documents.title: Average remaining life is not a retirement funding deadline: read the period table
documents.description: Four interactive graphics distinguish a precise population mean, conditional survival to later ages and a separate constant-cash illustration of longer planning horizons.
documents.body: Life expectancy is an average under a particular mortality schedule. A cash plan still needs explicit later-age scenarios and resources for the years that may extend beyond that average. Condition on the birthday already reached A retirement plan can run out of years before it runs out of arithmetic. If its final spending date is chosen only because a life-expectancy figure appears nearby, the plan may stop while the underlying life table still contains survivors. This article uses Canada’s preliminary 2022–2024 period estimates from Statistics Canada Table 13-10-0114-01 . At exact age 65, the both-sexes mean remaining life is 20.85 years. This is conditional on reaching 65; it is not obtained by subtracting 65 from life expectancy at birth. The source definition holds the mortality observed in the reference period across the hypothetical remaining lifetime. Adding 65 gives 85.85 as a conditional mean age under those assumptions. It is a period measure. It does not follow an actual birth cohort into its future or add assumptions about later mortality improvements. The age control selects the source row for an exact birthday between 55 and 80. It also changes the denominator of the survival calculations. It does not modify anyone’s health, alter the historical mortality schedule or predict how long a reader will live. Read survivor counts as a life-table construction The table begins with a hypothetical radix of 100,000 live births. Its survivor column records how many remain at each exact age under the table’s schedule. These figures are not counts of respondents, pension members or actual Canadians still alive from a particular group of births. In the selected both-sexes table, 88,760 survivors reach exact age 65 and 13,600 reach exact age 95. Dividing 13,600 by 88,760 produces a conditional table proportion of about 15.32%. The denominator is the survivors who already reached 65, rather than the original 100,000. The survival curve repeats that calculation at each later age. Its value is 100% at the conditioning birthday. From age 65, the same table gives approximately 57.15% reaching 85 and 3.53% reaching 100. An average remaining duration does not turn the later proportions into zero. The threshold bars are nested. A table survivor reaching 95 has also reached 90, so their percentages cannot be added as separate outcomes. The source sex categories are shown separately. No joint-life or couple probability is calculated from them. A narrow confidence interval is not a narrow range of personal lifespans The published margin for the both-sexes expectation at age 65 is 0.02 years. Applying it to 20.85 gives a 95% interval for that population mean of 20.83 to 20.87 years. The first chart retains those bounds, even though the whiskers are small on its zero-based axis. Statistics Canada’s life-table methods explain how the published margins support a 95% confidence interval. This describes precision of the estimated mean. It does not say that 95% of individuals will live between those two remaining durations. It also does not supply uncertainty around the derived survivor ratios. The article therefore shows no invented confidence band around that curve, and it does not reuse the expectation’s margin for a different statistic. The displayed source counts are rounded, so derived ratios should not be treated as exact personal probabilities. The reference period is preliminary according to metadata note 14, because late death registrations can lead to updates. The individual selected CSV status cells are blank; that does not override the period-level preliminary designation. The release date, reference period and review date remain distinct. Translate a chosen horizon into a separate cash scenario The final chart introduces an independent hypothetical input: an annual spending gap of CAD 40,000 in constant purchasing power. It applies no real investment return and simply multiplies that gap by the years between the starting age and each chosen endpoint. From age 65 to 85, twenty years at that gap total CAD 800,000. Extending the endpoint to 95 produces thirty years and CAD 1,200,000. The additional ten years add CAD 400,000 under these deliberately fixed assumptions. Those balances are not mortality-weighted present values, market quotations or claims about an adequate reserve. They also do not fund every possible lifespan. Their purpose is to expose how a chosen final age changes a simple cash requirement while keeping the statistical evidence separate. Changing the spending gap changes only this cash chart and its corresponding dollar metric. It does not change the official expectation, its margin or the conditional survival curves. Changing the conditioning age changes the statistical denominator and the length of each cash horizon, with the source period held fixed. Use later-age scenarios without treating one as a guarantee A household plan needs its own income sources, accessible assets, spending pattern and contingencies. The simple gap here could be replaced by a documented budget, but actual pension payments, tax, returns, care needs and inflation would need a fuller cash model. Examine what remains available at more than one later age. Identify income that continues for life, cash obligations that can change and resources that might be difficult to turn into spendable money. A positive balance at one endpoint does not settle the years after it. The plotted curve stops at exact age 100 because that is this article’s display boundary. It does not assume all remaining lives end there or renormalize the surviving fraction away. A longer planning horizon would need to be assessed explicitly. Finally, retain the table version and revisit the plan when circumstances or source estimates change. A population statistic can clarify the question being asked; it cannot select a personal death date, an insurance price or a universally sufficient retirement deadline.

documents.title: A brokered GIC in your name can share a coverage limit with your direct deposits
documents.description: Four charts group hypothetical eligible deposits by issuing CDIC member and category, combining direct and client-name brokered balances before applying a limit.
documents.body: Identify the issuing member, eligible deposit and recorded coverage category first. Buying through another channel does not automatically create another limit for a client-name deposit. Follow the deposit to its issuing member A brokerage statement can contain a GIC issued by another financial institution. A separate statement does not by itself establish a separate deposit-insurance limit. The issuer, recorded ownership and applicable category determine which balances need to be considered together. CDIC’s GIC guidance distinguishes deposits placed by a broker in the client’s name from deposits held by a broker as nominee. It states that client-name eligible deposits are combined with other deposits in the same insurance category at the same issuing member. This guide models only that client-name case. Begin the inventory with the issuing institution shown in the deposit documentation, rather than stopping at the platform or advisor that arranged it. Verify membership and the product’s eligibility independently. A brand, branch or statement label is not sufficient evidence that two rows belong to different members. Members A and B in the tool are invented and assumed genuinely distinct. They are not placeholders for a verified mapping of any named financial group. Nominee-name and trust arrangements require their own records and rules; this snapshot does not calculate their coverage. Put the balances into a member-by-category map The illustration uses one depositor and two qualifying categories at each member: eligible deposits in the one-name non-registered category and eligible deposits held in a TFSA. Direct and client-name brokered holdings are separate input channels inside each cell. CDIC’s overview states a CAD 100,000 limit, including principal and interest, for each covered category at a member institution. Its TFSA examples also distinguish eligible deposits from securities held inside the same wrapper. The account wrapper alone does not make every product an eligible deposit. All entered amounts are therefore assumed to be eligible deposits, already in place and correctly recorded in the stated categories. They include accrued interest through one common observation date. The calculator does not turn a security into a deposit, validate ownership or determine TFSA contribution room. The first stacked chart makes the grouping visible. A directly held deposit and a client-name brokered GIC in the same cell are two parts of one combined eligible balance. The channels remain visible for reconciliation while the coverage cap is applied to their sum. Reconcile the original four buckets Member A’s one-name cell contains CAD 60,000 directly and CAD 50,000 through the client-name broker channel. Its total is CAD 110,000, of which CAD 100,000 is within the modeled cap and CAD 10,000 is above it. A’s TFSA cell contains CAD 40,000 directly and CAD 70,000 through the client-name broker channel. It also totals CAD 110,000, with the same CAD 10,000 above its own separate modeled cap. At member B, the one-name cell combines CAD 30,000 and CAD 60,000, for CAD 90,000. The TFSA cell combines CAD 10,000 and CAD 20,000, for CAD 30,000. Both are within their respective assumed limits. The eligible total is CAD 340,000. Applying the cap cell by cell leaves CAD 320,000 within the modeled limits and CAD 20,000 above them. The second stacked chart shows those pieces without treating a second purchase channel as another category. Headroom belongs to the cell in which it exists The headroom matrix subtracts each combined balance from CAD 100,000. Member A’s cells each show negative CAD 10,000. Member B shows positive CAD 10,000 in one-name deposits and positive CAD 70,000 in TFSA eligible deposits. Adding those signed figures would produce positive CAD 60,000, but that does not erase the CAD 20,000 above A’s two limits. A positive amount in one member/category cannot simply be applied to another cell’s excess. The same point appears in the total-cap shortcut. Four assumed caps add to CAD 400,000, which exceeds the CAD 340,000 eligible balance. Yet the actual cell-by-cell illustration still has CAD 20,000 above individual limits. A combined maximum is not automatically usable when deposits are concentrated unevenly. The waterfall checks the correct sequence: begin with CAD 340,000, subtract each of the two CAD 10,000 excesses and retain CAD 320,000. Coverage is aggregated after each separate bucket is tested. The matrix describes an existing snapshot, rather than approving a move between institutions or account wrappers. Changing the channel alone does not change the combined balance Within the same client-name member/category, relabeling CAD 20,000 from directly held to brokered holdings leaves the combined balance and this model’s coverage result unchanged. Only the first chart’s channel composition changes. That invariance is useful for checking an inventory spread across several statements. Sum the compatible deposits before applying a cap. Do not count the same underlying deposit twice because it appears in a platform summary as well as an issuer record, and do not omit other eligible balances at that issuer. Use the legal issuer and ownership records to establish the grouping. CDIC’s public member list is the reference for current members and associated trade names; this article does not verify any actual names. If the documentation instead shows nominee ownership or a trust relationship, stop applying this client-name illustration to it and consult the relevant rules. Other registered categories, joint deposits, trust beneficiaries and provincial credit-union arrangements have separate requirements. They are outside this four-cell model. Their presence in a real household inventory calls for additional correctly classified rows, not an invented extra cap on an existing cell. Keep protection, balance growth and access on separate schedules The calculation is a same-date snapshot. It projects no interest, new deposit, withdrawal or tax payment. Future credited interest can change the balance relative to a cap, which is why the related headroom guide follows growth over time. An above-cap amount is not a predicted loss, and an amount within the assumed limits is not proof that it can be spent today. A non-redeemable GIC still has contractual access and maturity conditions. Deposit protection addresses eligible deposits in a member failure; it does not replace the household payment calendar. The useful review record identifies the observation date, issuer, ownership category, eligible product, principal and accrued interest. Keep the original documents that support those classifications, and check current CDIC guidance when circumstances or rules change. These four charts organize that review. They preserve the purchase channels for reconciliation, apply limits to the correct combined cells, and prevent unused headroom elsewhere from hiding an excess. The result is an inspectable planning illustration rather than a coverage certificate or a deposit-transfer recommendation.

documents.title: Two benefits plans do not turn one bill into two reimbursements: chart the coordination
documents.description: Split a hypothetical invoice between two plans and the household, compare standalone amounts with coordinated payments and stress unused maximums in four charts.
documents.body: The eligible expense, the order of payment, each plan’s remaining maximum and the coordination calculation all matter. Two headline percentages cannot simply be added to predict cash received. Establish the eligible expense and the plan order first Coverage under two health or dental plans does not mean the household can collect each plan’s headline percentage independently. The plans coordinate payments for the expense, and the actual outcome depends on the applicable terms. Canada Life’s coordination overview describes a primary payer, a secondary payer and submitting the first plan’s benefit statement with the remaining claim. Its examples also show that priority depends on the coverage circumstances. The calculator assumes the order has already been confirmed. The model does not choose which plan should pay first, check dependent eligibility or decide that a service qualifies. It begins with a common amount assumed eligible on the same basis under both plans. Actual plans can recognize different eligible amounts and require a different calculation. A fully reimbursed eligible amount may still leave part of the invoice The example has CAD 1,500 assumed eligible under both plans and a separate CAD 200 invoiced amount assumed ineligible under both. The total bill is therefore CAD 1,700 . Entering these separately prevents the entire provider charge being mistaken for an automatically covered expense. CLHIA’s consumer explanation notes that combined reimbursement cannot exceed the eligible expense and can be lower than the amount charged. A plan’s recognized fees and limits can matter even when another plan has already made a payment. The model’s CAD 200 is not a deductible or an estimate of a typical fee difference. It is an independent amount outside both plans’ assumed eligibility. Any actual difference between a provider’s invoice and each plan’s recognized expense needs confirmation from the benefit statements and plan documents. Write the secondary formula instead of assuming it In this teaching contract, the primary payment is the lesser of its percentage of the common eligible expense and its unused maximum available for the claim. The secondary standalone amount is calculated the same way using its own percentage and maximum. The coordinated secondary payment is then the least of three amounts: the unpaid part of the common eligible expense, the secondary standalone percentage amount and the secondary unused maximum. Its percentage applies to the original common eligible amount, rather than to the unpaid remainder. That is an explicit model convention. An actual plan may have different eligible fees, deductibles, limits or secondary-payment terms. The public source establishes the need for coordination; it does not certify these entered percentages, maximums or the result for a real claim. Follow one CAD 1,500 eligible expense through both calculations The primary rate is 70%. Applied to CAD 1,500, it produces CAD 1,050 before the unused maximum. The selected primary maximum is CAD 1,000, so the modeled primary payment is CAD 1,000 . CAD 500 of the common eligible expense remains unpaid. The secondary rate is 60%, giving a standalone percentage amount of CAD 900. Its unused maximum is CAD 1,000. Coordination limits the secondary payment to the remaining CAD 500, so it pays CAD 500 under the stated formula. The two payments total CAD 1,500. They fully reimburse the common eligible amount in this example while leaving the CAD 200 separately ineligible amount to the household. The first stacked bar therefore reconciles CAD 1,000 + CAD 500 + CAD 200 = CAD 1,700. Seventy percent plus sixty percent is not a 130% payment The second chart compares each plan’s modeled standalone amount with its coordinated payment. The primary’s CAD 1,000 amount stays unchanged. The secondary’s CAD 900 standalone amount becomes CAD 500 after applying the unpaid-expense ceiling. Adding the two standalone amounts would give CAD 1,900. That exceeds the common eligible expense by CAD 400. It describes an uncoordinated sum that the model does not pay, rather than extra money available to the household. The unused maximum is also different from a reimbursement percentage. A CAD 1,000 maximum does not mean that CAD 1,000 will be paid on any claim. The percentage calculation and the eligible amount can produce a smaller benefit before coordination is even considered. Use what remains available, rather than an original annual headline Reduce the secondary unused maximum from CAD 1,000 to CAD 200. Its potential standalone amount is now limited to CAD 200, and its coordinated payment is also CAD 200. The primary still pays CAD 1,000. The household then funds CAD 300 of the common eligible expense plus the separate CAD 200, for CAD 500 in total. A second plan exists, but that fact alone does not complete the reimbursement. The controls accept unused amounts available for this claim. They do not reconstruct earlier claims, reset benefits at a calendar anniversary or determine whether several services share one maximum. Verify the relevant benefit category and period before entering an amount from a coverage summary. Read the claim-size curve as separate scenarios The line chart increases the common eligible expense while holding rates, unused maximums and the separately ineligible amount fixed. It compares the household share with only the primary plan against the share with both modeled plans. At smaller claim sizes, the percentages can determine the result. At larger sizes, the selected maximums can limit both payments, leaving a growing amount for the household. With the default CAD 1,000 maximum available under each plan, combined payments cannot exceed CAD 2,000 even when the common eligible expense becomes much larger. These points are alternative claim sizes. They are not successive claims consuming an annual balance, observations of medical prices or predictions of what treatment will cost. The ineligible CAD 200 remains a fixed additional amount in every scenario. The final household share and the upfront cash need are different questions The matrix replaces the primary and secondary unused maximums. It leaves both rates and both expense inputs selected. Each cell reports the household share under the same teaching formula, including the amount ineligible under both plans. A small final household share does not prove that only that much cash is needed on the invoice date. If the household must first pay the full CAD 1,700 and reimbursements arrive later, it needs funding for that interval. Direct billing, assignment and claim processing need separate confirmation. The reimbursement-timing article covers that calendar. Confirm who is covered and which plan pays first. Read the eligible amount and first payer’s benefit statement. Check the secondary plan’s actual formula and unused limits. Keep any ineligible charges in the household budget. Match invoice and reimbursement dates before relying on the eventual payments. Neither the existence of two plans nor a combined percentage establishes complete coverage. A clear calculation and a dated cash plan make the remaining commitment visible.

documents.title: Homeownership rates by age: useful context, different from your purchase-cash plan
documents.description: Read twelve dated Canadian household ownership rates, distinguish percentage-point changes from personal transitions, and build a separate cash target with a monthly funding calendar.
documents.body: A household ownership rate describes a defined group at a past observation date. A purchase plan still needs its own cash amounts, monthly saving, retained reserve and financing assessment. Keep the statistical observation date visible A chart showing how common homeownership is at different ages can help describe housing conditions. It cannot specify when a particular person should buy or the amount of cash that a proposed purchase requires. The first figure retains twelve rates from Statistics Canada’s September 2022 Chart 2 : four selected age groups, each shown for 2011, 2016 and 2021. The underlying programs are the 2011 National Household Survey and the 2016 and 2021 Census of Population. For ages 25–29, the published rates are 44.1%, 39.6% and 36.5%; for ages 30–34, they are 59.2%, 55.0% and 52.3%. These are dated Canadian household statistics. They are not observations of the housing market in October 2026. The complete original chart includes additional ages. Selecting four groups makes this comparison readable without turning their unweighted average into a national rate. Read the household classification before interpreting the age label The age is that of the primary household maintainer. It is a way to assign an age characteristic to a household that may contain several people. It does not turn every resident of that age into a separate household observation. Statistics Canada’s study of multiple household maintainers explains that the primary maintainer is the first reported person contributing to housing costs. That status concerns housing payments and reporting order; it is not a verification of an individual’s legal ownership title. For example, a young adult living with parents might be part of an owner-occupied household while not personally owning the home. A roommate who helps pay bills need not be the person whose age classifies the household. The unit and classification matter before making a statement about people. Different studies may also use different denominators or exclusions. Retain the published series and its scope rather than combining a rate from one definition with a count from another. This article does not recompute the 2022 release using the later study’s alternative household classifications. Subtract rates without inventing a household transition The second figure calculates 2021 minus 2011 within each retained age group. For ages 25–29, 36.5% minus 44.1% equals a change of −7.6 percentage points . This is a difference between rates. It is not a 7.6% change in house prices, a count of households selling homes or a measured probability that a particular renter becomes an owner. A percentage change would use an additional denominator, and an ownership transition would require information linking the relevant household states over time. The people aged 25–29 in 2011 are not the same age group in 2021. Even comparing an age group ten years older would not, by itself, follow a fixed set of households: household formation, migration and composition can change. The charts provide no confidence intervals or statistical-significance tests. They display the source’s published rounded rates and their arithmetic differences. They also do not identify how much of a change was caused by prices, income, preferences, borrowing conditions or any particular policy. Build the independent purchase target from payments and cash kept afterward The editable example begins with CAD 80,000 chosen for a down payment, CAD 10,000 entered for other purchase payments and CAD 15,000 intended to remain available afterward. The combined funding target is therefore CAD 105,000 . These are independent scenario amounts, not estimates obtained from the ownership chart. The down-payment entry does not calculate a legal minimum or prove that financing will be available. The other-cost entry is not a province-specific tax or fee schedule. The retained CAD 15,000 is part of the target because it must remain after the first CAD 90,000 of payments. It is not another purchase expense. Reaching CAD 105,000 would fund those selected payments while leaving the chosen cash reserve, assuming no omitted costs. FCAC’s homebuying guide discusses upfront costs beyond the down payment. Use actual quotes and applicable rules for an implemented plan, and review the ongoing housing budget separately from the initial cash requirement. Count the month-end deposits needed to close the cash gap Opening cash assigned to this goal is CAD 45,000. Subtracting it from the CAD 105,000 target leaves CAD 60,000 to accumulate. New saving is CAD 1,200 at each month-end, after all other household commitments have been funded. With no interest or withdrawals, fifty deposits supply CAD 60,000. Cash first reaches the selected target at the end of month 50 . At month 49 it is CAD 103,800, still CAD 1,200 short. A fraction of a required deposit cannot move the funded date earlier in this monthly convention. The line runs through the chosen sixty-month window. It ends at CAD 117,000 because it keeps accumulating the stated saving; it does not execute a purchase at month 50. The target line also stays fixed. There is no forecast of house-price growth or automatic adjustment to purchase costs. If the entered opening cash already covers the entire target, the funded month is zero. If the chart ends before funding is complete, the headline reports that the target was not reached within the window and the note retains the remaining gap. A positive final balance alone does not mean the target is funded. Change the cash assumptions without changing the historical observations The matrix varies combined cash targets and new monthly saving while retaining opening cash. Each cell divides the remaining positive gap by monthly saving and rounds upward to the next whole deposit. A zero cell means that opening cash already covers that comparison target. The matrix does not apply an ownership percentage anywhere in this calculation. Some cells can require more months than the adjacent line chart displays. Those are conditional arithmetic comparisons, not extensions of a guaranteed saving commitment or estimates of a purchase date. Assign opening resources once. Cash counted here cannot simultaneously fund another goal unless that other goal’s allocation is reduced. Borrowing can provide funds while adding a debt obligation; it should not be relabelled as accumulated saving or assumed to remove affordability constraints. The model deliberately excludes investment returns, interest tax, unexpected bills and changes in saving capacity. Before relying on a date, identify the actual cash source, its accessibility, the timing of payments and the affordability of maintaining the chosen monthly contribution. Use group context to frame questions, then assess the actual plan A population comparison and a household budget serve different purposes. The first helps describe a defined group. The second asks whether specified resources can cover specified payments on the chosen schedule. An individual can have adequate purchase cash while facing an unaffordable ongoing mortgage. Another can have a workable monthly housing budget but insufficient closing cash. Neither condition is determined by how common homeownership was in a past age group. Record the property and transaction assumptions, verify financing separately, include recurring housing costs and preserve the cash needed for other priorities. Revisit the plan when those inputs change rather than treating an age-group bar as a deadline. The official charts remain dated context throughout that work. The independent cash illustration makes its own arithmetic inspectable without presenting a national historical rate as a personal forecast or a reason to enter the housing market.

documents.title: Positive equity can still fail a collateral test: separate repayment, new collateral and a sale
documents.description: Chart a fictional loan-to-collateral limit, compare two outside-resource adjustments, and calculate how an internal sale changes both the loan and its collateral.
documents.body: An account can have positive equity and still exceed a contractual debt ratio. Repaying debt, posting eligible collateral and selling assets to repay debt are different calculations. Separate the amount you own from the ratio the contract tests Suppose eligible collateral starts at CAD 100,000 and the loan outstanding is CAD 50,000. The entered pool initially has CAD 50,000 of equity and a 50% loan-to-collateral ratio. Those two descriptions use the same balance sheet, but they answer different questions. Now apply an immediate 30% collateral-price decline, with the debt unchanged. Collateral falls to CAD 70,000, leaving CAD 20,000 after subtracting the loan. Equity is still positive. Yet the debt ratio is CAD 50,000 ÷ CAD 70,000, or about 71.43%. The teaching contract permits a maximum ratio of 60%, so this case fails its test before equity reaches zero. That 60% is an original fictional input, not a margin requirement, an actual lender quote or a Canadian regulatory rule. The tool is a static cash-and-collateral illustration rather than an approval or enforcement model. Locate the collateral threshold without assigning a probability to the loss If debt is D and the maximum allowed debt ratio is c, the collateral value required by this particular test is D ÷ c . At the defaults, CAD 50,000 ÷ 60% gives CAD 83,333.33. Starting from CAD 100,000, a decline beyond about 16.67% crosses that threshold if nothing else changes. That percentage is a mathematical price boundary, not the chance of a call or a forecast drawdown. The chart varies an immediate decline while keeping debt fixed. A real loan can include other tests, valuation rules, interest accrual and changes in eligible assets that are outside this formula. The tool also permits a starting case that already exceeds the chosen limit. In that case, no further market decline is needed for the fictional test to fail. It does not imply that a lender would have approved those initial balances. Outside repayment changes the numerator With CAD 70,000 of collateral and a 60% limit, permitted debt is CAD 42,000. An outside cash repayment of CAD 8,000 reduces the original CAD 50,000 loan to that amount. The collateral stays CAD 70,000 and the ratio becomes 60%. The formula is max(0, D − cV) , where V is the stressed collateral value. This method changes debt while holding collateral fixed. It does not require a collateral sale within the entered pool, but it does require cash from somewhere outside it. Repayment is not a second investment loss. If a household uses its own outside cash, its cash and debt both fall by the same amount before fees or tax effects. Equity inside this particular pool rises from CAD 20,000 to CAD 28,000, while outside cash falls by CAD 8,000. The transfer does not create household wealth. Additional eligible collateral changes the denominator If the debt instead remains CAD 50,000, total eligible collateral must rise to CAD 83,333.33. Starting from CAD 70,000, the additional amount is therefore CAD 13,333.33 , assuming the new collateral receives its full stated value. The formula is max(0, D ÷ c − V) . It differs from the repayment formula because the denominator changes while debt stays fixed. At a 60% limit, one additional dollar of eligible collateral supports only 60 cents of debt capacity in this fictional test. Posting an outside asset moves it into the committed collateral pool. The asset remains owned in this model, but its availability for another bill has changed. It is not income, an expense equal to its entire posted value or newly created wealth. Actual eligibility, haircuts, transfer timing and acceptance must come from an actual agreement; the calculator assumes them only for its stated example. An internal sale changes both numerator and denominator A third mathematical method sells some of the existing collateral and applies all proceeds immediately to the loan. If the sale amount is s, the new ratio is (D − s) ÷ (V − s) . Subtracting s from the debt alone would miss the collateral leaving the pool. Solving for the amount that reaches the limit gives s = (D − cV) ÷ (1 − c) when the test is initially breached and a partial-sale solution exists. At the defaults, that is CAD 8,000 ÷ 40%, or CAD 20,000 . The remaining collateral is CAD 50,000, debt is CAD 30,000 and the ratio is 60%. Before costs, the pool’s equity remains CAD 20,000 because both assets and debt fell by the same CAD 20,000. Exposure is smaller, and future gains or losses apply to fewer assets. This method does not have the same resource path as contributing CAD 8,000 of outside cash or CAD 13,333.33 of outside collateral. If debt is at least the collateral value, no partial sale can restore a positive-collateral active loan ratio below 100% in this model. Selling everything either closes both balances when they are equal or leaves debt unpaid when debt is larger. The live assumptions state which case applies instead of showing a negative residual collateral balance as a workable solution. Read the response bars as alternatives, not charges to add together The grouped bars compare outside repayment with an outside collateral addition at several price stresses. Their different heights are a consequence of the different equations. They are not two amounts due together, nor do they prove that either resource is available to the household. The matrix then changes the fictional ratio limit as well as the price decline. A tighter limit can increase the cash needed even at the same asset price and debt. The equity bridge, by contrast, is unchanged when only the limit changes. A contract test and a balance-sheet loss remain separate dimensions. A response amount should therefore be matched to actual access to funds. An asset already assigned to another goal cannot also be counted as free collateral, and an unused borrowing limit does not establish that cash will remain available during the same stress. Bring the actual agreement and transaction timing back into the plan The SEC’s Investor.gov margin-account bulletin explains, in its U.S. investor-education context, that borrowing against securities can require additional funds or asset sales when prices decline. It also describes firm actions and changing requirements. This guide uses that source for broad risk context and does not reproduce its regulatory thresholds as this model’s contract. The four charts assume a constant debt balance, immediate execution at entered values, fully eligible collateral, and no interest, tax, fees, slippage or price movement during an adjustment. They do not grant a right to select a response, promise a deadline or extension, or determine what a lender can accept or sell. Read the actual debt-ratio definition and eligible-value rules. Check when debt, interest and collateral are measured. Separate a cash repayment from a collateral transfer or internal sale. Identify available outside resources without counting them twice. Test the household’s bill payments alongside any contractual funding demand. The result is a transparent set of conditional calculations. A workable borrowing plan still requires the actual terms and a cash path that can be executed when needed.

documents.title: An equity-ratio shortfall: why repaying debt, adding collateral and selling assets need different amounts
documents.description: Compare three original balance-sheet adjustments after an asset-price decline, inspect their different denominators, and reconcile new outside cash without treating it as recovered investment performance.
documents.body: An equity ratio can improve by changing debt, assets or both. The amount required depends on which balances change, while new funding does not reverse the investment loss. Identify the assets, debt and equity before calculating a shortfall A collateral ratio combines two balances. In this illustration, equity equals the value of assets in the account minus the loan, and the required ratio is equity divided by total collateral assets. Changing either assets or debt can therefore change the ratio. The SEC’s margin-account bulletin explains borrowing against an investment account and the possibility of demands for additional resources or asset sales. Its margin-call glossary also notes that a firm can change its threshold. These US investor-education sources provide general context, not the requirement used here. The entered equity requirement is deliberately hypothetical. Real arrangements can apply different collateral eligibility, haircuts, cash-netting rules and rights of sale. This tool compares arithmetic under one simplified rule; it does not determine a regulatory requirement or recommend a response to a real lender. Trace the default decline before adding any new money The account begins with CAD 60,000 of assets, financed by CAD 30,000 of borrowing and CAD 30,000 of investor capital. After a 30% asset-price decline, the assets are worth CAD 42,000. The loan stays at CAD 30,000, leaving CAD 12,000 of equity. The asset lost CAD 18,000, while the investor’s initial CAD 30,000 of equity fell by 60%. Interest and costs are excluded from this instantaneous example. The resulting equity-to-assets ratio is CAD 12,000 divided by CAD 42,000, or about 28.57%, below the invented 40% requirement. Under that fixed loan and ratio, the boundary asset value is loan ÷ (1 − required ratio) . Here it is CAD 50,000, corresponding to a decline of about 16.67% from the original CAD 60,000. This boundary comes from the selected equation. It is not a quotation of a brokerage firm’s actual trigger price. Distinguish cash that reduces debt from cash that increases collateral assets If new outside cash is used directly to repay the loan, the asset denominator stays at CAD 42,000. Equity must reach 40% of that amount, or CAD 16,800. A CAD 4,800 repayment reduces the loan to CAD 25,200 and produces that equity amount. The separate held-cash illustration assumes new cash is added to collateral assets while the loan remains unchanged. The cash increases both assets and equity. Solving (equity + cash) ÷ (assets + cash) = required ratio gives CAD 8,000. Assets become CAD 50,000, debt stays CAD 30,000 and equity becomes CAD 20,000, again 40%. Those are different accounting treatments. A firm may apply a cash deposit against its debit balance instead of allowing the assumed held-cash arrangement. In that situation, use the repayment treatment. Adding a deposit to assets while also subtracting the same money from debt would count one contribution twice. The model does not establish which treatment an actual agreement permits. A sale followed by loan repayment reduces both sides of the ratio In the sale-only case, assets are sold at their current assumed value and every dollar of proceeds repays the loan. A CAD 12,000 sale reduces assets from CAD 42,000 to CAD 30,000 and the loan from CAD 30,000 to CAD 18,000. Equity remains CAD 12,000. Dividing it by the smaller CAD 30,000 asset balance gives 40%. The sale repairs the ratio without new outside cash in this example, but it does not recover the CAD 18,000 price loss. It also leaves less of the original investment inside the account. The sale proceeds are assigned to the loan, rather than becoming money for household bills. A sale alone cannot restore a positive ratio in a remaining funded account when equity is zero or negative. For example, assets of CAD 24,000 against a CAD 30,000 loan leave negative CAD 6,000 of equity. Selling all assets still leaves CAD 6,000 of debt. The tool marks that sale-only repair unavailable; closing an empty, exactly settled account is also different from restoring a positive equity ratio. Subtract new outside funding before describing the remaining investment equity The three default adjustments show different account-equity amounts: CAD 16,800 after loan repayment, CAD 20,000 after adding held cash, and CAD 12,000 after the sale. Comparing those figures without their funding sources would favor whichever account received the most new money. Subtract the CAD 4,800 outside repayment from the first amount and the CAD 8,000 outside cash contribution from the second. Each leaves CAD 12,000, matching the sale case, which received no new cash. The signed-bar chart performs that reconciliation and keeps the original CAD 30,000 investor capital beside it. This is an accounting identity under unchanged execution prices, rather than a full household wealth forecast. Tax, transaction costs and subsequent price movements would create additional changes. Outside money may also have an existing purpose elsewhere in the household plan. Improving a ratio by transferring that money does not make its previous obligation disappear or establish that the investment has earned back its loss. Use the profile and matrix to inspect the assumed rule The ratio profile holds the original loan fixed while changing the asset-price move. Negative ratios indicate debt greater than asset value. The horizontal requirement is another assumption, so moving it changes the illustrated shortfall without changing what the investment is worth. The matrix reports only outside cash applied to debt repayment. Its rows replace the asset-price decline and its columns replace the required equity ratio. The other two treatments require their own equations, which is why the matrix is not labelled simply “the margin-call amount.” Zero means no adjustment is needed for that particular assumed rule at that point. An actual lender can have different eligible collateral, requirements, deadlines and execution rights. A favorable calculation here does not secure time to act or guarantee that a selected sale is available. Keep the three questions distinct: what the account currently owns and owes, which balances a proposed adjustment changes, and what the actual agreement requires. The charts make the first two inspectable while leaving the third to current contractual evidence.

documents.title: Buybacks and dilution: what changes for each share?
documents.description: Use five charts to reconcile repurchases and issuance, time-weight the EPS denominator, and distinguish EPS growth from a conditional equity-value-per-share result.
documents.body: The repurchase announcement is the beginning of the analysis. The price paid, net share reduction and source of funding determine the economics. Start with earnings and the share denominator When a company earns the same profit with fewer shares outstanding, earnings per share can rise without any improvement in total operating profit. This is arithmetic, and it can be economically useful. It does not establish that the repurchase price was attractive. The SEC financial-statement guide describes the relationship between earnings and shares and points readers to stock-option disclosures. In a full issuer analysis, use the reported weighted-average basic and diluted share counts, and distinguish them from the shares outstanding at the reporting date. EPS growth factor = net-income growth factor ÷ share-count growth factor For example, 6% net-income growth and a 2% decline in the comparable share denominator produce 1.06 ÷ 0.98 − 1 = 8.16% EPS growth. Adding 6% and 2% is a rough approximation. The exact calculation preserves the interaction. Reconcile the gross buyback with net dilution Our invented company begins with 100 million shares and annual net income of 500 million. It spends 300 million to buy six million shares at 50 each, while adding two million fully issued shares with zero modeled cash proceeds. Assume all changes happen at the start of the modeled year and profit is unchanged. The gross repurchase removed 6% of opening shares. Net shares declined 4%. Neither figure is the same as the 4.17% EPS increase. A research note should state which quantity it means instead of calling all three “buyback yield.” Actual weighted-average share counts reflect transaction dates. Potential dilution can depend on award terms and the applicable accounting method. Our simplified closing-share calculation is a teaching scenario, not a reconstruction of a company’s reported diluted EPS. For the interactive extension, monetary totals are CAD millions, share counts are millions and prices/EPS are CAD per share. The issued-share input does not calculate an award’s value, service cost, vesting or accounting expense. Repurchased shares leave the modeled outstanding count; legal retirement or treasury treatment requires the actual issuer’s reconciliation and jurisdiction. Period-end shares are not automatically the EPS denominator The IFRS Foundation’s public IAS 33 summary identifies weighted-average shares and separate basic/diluted EPS calculations. The timeline here is much simpler: both modeled count changes occur at one instant, and the resulting count applies for the entered fraction of the earnings period. At the default full-period fraction, 96 million shares apply throughout, so 500 ÷ 96 = 5.2083. If that same count applies for half the period, weighted-average shares are 100 × 0.5 + 96 × 0.5 = 98 million. Modeled period EPS is then 500 ÷ 98 = 5.1020. The period-end snapshot still contains 96 million shares. At a zero fraction, the changes have no weight in that simplified earnings period, so period EPS stays at 5.00 even though ending shares have changed. The dashed line shows net income divided by ending shares as a snapshot proxy. It must not be relabeled as actual reported diluted EPS. The model contains no preference claims, splits, options, unvested awards or multiple transaction dates. Its weighted denominator teaches the timing distinction, rather than implementing a complete accounting-standard calculation. Charge the repurchase for its funding In a separate invented funding case, assume borrowing of 300 million costs 6% annually and a fictional 25% offset reduces that cost. This is a numerical assumption, not a claim that interest is tax-deductible in an actual case. The annual after-tax interest cost is 13.5 million. Under the same immediate-timing assumption, net income falls to 486.5 million and EPS becomes 486.5 ÷ 96 = 5.0677. EPS accretion falls to 1.35%. That calculation omits issuance fees, refinancing risk, changes in credit quality, and any operating effect of the awards. It isolates the funding cost. If cash funds the repurchase, test foregone after-tax interest or the value of an alternative use of that cash rather than assuming a zero opportunity cost. Debt maturity and liquidity matter independently of EPS. A small per-share earnings improvement can coexist with a weaker ability to withstand a downturn. Extend the model through a lower-profit year and a higher refinancing rate before treating leverage as a permanent enhancement. This funding calculation is separate from the interactive controls, which hold annual net income fixed at 500 and assume cash is already available. Changing transaction timing there changes the share weighting only; it does not calculate interest, tax, foregone cash income or a new earnings forecast. Add a stated value assumption before comparing per-share outcomes The interactive charts extend the original EPS case with a new assumption: pre-event total common-equity value is 5,000 million, including the cash available for the 300 million repurchase. With 100 million opening shares, that assumed value is 50 per share. Spending 300 leaves total assumed equity value of 4,700. After repurchasing six million shares and adding two million, 96 million shares remain. Value per share in this static thought experiment is 4,700 ÷ 96 = 48.9583, a decline of about 2.08%, while the full-period EPS calculation rises about 4.17%. That contrast is conditional arithmetic. The 5,000 input is not a measured intrinsic value, enterprise value, book-equity balance or a predicted market capitalization. Annual profit of 500 is not added again to this independently assumed transaction snapshot. Sufficient cash for the repurchase is assumed separately; equity value alone cannot establish liquidity. The new shares bring zero modeled cash proceeds and no separate value is assigned to employee services or other consideration. This limitation does not imply that real services have no economic value. The IFRS Foundation’s public IFRS 2 summary describes share-based payment as a financial-reporting matter; an issued-share count alone cannot reconstruct its expense. Compare the repurchase price with a value range A separate, deliberately simplified thought experiment shows why the price matters. Assume total common-equity value is 1,000 million, including 200 million of excess cash, and there are 100 million shares. The starting assumed value is 10 per share. Ignore tax, signaling, transaction costs, and any change in operating value. Spending 200 million at 8 per share removes 25 million shares from the modeled outstanding count. Remaining equity value is 800 million across 75 million shares: 10.67 per share. Spending the same cash at 12 removes only 16.67 million shares from that count, leaving approximately 9.60 of value per remaining share. The total assumed equity value has fallen by the cash spent in both cases. The different per-share outcomes arise from the price paid. This is our own conditional valuation example; it does not establish an observable intrinsic value or justify a company-specific price target. The 1,000 equity/200 cash/100 shares thought experiment is a separate original case. It does not supply the 5,000 total-equity input added to the interactive EPS example, and its repurchase prices of 8 and 12 must not be confused with the other case’s price of 50. Compare the quantities without adding them into an extra return The share bridge reconciles opening, repurchased and newly issued shares. The separate equity bridge deducts the same cash payout from the assumed value once. The EPS timeline changes a period denominator; the value matrix changes the assumed repurchase price and issuance at a transaction snapshot. The signed bars compare percentage changes from each measure’s own starting baseline. They are separate quantities, with different definitions, rather than components to add into shareholder return. Neither is a historical observation or a recommendation to buy at a stated price. The controls impose numerical boundaries so the company never repurchases all opening shares before issuance and the modeled equity value remains positive. Those are computational limits, not recommended payout ratios. There is no financing, cash-interest, tax, valuation-response or price-impact model behind the controls. A no-issuance repurchase at the initial assumed value per share is neutral for that assumed value under these conditions. Adding zero-cash shares can offset that benefit, while changing the value input can change the conclusion. This dependence is why EPS growth alone cannot settle whether an actual repurchase improves continuing shareholders’ economics. Keep the return model internally consistent If forecast EPS already includes the assumed decline in shares, terminal EPS multiplied by an exit P/E already reflects that per-share benefit. Adding a separate repurchase yield as an extra shareholder return can count the same mechanism twice. Alternatively, begin with aggregate earnings, model the cash allocated to repurchases, estimate the price paid each year, and calculate the resulting share path. Reconcile this with dividends, reinvestment, and debt changes. A dollar cannot simultaneously fund a dividend, an acquisition, and a repurchase. Authorization is also different from execution. Record the announced capacity, actual spending, average price, period-end shares, and diluted weighted-average shares as separate fields. A large remaining authorization alone is weak evidence for future share reduction. Questions to answer before rewarding the buyback How much of gross repurchasing offsets employee issuance or other dilution? What earnings and cash-flow assumptions fund the program? How does the price paid compare with a defensible range of estimated value? What changes in debt, liquidity, and financial flexibility? Does the EPS forecast already incorporate the share-count effect? Track the answers over several reporting periods. A disciplined program can reduce purchases when valuation is demanding and increase them when cash is truly surplus and the price is attractive. The useful evidence is the realized allocation record and its effect on continuing owners, assessed alongside the business’s investment needs.

documents.title: Average purchase cost needs units: four equal-cash purchases, four different prices
documents.description: Four charts trace equal cash purchases into unit counts, ownership shares, average cost and final market value without treating a price average as an investment return.
documents.body: Divide total purchase cash by total units acquired. A lower average cost than the simple mean of quoted prices is an accounting result, and does not guarantee a profit or prove one investment schedule is better. Start with the cash bought and the units received Buying the same dollar amount at regular intervals does not buy the same number of units. The price at each purchase date determines how many units that cash can acquire. An average of price observations therefore answers a different question from the average cost of the units actually owned. Investor.gov defines dollar-cost averaging through equal portions invested at regular intervals. Its description explains the basic quantity effect: the same money buys more units at a lower price and fewer at a higher price. This guide uses that relationship for an accounting illustration, rather than predicting a benefit for a real investment. The original example makes four purchases of CAD 1,000 each. Its entered prices are CAD 20, CAD 10, CAD 25 and CAD 20 per unit. All units belong to one hypothetical unit class, and fractional purchases are allowed. No fee, spread, tax, distribution or currency conversion changes the cash invested. Each CAD 1,000 becomes available at its purchase date. The model does not begin with CAD 4,000 of cash held from day one or compare investing an existing lump sum immediately with holding it for later. Those are different funding assumptions addressed in the related timing guide. Add unit quantities before calculating cost per unit For each purchase, units acquired equal cash invested divided by price. The four purchases acquire 50, 100, 40 and 50 units. Together they cost CAD 4,000 and acquire 240 units. Average purchase cost is therefore CAD 4,000 ÷ 240 = approximately CAD 16.67 per unit . Calculations retain full precision even though the displayed currency is rounded. The first bar chart shows the different quantities directly. The CAD 10 purchase accounts for 100 units, twice the quantity bought by CAD 1,000 at CAD 20. The CAD 25 purchase accounts for only 40 units. These unequal quantities are the weights missing from a simple average of prices. The mechanics assume every order executes fully at its entered price and can buy arbitrary fractions. Actual products may have order sizes, dealing times, spreads, commissions or fractional-unit restrictions. Those conditions can change both the cash used and the quantity received. Cash shares and unit shares have different denominators Every purchase supplies 25% of the total cash because all four cash amounts are equal. The unit shares are approximately 20.83%, 41.67%, 16.67% and 20.83%. Each list separately adds to 100% before rounding. The grouped chart keeps those denominators apart. A purchase can supply one-quarter of the money and more than two-fifths of the units. A percentage is interpretable only after its denominator is named. The simple mean of the four prices is (20 + 10 + 25 + 20) ÷ 4 = CAD 18.75 . It gives each date’s price one equal weight. It does not give each acquired unit one equal weight, so it is not the average cost of the 240 units. The unit-weighted price calculation does reconcile with the cash ledger: (20 × 50 + 10 × 100 + 25 × 40 + 20 × 50) ÷ 240 is CAD 4,000 divided by 240. Adding price observations without those unit weights describes the observations, not the purchase cost. The harmonic mean is an identity under these limited assumptions When the same cash amount B is invested at four positive prices, acquired units sum to B × (1/p 1 + 1/p 2 + 1/p 3 + 1/p 4 ) . Dividing the total 4B cost by that quantity cancels B. The resulting cost per unit is 4 ÷ (1/p 1 + 1/p 2 + 1/p 3 + 1/p 4 ) , the harmonic mean of the prices. With positive prices it cannot exceed their arithmetic mean, and it equals that mean when all four prices are identical. This mathematical comparison does not establish that an investor earned an excess return or chose a better trading plan. The two means are statistics calculated from the same executed purchases. An alternative strategy comparison would need consistent available resources, dated orders, waiting cash and the same endpoint. Changing the cash purchase amount scales quantities and dollar results without changing this frictionless cost-per-unit statistic. It still changes the household money committed. Equal averages do not make two differently sized positions equally important to a financial plan. Mark all accumulated units at the final price At the fourth price of CAD 20, the 240 units have a market value of CAD 4,800. Compared with CAD 4,000 of contributed cash, the final dollar difference is positive CAD 800. The line chart shows the cumulative cash and the marked position after each purchase. After the second purchase, 150 units at CAD 10 are worth CAD 1,500, below the CAD 2,000 already contributed. Buying additional units does not remove the loss on earlier units when the current price is lower. Change the fourth price to CAD 5 and the result becomes a loss. The four purchases then acquire 390 units, with a final market value of CAD 1,950 against CAD 4,000 of contributions. Having more units and a lower average cost does not ensure that the final price is above that cost. The dollar gap is not an annualized, time-weighted or money-weighted return. Cash arrived on four dates, and the tool does not assign calendar spacing for a rate calculation. It also does not calculate cash available after a sale, tax payable or a tax adjusted cost base. Use the accounting before choosing an investment schedule For a real record, reconcile each trade’s cash, execution price and units with its confirmation. Keep fees, distributions, currency conversions and corporate actions in the appropriate ledger. Do not combine incompatible unit classes or unadjusted prices across an event that changes unit counts. FINRA’s discussion distinguishes investing money as it becomes available from intentionally delaying investment of cash already held. It also notes that repeated transaction costs and waiting cash can affect a schedule. These implementation issues remain outside the frictionless four-purchase identity. Neither the chosen price path nor the fact that its harmonic mean is lower than its arithmetic mean supplies evidence about future market direction. A plan must still consider the investment’s suitability, diversification, time horizon, cash needs and the ability to keep funding purchases. The useful accounting sequence is concrete: record the cash invested, calculate and add the units, divide cost by units, then mark the entire position at the valuation price. The four charts preserve those steps so that a price average, unit quantity and dollar gain are each given the meaning their calculation supports.

documents.title: Wealth concentration: read the household share, the group mean and the missing detail
documents.description: Compare dated official wealth-group averages, derive approximate group shares, and trace cumulative wealth only at the boundaries the published extract supports.
documents.body: A group’s average wealth and its share of national wealth answer different questions. Neither reveals a family’s usable cash or the distribution hidden inside that group. Read the reference quarter and the ranking variable first A statement about the wealthiest 20% describes households ranked by net worth. It does not identify the highest-income 20%, the oldest 20% or the households with the largest bank deposits. The sorting variable belongs beside the percentage before any planning interpretation is attempted. This guide uses Statistics Canada’s release table 3 published on 13 April 2026. It contains average net worth per household for the fourth quarters of 2024 and 2025. The selector changes between those two dated snapshots; it does not estimate a current account balance or create a later observation. The source groups the least wealthy 40% together and shows the next three wealth quintiles separately. A quintile represents one-fifth of the household distribution, while that combined first group represents two-fifths. The four rows therefore have different household weights even though they occupy equal space in a chart. A group average is neither its entry threshold nor its median For Q4 2025, the published mean is CAD 81,650 within the bottom 40%, CAD 526,185 within the third quintile, CAD 1,160,145 within the fourth quintile and CAD 3,543,579 within the top quintile. The published all-household mean is CAD 1,078,642. The top-group mean does not tell you the minimum net worth required to enter that group. It also does not tell you the net worth of its middle household. A few very large values can affect an average substantially, and these grouped means do not reveal the observations needed to reconstruct a median, a percentile threshold or an individual distribution. Net worth is a balance-sheet amount: assets less liabilities. It can contain property and other assets whose value cannot be spent immediately without a transaction. A wealth-group mean therefore cannot be copied into a household cash plan as if it were an available bank balance. Use household weights when moving from group means to approximate shares To derive a group’s contribution to the overall mean, multiply its published mean by its household weight. For the top group in Q4 2025, the contribution is 20% × CAD 3,543,579 = CAD 708,715.80. For the combined bottom group, it is 40% × CAD 81,650 = CAD 32,660. Adding the four weighted contributions gives CAD 1,078,641.80. That is 20 cents below the separately published all-household mean, reflecting rounding in the displayed inputs. The website divides each contribution by this weighted sum so that the four approximate derived wealth shares add to 100%. The results are about 65.70% for the top 20% and 3.03% for the bottom 40%. The accompanying release describes those shares at rounded headline precision as 65.7% and 3.0%. The website’s extra decimal place is arithmetic from rounded means, not evidence of a more precise official estimate. The grouped chart places household shares beside wealth shares. A bar at 20% in the first series and about 65.70% in the second uses two different denominators: households and net worth. It does not mean that 65.70% of households are in the top quintile. Trace only the cumulative boundaries the extract actually provides The cumulative chart begins at zero, then adds the wealth shares at 40%, 60%, 80% and 100% of households, ordered from least to most wealthy. The equality reference is a diagonal: under equal net worth per household, a given household share would hold the same share of wealth. The displayed curve is a grouped-boundary picture. Straight connecting segments help locate the known endpoints but do not recover what happens inside each group. In particular, this extract has no separate 20% boundary. Filling it in with half the bottom-40% share would silently assume away within-group inequality. The release explains that the lowest two quintiles are combined because the lowest quintile’s average liabilities exceeded its assets. A positive average for the combined bottom 40% therefore does not establish that its least wealthy households have positive net worth. The missing detail matters. This chart does not calculate an individual-level Lorenz curve or a Gini coefficient. Computing such a statistic from the few straight segments and presenting it as the country’s actual inequality measure would give the unobserved within-group distribution an unwarranted role. A rise in a group mean is not an investment return for its members The final chart retains the source’s rounded changes in group mean net worth from Q4 2024 to Q4 2025: 2.1% for the bottom 40%, 3.2% for the third quintile, 4.4% for the fourth and 6.0% for the top quintile. It compares the same quarter of two years and stays fixed when the snapshot selector changes. Those figures do not show what happened to every household that started in a particular group. Households can move between groups, and a group’s net worth can change through asset values, saving, borrowing and changes in its composition. The chart is a comparison of group averages at two dates, rather than an account statement following the same investors. The values are nominal. They have not been adjusted for inflation. They should also not be read as a return that a family could earn by adopting the financial habits or assets associated with a higher-wealth group. Keep estimation limits visible beside the concentration story The release’s notes describe a distributional economic-account system using different data inputs, models and assumptions, with some components relying on information from earlier periods. These are estimates that can be revised. The release table provides no confidence bounds for the selected means, so none are drawn or inferred here. The grouping is useful for describing concentration at the supported level of detail. It does not establish why an individual household has a particular amount of wealth, forecast where that household will rank later or show its ability to meet next month’s expenses. For a personal plan, prepare a separate list of assets, debts, access conditions and dated cash needs. Distinguish property value from net sale proceeds, a restricted asset from cash available now, and a debt balance from the payment calendar. A national wealth share provides context for that work; it does not replace it. Record the reference date and the variable used to rank households. Keep a group mean separate from a threshold, median or share. Use the correct group weights and disclose rounding in derived shares. Leave unsupported within-group detail unknown. Build the household’s own liquidity plan from its own evidence.

documents.title: Regular investing: average quoted price is different from your cost per unit
documents.description: Track six equal cash purchases through fractional units, arithmetic and harmonic averages, fixed transaction fees and a separate market valuation in four interactive charts.
documents.body: Divide the relevant cash amount by the units actually acquired. A lower purchase-price average than the arithmetic average does not establish a profit or a superior investing schedule. Give the cash and the units their own records Suppose you invest the same cash amount every month while the unit price changes. Averaging the quoted prices gives each month equal weight. Dividing your purchase spending by your acquired units gives a different average because a lower price allows the same cash to buy more units. The distinction is arithmetic, not evidence that a particular schedule is profitable. A useful record identifies execution prices, cash available, charges, units bought and the price later used to value those units. Investor.gov’s dollar-cost-averaging explanation describes equal purchases at regular intervals and the resulting change in units when prices move. This article uses that mechanism in six original monthly transactions. It does not compare investing an existing lump sum with investing future earnings. The default assigns CAD 200 to each purchase, including a CAD 2 transaction fee. Net security-purchase cash is therefore CAD 198 per order. The six execution prices are CAD 20, 16, 12, 18, 24 and 20 per unit. These are authored numbers, not observations from a fund. Follow each execution before calculating an average At CAD 20, net cash of CAD 198 buys 9.9 units. At CAD 16 it buys 12.375 units; at CAD 12, 16.5 units. The fourth, fifth and sixth purchases add 11, 8.25 and 9.9 units respectively. Total units are 67.925 . Security-purchase spending is six times CAD 198, or CAD 1,188 . Fees total CAD 12, bringing total household cash spent to CAD 1,200 . The unit bars make the changing quantities visible. They should not be interpreted as changes in the amount the household saved: each monthly cash assignment is still CAD 200. The fee is paid from that assignment before the units are acquired. The example allows any fractional unit amount and retains calculation precision. Actual brokers, plans or securities may impose whole-unit orders, rounding rules or minimums. Those restrictions would require a separate cash-residue ledger and could change the units obtained. Identify the numerator before reporting a unit cost The simple arithmetic average of the six execution prices is their sum divided by six: CAD 110 ÷ 6, or approximately CAD 18.33 per unit . It describes this list of prices, with equal weight assigned to every purchase date. The actual purchase-price amount per acquired unit is CAD 1,188 ÷ 67.925, or approximately CAD 17.49 . This is a unit-weighted average: multiplying each execution price by its purchased units reconstructs the CAD 1,188 security spending. Total household cash per unit includes the fees. CAD 1,200 ÷ 67.925 is approximately CAD 17.67 . It exceeds the purchase-price average because the same acquired units must account for an additional CAD 12 of cash spent. The three headline figures are all CAD per unit. None is an account balance or a percentage investment return. The line chart traces their cumulative versions after each purchase so a reader can see how the records develop, rather than replacing the underlying transactions with one unexplained average. Use the harmonic mean only when its equal-cash condition holds Write the six positive prices as P₁ through P₆ and equal net purchase cash as C. Total units are C ÷ P₁ + C ÷ P₂ + … + C ÷ P₆. Total security spending is 6C. Dividing spending by units cancels C and gives 6 ÷ (1/P₁ + 1/P₂ + … + 1/P₆) . This is the harmonic mean of the six positive prices, matching the definition in NIST’s harmonic-mean reference . The identity applies here because equal household cash and an identical fixed fee leave equal net cash at every execution. If the amounts or fees vary between purchases, calculate total actual spending divided by total actual units directly. An unweighted harmonic mean would then generally answer a different question. For positive prices, the harmonic mean is no greater than the arithmetic mean, with equality when all the prices are identical. That mathematical comparison is between two averages of the same price list. It does not compare this schedule’s realized return with another strategy, and it does not remove the effect of charges. Reconcile the separate valuation without treating costs as profit The valuation input is independent of the six execution prices. At the default CAD 20 per unit, the 67.925 units have market value of CAD 1,358.50 . Compared with CAD 1,200 of household cash spent, the unrealized cash gain is CAD 158.50. The waterfall starts with that CAD 1,200, subtracts the CAD 12 paid in fees and adds CAD 170.50 of price change across the purchased units. The resulting CAD 1,358.50 is the market value, with the fee deducted once. Change only the valuation price to CAD 15. Market value becomes CAD 1,018.875 before display rounding, and the unrealized cash result becomes a loss of CAD 181.125. The six-price arithmetic average and purchase-price harmonic mean have not changed. A purchase average below an arithmetic average can therefore coexist with an investment loss. The separate valuation is not an executed sale. Selling costs, tax and access to cash remain outside the illustration. The all-in cash figure is not a determination of the asset’s tax adjusted cost base. Test identical prices and fee drag before drawing a conclusion The variation control scales the authored deviations from the first-price base. At 100%, the default six-price shape is 1, 0.8, 0.6, 0.9, 1.2 and 1 times the base. Zero variation makes all execution prices equal. Changing it does not select a historical market episode or assign probabilities to a decline. With zero variation, a CAD 20 price and the unchanged CAD 2 fee, every purchase buys 9.9 units. Both the arithmetic price and the purchase-price average are CAD 20, while household cash per unit is approximately CAD 20.20. Valuing the units at CAD 20 leaves a CAD 12 loss, exactly equal to the six fees. The signed matrix changes the valuation price and fee while preserving the selected execution prices and monthly cash. Its rows are explicit comparison prices, not confidence bounds. A larger fee reduces the units bought from the fixed budget; a higher valuation price raises their market value. FINRA’s discussion of regular investing identifies transaction costs and the distinction between existing cash and money invested as it is earned. Those practical considerations require their own records. This calculation supplies neither a guarantee of profit nor an allocation or timing recommendation.
