documents.title: One project can have two internal rates of return: keep the later payment in the picture
documents.description: Three charts follow an initial outlay, a later receipt and a final obligation, then reveal why the same cash flows can have more than one nonnegative IRR.
documents.body: An IRR is a discount rate that makes a cash-flow valuation equal zero. With a later outflow, there may be several such rates, so read the dated cash flows and NPV profile before relying on one percentage. Put the final obligation on the timeline A project can require cash now, return cash later and still leave another payment due. Ending an analysis at the first receipt can hide that obligation and turn a partial cash-flow record into an apparently attractive return. The original example pays CAD 10,000 immediately, receives CAD 23,000 at the end of year one, and requires CAD 13,200 at the end of year two. The last amount could represent an independently estimated closing or restoration obligation in a hypothetical project. It is entered as a required payment rather than treated as an optional use of profit. The first chart shows the signs from the participant’s perspective: negative, positive, negative. A payment and a receipt one year apart cannot simply be netted as though they occur on the same date. That separation matters to both valuation and the eventual cash required. No actual project, security or contract is being offered. The amounts are fixed teaching assumptions, with no claim that the receipt or final bill is certain in real life. A practical review would need complete cash-flow evidence, taxes, financing conditions, risk and other obligations. NPV values all the flows at one stated discount assumption Net present value converts future flows to a common starting date. For an effective annual discount assumption r, this example uses −10,000 + 23,000 ÷ (1 + r) − 13,200 ÷ (1 + r) 2 . At 15%, the year-one receipt has a present value of CAD 20,000. The year-two payment has a present value of approximately CAD 9,981.10. Subtracting the immediate CAD 10,000 payment leaves NPV of approximately CAD 18.90. The waterfall displays those three components separately. The small positive endpoint means the modeled discounted receipt exceeds the modeled discounted payments by that amount at the selected assumption. It is not a cash account holding CAD 18.90 or a guarantee that the project can pay its last bill. The undiscounted sum is negative CAD 200. That different result uses no time adjustment. Neither measure should be relabeled as the other. OpenStax’s NPV discussion provides the general valuation framework; all amounts and calculations in this article are independently authored. IRR solves for a zero valuation instead of accepting a discount input An internal rate of return is a rate at which the NPV equation equals zero. For the original cash flows, 10% is one solution: the CAD 23,000 receipt discounted one year and the CAD 13,200 payment discounted two years exactly reconcile with the initial outlay. But 20% also makes the same equation zero. The cash-flow pattern therefore has two distinct nonnegative annual IRRs. Reporting only whichever rate a trial-and-error routine happens to find would conceal another mathematical solution. The reason can be checked algebraically. Let g = 1 + r. Multiplying the zero-NPV equation by g squared gives 10,000g 2 − 23,000g + 13,200 = 0 . It factors into growth factors of 1.10 and 1.20, corresponding to the two rates. The rate metric solves that quadratic directly. It does not search only the plotted grid or treat two adjacent plotted values as proof that a unique rate exists. Depending on the entered flows, the stated nonnegative domain can contain zero, one or two distinct rates. The NPV profile explains why one higher-rate rule can fail The line chart evaluates the entire three-flow NPV at a range of annual discount assumptions. In the original example, NPV is negative at 0%, zero at 10%, positive around 15%, zero again at 20%, and negative beyond the upper root. The later payment is discounted for two years while the receipt is discounted for one. Raising the rate reduces the present value of both. Their competing effects mean the total need not fall continuously as the rate rises. A rule learned for an initial outflow followed only by inflows cannot be applied automatically to every sign-changing pattern. OpenStax’s IRR discussion identifies multiple mathematical solutions as a limitation when later negative flows occur. This article uses that mathematical fact to inspect one original example; it does not turn the higher root into a superior choice or recommend a discount rate. The profile starts at 0% and extends to at least 30%. If the selected discount input is higher, it extends to that input. A listed root beyond the visible range remains a root even though the line chart does not show it. The metric states that only nonnegative rates are listed; a negative solution is outside this guide’s chosen domain. A repeated root and no admissible root are meaningful outcomes Change the final payment to CAD 13,225 while retaining the original initial cost and receipt. The two growth-factor roots meet at 1.15. The solver lists a single distinct 15% rate, and the NPV curve touches zero there rather than crossing into a positive region. This is why counting visible crossings is insufficient. A tangent zero is still a mathematical solution. A repeated solution should also not be presented as two different rates merely because a quadratic formula returns it twice. Other entries can produce no nonnegative solution. A positive year-two obligation with too little earlier receipt may leave NPV below zero for every nonnegative discount rate. If the final payment is zero, the remaining two-date problem can instead have one nonnegative IRR, depending on the receipt relative to the initial outlay. Scaling every cash amount by the same positive factor leaves the roots unchanged while scaling NPV by that factor. A percentage therefore does not measure the dollar size of a project’s value or funding requirement. Two opportunities with equal rate roots can still place very different amounts of household money at risk. Add the cash plan before interpreting a return The year-one receipt is not automatically available for unrestricted spending. In the original example, a required payment remains due one year later. The household needs a supported plan for that date even when a valuation metric is positive. This calculator does not hold the receipt in an account, assign it a reinvestment rate or compute final wealth. It also does not obtain credit for a later shortfall. A dated cash plan would separately identify available starting resources, what happens to the receipt, and how the final payment is funded. The discount input is an assumption used for valuation. Selecting a higher number does not make a project safer, increase its actual receipts or remove an obligation. The appropriate treatment of risk and the comparison with other uses of money require facts beyond these three entered flows. Use the charts to check completeness before relying on a quoted percentage. Keep every material inflow and outflow at its own date, inspect whether more than one admissible rate exists, and read NPV at explicitly supported assumptions. Then evaluate the actual contract, uncertainty and payment capacity as part of the wider decision.

documents.title: Repair or replace: compare future cash, current resale value and a common exit date
documents.description: Use cash-flow bridges, cumulative costs and a signed sensitivity matrix to separate an old purchase price from the money that changes in today’s repair decision.
documents.body: Begin the comparison today. Include a repair quote, replacement costs, sale proceeds and future running costs once, using the same service requirement and exit date. Write the two forward alternatives before looking at the original receipt An expensive item can feel worth repairing because it cost a lot when new. A disappointing past purchase can also make replacement feel like an admission of loss. The forward cash question is more concrete: what money changes from today if the household repairs and retains the item, compared with replacing it now? The illustration assumes that either alternative provides the same required service for five more years. The old item can be repaired for CAD 450. A replacement costs CAD 1,600, with CAD 150 of delivery and installation. Its assumed annual running cost is lower. Both alternatives are evaluated at the same final date, including independently entered net sale values. The original CAD 2,200 purchase payment is already paid and unrecoverable. The context field lets you change that past amount, but doing so intentionally leaves every cost metric and chart unchanged. The numbers that can change the forward choice have their own inputs. Distinguish an unrecoverable past payment from sale proceeds available today ACCA’s relevant-cost guidance distinguishes past costs from changes in future cash and explains the opportunity cost of keeping an asset that could otherwise be sold. That distinction is the accounting context for this original household example; the source does not provide the repair quotes, resale estimates or discount rate used here. The old item’s assumed net sale value today is CAD 100. Replacing it allows that receipt now, so the replacement cash calculation is CAD 1,600 + CAD 150 − CAD 100 = CAD 1,650 . Repairing it uses CAD 450 and keeps the item. The initial replacement outlay is therefore CAD 1,200 higher. The CAD 100 is relevant because the two choices change whether it is received today. It is different from the historical CAD 2,200 payment. No fraction of the original receipt is added to today’s repair payment merely because that receipt once existed. Count the current resale opportunity once The same initial difference can be expressed using two consistent ledgers. The cash ledger compares CAD 450 to repair with CAD 1,650 to replace after selling the old item. An equivalent opportunity-cost ledger adds the common CAD 100 resale baseline to both sides: CAD 550 for retaining and repairing the old item, versus CAD 1,750 for acquiring and installing the replacement before sale proceeds. Both comparisons give the same CAD 1,200 difference. The opportunity-cost presentation makes the sale receipt forgone by retaining the item visible; it does not create another CAD 100 invoice. Combining the two ledgers incorrectly would add the CAD 100 forgone sale to repair and subtract it from replacement. That would count the same opportunity twice and produce a false CAD 1,100 difference. The calculator uses the cash ledger throughout: the old sale appears once as a receipt in the replacement alternative. Follow running costs and the final sale through the same five years After repair, the old item has an assumed constant running cost of CAD 320 per year. The replacement costs CAD 180 per year to run. These are all-in scenario inputs, not measured electricity consumption, market tariffs or quoted maintenance plans. They can include the recurring costs relevant to the comparison if the same categories are used on both sides. The old item’s assumed final net sale value is zero, so its five-year undiscounted net cost is CAD 450 + 5 × CAD 320 = CAD 2,050 . The replacement has an assumed CAD 400 final sale receipt, giving CAD 1,650 + 5 × CAD 180 − CAD 400 = CAD 2,150 . The replacement line falls from CAD 2,370 at year four to CAD 2,150 at year five because the final CAD 400 receipt exceeds that last year’s CAD 180 running cost. The decline does not mean a negative operating bill. A sale receipt is included only at the selected final date, after the last running-cost payment. Compare present values without adding them to the cash bills The default effective annual nominal discount rate is an assumed 4%. Initial payments remain at today’s value. Annual running payments are discounted from each year-end, and final sale receipts from the common exit date. Under those assumptions, repair has a present net cost of about CAD 1,874.58 and replacement about CAD 2,122.56 . The replacement-minus-repair bridge begins with CAD 1,200 of additional initial cash. The present value of its CAD 140 annual running-cost reduction subtracts about CAD 623.26. Its additional CAD 400 exit receipt subtracts about CAD 328.77 after discounting. The remaining difference is about CAD 247.97 of higher present cost for replacement. That differs from the CAD 100 undiscounted difference because the replacement’s offsetting savings and sale receipt occur later than its additional initial payment. Present value is an alternative valuation of the same cash schedule. It is not another charge, an interest bill, a promised investment return or permission to ignore the cash needed now. Stress the uncertain quote and running cost before interpreting the answer The matrix replaces the repair quote and the replacement’s annual running cost. It holds the selected horizon, old running cost, discount rate, current sale receipt and both final sale values fixed. Each cell is replacement present cost minus repair present cost: a positive amount means replacement costs more in the model; a negative amount means it costs less. A lower running-cost estimate cannot by itself establish that a replacement is preferable. The price difference, timing and exit values still enter the same comparison. Likewise, a higher repair quote can change the result without changing the amount originally paid for the old item. The five-year service assumption is a condition of the illustration, not a reliability finding. A repair that provides less service, another breakdown, a different replacement cycle or a change in usage needs additional dated cash flows. Changing the horizon also requires reviewing both final sale values rather than treating them as guaranteed amounts at any date. Make the forward comparison usable in a household budget Confirm the required service and a common comparison date. Obtain current repair, purchase, delivery and installation amounts. Use net sale receipts after selling costs, with realistic receipt dates. Compare running costs on the same usage and dollar basis. Review final values, remaining service life and the cash available today. The calculator assumes cash settlement today and no financing, tax calculation, refund, warranty recovery, inflation or another failure. It does not value convenience, downtime or differences in product quality. If the old item’s sale receipt arrives after the new purchase payment, the upfront bridge understates the interim cash needed and a separate timing plan is required. A forward cost comparison helps identify the amounts that matter. The household still needs a workable payment plan and evidence that each option can provide the service being compared.

documents.title: Borrow the project budget now or draw it in stages? Follow debt, unused cash and carrying costs
documents.description: Compare an immediate project-loan draw with three draws tied to bills, then reconcile interest, draw fees, interest on idle borrowed cash and the principal still owed.
documents.body: Borrowed cash comes with matching debt. Aligning draws with bills can change carrying costs, but an undrawn limit is a different resource and the final project debt still needs repayment. Separate the approved limit, the borrowing transaction and the project bill A project budget can be known well before all of its bills are due. Borrowing the full amount immediately creates cash in an account, but it also creates debt immediately. Drawing only when a bill is due leaves less debt outstanding earlier, provided those later draws remain available under the actual arrangement. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s line-of-credit explanation distinguishes a credit limit from money borrowed and explains that interest applies to drawn amounts. It also identifies possible fees and the consequence of paying interest without reducing principal. Those general mechanics provide the context for this illustration. The model compares two schedules on an assumed facility, rather than two actual loan offers. Each finances the same CAD 60,000 project. One draws CAD 60,000 now; the other draws CAD 20,000 for each of three bills. Approval, continued access and payment of every bill are assumptions that require separate evidence in an actual plan. Put the three bills at explicit points inside the year The default bills arrive at the start of months three, six and nine. The first two monthly periods therefore pass before the first bill. Changing the spacing moves all three dates together while keeping their amounts equal. A spacing of four places the final bill at the start of month twelve. The immediate-draw schedule owes CAD 60,000 throughout the year. Its borrowed project cash falls to CAD 40,000 at the first bill, CAD 20,000 at the second and zero at the third. Paying a contractor uses the cash; it does not repay the lender. The staged schedule owes nothing in the first two monthly periods, CAD 20,000 in months three through five, CAD 40,000 in months six through eight, and CAD 60,000 in months nine through twelve. Every draw goes straight to the associated bill. Both schedules therefore finish with the same amount spent on the project and the same principal owed. Charge interest to the debt that is actually outstanding The default annual borrowing input is 8%, with one twelfth applied to each monthly period. The immediate schedule pays CAD 400 of interest per month and CAD 4,800 over twelve months. The staged schedule pays interest on its smaller early balances and pays CAD 2,800 over the same horizon. This is a deliberately uniform monthly convention. FCAC describes interest running from withdrawal until repayment; actual agreements may calculate it daily and apply variable rates. The illustration holds its rates fixed and does not claim that each real calendar month has the same day count. All borrowing interest is paid from separate household cash. It is not added to principal, funded by another draw or deducted from the cash earmarked for bills. That keeps the full project funded in both schedules, but it also means the household needs another budget line for those monthly payments. Counting the project loan as sufficient to cover both the bills and those separate interest payments would overstate the funds provided. Include interest on unused borrowed cash without counting it twice The immediate schedule holds borrowed money before the project needs it. At the hypothetical 2% annual cash-interest input, its unused project cash earns CAD 500 over the modeled year. The interest is paid out to separate household cash and is not compounded or used to change the project’s bill amounts. The cash pot contains CAD 60,000 for two monthly periods, CAD 40,000 for three, and CAD 20,000 for three. Multiplying those balances by their periods and the monthly cash rate gives the CAD 500 amount. The staged schedule has no idle project cash because each draw immediately pays a bill. The income offsets part of the immediate schedule’s borrowing cost, but it does not turn borrowed principal into new household wealth. At the initial draw, CAD 60,000 of cash and CAD 60,000 of debt arise together. The model also makes no assumption that project spending creates an asset worth its cost. Any market value, resale proceeds or tax treatment would need its own evidence. Reconcile fees before describing the net saving A hypothetical CAD 50 fee applies to each positive draw and is paid from household cash. The immediate schedule has one fee of CAD 50. The staged schedule has three fees totaling CAD 150. These are entered assumptions, rather than a claim about common lender pricing. The immediate schedule’s net carrying cost is therefore CAD 4,800 of borrowing interest plus CAD 50 of fees minus CAD 500 of cash interest, or CAD 4,350. The staged schedule costs CAD 2,800 plus CAD 150, or CAD 2,950. Staged cost less immediate cost is negative CAD 1,400 under the default inputs. The waterfall reconciles that signed difference. It adds staged interest and fees, subtracts the immediate schedule’s interest and fee, then adds back the income already deducted from the immediate cost. This last sign matters: ignoring the income would exaggerate the staged schedule’s advantage. No extra principal deduction belongs in the comparison because the same CAD 60,000 debt remains in both alternatives. Test the bill dates and rates, then plan the debt repayment The matrix replaces the borrowing rate and the bill spacing while holding project size, cash yield and draw fee selected. Later bills leave more borrowed money idle under the immediate schedule. A larger borrowing-rate margin over the cash rate increases that carrying-cost difference, while extra draw fees can offset it. The cells are alternative calculations, not forecasts of rates or approval. An entered cash rate above the borrowing rate can even produce negative net carrying cost for the immediate schedule. That is a mathematical consequence of the assumptions, rather than evidence that such an arrangement is available, permitted or attractive after tax and other costs. The final planning task remains principal repayment. The calculation stops after twelve months with the project paid and its debt outstanding. It does not assume a home sale, refinancing, future income increase or another loan will clear that balance. Keep the draw calendar, monthly carrying budget and eventual repayment source together. A lower first-year financing cost can improve the cash plan while leaving the same long-term debt obligation.

documents.title: An inflation-linked bond has three different amounts: adjusted principal, coupon cash and redemption
documents.description: Use four interactive USD charts to separate an index adjustment from spendable coupon cash, apply a maturity principal floor and compare redemption with an independently entered purchase outlay.
documents.body: Match a spending date with an actual cash payment. Index-adjusted principal, market value and purchase outlay are different amounts, and a floor on original face does not promise every purchase price back. Start with the cash-flow question, then identify the amount A retirement budget may need money this month, while a bond’s principal is scheduled to be repaid years later. An increase in an indexed principal amount does not itself fill that month’s spending account. The useful first question is when cash is actually paid. TreasuryDirect’s TIPS overview describes U.S. Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities: principal adjusts with inflation or deflation, the coupon rate is fixed, and interest is paid every six months on adjusted principal. At maturity, principal redemption is the greater of the adjusted amount and original principal. The charts use those basic distinctions in an authored USD example. They do not reproduce a security’s daily index ratios or a market quotation. Keep four labels separate: original face, index-adjusted principal, coupon receipts and the amount actually paid to buy the bond. A secondary-market sale value would be another amount requiring its own calculation. Specify the reference index and the payment convention The default begins with USD 10,000 of original face and a reference index of 1. Its illustrative index rises at a constant 3% annually over five years. Half-year checkpoints use fractional compounding, so the index at time t is 1.03 raised to the power t . At year five, adjusted principal is approximately USD 11,592.74. The increase above USD 10,000 remains part of the principal calculation; it has not also been paid as five separate annual cash bonuses. The first chart therefore shows principal amounts rather than a bank-account balance. For an actual TIPS, TreasuryDirect provides security-specific daily index ratios . A real calculation requires the matching security and payment date. This model substitutes a smooth authored index and omits reference-CPI publication lag, daily interpolation and settlement rounding. Its index is neither observed U.S. inflation nor a forecast. Multiply the fixed coupon rate by the changing principal base The selected annual coupon rate is 2%. A half-year payment is adjusted principal on that payment date multiplied by 1%. It is not 1% of the purchase price, and a principal index increase is not another coupon. TreasuryDirect’s pricing explanation uses original principal times the applicable index ratio, then half the stated annual coupon rate, to calculate a TIPS payment. The chart’s simpler index follows that multiplication structure without claiming to reproduce an actual payment. The grouped bars total the two nominal coupons received in each model year. Beside them, each coupon is divided by the illustrative index at its own payment date before the two reference-date amounts are added. That comparison remains USD 200 per year. It describes the purchasing power of the payment flows under the same index, rather than the later value of accumulated cash. Apply the original-face floor at redemption, not at every checkpoint Change the annual index movement to a negative figure. Adjusted principal declines, and so do nominal coupon payments. The dashed original-face reference does not stop that interim decline. In this illustration, the final coupon is still calculated from adjusted principal even when it is below face. At maturity, the separate principal payment is the larger of adjusted principal and original face. Under five years of constant 4% annual deflation, for example, adjusted principal is about USD 8,153.73, while the modeled principal redemption is USD 10,000. The floor supplies the difference at that date. That maturity calculation is not a quote for selling the bond earlier. Nor does it guarantee that an amount paid above original face will be returned as principal. The matrix compares redemption with several authored purchase outlays and excludes coupons explicitly. A negative cell identifies a principal-only difference; it does not establish the full investment loss. Count coupons and redemption once, then subtract the purchase outlay The default purchase outlay is 105% of original face, or USD 10,500. This amount is entered independently. The model does not solve for a market yield, assess whether that price is attractive or imply that coupon rate equals return. The waterfall adds all received coupons and the maturity principal payment, then subtracts the purchase outlay. It assumes every coupon is retained as cash earning zero interest. The maturity payment already contains the applicable index adjustment or original-face floor, so adding a separate inflation uplift would count part of principal twice. The resulting nominal cash difference is not an annualized or inflation-adjusted return. Coupons arrive at different dates, and cash held without interest can lose purchasing power during inflation. Spending those coupons would reduce the cash still available at maturity. Reinvesting them would require a separate rate and timing assumption; neither action is silently included here. Match the currency, price index and payment date to the actual need To use this distinction in a financial plan, list the dates and currency of the required payments. Place expected coupon receipts beside those dates, and reserve the principal payment for maturity. A bill due earlier needs another identified source of cash or an explicit sale assumption. These USD charts do not demonstrate protection for a Canadian-dollar bill. Currency conversion changes the CAD amount received, while a household’s spending basket can move differently from a broad consumer price index. Taxes and transaction costs can also separate gross contractual payments from spendable household cash; neither is calculated here. The related bond-horizon article examines sale values and reinvestment separately, and the currency guide explains translation into CAD. This page stops at contractual cash-flow arithmetic under its selected index. It supplies no actual bond price path, fund return, tax estimate or personal allocation target. Use a real security’s terms and dated index ratios before treating a chart as a payment forecast.

documents.title: Fraud reports, victims and losses: three numbers that need different planning questions
documents.description: Three source-backed charts explore the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre’s 2025 category tables, with a display control that preserves the original observations.
documents.body: A reported loss ranking can identify serious patterns. It cannot supply your personal chance of being defrauded, the typical loss of a household, or a guarantee that money will be recovered. Start with the reporting system and the reference year A financial-safety plan benefits from evidence about fraud, but a headline must be matched to the question it can answer. A reported dollar loss describes a financial amount. A report count describes entries received by a reporting system. Neither is automatically a probability for one person receiving a suspicious message. The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre’s 2025 top-ten page reports more than CAD 704 million of losses and over 112,000 reports across its system. Its category tables are the controlling source for the charts here. The page was issued and modified on 25 February 2026; the observations concern calendar 2025. The display control selects between three and ten categories from the published dollar-loss ranking. It does not change any observation or construct a household scenario. Five categories appear in the original view. The count chart keeps their dollar-loss order so that the reader can compare the same rows, while the derived-ratio chart deliberately uses its own ordering. These are administrative reported observations, not a representative sample of every Canadian household or every encounter with a scam. The charts provide neither a population exposure count nor the total number of unreported incidents. A denominator needed for a personal victimization probability is absent. Keep the loss amount, report count and victim count separate The first chart ranks selected categories by reported dollar amount. The grouped chart places the source’s report and victim columns beside each other. Different quantities can move differently: a category with fewer listed reports can still have substantial financial losses. Do not add report counts and victim counts together. They describe different units. Nor does a category table establish that every listed victim is a distinct person across all categories, that every report concerns one household, or that the counts represent the number of people who encountered an attempt. The control preserves a common set of categories across all three charts. Expanding to ten reveals more of the source’s loss ranking; it does not turn the selection into the entire reporting system. The selection is by dollar loss, so it should not be presented as the ten most frequent categories or as a ranking of how likely one household is to encounter each type. The first two bar charts begin their magnitude axes at zero. Their different units remain explicit. A long dollar-loss bar and a short count bar cannot be divided visually to obtain a precise rate; the derived calculation needs the actual values and a stated denominator. A loss-per-count ratio is an average of reported aggregates The third chart divides each rounded category loss by its listed victim count. It then rounds the result to the nearest CAD 100. That additional rounding avoids showing cents of precision unsupported by a source that publishes losses in rounded millions. The calculation changes the question from total reported financial scale to reported loss per listed victim count. It can therefore change the category order. That is an arithmetic consequence of choosing another denominator, rather than a contradiction between charts. The result is not a median, a typical household outcome or the cost a particular person should expect. A small number of very large losses can influence an aggregate ratio, and the table does not supply the individual loss distribution needed to inspect that effect. It also supplies no uncertainty interval for the displayed comparison. Reported aggregates should not be treated as independent, identically exposed household observations. Reporting behaviour, category definitions and the underlying incidents can differ. The ratio is useful as a clearly named descriptive calculation, with those limitations retained, rather than as an actuarial price for an individual’s risk. Preserve unavailable amounts and lower-bound headlines The source also publishes a separate frequency table containing N/A dollar-loss entries. An unavailable amount is not the number zero. It should not become a zero-height loss bar, a claim that no harm occurred, or a zero average obtained by dividing it by a count. This article therefore uses the source’s dollar-loss ranking for the selected loss comparisons and preserves the unavailable entries in its source extract. It does not merge the two top-ten selections into a single invented population. The all-category loss headline says more than a stated amount. It is not an exact total with which to calculate exact category shares. Rounded category amounts add another precision limit. The article avoids a pie chart or an exact percentage of all national losses. The Competition Bureau’s March 2026 release describes substantial underreporting. That makes the reporting-system boundary material. It does not justify multiplying every category by one assumed reporting factor or converting the published totals into a new national-loss estimate. Such a calculation would require defensible assumptions about which incidents are missing and how their losses differ. Use the evidence to review a payment process A household can use the patterns as a reason to examine how unusual requests reach its money. The practical record might identify who can approve a large transfer, how an unexpected caller is verified, and which independently obtained contact details are used to check a request. CAFC’s fraud-investigator guidance explains that criminals may impersonate trusted investigators or financial institutions. Verify an unexpected request through a channel you obtain independently, rather than treating a caller’s claimed role or displayed number as proof. The relevant question is whether the request has been authenticated before money or account access is supplied. CAFC’s investment-fraud guidance also supports checking a proposed investment and the people offering it. A polished page, a persuasive introduction or an apparent account balance does not itself verify an opportunity. Use the current official guidance linked below when a specific proposal needs checking; these charts do not assess an actual person or product. The controls and reserves in a financial plan have separate roles. Access to an emergency account can help meet legitimate bills after a disruption, but it does not validate a request to move money. Keeping another account balance on a chart is not evidence that a suspicious transfer can safely be made. Keep reporting, recovery and future planning distinct Reporting an incident helps establish a record; it does not promise recovery or determine reimbursement rights. The official CAFC page links to the reporting service and advises contacting local police when fraud or cybercrime is suspected. Use those official channels and retain relevant transaction records when an actual incident occurs. When planning after a loss, distinguish confirmed available money, disputed transactions and possible recoveries. An amount under investigation should not automatically be treated as cash for next month’s bills. Any reimbursement assumption needs its own support and payment date. Return to the dated source when updating the article. A later release, a partial-year update and an annual table can cover different windows or classifications. Do not splice them into a trend without first checking those definitions. A change in reported totals can reflect reporting as well as the underlying harm. The useful output of these charts is a better set of questions: which unit is being counted, which incidents are represented, how much rounding is present, and what action is supported by the evidence. Keeping those questions visible makes the statistics relevant to a household safety process without pretending they predict one person’s outcome.

documents.title: One saving headline, five different group averages: read the distribution before setting a target
documents.description: Explore 25 official annual net-saving observations, compare income-group means, trace one group and distinguish a negative level from a worsening change in four charts.
documents.body: A negative income-group average describes an aggregate accounting result. It cannot tell you how many households are in deficit or prescribe a saving amount for one family. Start with the annual measure and its release vintage Statistics Canada’s average household net-saving chart , released on 13 April 2026, reports five annual observations for each of five income quintiles. The source is Table 36-10-0587-01 within the Distributions of Household Economic Accounts. The article preserves that release vintage rather than mixing revisions from different downloads. The chart’s unit is current Canadian dollars per household per year. It is not a percentage, thousands of dollars, total saving for an entire group or a quarterly amount. The default controls display 2025, compare it with 2021 and trace the middle income group through all five years. These are national-accounts estimates distributed across household groups. They are not the answers to a survey question asking how much each respondent transferred into a savings account. The separate aggregate-saving-rate article explains the accounting distinction and its pension-entitlement adjustment. Read the sign before comparing the sizes For 2025, the source reports average annual net saving of −CAD 38,907 for the lowest income quintile, −CAD 19,944 for the second and −CAD 10,092 for the middle group. The fourth group is positive CAD 18,912 and the highest is positive CAD 75,469. The signed bars retain both sides of zero. A negative mean is net dissaving on the source’s definition. It is not a negative bank-account balance, a household’s end-of-year net worth or a statement that every member of the group had the same result. The highest-minus-lowest difference is CAD 75,469 − (−CAD 38,907) = CAD 114,376 . That subtracts two group means. It is not the income cutoff separating those quintiles, an amount owed between groups or a recommended annual saving target. An improving figure can remain below zero The difference chart subtracts the reference-year mean from the selected-year mean for each group. With 2021 as the reference and 2025 selected, the lowest group moves from −CAD 24,400 to −CAD 38,907, a difference of −CAD 14,507. The highest moves from CAD 59,395 to CAD 75,469, a positive difference of CAD 16,074. Try changing the reference year to 2024. The middle group then moves from −CAD 10,387 to −CAD 10,092, an improvement of CAD 295. Its level is still negative. Calling every negative mean a worsening result would miss this distinction. The controls allow either year to serve as the reference. Comparing a selected earlier year with a later reference reverses the subtraction. Selecting the same year twice produces zero in the change chart, while the level chart continues to show the actual group means for that year. Use a history and a matrix for different reading tasks The line follows the selected group’s five annual means from 2021 through 2025, with an explicit zero comparison. It helps distinguish the direction of a change from the sign of the level. Exact calendar years and values remain in the data table. The matrix displays three fixed snapshots—2021, 2023 and 2025—for all five groups. Its signed labels remain visible alongside the colour encoding. It supplies context when the controls focus on a different year or a single group. Neither visual follows the same individual families over time. A household can move between income groups, and the composition of each group can change. A line connecting group averages therefore cannot establish how the finances of one unchanged set of households evolved. Three negative group means do not establish that 60% of households are in deficit A mean summarizes the sum divided by the number of observations. It does not preserve the count on either side of zero. Knowing that three income-group means are negative is insufficient to determine how many individual households have negative net saving. Consider two original mathematical examples, separate from the official data. Set A contains five annual amounts: −500, −500, −500, −500 and +1,500. Their sum is −500 and their mean is −100. Four of the five values are negative. Set B contains −4,000, +875, +875, +875 and +875. Its sum is also −500 and its mean is also −100. Only one value is negative. The identical mean coexists with negative shares of 80% and 20% in these invented sets. The official chart does not supply the within-group observations needed to recover such shares. It also does not supply medians or the spread of individual outcomes. Do not turn a group mean into a claim about a typical family or a precise prevalence of financial difficulty. Keep the income grouping separate from wealth and liquidity An income group and a wealth group classify different quantities. The associated DHEA release discusses both, but the net-saving chart here uses income quintiles. Its labels cannot be silently replaced with “poorest” and “richest” by net worth. A household with substantial existing assets can have a low-income year. Another with strong current income may also have large debt payments or near-term obligations. The group chart does not identify those individual circumstances or reveal the money available for the next bill. The explorer supplies no income thresholds and does not assign the reader to a quintile. Choosing group three means “display the source’s third group,” rather than a determination that a particular salary, household size or bank balance belongs there. Use the estimates without treating them as a causal experiment Statistics Canada describes DHEA as combining macroeconomic accounts with distributional information. Some components use timely microdata or models; others rely on assumptions or information from earlier reference periods. The release also notes revisions to prior estimates. The annual values shown here are nominal. A change between 2021 and 2025 has not been adjusted for price inflation. The charts contain no confidence intervals or significance tests, and the subtraction does not establish which policy, price, job event or spending decision caused the difference. Lower-income pressure and wider differences between group means are useful economic context. Assessing their causes requires more evidence than these 25 observations. Assessing one family’s funding capacity requires its actual receipts, obligations and payment dates. Use the group context to ask better household questions The source does not imply that every household can solve a negative cash plan by choosing a different saving percentage. It also does not establish that a positive group average makes a particular household’s goals adequately funded. For a personal plan, start with cash actually received, list required costs, separate debt principal from interest, reserve for predictable irregular bills and write each goal in dollars with a date. Then check whether the proposed contribution fits the remaining cash. Those steps use a separately defined household ledger, rather than importing a group mean as a payment instruction. Keep the statistical release date and the annual reference year beside any number reused elsewhere. The four charts show how outcomes differ across groups and time while preserving what the evidence cannot identify about an individual household.

documents.title: A disability prevalence statistic is not your future income-loss probability
documents.description: Read official age-group estimates with their published confidence intervals, distinguish percentage points from percent changes, and explore how an invented age mix changes an aggregate.
documents.body: A survey’s population, definition and reference year belong beside the percentage. Use disability prevalence as context, then build an income-interruption cash plan from separate evidence. Ask what the percentage actually measures A statement that 27.0% of a covered population had a disability in 2022 does not mean that a currently employed person has a 27.0% chance of losing all income next year. Those statements have different outcomes, populations and time periods. Substituting one for the other can make a precise-looking financial projection answer the wrong question. Statistics Canada’s Table 1.1.A reports a 2022 disability prevalence estimate of 27.0% for its total aged-15+ population, compared with 22.3% in 2017. This guide uses selected all-gender age-group rows from that dated table. It is not a release of new 2026 observations, an insurance-claims dataset or a measure of the probability of a future earnings interruption. The first chart retains both survey years and the source’s published uncertainty. The later interactive example asks a separate arithmetic question about population composition. Its controls do not change the historical estimates. Keep the survey definition and coverage beside the numbers The 2022 Concepts and Methods Guide describes activity limitations connected with a long-term condition or health-related problem. Its framework considers the interaction between functional limitations and environmental barriers. That is a broader subject than a particular insurance contract’s definition of a payable claim. The methods guide describes coverage of people in private dwellings and exclusions including institutional and other collective dwellings, as well as First Nation reserves. Its sample frame was linked to the 2021 Census, with the stated age eligibility based on that census date. A headline label such as “Canadians” should not erase those coverage details. For a planning decision, the event needs its own definition: reduced hours, no earnings, additional support costs or a particular benefit becoming payable. A prevalence measure alone does not specify which of those events occurs, its start date, its duration or the money received during it. An age-group comparison is not an individual lifetime path The selected 2022 estimates are 20.1% for ages 15–24, 24.1% for ages 25–64 and 40.4% for ages 65+. The denominators differ by age group. These rows cannot be added together, and an unweighted average would assign each group equal population weight whether or not that matches the population being discussed. A comparison between people aged 25–64 and those aged 65+ also does not follow the same people into retirement. It does not reveal how many people newly developed a limitation during a year, how long it lasted or whether it interrupted paid work. Those transition questions require information beyond the displayed prevalence estimates. The 2024 analytical profile examines demographics, employment and income as distinct dimensions. Its scope is a reminder to keep the measured condition separate from a financial consequence that a household may need to model. Read the interval as uncertainty about the survey estimate The table gives the 2022 ages-25–64 estimate as 24.1%, with a published 95% confidence interval from 23.7% to 24.5%. For ages 65+, it gives 40.4%, with bounds of 39.6% and 41.3%. The whiskers preserve those asymmetric limits rather than replacing them with visually convenient equal margins. The survey’s data-quality chapter describes a complex sample design and bootstrap-based estimation of sampling error. This website copies the published intervals. It does not recalculate them as if every plotted percentage came from a simple unweighted sample with a known denominator. These intervals concern survey estimation uncertainty. They are not a range of outcomes for one person’s future health or income. They also do not make coverage exclusions or other non-sampling errors disappear. Testing a difference requires the appropriate comparison evidence; it cannot be replaced with a visual judgment about whether two separate intervals overlap. A percentage-point change and a percentage increase use different arithmetic For ages 15–24, the published levels rise from 13.1% to 20.1%. Subtracting them gives an increase of 7.0 percentage points . Dividing that 7.0-point difference by the starting 13.1% gives a relative increase of about 53.44% . Both describe the same two published levels, with different scales and denominators. Neither result is a yearly probability of developing a disability. The five-year gap between survey dates is not permission to divide a prevalence change by five and label it an annual incidence rate. The displayed age-group populations can change between surveys, and prevalence combines more than the arrival of new cases. The change chart therefore uses an explicit percentage-point unit. Statistics Canada flags the three selected age-group year comparisons as significantly different at p < 0.05 in this table. No confidence interval for each difference is supplied here, and none is manufactured by subtracting the separate estimate bounds. Change the population mix while holding subgroup estimates fixed The interactive illustration contains only two groups: ages 25–64 and ages 65+. It is an invented ages-25+ population, excluding youth. The subgroup estimates remain fixed at the published 2022 values of 24.1% and 40.4%. Only the population weights change. Population A assigns an invented 20% weight to ages 65+ and 80% to ages 25–64. Its weighted aggregate is 80% × 24.1% + 20% × 40.4% = 27.36% . Population B uses a 40% older share and a 60% working-age share, giving 30.62% . The 3.26-point difference arises entirely from the chosen weights while both subgroup estimates remain unchanged. These are not observed Canadian age shares, a reconstruction of the national aged-15+ result or an official age-standardization calculation. Nor do they decompose the actual change from 2017 to 2022. The contribution bars explain a weighted mean; the sensitivity line shows every invented older share from zero to 100%. No aggregate confidence interval is inferred by averaging subgroup bounds. Translate a defined income interruption into cash separately A household cash stress needs amounts and dates. For example, assume essential spending of CAD 4,000 a month, other continuing net receipts of CAD 1,500, and three months before any additional receipt is available. The conditional funding need is CAD 2,500 a month, or CAD 7,500 over that assumed window, before considering the starting reserve. That calculation describes the cash consequence if the assumed interruption occurs. The survey prevalence percentages do not supply its event probability, establish benefit eligibility or identify the payment date. A complete plan needs the household’s actual budget, accessible funds and applicable benefit or contract details. Record the statistic’s population, definition and reference date. Keep prevalence, new-event incidence and a future transition probability distinct. Inspect subgroup weights and published uncertainty before interpreting an aggregate. Define the household event and its cash consequences using separate evidence. The related waiting-period and joint-income tools provide separate hypothetical cash scenarios. They do not convert this survey extract into a personal probability estimate.

documents.title: Capital gains: compare annual sales with a final sale using after-tax values
documents.description: Explore two invented realization schedules with the same starting capital, price appreciation and assumed tax on gains, then reconcile gross growth, tax payments and final spendable resources.
documents.body: The date tax leaves an investment can affect later compounding. Compare both cases after their remaining gain tax, and distinguish a larger tax bill from a smaller after-tax outcome. Begin with the same capital and an explicitly limited return assumption A tax-timing comparison can be distorted if one investment is shown before tax while another has already paid it. Start with the same resources, use consistent return assumptions and identify any tax still embedded in the ending market value before comparing the two outcomes. This example places CAD 100,000 in each of two non-registered capital-appreciation scenarios. Opening adjusted cost base is also CAD 100,000. There are no new contributions, distributions, withdrawals for spending, fees or losses. Both holdings receive the same constant 5% annual price appreciation. The independently selected tax assumption is 25% of each full dollar of realized gain. It is not a capital-gains inclusion rate or a personal marginal tax rate. The calculator neither combines those two concepts nor estimates a household’s actual tax. The assumption remains identical in both cases throughout the illustration. Follow tax paid from each annual sale before reinvesting The first case sells all its holdings at every year-end. It calculates that year’s gain relative to its current cost base, pays the assumed tax immediately from sale proceeds and reinvests the remainder. That reinvested amount becomes the new cost base for the following year. In year one, CAD 100,000 grows to CAD 105,000. The CAD 5,000 gain produces CAD 1,250 of modeled tax, leaving CAD 103,750 invested. No extra household money pays that tax outside the scenario. Year two therefore earns 5% on CAD 103,750, rather than on CAD 105,000. Its gain is CAD 5,187.50 and modeled tax is CAD 1,296.875 before rounding. The process continues for the selected horizon, with calculations retaining full precision. At the default ten years, the annual-sale case ends with approximately CAD 144,504.39 after all its modeled gain taxes. The tax-payment dates are an arithmetic convention, rather than actual withholding or filing deadlines. Deduct the accumulated gain tax from the final-sale case The other case makes no intervening sale and receives no distribution or other taxable event under the stated assumptions. Its cost base remains CAD 100,000. Market value compounds at the full selected price-appreciation rate until the final sale. After ten years, that market value is CAD 100,000 × 1.05 to the tenth power, or approximately CAD 162,889.46. Its remaining gain is CAD 62,889.46. Applying the same 25% assumption produces CAD 15,722.37 of modeled tax at liquidation. The after-tax endpoint is approximately CAD 147,167.10, rather than the entire CAD 162,889.46 market value. It exceeds the annual-sale endpoint by about CAD 2,662.70 under these specific assumptions. The waterfall taxes the gain, not the original capital. It adds gross appreciation to the initial cost and subtracts the modeled final tax once. The original principal is not subjected to that gain-tax fraction a second time. Explain why the larger tax payment does not reverse this comparison The annual-sale case earns approximately CAD 59,339.19 of cumulative gross appreciation on its changing invested balance. It pays approximately CAD 14,834.80 of modeled tax and retains CAD 44,504.39 of net growth. The final-sale case earns more gross appreciation because its earlier gains remain invested without the intervening tax outflows. Its CAD 62,889.46 gross increase produces the larger CAD 15,722.37 tax payment, while still leaving the larger after-tax endpoint. The grouped bars keep each case’s own gross growth, tax and net increase together. Within a row, net increase equals gross appreciation less modeled tax. Those three bars should not be added as separate sources of wealth. Comparing only cumulative tax dollars would miss the additional growth. Comparing only gross market values would miss the remaining liability. Tax also occurs at different dates, so a simple total of payments is not a present-value measure of their cost. Read intermediate liquidation values as valuations rather than repeated sales The line chart shows the annual-sale balance, the final-sale case’s gross market balance and that same final-sale case’s hypothetical after-tax liquidation value at each completed year. The last line asks what would remain if that position were sold at the indicated year. It does not pay all those intermediate hypothetical tax amounts and then pay them again at the selected finish. There is only one final sale in that scenario. The matrix changes the holding horizon and the tax fraction for both cases together, while keeping initial capital and appreciation selected. One year produces no timing difference because both cases sell at the same date. A zero tax assumption or zero appreciation also removes the modeled advantage. The cells do not assign probabilities to returns or identify a future tax rate. A longer horizon magnifies the effect of constant compounding in the illustration, while real returns, laws, cash needs and portfolio choices can change during that time. Keep actual taxable events and investment decisions outside the shortcut The CRA’s Capital Gains guide explains that a gain or loss usually arises when capital property is sold or considered sold. This article does not model deemed dispositions, reserves, exemptions or other special treatment. It uses the general gain concept with original hypothetical tax inputs. Holding a fund without selling its units does not establish that every return can remain untaxed until a final sale. The CRA’s mutual-fund guidance discusses distributions while a holding is owned, including reinvested amounts. Those events and their cost-base adjustments are deliberately absent here. Reconcile actual income categories, transactions, cost records and payment dates before estimating a real after-tax goal amount. Investment suitability, diversification, fees and the need to sell can matter independently of this timing effect. The comparison isolates one mechanism; it does not determine whether postponing a particular sale is appropriate.

documents.title: The investment is sold: when does its cash actually reach the bill-paying account?
documents.description: Use five charts to separate trade execution, settlement and bank receipt, then test whether a weekend or processing delay creates an earlier bill-payment gap.
documents.body: A sufficient eventual sale receipt can arrive too late for an earlier bill. Check the bank-receipt date as well as the trade and settlement dates. Start with the account that must pay the bill A portfolio can contain enough value to cover a purchase while the spending bank account lacks the cash on the bill’s due date. Before relying on a sale, separate an order submitted, a trade executed, settlement completed, withdrawal eligibility and usable cash received at the bank. The model begins with an assumed executed sale . It does not place an order, assume that a submitted limit order fills, or price the security. The proceeds input is a separately determined net receipt. Costs, tax earmarks and registered-account consequences require their own review; the linked sale-proceeds guide addresses a different part of that work. The financial-planning question here is narrower: does the money reach the account that must pay this one bill in time? A balance available to buy another security need not be available to withdraw to an external bank at the same moment. T+1 describes settlement, rather than external-bank arrival The Canadian Securities Administrators announced Canada’s shorter settlement cycle effective 27 May 2024 . The Canadian Capital Markets Association’s implementation release describes the one-business-day cycle and includes ordinary exchange-traded securities such as ETFs. This is context for an ordinary secondary-market Canadian-listed stock or ETF sale subject to the applicable regular T+1 terms. It does not establish the timetable for every mutual fund redemption, cross-border trade, new issue, special settlement arrangement or foreign-currency transaction. T is the executed trade date. In a one-business-day example, settlement counts the next open business day after it, rather than simply adding 24 hours. Friday can therefore settle on Monday when the intervening weekend is closed. Real securities and banking calendars may differ and can contain holidays, cutoffs or other restrictions. The control’s default settlement count is one. Increasing that count is an assumed operational stress for this calendar, not a choice of an alternative regular settlement rule for the same actual trade. Confirm the executed trade’s settlement date from the actual transaction record. Keep the post-settlement wait as a separate assumption Wealthsimple’s sale guidance distinguishes cash balance, available-to-trade funds and available-to-withdraw funds. Its withdrawal guidance describes separate processing considerations and reasons balances can differ. Those are first-party explanations for that broker, not a service promise for every account. The second delay is therefore labeled assumed post-settlement wait until bank receipt . It can represent separately checked availability restrictions, broker processing and transfer transit. The tool does not infer withdrawal eligibility from settlement or quote an actual transfer service. A zero wait means the illustration assumes usable bank cash on the settlement day. It does not mean any provider promises such a service. For a real payment, verify the actual account’s holds, available balance, request cutoff, transfer method and receiving-bank usability. Read a fictional calendar before counting its days Day 1 is a fictional Monday. Days 6 and 7 are the first weekend; Days 13 and 14 are the second. The first-week trade choices are Monday through Friday, so the assumed execution is always on an open model day. The closure control can add zero to three fictional closed weekdays beginning on Day 8, the second Monday. One extra closure closes only Day 8; two close Days 8 and 9. These are invented operational sensitivities, not actual 2026 holidays. A single shared calendar is used for settlement and bank processing to make the arithmetic inspectable. A positive wait excludes its starting day, then counts only subsequent open model days. A zero post-settlement wait returns the settlement day. The separate calendar matrix marks open days as 1 and closed days as 0, so a weekend is not silently counted as a processing day. The bill occurs on its entered calendar day even if that day is closed. Within a day, assumed bank receipts arrive before the bill. Those are explicit teaching conventions; actual bill debit rules and posting order must be checked rather than inferred from a day-end balance. The same endpoint can hide a CAD 3,000 earlier gap The default bank balance is CAD 1,000. The assumed net sale proceeds are CAD 5,000, and a CAD 4,000 bill is due on Day 10. The executed sale is Friday, Day 5. With one settlement business day and two further business days until bank receipt, settlement is Monday, Day 8 and receipt is Wednesday, Day 10. Under receipt-before-bill posting, bank cash first becomes CAD 6,000 on Day 10, then falls to CAD 2,000 after the bill. No additional opening cash is needed for this one obligation. Add one fictional Day-8 closure. Settlement moves to Tuesday, Day 9 and bank receipt to Thursday, Day 11. Only CAD 1,000 is available for the CAD 4,000 bill on Day 10, leaving an unfunded CAD 3,000 position. Receipt on Day 11 restores the scheduled ledger to CAD 2,000, but it cannot fund the prior day retroactively. Both cases end with the same arithmetic: 1,000 + 5,000 − 4,000 = 2,000. The earlier funding requirement differs. A negative line segment records that missing resource; it is not an approved overdraft, an instruction to pay an unfunded bill or a prediction that a bank will allow the transaction. Do not count the same sale proceeds in three places After execution and before settlement, the illustration classifies the proceeds as an unsettled receivable. After settlement and before bank receipt, it places them in one off-bank processing category. At bank receipt, that same amount becomes the received bank component. The stage chart shows successive snapshots of this one receipt before allocating it to household spending. Its rows must not be added into a larger household balance. The middle category can include transfer transit; it does not claim the money remains withdrawable brokerage cash after a transfer debit. If settlement and bank receipt are on the same modeled day, the settled snapshot already shows bank receipt and the off-bank interval disappears. No additional receipt is created. The bank ledger, separately, deducts the bill once. Selling an investment changes the form of existing assets. Transferring the proceeds between accounts changes their location. Neither operation creates the sale amount as new earned income. This tool tracks a receipt’s timing without reconstructing the unsold security’s value or the household’s total net worth. Keep an arrival beyond Day 14 outside the ledger The charts display fourteen calendar days, but the calendar continues counting when processing lasts longer. With the default Friday trade, one Day-8 closure and six post-settlement business days, receipt is Day 17. It is not moved backward to Day 14 to make the diagram balance. In that case, Day-14 scheduled bank cash remains negative CAD 3,000 and the entered CAD 5,000 receipt is still off bank. An eventual endpoint after receipt would answer a different horizon. Read the arrival-day metric and pending-receipt note with the bank ledger. The sensitivity matrix changes the trade weekday and post-settlement wait while keeping the bill, opening cash, proceeds and selected calendar assumptions fixed. Each cell is an independent scenario, with no probability assigned. The weekday comparison separately contrasts weekends only with exactly one fictional Day-8 closure. Turn a confirmed bank receipt into the spending plan Confirm that the sale executed and read its actual settlement terms. Check withdrawable cash and any account-specific eligibility, holds or restrictions. Verify the request cutoff, transfer route and receiving-bank availability. Determine net spendable proceeds and any tax reserve separately. Match the confirmed usable-cash date with the bill’s debit date and posting order. This is a partial one-bill cash exercise. Other payments, income, emergencies, tax, exchange rates and changes in investment value are omitted. For a real household calendar, add the confirmed receipts and obligations rather than treating this illustration as a complete liquidity assessment.

Each cell is a separate timing scenario with no assigned probability. Receipt-before-bill posting applies if both fall on the same day.

documents.title: Cash now or payments later: compare present value without losing the receipt calendar
documents.description: Compare an immediate lump sum with a finite annual payment stream, discount each receipt to the same date, and distinguish eventual totals from the cash available for current bills.
documents.body: An eventual payment total, its present value and the amount available today answer different questions. Keep all three beside the actual receipt dates. Write down the receipts before choosing a valuation method Suppose a household can receive CAD 50,000 immediately or CAD 12,000 once a year for five years, with the first payment one year from now. The second option totals CAD 60,000. That larger numeral alone does not tell us whether it is more valuable today or whether it can meet a bill due next month. The alternatives have different dates as well as different totals. An immediate receipt can be assigned to a current need. A future receipt is assumed to arrive only on its stated date. This guide keeps a cash calendar beside a present-value comparison so the valuation does not erase that distinction. The tool assumes that the alternatives are mutually exclusive and every scheduled payment is made in full. Enter amounts on the same spendable basis. It does not estimate taxes, establish a right to choose a different payment form, or value a life-contingent pension. A real contract must first identify what is payable, when it is payable and under what conditions. Convert each payment to the same date exactly once The OpenStax discussion of annuities explains how a stream of fixed payments can be valued by discounting each receipt. Its cash-flow timing chapter also shows why a dated timeline matters when amounts occur in different periods. This guide applies that method to an independently authored example. A payment due in year t has a time-zero value of payment ÷ (1 + effective annual discount rate) t . The immediate amount is already at time zero, so it is not discounted for another year. A payment received now likewise has an exponent of zero. The selected discount rate is a valuation assumption. It does not guarantee that the household can earn that rate, and it does not automatically incorporate tax, default risk or inflation. Choosing a rate appropriate to an actual decision needs a separate assessment of its cash flows and alternatives; this illustration does not supply a market quote. Keep the analytical discount rate separate from a price-year conversion. Expressing a future receipt in constant purchasing power requires a specified inflation path. Comparing its value with an alternative use of money requires a consistent valuation assumption. If amounts have already been converted to constant-price dollars, applying a rate on a different price basis can combine inconsistent units. This tool uses payment-year dollars, a discount rate on that basis and no second inflation conversion. Explain the default result through individual discounted receipts At a hypothetical 5% effective annual discount rate, the first CAD 12,000 payment has a present value of approximately CAD 11,428.57. The fifth payment has a present value of approximately CAD 9,402.31 because its receipt is five years away. Adding all five discounted payments produces about CAD 51,953.72. Subtracting the immediate CAD 50,000 alternative leaves a positive valuation difference of about CAD 1,953.72. The waterfall shows each discounted payment and the final subtraction, so the result can be traced without treating the entire CAD 60,000 as money received today. This is an arithmetic comparison under the stated assumptions. It does not create CAD 51,953.72 of accessible cash, nor does it establish that borrowing against future receipts would be available or inexpensive. Discounting a payment to time zero and then deducting an additional generic “waiting cost” would also count the same selected time-value assumption twice unless that cost represents a separate identified cash flow. Keep the cumulative receipt line separate from an investment account The cumulative chart begins with CAD 50,000 received under the upfront alternative and zero received under the default delayed alternative. The latter rises by CAD 12,000 at each annual receipt. It reaches CAD 60,000 after the fifth payment. No return is earned in that chart. The upfront line stays at CAD 50,000 because it records total receipts, rather than a growing investment. Spending is also absent, so neither line is a forecast of the bank balance remaining after bills. A household that spends an immediate receipt will not still own all of it simply because its cumulative-receipts line stays level. A larger eventual receipt total can coexist with a lower present value. At an 8% discount rate, the same five payments are worth about CAD 47,912.52 today, below the CAD 50,000 alternative. The receipt dates and total have not changed; the analytical rate used to compare them has. The matrix makes that sensitivity visible. Shift the whole payment calendar instead of adding an unexplained adjustment The first-payment control can move the equal stream while retaining its size and count. With five payments starting in year zero, the dates are zero through four. Starting in year one gives dates one through five. Starting in year three gives dates three through seven. At 5%, moving the default stream two years later reduces its present value from CAD 51,953.72 to about CAD 47,123.56. This equals the original present value divided by 1.05 squared. The undiscounted total remains CAD 60,000 because no payment has been removed or reduced. At a zero discount rate, the model values every dated dollar equally, so the timing rows show the same difference for a given total. That does not eliminate a household’s need for cash before a payment arrives. It shows the consequence of using zero as the analytical rate. The schedule still identifies those earlier periods without receipts. Check the current spending need and payment conditions separately A household may prefer a regular receipt pattern for budgeting, or need more money immediately for a known obligation. Those practical needs should be specified directly. They are not automatically settled by the sign of a present-value difference. For example, a CAD 15,000 bill due now cannot be paid from the first default installment one year later. Funding that bill from existing savings changes how much of those savings remains for other needs. Borrowing instead introduces its own proceeds, interest and repayment dates. Neither action is assumed in this receipt-only comparison. Before applying the method to an actual offer, check payment certainty, gross versus net amounts, fees, any indexing, transfer restrictions and the consequences of a recipient’s death. A finite stream assumed fully payable differs from a payment that depends on continued survival or another condition. Record those terms alongside the timeline, then value the resulting cash flows on a consistent date. The charts explain the method while leaving those contract-specific facts to the actual evidence.
