documents.title: Your hourly quote applies to billable hours: plan for the rest of the working year
documents.description: Four interactive charts turn leave, downtime, unpaid work and business costs into an annual pre-tax cash budget and a conditional hourly-rate requirement.
documents.body: A quoted hourly rate becomes annual cash only through hours you can sell and collect. Budget unpaid work and fixed costs before treating the quote as a household income rate. Separate the work relationship from the pricing arithmetic An hourly quote is a unit price, not a promise of forty paid hours every week. Before building a household budget around it, establish how many hours can produce collected fees and what those fees must fund. Worker status is a separate question. The CRA’s Employee or Self-employed guide says the facts of the working relationship as a whole decide employment status. A chosen contract label or a favourable calculator result does not settle it. The guide also explains the option of requesting a CPP/EI ruling when status is uncertain. This tool assumes an independently established sole-operator business arrangement. It performs annual capacity and cash-allocation arithmetic. It does not determine employment status, statutory contributions, labour-law rights, tax deductions or the value of an actual employee benefit. Build the time budget before multiplying by the hourly rate The example uses a simple fifty-two-week template, with forty hours assigned to each available workweek. Five weeks are reserved for leave and four other weeks for downtime. These categories are assumed not to overlap, leaving forty-three working weeks. That produces 1,720 working hours. A quarter of them, or 430 hours, is assigned to work that cannot be billed: for example, administration, business development or maintaining systems. The remaining 1,290 hours are the billable capacity used by the model. The time chart also shows 360 hours of no-work capacity. That is nine unavailable weeks multiplied by the forty-hour template; those hours are not actually worked. Billable hours, unpaid working hours and no-work capacity together reconcile to the template’s 2,080 hours. All 1,290 billable hours are assumed to find buyers and be collected in the same year. This is a strong assumption. Time available to sell a service does not establish demand, and an invoice does not establish collection. Use the separate invoice-cash guide to test when money reaches the bank. Follow collected fees through the costs they must cover At CAD 100 per billable hour, the selected capacity generates CAD 129,000 of collected fees, excluding sales tax. Variable business cash costs take 8%, or CAD 10,320. Annual fixed business cash costs take another CAD 12,000, leaving CAD 106,680 before a separate personal allocation. The example then assigns CAD 12,000 to a personal provision. This might represent a separately budgeted amount for protection or saving, but the tool gives it no automatic tax treatment and assumes no equivalence with employer benefits. Counting it as a cash allocation keeps it from being spent again elsewhere. After that provision, CAD 94,680 remains before personal income tax, CPP/QPP, EI and other personal liabilities. It is not take-home pay. It includes the cash available to reward the owner’s work and bear business risk; no separate owner wage has been deducted. BDC’s pricing overview explains the need to account for costs and overhead when examining a break-even point. The waterfall here uses a deliberately simple cash structure, rather than reproducing a formal cost-of-sales statement or claiming that every entered expense is deductible. Solve for a rate only after stating the annual target The target input asks for annual cash remaining after the entered business costs and personal provision, but before personal tax. Its default is CAD 80,000. This target is separate from the CAD 12,000 provision, so the model does not quietly count that allocation twice. To solve for the rate, add the target, fixed business costs and provision. Divide their CAD 104,000 total by the billable hours multiplied by the 92% left after variable costs. The required rate is approximately CAD 87.63 per billable hour under these assumptions. The line chart varies the quote and shows where annual remaining cash meets the target. A crossing above the displayed range can still produce a numeric required rate. That calculation does not make the price commercially attainable or prove that the assumed number of hours will sell. When there are no billable hours, the tool reports that no billable hours are available rather than dividing by zero. Fixed cash costs and the chosen provision remain in the budget. They do not disappear merely because all working time becomes unpaid or every week is unavailable. Use the sensitivity grid to choose what needs better evidence The matrix changes the quote and the unpaid share together. A larger unpaid share leaves fewer hours producing fees while fixed costs continue. A higher quote raises modeled revenue only because the grid holds sold hours unchanged. It does not model customers buying fewer hours at a higher price. Before relying on a cell, check recent time records, confirmed bookings, cancellation terms, collection experience and the costs that continue during downtime. Keep leave and other unavailable weeks distinct so the same week is not removed twice. For household planning, add a separate assessment of personal tax, statutory contributions, protection needs and the timing of withdrawals. A full year’s positive result may still coexist with an early cash shortage. The useful output is a documented capacity budget and a set of assumptions to verify, not a salary comparison or an instruction to charge a particular rate.

documents.title: Budgeting for a repair: compare expected cost with the cash reserve needed
documents.description: Four charts compare two hypothetical repair outcomes, the probability needed for equal expected cost, and the cash still required when a repair occurs.
documents.body: A probability-weighted average helps compare modeled cost. It does not tell you whether one household can pay the actual repair bill, or whether a real contract will cover it. Define the comparison period and the repair before assigning a probability An extended warranty or repair service contract can exchange a known upfront payment for help with certain future repair costs. Whether a quoted contract addresses a household’s risk depends on its actual terms, existing coverage and the cost of paying directly. The Office of Consumer Affairs recommends checking the period, parts, service, repair arrangements and additional costs, and considering repair costs and possible overlapping coverage. Those questions establish the contract being compared. They do not supply a failure rate for a particular appliance or vehicle. This guide uses one fixed comparison period with only two possible outcomes: no eligible repair, or one eligible repair costing CAD 800. The original assumed probability of that repair is 20% over the entire period. It is not an annual probability, a measured product statistic or an estimate based on an actual claims file. The hypothetical contract costs CAD 180 upfront and leaves CAD 100 of the modeled repair for the household to pay. It accepts the claim and directly pays the remaining CAD 700. These generous simplifying conditions must be visible before interpreting any saving. Additional repairs, rejected claims, shipping, service delays, benefit limits and provider failure sit outside the model. Read the actual outcome costs before reading their average Without the contract, the modeled no-repair state costs zero and the repair state costs CAD 800. With the contract, the no-repair state costs CAD 180 because the fee has already been paid. The repair state costs CAD 280: the same CAD 180 fee plus CAD 100 out of pocket. The first grouped chart keeps both states visible. The provider’s assumed CAD 700 payment reduces the repair-state burden, while the fee adds a cost to the no-repair state. Buying the contract changes the shape of the possible household outlays, rather than simply removing every repair cost. The out-of-pocket input is capped at the repair amount. If the repair costs less than the stated deductible, the model makes the household pay the repair cost and assumes no covered amount. It never credits the household with a payment larger than the repair or treats unused deductible capacity as cash. All amounts are nominal and undiscounted. The original purchase price of the product is common to both choices and excluded. No borrowing, fee financing, cancellation refund or investment return is inserted. Actual differences in service quality, repair timing or replacement value require separate evidence. Calculate the probability-weighted cost without turning it into a guaranteed bill For this two-state example, expected direct-repair cost is probability × repair cost . At 20%, that is 0.20 × CAD 800 = CAD 160. Expected contract cost is upfront fee + probability × out-of-pocket repair amount , or CAD 180 + 0.20 × CAD 100 = CAD 200. The contract therefore has CAD 40 more expected cost under the original assumptions. That calculation does not mean every buyer loses CAD 40 or receives a CAD 200 invoice. One household pays either zero or CAD 800 directly; under the assumed contract it pays either CAD 180 or CAD 280. The line chart recalculates the expectation across alternative probabilities for the same period. It is an arithmetic sensitivity analysis, not a forecast curve. The selected probability determines the current metric, while the full line shows what different assumptions would imply. An average cost cannot resolve a household’s ability or willingness to absorb a large payment. Expected cost, available reserves, the practical value of a service and exposure to unmodeled contract problems answer different questions. The St. Louis Fed’s consumer-education discussion similarly separates risk preferences, potential repair savings and the costs or limitations of service contracts; its older survey figures are not used here. Use the equality threshold to identify the assumption doing the work When the contract covers a positive part of the repair, equal expected costs occur at fee ÷ (repair cost − out-of-pocket amount) . In the original example, CAD 180 ÷ CAD 700 is approximately 25.71%. At that probability, both expected costs are approximately CAD 205.71. Below it, paying directly has the lower modeled expectation; above it, the contract does. Equality at one point is not evidence that the actual probability is near that point or that either option is suitable. A fee larger than the maximum modeled covered repair amount produces no equality within 0–100%. If the contract pays none of the repair, it cannot reduce expected repair costs in this model; a positive fee only adds expense. With no fee and no covered amount, the two choices are equal for every probability. The matrix varies the repair cost as well as its assumed chance. It holds the selected fee and deductible constant. A repair amount below the deductible leaves no covered portion, while a more expensive eligible repair can change the comparison sharply. The matrix therefore helps locate which severity and probability assumptions support a result, without assigning confidence to any cell. Test the full repair-state cash requirement against the same reserve The original household has CAD 500 available before any contract fee is paid. With no repair, paying directly leaves CAD 500 and the contract leaves CAD 320. If the modeled repair occurs, direct payment requires CAD 800 and leaves a CAD 300 funding gap. The contract’s total CAD 280 outlay leaves CAD 220. The final signed chart displays the reserve less each state’s complete outlay. A negative amount is money still needed, not an assumed overdraft or an available loan. If the upfront fee alone exceeds the reserve, even the no-repair contract state has an initial funding problem. Changing the probability changes expected cost but not the cash required in a specified repair state. Likewise, increasing the reserve improves payment capacity without changing the contract’s expected cost difference. Keeping those controls independent prevents a larger cash balance from being mistaken for better coverage or a lower failure rate. The contract assumes direct settlement of the covered amount. If an actual provider reimburses later, the household may need the full repair bill first. This model also contains no later deposits, so it does not assess how a reserve could be rebuilt over a multi-year coverage period. Replace the two-state example with the facts of the actual decision Before using the comparison, verify what already protects the product, the dates of that protection and whether extra coverage overlaps it. Read the covered parts, excluded causes, required maintenance, approval steps, service locations, claim limits and the amount payable per visit or repair. The Office of Consumer Affairs advises checking whether shipping and service costs are included and whether card-provided protection already applies. These are questions for the actual terms; this article does not determine anyone’s legal entitlement or cancelation rights. Use an independently supported repair estimate and a probability definition matched to the same product, condition, use and period. If there is no reliable probability evidence, retain several clearly labeled scenarios instead of presenting one assumption as a measured rate. More than one potential failure, varying repair severity or a coverage cap requires a richer outcome model. The four charts help separate cost, uncertainty and liquidity. They do not value peace of mind, guarantee claim acceptance or identify the best provider. A useful decision record states the coverage being compared, the modeled outcomes, the assumption driving the cost threshold and the cash available if the less convenient outcome occurs.

documents.title: CAD 20,000 now or CAD 24,000 later? Compare the date before comparing the dollars
documents.description: Use a discount-rate curve, common-date value bars, a present-value waterfall and a rate-and-wait matrix to examine an immediate versus deferred lump sum.
documents.body: A larger later payment is not directly comparable with cash today. Put both alternatives on one date, show the implied annual rate, and separately check payment reliability and access. Write two alternatives, rather than one combined balance The example offers one of two receipts: CAD 20,000 today or a single CAD 24,000 payment in three years. Receiving one means giving up the other. Adding them into CAD 44,000 of household resources would count an alternative that was never available alongside the first. The nominal difference is CAD 4,000, or 20% of the immediate amount. That 20% covers the entire three-year wait. It is not a 20% annual return. The dates are part of the comparison, just as surely as the amounts. The CFA Institute’s public time-value overview connects current values, future cash flows and implied returns. Here, the calculator applies those principles to a simple original example with one payment under each alternative. Convert the later receipt into a value measured today Let L be the later payment, r the effective annual comparison rate as a fraction, and n the number of years. The present value is PV = L ÷ (1+r) n . This discounts the later amount over the actual waiting period. At the default 5% comparison rate, CAD 24,000 divided by 1.05³ equals approximately CAD 20,732.10 . Compared with CAD 20,000 today, the present-value difference is about CAD 732.10 in favour of the later receipt under the stated assumptions. That value is not a deposit already held in an account. It is today’s equivalent on the selected valuation basis. A household cannot send CAD 20,732.10 to pay an earlier bill merely because the calculator displays that present value. A discount-rate curve shows which assumption changes the answer The first chart recalculates the later receipt’s present value at rates from 0% to 20%. The immediate CAD 20,000 remains a horizontal comparison. At a zero rate, the later receipt has a present value equal to its CAD 24,000 nominal amount. As the rate rises, its present value falls. The crossing is useful because it identifies the rate at which the two valuations are equal. Below that rate, the later receipt has the greater present value. Above it, the immediate cash has the greater present value. Those statements hold for these fixed amounts and dates with full payment assumed. The selected rate needs a reason. It might represent an independently assessed opportunity cost on a consistent cash basis, but the calculator does not identify an available deposit, achievable investment return or appropriate risk premium. An uncertain investment forecast cannot be turned into a guaranteed alternative simply by entering its average return here. Moving both alternatives forward gives the same ordering The common-date bars perform the comparison at the end of year three instead of today. Compounding CAD 20,000 at 5% for three years gives CAD 23,152.50 . The alternative later receipt is CAD 24,000, leaving a future-date difference of CAD 847.50 . The present-date difference was CAD 732.10, not CAD 847.50. The two figures use different dates. Multiplying the unrounded present-value difference by 1.05³ converts it into the future-date difference. It does not create an extra source of profit. The bars assume the immediate receipt remains invested at the entered constant rate with no withdrawals. If the cash is used for living costs, the resulting future balance will differ. Actual spending may meet a real need, but it cannot simultaneously remain available to compound toward the later comparison. Solve for the annual rate instead of dividing 20% by three The break-even annual rate solves cash now × (1+r*) n = later cash . Rearranging gives r* = (later cash ÷ cash now) 1/n − 1 . For CAD 20,000 and CAD 24,000 three years later, the result is approximately 6.26586% effective annually . Compounding at that rate for three years produces the full 20% cumulative increase. Dividing 20% by three gives a simple average of about 6.67%, which does not preserve the compounding equation. The rate is implied by the two offered amounts and their timing. It is not a separately earned coupon or an assurance that anyone will pay it. The California Board of Equalization’s time-value summary explains compounding and discounting as opposite movements between dates. This example uses annual effective compounding consistently in both directions. Keep the future amount fixed when testing a longer delay The matrix changes the waiting time and the comparison rate while retaining the same two receipt amounts. Every cell reports the later receipt’s present value minus the cash-now alternative. A longer wait does not automatically earn a larger payment in this exercise. At a positive rate, postponing the same future amount reduces its present value. At a zero rate, changing the wait leaves the present-value amount unchanged, although the actual availability date still moves. This separates the valuation calculation from the practical need to use money before it arrives. The matrix has no probabilities attached to its cells. It does not forecast which date or rate will occur. It helps reveal whether a conclusion depends strongly on a short delay or a particular valuation rate. A break-even rate can sit outside the plotted range If the two nominal amounts are identical, their implied break-even rate is zero. If the later amount is smaller than the immediate amount, the implied rate is negative. A nonnegative comparison rate will then favour the immediate amount on this narrow valuation basis. A very large later amount over a short period can imply a break-even rate above the graph’s 20% ceiling. The metric still reports the calculated rate, while the chart shows only its stated 0% to 20% range. No crossing inside the visible graph should be invented. These mathematical controls help interpret the output without treating an unusual implied rate as evidence that a high-return product exists. The legal terms, payment source and reliability of an actual offer require their own evidence. Bring the valuation back to the household’s required dates A bill due in six months cannot be paid directly by a receipt arriving in three years. A positive present-value difference does not supply a bridge loan, change the bill’s due date or make the later promise transferable. The calculator includes none of those arrangements. Compare the actual net receipts on the same tax and cost basis. The model does not calculate tax, fees, inflation or default losses. It also does not convert nominal future cash into inflation-adjusted purchasing power; adding such a comparison would require a consistent real-cash and real-rate calculation. Confirm which receipts are mutually exclusive and when each is usable. Put their amounts on a consistent net-cash basis. Document the reason for the comparison rate. Check both present-date and common future-date values. Review payment reliability and earlier cash obligations separately. The result is a transparent valuation comparison. The choice still has to support the actual payment calendar and the terms of the available alternatives.

documents.title: A TFSA investment loss changes your wealth, not your unused contribution room
documents.description: Use four graphics to separate investment value, cash withdrawn and the ordinary withdrawal amount added back as room in the next calendar year.
documents.body: A loss inside a TFSA is not a withdrawal. A later ordinary withdrawal adds back the amount actually withdrawn next year, rather than automatically restoring the original contribution. Keep value, cash movements and contribution room in separate records A TFSA can have one account value and a different amount of unused contribution room. An investment loss changes the value of what is held. A withdrawal moves money out. The room record follows the applicable contribution and withdrawal rules, rather than simply mirroring the account balance. CRA’s contribution guidance states that investment-value changes do not affect TFSA contribution room and that an investment loss does not count as a withdrawal. The loss itself is not added back as room. The tool begins just after one assumed lawful contribution. Its unused-room input is already reconciled across the holder’s TFSAs after that contribution. It does not establish eligibility or reconstruct anyone’s full contribution history. Follow the investment change before making any withdrawal The default opening contribution is CAD 10,000, assumed permitted using previously available room. A 20% investment decline reduces the account value by CAD 2,000 to CAD 8,000. No money has been withdrawn at this stage. The room amount entered after the opening contribution remains unchanged. With the default of zero unused room, the loss does not create a new CAD 2,000 deposit allowance. Replacing the lost value with new money would require room available for that contribution through the applicable record. The waterfall shows only the value arithmetic: CAD 10,000 minus CAD 2,000 equals CAD 8,000. It does not record the loss as a cash payment to the holder or a transaction that restores contribution capacity. Use the amount actually withdrawn for the next-year addback The default then withdraws 100% of the remaining CAD 8,000 as an ordinary withdrawal. Account value falls to zero and CAD 8,000 becomes cash held outside the TFSA. Under the reviewed ordinary-withdrawal framework, that CAD 8,000 is the amount added back as room on the next 1 January. CRA’s withdrawal guidance explains that an ordinary withdrawal does not create new room immediately. Re-contributing during the same calendar year requires sufficient unused room already available. The related calendar guide examines that timing constraint in more detail. The withdrawal-based addback in this example is CAD 2,000 below the original CAD 10,000 contribution. That comparison concerns this selected withdrawal only. It is not a complete next-year contribution limit, a required deposit or an estimate of how much the investment could later recover. Room returning does not restore money lost The stacked bars track financial resources separately from the room bars. Before the withdrawal, CAD 8,000 is inside the account. Afterward, CAD 8,000 is outside as retained cash. The total is unchanged by the withdrawal because the model assumes no fees or spending. On the next 1 January, the ordinary withdrawal affects the room record, but there is still only CAD 8,000 of financial resources in this illustration. Adding the room amount to the cash amount as though both were assets would count permission to contribute as money. Rebuilding wealth requires investment changes or additional saving. The model does not project a recovery or recommend keeping, selling or replacing an investment. Its purpose is to keep the value and room calculations from being confused. Test partial withdrawals and gains without changing the rule Change the withdrawal share to 50% while keeping the default 20% decline. The ordinary withdrawal is then CAD 4,000, with CAD 4,000 still in the TFSA. The withdrawal-based next-year addback is CAD 4,000, not the whole remaining account value and not the original contribution. Now try a 20% investment gain and a full ordinary withdrawal. The account reaches CAD 12,000, and the assumed withdrawal is CAD 12,000. The gain alone did not change room while it remained invested; the amount actually withdrawn is what enters this ordinary-withdrawal addback illustration. The matrix combines several value changes and withdrawal shares. Every cell holds the original contribution fixed and calculates the assumed withdrawal after the selected move. It contains neither a future annual dollar limit nor probabilities for market outcomes. Complete the room calculation with the actual record before contributing The room chart deliberately excludes the new calendar year’s annual dollar limit. It also excludes other contributions, withdrawals, transfers and adjustments. Its final bar is only a subtotal of carried unused room plus this one ordinary withdrawal. For example, entering CAD 3,000 of unused room after the original contribution would leave that amount unchanged by the market decline and the same-year withdrawal. Adding the default CAD 8,000 ordinary withdrawal next year produces a CAD 11,000 subtotal before the omitted annual limit and any other adjustments. CRA recommends reconciling contribution room using the holder’s own records. The model assumes Canadian residency and eligibility throughout, and it excludes specified distributions, transfer treatment, excess histories and other special situations. Use the applicable full record rather than an account value or this partial illustration before making a real contribution.

documents.title: An extended warranty has a certain price and a conditional benefit: chart both
documents.description: Use a three-state probability model, owner-cost bars, a cost bridge and sensitivity charts to separate repair risk, eligible claims and the cash a contract can save.
documents.body: Expected repair cost, a payable benefit and the cash needed in an actual failure are three different amounts. A contract price buys only the protection its terms actually add. Start with the protection window and the protection you already have A checkout offer can make an extended warranty sound like a simple comparison between a small price now and a large repair later. The useful comparison is more specific: which repair, during which period, under which conditions, and how much of that repair would this extra contract actually fund? The Government of Canada’s warranty guide distinguishes included manufacturer protection from extra-cost extended coverage and asks consumers to review terms, repair costs and possible credit-card overlap. A purchased contract should therefore be evaluated for its additional protection rather than credited with every repair benefit associated with owning the product. This tool uses one common comparison window and a deliberately simplified event structure. There is either no modeled repair, one eligible repair, or one excluded repair. A repair has the same entered cost in the two repair states. The product purchase price is common to both alternatives and excluded. Existing legal, manufacturer and card protection are outside the calculation; the example does not decide anyone’s rights or whether a claim meets a real contract. Separate the chance of a repair from the chance that a repair is eligible The default repair-event probability is an assumed 40% over the entire comparison window. The assumed eligible share is 70% of those repair events. Multiplying them gives a 28% eligible-event probability. The excluded-event probability is 40% × 30%, or 12%, and the no-repair probability is 60%. These are original teaching inputs, not a product failure study, a claim-approval statistic or an annual risk estimate. A different window, product age or definition of an eligible event would need its own evidence and assumptions. The model does not automatically convert a multi-year event probability into an annual rate. The first chart keeps the denominator visible. “70% eligible” refers to the repair branch, not to every product bought. Treating it as a 70% chance of receiving a payment would confuse a conditional share with the overall probability. Even an eligible event can produce a zero payment if the deductible absorbs the entire repair cost. Apply the deductible and payment cap before valuing the contract The example repair costs CAD 800. The owner deductible is CAD 50, leaving CAD 750 before the cap. The provider-payment cap is CAD 500, so the modeled payment is CAD 500, not CAD 750 and not the full CAD 800. The owner retains CAD 300 of repair cost even in the eligible state. The precise convention matters. This illustration defines the cap as a maximum provider payment after subtracting the deductible: payment = min(cap, max(0, repair cost − deductible)) . It does not model a policy that first caps eligible repair charges and then subtracts a deductible. Read an actual contract before using either interpretation. Raising the entered cap beyond CAD 750 cannot increase the default eligible payment because there is no more modeled eligible cost left to fund. Likewise, if the deductible reaches or exceeds the repair cost, the modeled payment becomes zero. A large number printed as a limit is not automatically a large economic benefit. Keep the upfront price in every outcome The contract costs CAD 180 at the start, with no refund in this illustration. If no repair occurs, the owner pays zero repair cost without the extra contract and CAD 180 with it. In the eligible repair state, the comparison is CAD 800 without the contract versus CAD 480 with it: CAD 180 plus the CAD 300 repair remainder. In the excluded repair state, the owner pays CAD 800 without the contract and CAD 980 with it. The extra contract has not removed that repair exposure, and its initial price has already been spent. These bars show total nominal owner cost over the comparison window, not an estimate of an average bill. They also do not show peak cash needed. A provider that reimburses later can leave the owner paying a larger invoice first. Repair timing, claims processing, downtime and shipping are excluded from the arithmetic. Those operational terms need a separate cash-access review even when a final payment is expected. Reconcile the expected cost without turning it into a reserve target Without the contract, expected repair cost is 40% × CAD 800, or CAD 320. The expected provider payment is 40% × 70% × CAD 500, or CAD 140. Expected owner cost with the contract is therefore CAD 180 + CAD 320 − CAD 140 = CAD 360, which is CAD 40 higher than the no-contract expected cost. The waterfall makes the certain price and the contingent payment separate steps. A CAD 140 expected provider payment does not mean the provider pays CAD 140 when a repair occurs. In this restricted model, it pays either zero or CAD 500. Likewise, setting aside CAD 320 does not fully fund the possible CAD 800 repair. Expected cost is one comparison, not a complete decision rule. A household may value reducing a particular cash exposure, convenience or service support, but those features need evidence in the actual offer. The tool places no dollar value on them and does not identify a contract that should be purchased. Read the crossover as an assumption threshold, not a reliability estimate Let W be the upfront contract price, p the whole-window repair probability, q the eligible share and P the provider payment in an eligible event. Expected extra owner cost is W − p × q × P . If qP is positive, cost equality occurs at p = W ÷ (qP) . At the defaults, CAD 180 ÷ (70% × CAD 500) gives about 51.43%. That threshold is above the selected 40% assumption. It does not show that the product’s actual repair probability is 51.43%, and it is not evidence for moving the probability input to make an offer look attractive. A threshold above 100% cannot be reached within this single-event model. If no provider payment is available, a positive contract price cannot be recovered through modeled payments at any event probability. A zero-price, zero-payment contract ties the repair-cost baseline at every probability. These boundary cases are stated explicitly beside the charts. Use the charts to ask better questions about the offer Define the comparison period and remove benefits already provided by other protection. Read the deductible, payment limit, eligible repairs and claim process in the actual terms. Keep the failure probability and conditional eligibility assumption separate. Compare the actual failure-state cash with the probability-weighted average. Test a lower eligible share and a smaller payment cap before interpreting the crossover. The matrix changes eligibility and the payment cap while holding the selected repair probability fixed. Its signed cells report extra expected owner cost, so a negative value means lower modeled cost with the contract. It is not a product rating or a probability forecast. Multiple repairs, replacement instead of repair, depreciation, financing and the opportunity cost of the upfront price require a fuller model.

documents.title: A GIC ladder can keep its principal while its interest income falls after renewal
documents.description: Four charts follow a hypothetical renewing five-rung ladder, separating interest receipts, rolled principal and the outside reserve needed when new rates differ.
documents.body: A maturity date gives a choice about principal. If that principal is reinvested, the same dollars are unavailable for spending, and the new interest income still depends on the renewal rate. Distinguish a guaranteed term from an unknown renewal rate A fixed rate for one deposit term does not specify the rate available when that term ends. A plan that intends to reinvest principal needs a separate assumption for the next contract. The Ontario Securities Commission’s investor-education guide describes reinvestment risk as the possibility of reinvesting principal or income at a lower rate. This article isolates principal renewal while interest is paid out for spending. It makes no prediction about future market rates. A ladder spreads initial maturity dates across several years. That changes when different parts of principal encounter the renewal assumption. It does not lock every later term at today’s selected rate or turn an entered future rate into a guarantee. Write the five-rung schedule before counting the receipts The example divides CAD 50,000 equally into five CAD 10,000 rungs. Their initial terms mature at the ends of years one, two, three, four and five. All five initially pay 4% in annual cash interest, even though the terms differ. That equal-rate starting point is a teaching assumption, not a set of available quotes. At each maturity, the whole CAD 10,000 principal is immediately renewed for five years at the selected 2%. One rung therefore matures each year, including years six through ten. Later renewals use the same 2% assumption, with no new rate scenario introduced. OSC’s GIC explanation describes staggered maturities and choices at maturity, including reinvestment or taking cash. Here renewal is an explicit instruction in the model. The charts do not infer an actual bank’s automatic-renewal terms. Keep the old rate through the final year of its original term Year one receives five interest payments of CAD 400, for CAD 2,000 in total. The first rung matures only after paying that year’s interest. Its renewed rate therefore begins contributing to the cash schedule in year two. Year two has four original payments of CAD 400 and one renewed payment of CAD 200, totaling CAD 1,800. Year three has three original and two renewed payments, totaling CAD 1,600. The later totals are CAD 1,400 in year four and CAD 1,200 in year five. In year six all five rungs pay CAD 200, so annual interest is CAD 1,000. With every later renewal held at 2%, income stays at that level through year ten. The composition chart explains the transition rather than implying that all the original 4% income disappears at the first maturity. Do not spend the same matured principal that the model renews Each year CAD 10,000 comes due and is immediately committed to another five-year term. It is a return and reinvestment of principal, not new interest earned. Counting it as spending money while also retaining the renewed rung would create resources twice. Across ten years the schedule rolls CAD 100,000 of gross maturity principal. That does not mean the household began with CAD 100,000 or earned that much. The original CAD 50,000 is being reused as different rungs reach maturity again. Nominal principal remains CAD 50,000 throughout this illustration, while total interest paid outside it is CAD 13,000. That interest is a distinct stream. The tool does not compound it back into the ladder, assume access to locked principal, or replace a spending shortfall with a redemption. Put the interest income beside the spending assigned to it The selected annual cash need is CAD 2,000, received interest arrives before that year’s spending, and the outside reserve starts at CAD 1,000. Year one uses its CAD 2,000 interest without drawing the reserve. Later income falls while the assigned need stays fixed. The first gaps are CAD 200, CAD 400 and CAD 600 in years two, three and four. Outside cash is therefore CAD 800, CAD 400 and negative CAD 200 after those years. An unchanged principal does not remove that spending shortage. By the end of year ten, cumulative gaps total CAD 7,000: CAD 20,000 of assigned spending less CAD 13,000 of interest. The required outside opening reserve is CAD 7,000, while the entered CAD 1,000 leaves CAD 6,000 still to fund. The matrix varies renewal rates and annual needs to show how that requirement changes. Holding the initial 4% and CAD 2,000 annual need unchanged, a 1% renewal assumption requires CAD 10,500 outside the ladder. A 3% assumption requires CAD 3,500. Both cases preserve the same CAD 50,000 of nominal principal. The difference comes from thirty-five renewed rung-years across the ten-year window: one extra percentage point on each CAD 10,000 rung supplies CAD 3,500 more interest in total. That is a sensitivity of the selected calendar, rather than a claim that a higher rate will be available. These annual points also simplify payment timing. An interest deposit at year-end cannot pay a bill due months earlier. A real implementation needs exact interest dates, a within-year cash calendar and a separate review of whether preserving every rung’s principal remains appropriate. Review the actual maturity instructions and the wider plan FCAC’s GIC rights guide identifies information about the term, principal repayment, interest payments and renewal conditions that applicable federally regulated institutions must disclose. Read the new rate and instructions before treating a maturity as a continuation of the same income. The tool excludes tax, inflation, fees, issuer failure, insurance eligibility and any market value before maturity. The nominal principal line is therefore not proof of maintained purchasing power, complete protection or personal suitability. The interest figures are before tax, and annual spending does not rise with prices. Record the intended job of each maturity: renewal, spending or another goal. Then use the corresponding cash treatment consistently. Stress the rate that would fund the next term, and keep reserves already assigned to other bills separate. A ladder is a schedule to manage, rather than a promise that its first year’s income continues indefinitely.

documents.title: Paying more for a refundable booking: compare the outcome, the assumption and the cash wait
documents.description: Four charts compare two hypothetical booking contracts, separating upfront prices, cancellation costs, assumed probability-weighted amounts and cash waiting for a refund.
documents.body: A refund promise changes a cancellation outcome, while the higher price still has to be funded immediately. Check the contract and the cash calendar before interpreting an average cost. Define whose cancellation and which refund the comparison assumes A booking can have several different cancellation situations. This exercise considers a traveler choosing to cancel before using a booking, with the seller accepting an eligible cash refund under the assumed contract. It does not calculate rights when a supplier cancels or changes the service. The Canadian Transportation Agency’s traveler tips recommend reading ticket rules and the tariff, including restrictions and penalties. A broad label such as “flexible” does not supply the exact percentage, fee, deadline or payment form needed by a cash calculation. If the contract returns only a travel credit, that amount cannot simply be inserted as a cash refund. Check what it can purchase, any expiry or transfer restrictions, and whether using it requires another payment. A credit reserved for a future trip also cannot pay an unrelated household bill while the family waits. Every price and refund in these charts is hypothetical. Before using an actual quote, identify the amount refundable, conditions for cancellation, any deduction and whether repayment means cash or a restricted credit. The model accepts cash refunds only and makes no finding about a real booking’s legal terms. Keep the used-booking and cancellation branches separate The default lower-priced booking costs CAD 1,800 and has no modeled refund for an eligible voluntary cancellation. The alternative costs CAD 2,100: a CAD 300 premium. It refunds 100% of its price less CAD 100 retained from that refund. If the booking is used, the cash costs are CAD 1,800 and CAD 2,100. If the traveler cancels under the assumed eligible conditions, they remain CAD 1,800 for the lower-priced contract and become CAD 100 for the alternative. The alternative’s net refund is 2,100 − 100 = CAD 2,000 . The first chart shows those two branches rather than adding them. It also avoids counting the retained amount twice: the CAD 100 has already reduced the refund. The formula floors a refund at zero, so a large retained fee cannot generate another bill in this illustration. A real contract that charges an additional amount needs a different cash model. Treat the cancellation chance as an uncertain assumption The probability control starts at 20%. It is chosen for the example, not estimated from travelers, destinations, health information or a booking provider. Moving the control tests a different assumption; it does not make the chosen probability more reliable. Probability-weighted cost equals the used-booking cost times the chance of using it, plus the cancellation cost times the assumed chance of cancelling. The same calculation can be written price − probability × net refund . At 20%, the default lower-priced booking remains CAD 1,800. The alternative becomes 2,100 − 0.20 × 2,000 = CAD 1,700 . One actual booking does not produce an automatic CAD 1,700 invoice: under these assumptions, the alternative costs either CAD 2,100 if used or CAD 100 if cancelled with the refund received. Read a crossing as arithmetic, rather than a decision rule In the default comparison, the alternative costs CAD 300 more initially and returns CAD 2,000 more if an eligible cancellation occurs. Equal probability-weighted costs occur at 300 ÷ 2,000 = 15% . Below that assumed chance, its weighted cost is higher; above it, lower. The matrix changes the premium and the cancellation assumption. A different premium also changes the alternative’s price and therefore the base used by its refund percentage. Holding that refund fixed while changing the full-refundable price would compare inconsistent contracts. Other inputs can remove a crossing from the 0–100% range. Two contracts can also have equal weighted costs at every assumption. The tool reports those cases directly rather than displaying an impossible probability as a personal forecast. Money is only one part of a booking choice. The comparison assigns no value to the trip, schedule certainty, convenience, provider reliability or flexibility beyond the stated cash refund. An average-cost equality cannot determine how much a particular household values avoiding a large cancellation loss. Fund the premium before relying on the later refund Both bookings are paid in full at time zero. With CAD 2,500 assigned to the purchase, the lower-priced choice leaves CAD 700 and the alternative CAD 400 immediately. The conditional cash chart assumes cancellation in month two and refund two months later. The alternative’s cash stays at CAD 400 until month four, then rises by CAD 2,000 to CAD 2,400. The lower-priced path stays at CAD 700 because its modeled refund is zero. These lines condition on the cancellation branch; they are not the probability-weighted averages from the previous chart. A longer refund wait delays the recovery without changing these undiscounted endpoint costs. Reducing initial cash to CAD 2,000 produces a CAD 100 upfront shortage under the alternative, even though a large refund might arrive later. The calculator labels that shortage without assuming a credit-card advance, asset sale or help from another goal. Keep a refund clause separate from insurance and the rest of the trip Travel.gc.ca distinguishes trip cancellation coverage from trip interruption and medical coverage and emphasizes reviewing policy terms, conditions, exclusions and requirements. A booking’s refund clause and a separate insurance policy need their own review. No insurance premium or claim is included here. Nor are vouchers, exchange rates, rebooking costs, partially used travel, meals, accommodation or other prepaid commitments. A refund for one item cannot be assumed to repair the entire trip budget. For a real plan, list each payment and its cancellation conditions, record the required notice date, and keep confirmation of the promised repayment form. Put any expected cash receipt on its own date. Use a range of cancellation assumptions to understand the price trade-off, then check that the chosen upfront bill fits resources still available after other household commitments.

documents.title: Financial advice bills: compare monthly and asset-linked fees with outside cash
documents.description: Four charts separate Canadian advice-source statistics from hypothetical project, monthly and asset-linked charges, then test the outside cash assigned to each schedule.
documents.body: A popular advice source is not a price quote. Compare the written service scope, translate the full fee into dollars and place its due dates beside cash that can actually pay it. Read advice-source use without turning it into a quality ranking FCAC’s 2024 survey summary supplies the first chart’s eight advice-source percentages. They add to 142%, reflecting overlapping source use. Treat them as mentions, rather than eight slices of one 100% total. The chart measures neither prices nor provider quality. A source someone consults is different from the work a household needs completed. A budgeting conversation, a retirement projection and implementation of an investment account can involve different tasks, responsibilities and charges. Write the question to be answered before comparing the amount on an invoice. The fee controls below start a separate exercise. They do not estimate what survey respondents paid or attach a financial outcome to any of the survey’s categories. Editing a fee leaves the historical bars unchanged. Specify the work before comparing payment labels The age-group and project-review guide examines different survey cuts and the present cost of periodic reviews. Here the focus is a monthly retainer, a fixed asset-based bill and the outside cash that funds those invoices. A one-time project and an ongoing engagement need not provide the same service. A project may end after a defined report or meeting. An ongoing arrangement may include scheduled updates, access between reviews or implementation work. Those details need written confirmation rather than an assumption based on the billing label. FCAC’s advisor-selection guide recommends understanding the services, their cost and how payment works. It also suggests asking about qualifications, compensation and the working relationship. Use the actual engagement terms to establish what is included and which questions need another specialist. In this calculator, the project has no automatic renewal; the retainer continues for every selected month; and the asset-linked charge continues over the same period. These are three hypothetical schedules. The tool does not assert equivalent deliverables, value the advice, or identify which arrangement is suitable. Turn the percentage into dollars using its actual base The default project costs CAD 2,500 immediately. The alternative retainer costs CAD 200 each month. The third schedule applies an annual 0.8% to an unchanged CAD 400,000 calculation base, divided into twelve monthly bills. That last calculation is 400,000 × 0.008 = CAD 3,200 a year , or about CAD 266.67 per modeled month. Over the selected twenty-four months, the totals are CAD 2,500, CAD 4,800 and CAD 6,400. The lines reconcile those amounts without assuming an investment return. The asset figure only calculates a bill. It is not an extra reserve that the cash chart can spend. Every fee in this illustration is paid from outside cash, so the model does not deduct the same charge from the portfolio again. Product expenses, commissions, account charges and taxes are also excluded rather than silently bundled into the selected percentage. Check the first invoice as well as the two-year total The default outside reserve is CAD 2,000. Another CAD 150 becomes available each month before any recurring bill. The full project fee, however, is due at time zero, before those future additions arrive. The project’s initial funding gap is CAD 500. Its outside cash later recovers to CAD 3,100 after twenty-four monthly additions. That positive endpoint does not supply the missing cash on the original invoice date. Under the stated order, the project needs CAD 2,500 available at the start. The retainer uses CAD 50 more than the monthly addition, so its opening-cash requirement over twenty-four months is CAD 1,200. The asset-linked bill uses about CAD 116.67 more each month, requiring CAD 2,800 initially. The entered CAD 2,000 therefore leaves that path CAD 800 short by the end. These requirements cover only the displayed advice bills. Cash already promised to rent, taxes or another goal cannot also pay these invoices. Negative values identify an unresolved funding need; the calculator does not sell assets, open a credit line or postpone a contractual bill. Use a cost-equivalent asset base as a question, not a verdict The matrix translates three annual percentages and three unchanging asset bases into annual dollar charges. It helps expose the denominator: the same percentage can produce very different invoices when the amount subject to the fee changes. At the default 0.8%, CAD 300,000 would produce CAD 2,400 a year, equal in dollars to a CAD 200 monthly retainer. This is a cost-equivalent base for the selected numbers. It does not establish equivalent service or make either structure preferable above or below that amount. At only three months, the selected retainer totals CAD 600 and the asset-linked schedule CAD 800, while the project still costs CAD 2,500. The thirteenth retainer bill brings cumulative charges to CAD 2,600, passing the project amount. A crossing of selected cash totals does not turn a one-time engagement into thirteen months of support. The horizon and the work promised both matter. Actual terms can use average balances, quarter-end values, tiered rates, minimum fees or a different billing frequency. Assets can also change through markets, deposits and withdrawals. The model holds the base fixed to isolate the arithmetic. Before using a real percentage, confirm which assets enter the base and whether additional charges apply. Bring a complete fee calendar into the household plan Record the initial amount, recurring amount, billing dates and expected length of the engagement. Identify any separately quoted follow-up, implementation or product costs. Ask how a change in scope or an end to the relationship affects future invoices and work already paid for. Keep a separate list of deliverables and responsibilities: what information will be reviewed, what written output is expected, who implements changes, and when the plan is revisited. A cheaper bill cannot answer those questions, and a more expensive bill cannot establish better results. The calculator deliberately assigns no extra return, tax saving or avoided loss to an advisor. A claim about financial benefits needs evidence of its own and cannot be reverse-engineered from the fee. Start with a clear task and a complete quote, then reconcile the chosen payment schedule with the rest of the household’s commitments.

documents.title: One payment or monthly income: chart the cash calendar before comparing illness cover
documents.description: Four interactive graphics compare two independently approved benefit schedules, their cash paths, required opening reserves and the effect of a delayed one-time receipt.
documents.body: A lump sum and a stream of monthly receipts meet different cash calendars. Confirm the claim conditions first, then compare spendable amounts and dates with the costs they must fund. Begin with the payment trigger, before the amount The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s health-insurance overview describes critical illness insurance as usually providing a one-time payment following a covered diagnosis. Definitions and covered conditions vary by insurer. A policy document and a claim decision determine whether a particular event qualifies. FCAC’s disability-insurance overview describes protection when a person cannot work and earn income. Definitions, payment limits, duration and receipt delays require checking. A diagnosis and an inability to work are different questions; neither by itself establishes that both contracts will pay. The calculator begins after those questions have been resolved for each alternative. Scenario A receives one independently entered net amount. Scenario B receives a net monthly amount for an independently entered number of months. It does not add the alternatives together. Any tax and offset adjustments must already be reflected in the supplied receipts. Put the household costs on the same monthly calendar The example runs for eighteen whole months. Recurring spending is CAD 4,500 a month, while other spendable income contributes CAD 1,500. A separate CAD 6,000 cost occurs in month one. The household begins with CAD 10,000 of accessible cash. Scenario A receives CAD 50,000 in month two. Scenario B receives CAD 4,500 a month beginning in month four, with twelve payments ending in month fifteen. Their benefit totals are therefore CAD 50,000 and CAD 54,000 within the displayed window. These numbers are authored examples, not advertised benefits or estimates of an actual claim. The event chart highlights months around the first payment, the one-time receipt and the monthly stream’s end. It shows benefit receipts only. The complete month-end cash paths then add other income and subtract both recurring and initial costs. Keeping those two views distinct helps explain why a large benefit bar need not mean a large remaining balance. Every month receives its inflows before its costs are paid. That is a simplifying order. If rent leaves before a benefit arrives in the same month, the practical bank balance may need an additional buffer. Use actual dates for an implemented household plan. Find the deepest shortfall rather than reading only the final balance Before any benefit receipt, month one uses CAD 9,000 more than other income supplies. Under the one-time scenario, the month-two payment replenishes cash, but continuing spending draws it down again. The path ends month eighteen with CAD 0 at the selected CAD 10,000 opening balance. The monthly scenario must first fund three months before its first benefit receipt. Those months create a cumulative CAD 15,000 deficit. During months four through fifteen, benefit payments and other income exceed recurring spending by CAD 1,500 a month. The final three months have no modeled benefit and consume CAD 3,000 each. The ending balance is CAD 4,000, but an earlier point still falls below zero. Scenario A requires CAD 10,000 at the start to fund its entire calendar. Scenario B requires CAD 15,000, making its additional requirement CAD 5,000 above the selected cash. The higher ending balance in B does not make the early payments affordable on their due dates. Required opening cash is the largest cumulative shortfall across the horizon, with a floor of zero. Additional opening cash subtracts the accessible reserve already entered. A negative plotted position remains an unfunded need; the tool creates no overdraft, borrowing facility or interest charge to fill it. Test what changes when a payment arrives later The matrix changes only scenario A’s net amount and receipt month. Spending, other income, the initial cost and accessible cash stay fixed. Each cell reports additional opening cash, rather than total benefits or a probability. A larger payment can improve the final balance without funding the months before it arrives. Moving the same CAD 50,000 receipt from month two to month twelve leaves eleven earlier months to finance. Their cumulative deficit is CAD 39,000, so the extra opening requirement becomes CAD 29,000 above the selected CAD 10,000. The columns are stress assumptions. They do not represent promised insurer processing times or contractual choices. If a selected receipt falls after the displayed horizon, it contributes nothing within that window. The tool does not credit a future payment against an earlier deficit or assume the household can borrow against it. Likewise, the monthly stream’s maximum payment count is an entered calendar limit. It does not calculate an expiry age, a change in the definition of disability or an extension of coverage. Changing the horizon can expose months after the entered stream has ended. Take the calendar back to the actual contracts and budget Confirm the covered event, required evidence, applicable conditions, benefit amount and timing separately for each contract. FCAC identifies tax treatment and benefit offsets as points to check for disability cover. Do not enter a gross quoted amount as spendable cash unless the deductions have been assessed. Next, replace the example’s costs with a household budget. Separate recurring commitments from one-time changes, identify income that would continue, and count only accessible resources assigned to this purpose. Property value or an inaccessible retirement balance cannot automatically pay this month’s bill. Finally, compare premiums, exclusions and protection periods outside this cash exercise. A smaller reserve need under one assumed claim does not establish that a product offers broader cover or better value. These graphics explain payment shape and funding timing; they cannot select insurance or resolve a claim.

documents.title: Buying, repaying and saving: stop counting the same credit-card purchase twice
documents.description: Five charts reconcile a year of purchases with bank payments, card liabilities and savings transfers, then show what changes when the final bill is paid.
documents.body: Record a purchase once as consumption, track the card liability until repayment, and treat transfers between your own accounts as account movements. The bank balance alone is only one part of the household picture. Ask three questions about each transaction A budgeting app can show a grocery purchase on a card, a later payment from chequing to the card, and a transfer to savings. All three change an account, but they do not all measure new consumption. Treating every debit as another household expense can make a balanced plan look as if money disappeared twice. For each entry, ask what was consumed, which account moved and whether a liability changed. A consumed card purchase creates a liability without immediately reducing the bank account. Its repayment later reduces both cash and that liability. A transfer to your own savings account moves an asset between two locations. FCAC’s budgeting guidance supports reviewing income, savings and expenses against actual statements. This guide adds an original consolidated ledger to explain how those statements fit together. It is a teaching model rather than a prescribed accounting standard or a tax calculation. Define the twelve-month window and the nested spending shares The original example receives CAD 5,000 of take-home income at the start of each model month. It spends 60% directly from chequing, or CAD 3,000. The card-purchase input then applies to the CAD 2,000 that remains. A 40% card share therefore means CAD 800 of card purchases, not another 40% of the original CAD 5,000. Total monthly consumption is CAD 3,800, leaving CAD 1,200 after both purchase categories. The saving-transfer input moves 50% of that surplus, or CAD 600, from chequing to a separate savings account. The other CAD 600 remains in chequing after the ordinary monthly flows have settled. These nested shares make consumption no larger than current income within this limited example. They do not establish an appropriate spending target or prove that a real household can meet all its obligations. The tool omits additional loans, taxes beyond the entered take-home amount, emergencies and other accounts. Opening chequing is CAD 10,000, separate savings are CAD 5,000, and the card starts with no purchase liability. Neither bank account earns interest. Every modeled purchase is consumed, with no continuing vehicle, inventory or other asset value. Buying a retained asset would need a different ledger. Separate the purchase month from the repayment month The card’s new purchases are paid in the next model month. Month one therefore consumes CAD 3,800 while only CAD 3,000 leaves the bank for merchants or the card issuer. The difference is CAD 800 owed for purchases already consumed. That amount is not an extra saving created by choosing the card. Each of months two through twelve pays the prior CAD 800 card bill and makes another CAD 800 of card purchases. Consumption and purchase-related bank outflow are both CAD 3,800 in each of those ordinary months, even though the particular purchases being paid are different. The first chart groups those three distinct cases: the first month, each recurring month and a final settlement-only event. Its middle row is a per-month amount, not the eleven-month total. The cumulative chart then shows the complete twelve-month amounts and the remaining timing gap. The model assumes no card interest or fees. FCAC explains the conditions and limits of purchase grace periods, including the need to pay the required balance by its due date. A one-month teaching lag does not calculate an actual grace period. Existing revolving debt, cash advances, cash-like transactions, fees or missed due dates need a separate calculation using the agreement. Match the measure to the question before adding transactions Across twelve months, direct purchases total CAD 36,000 and card purchases total CAD 9,600. Consumption recorded once is therefore CAD 45,600. The bank has paid CAD 36,000 directly and CAD 8,800 to settle eleven earlier card-purchase batches, for purchase-related cash outflow of CAD 44,800. Both totals answer useful questions. CAD 45,600 measures consumption assigned to the window; CAD 44,800 measures the relevant bank outflows inside it. Their CAD 800 difference is exactly the remaining purchase liability. A bank-only report has a timing difference from a consumption report, rather than necessarily containing a transaction error. Adding the CAD 8,800 repayments to the CAD 45,600 purchases produces CAD 54,400. That calculation counts purchases once when incurred and again when the associated liability is settled. The third chart makes this recording mistake visible beside the two correctly named measures. A system that records only bank outflows can still be useful for cash planning. It needs the opening and closing liabilities to explain the boundary between reporting periods. A system that categorizes card purchases when they occur should classify subsequent repayments consistently so that the same consumption is not counted again. A savings transfer changes the location of money The household transfers CAD 7,200 into savings over the year. That is an account-level saving action, but it is not an additional CAD 7,200 cost to the consolidated household. Each transfer lowers chequing and raises savings by the same amount. At month twelve, chequing holds CAD 18,000 and savings hold CAD 12,200. Subtracting the CAD 800 card purchase liability gives CAD 29,400 of listed net financial assets. Relative to the opening CAD 15,000, the increase is CAD 14,400. The waterfall independently reconciles that increase: CAD 60,000 take-home receipts minus CAD 45,600 consumed purchases equals CAD 14,400. Card repayments and internal savings transfers each have zero immediate net effect on this consolidated measure. That does not make their dates irrelevant to the accounts that must fund them. FCAC defines net worth as assets less liabilities. This example includes only two bank accounts and one card purchase liability, so its result is deliberately called listed net financial assets. It is not a complete household balance sheet. An unpaid purchase liability still belongs in the model even when its assumed payment deadline has not yet passed. Settle the final bill without inventing another expense Position thirteen pays the last CAD 800 card bill. It supplies no new income, purchase or savings transfer. Chequing falls to CAD 17,200, savings stay at CAD 12,200 and the card purchase liability becomes zero. The combined net amount remains CAD 29,400. The final position is a settlement event, not a forecast that ordinary life pauses for a thirteenth month. It closes the twelve-month purchase cohort so that total bank outflow eventually equals that cohort’s consumption. A real following month would add its own income, purchases and other obligations. When applying the idea to statements, retain transaction dates, statement dates and actual processing dates. Match card payments to the corresponding liabilities and distinguish refunds, interest, fees and asset purchases from this guide’s simple consumed purchases. Check that opening balances reconcile before interpreting a later difference. The monthly model receives income before its payments. It cannot establish that the actual bank account stays above zero between paydays or that a payment will reach the issuer on time. Use the related dated cash tools for that task. The purpose here is to make each transaction’s role visible, so that consumption, payments, transfers and balances can all reconcile without counting the same purchase twice.

documents.title: Three months of savings: Canada’s asset-resilience statistics and your household cash target
documents.description: Explore official Canadian asset-resilience estimates with published confidence intervals, then compare an invented threshold, household income and essential spending using a separate cash-buffer illustration.
documents.body: A reserve statistic needs a population, asset definition, threshold and reference year. A household cash target also needs its own spending calendar; the same number of months can describe very different amounts. Ask what the reserve is supposed to replace “Three months of savings” sounds like a single target. It can instead mean three months of a low-income threshold, three months of usual household income, or three months of bills that still need paying during an interruption. The time unit matches while the dollar amounts differ. Statistics Canada’s protection-from-income-shocks indicator uses liquid assets relative to the after-tax low-income measure. It is a population measure of financial resilience. It does not establish that a particular household can fund three months of its actual lifestyle or contractual payments. The first two charts preserve the published statistical definitions. The last two let readers inspect independent invented budgets. Keeping those questions distinct makes both more useful: the survey describes an aggregate pattern, while a household plan identifies cash amounts and dates that its own resources must cover. Read six survey waves without inventing the years between them The three-month LIM-based estimate rises from 63.6% in 1999 to 71.4% in 2023, a difference of 7.8 percentage points. The chart shows all six published reference years in the selected series. It does not fill missing years with modeled observations or imply uninterrupted annual improvement. The denominator is persons of all ages in all family types across the ten provinces. The three territories are excluded. A percentage of persons is not interchangeable with a percentage of households: households of different sizes can contribute different numbers of people to a person-based measure. Whiskers show the supplied 95% confidence bounds. They describe uncertainty around estimated population shares, rather than the range of savings balances held by individuals. The chart does not calculate a formal difference test, establish why the estimates changed, or show that the same people became more resilient. Its latest observation is 2023, even though this guide was reviewed in October 2026. Change one definition before comparing a headline The 2023 chart varies both the required duration and the published income basis. Longer coverage requires more assets when the other definition stays fixed. Changing the income basis changes the benchmark against which those assets are assessed. For three months, the published share is 71.4% on the national after-tax low-income-measure basis and 63.6% on the household-income basis. That difference is not a count of households missing a recommended target. These are overlapping survey classifications, and their percentages cannot be added into separate population groups. The LIM benchmark reflects household-size adjustment and a national income distribution. The household-income measure uses after-tax income and excludes capital gains. Neither is identical to an itemized essential-expense budget. Before comparing an article, dashboard or social-media headline, record its denominator, benchmark, duration and year rather than relying on the word “savings” alone. Translate three independent benchmarks into dollars The interactive example starts with CAD 10,000 of cash assumed available after withdrawal costs and tax. Its invented annual benchmark is CAD 30,000, its entered annual household income after tax is CAD 72,000, and its entered monthly essential expenses are CAD 4,500. These inputs are not estimates taken from the survey. For three months, the resulting targets are CAD 7,500, CAD 18,000 and CAD 13,500 respectively. The same CAD 10,000 balance exceeds the first target, falls CAD 8,000 below the income-based target and falls CAD 3,500 below the essential-expense target. Passing one comparison therefore does not settle the others. The invented benchmark is deliberately labelled. It is not a current official LIM amount, and the tool does not implement household-size equivalization or classify the reader under Statistics Canada’s methodology. The cash bar is also repeated for visual comparison, rather than allocated three times. A plan still has only the original CAD 10,000 available. A payment calendar can also reveal costs hidden by a monthly average. Suppose the CAD 4,500 monthly figure excludes a separate CAD 1,200 obligation due in the second month. Three months then require CAD 14,700, leaving CAD 4,700 to fund. Entering CAD 400 more per month reproduces that three-month total, but spreads the obligation across dates. That shortcut cannot establish whether enough cash is available on its actual due date. Separate counted assets from money available for the next bill The source indicator’s liquid-asset definition includes deposits, securities and registered savings. For a household payment calendar, an asset’s quoted value and its usable cash proceeds can differ. A security may change in price before sale; an account can involve withdrawal tax, settlement time or access conditions. The cash input assumes those practical questions have already been resolved. It accepts an amount available when needed after relevant costs and tax, rather than applying an automatic haircut to every type of asset. It also assumes the amount has not already been reserved for an unrelated bill. The earmarking guide illustrates that separate allocation problem. At the default essential-spending input, CAD 10,000 funds about 2.22 months. This is a continuous expense ratio, not a guaranteed date at which money runs out. Actual rent, loan payments and annual bills arrive on particular dates. Replacement income or benefits would require a dated cash-flow schedule; none is silently assumed here. Stress the cash target without treating the grid as a forecast The matrix compares fixed essential-expense rows with one, three, six and nine months of coverage. Every cell subtracts the same entered cash from that scenario’s expense requirement and floors the additional amount at zero. A zero does not report zero risk; it says only that the entered cash covers the selected arithmetic target. For example, CAD 4,500 of monthly essentials requires CAD 27,000 for six months. With CAD 10,000 already available, the additional amount is CAD 17,000. At CAD 6,000 per month, the same six-month duration needs CAD 26,000 more. The darker cells indicate larger cash shortfalls, not more likely events. A future saving plan is another separate question. Adding CAD 500 at each month-end would close a CAD 3,500 shortfall after seven deposits if the target stays fixed and no cash is withdrawn. Those promised deposits do not enlarge the amount available for an emergency today. Use the official charts to understand what a reserve statistic measures and the hypothetical charts to ask a narrower budget question. A workable next calculation starts with essential payments, realistic incoming cash, access dates and existing earmarks. A national share can inform that discussion, but it does not choose a household’s reserve target or replace its own cash calendar.
