documents.title: Two incomes, one reserve: compare separate and overlapping income interruptions
documents.description: Use a four-cell probability grid, cash-need bars and two sensitivity curves to see how an independence assumption changes a household reserve stress test.
documents.body: Knowing each income’s individual absence probability does not tell you how often both disappear together. Inspect the joint states, cash needs and probability-weighted average separately. Define the four receipt patterns before entering probabilities A household with two incomes can face four simplified receipt patterns: both continue, only A is absent, only B is absent, or both are absent. Each pattern can create a different cash need even when the household’s ordinary monthly spending is unchanged. The tool assumes one pattern begins at the start and persists throughout the selected window. An absent income contributes zero; a retained income continues at the entered monthly net amount. Partial income reductions, a later interruption and returning to work are outside this model. The four states are a deliberately restricted planning universe, not a complete description of actual employment paths. Every probability is an assumption for that entire window. A 10% input is not a current unemployment statistic, an annual job-loss rate or a probability inferred from your occupation. Changing the number of months changes the meaning of the event, so the probability assumptions need reconsideration too. The tool has no employment dataset from which to estimate them. An independence assumption supplies an overlap that individual risks do not If each income has an assumed 10% absence probability, independence gives a 1% probability that both are absent: 10% multiplied by 10%. The remaining cells are 9% for A only, 9% for B only and 81% for neither. Independence is the extra assumption connecting the two individual probabilities. The Penn State lesson on two-way tables defines statistical independence through joint probabilities equalling the products of their marginal probabilities. That mathematical definition supports the grid’s independent case; it does not establish that a particular household’s incomes behave independently. The default stress setting of +50 instead places the joint absence probability halfway between independence and the largest feasible overlap. With two 10% marginal risks, that gives 5.5% for both absent, 4.5% for A only, 4.5% for B only and 85.5% for neither. Each income’s individual absence probability remains 10%. The model changes how the events overlap, rather than quietly increasing both risks. Use the remaining income before drawing from the reserve The example has monthly net income of CAD 3,500 from A and CAD 2,500 from B, essential spending of CAD 4,500, and a six-month window. If A is absent, B’s income reduces the monthly gap to CAD 2,000, creating a CAD 12,000 window need. If B is absent, the gap is CAD 1,000 per month, or CAD 6,000. If both are absent, the need is CAD 27,000. A CAD 15,000 starting reserve covers either single-income absence in full but leaves CAD 12,000 unfunded in the joint absence state. The cash bars show the part covered by the reserve and the amount still needing a workable funding response. These bars are alternative scenarios, not bills to add together. A zero-probability state can still be displayed as a counterfactual cash stress. No loan is automatically created for an unfunded amount. The FCAC emergency-fund guide provides general context for preparing for unexpected costs and lost income; it does not supply this model’s risk assumptions. A weighted average is not the amount needed in the bad state With the default reserve, only the joint absence state creates an unfunded need. Under independence, its 1% probability multiplied by CAD 12,000 produces an expected unfunded amount of CAD 120. At the selected +50 stress, 5.5% multiplied by CAD 12,000 gives CAD 660. Neither number is a sufficient reserve target or a forecast invoice. In this example the possible unfunded amounts are zero and CAD 12,000; no state has a CAD 660 deficit. The expectation is an average across the assumed probability distribution. A household experiencing the adverse state still needs to address that state’s actual cash gap. The two curves therefore show different summaries: the probability of any inadequacy and the probability-weighted unfunded dollars. Both span the full dependence-control range at the selected cash assumptions. Changing only the chosen setting updates the grid and headline metrics while leaving those full-range comparison curves in place. A lower probability of any shortfall can accompany a larger expected shortfall Set the reserve to zero while keeping the other default inputs. Under independence, at least one income is absent in 19% of the assumed states, and expected unfunded need is CAD 1,890. At the +50 setting, the probability of any absence falls to 14.5%, yet expected unfunded need rises to CAD 2,295. The larger overlap concentrates more probability in the state where both incomes are absent. At the same time, the fixed individual absence probabilities require less probability in the two single-absence states and more in the neither-absent state. There are fewer windows with any absence, but a greater weight on the more severe joint outcome. This is why a headline about the chance of a bad event cannot replace the distribution of its consequences. The result is a property of these entered amounts and probabilities, not an empirical claim about households. Read the state bars beside both curves before describing one scenario as safer. The stress dial stays within feasible probability bounds Let a and b be the two individual absence probabilities and j their overlap. The four cells are 1 − a − b + j , a − j , b − j and j . Keeping every cell non-negative gives max(0, a + b − 1) ≤ j ≤ min(a, b) . Setting zero uses j = ab. Positive settings move from that independent value toward the upper bound; negative settings toward the lower bound. +100 means the greatest feasible overlap, and −100 the smallest. This artificial interpolation scale is not a measured Pearson correlation coefficient. With unequal individual probabilities, the maximum overlap does not mean that the two receipt states always match. At an individual probability of zero or 100%, the bounds can force the joint distribution so that the dial has no effect. That is a constraint of the chosen probabilities rather than a malfunction. The grid and its data table let you check the row sums, column sums and total directly. Use the model to expose assumptions in a broader cash plan Build essential expenses and available net receipts from an actual household budget. Separate a probability assumption from an estimate supported by evidence. Stress overlapping interruptions as well as isolated ones. Compare the size of an unfunded need with the chance assigned to it. Review benefits, replacement income, bill dates and recovery timing separately. The illustration offsets receipts and spending within each month, uses only the starting reserve and ignores ordinary surplus saving. It does not determine benefits, severance, insurance claims, tax or access to credit. Earlier bill dates can need another timing buffer. The purpose is to make the joint-risk assumption visible before a more complete, evidence-based household plan is prepared.

documents.title: Fund cost records: reinvested distributions and return of capital can change the sale gain
documents.description: Follow an invented non-registered mutual-fund ledger from opening purchase through reinvestment, cash return of capital and sale, keeping units, cost base and market value separate.
documents.body: Original cash invested is not always the current adjusted cost base. Reinvestment can add cost and units, while return of capital can reduce cost without changing the unit count. Keep the unit count, market value and cost base in separate records A fund statement can show the current value of an investment without explaining every adjustment needed for its cost record. The amount first paid, the units now owned and the adjusted cost base can change in different ways after distributions and later transactions. Adjusted cost base, or ACB, is a cost measure used in calculating a capital gain or loss. It is not a continuously updated market valuation. A rise or fall in the quoted unit price does not by itself update that cost record. The CRA’s mutual-fund guidance explains reinvested distributions, returns of capital and average cost for identical fund units. This article uses those mechanics in an independent non-registered illustration with one holding, rather than recreating an issuer’s transaction history or completing a tax return. Add the actual amount reinvested and the units it purchases The example buys 500 units at CAD 20 each, for an opening cost of CAD 10,000. It later receives a taxable distribution with an actual cash-equivalent amount of CAD 500, all of which is reinvested at a post-distribution NAV of CAD 20. Reinvestment buys twenty-five additional units, taking the total to 525. Total cost increases by the amount used to acquire those units: CAD 10,000 + CAD 500 = CAD 10,500 . The average cost remains CAD 20 per unit at this particular stage. The illustration assumes a pre-distribution NAV of CAD 21 for the original 500 units. Paying CAD 1 per original unit transfers CAD 500 out of that value; immediate reinvestment at CAD 20 purchases the additional units. It does not create CAD 500 of value on top of a fund already worth CAD 10,500. CRA also explains that reinvesting a distribution does not remove the applicable income-reporting requirement. The input is the actual amount reinvested, not a dividend gross-up, tax bill or assumed after-tax amount. Any tax funding would need its own cash ledger. Record a later cash return of capital without buying more units The next event is a CAD 200 return of capital paid in cash and retained outside the fund. It does not purchase additional units, so the holder still owns 525. It reduces total ACB from CAD 10,500 to CAD 10,300. Average cost becomes approximately CAD 19.619048 per unit. The hypothetical market NAV also falls by CAD 200 divided by 525 units when that cash is transferred out. The grouped bars show book cost and NAV separately, even though they happen to coincide again after this event under the chosen assumptions. That equality is not a general rule. An actual fund can have market gains or losses unrelated to its holder’s cost record. Likewise, a falling NAV alone cannot establish whether a payment is return of capital. Use the reported classification and relevant records rather than guessing the character from the price chart. The controls keep total ACB positive. Cases where adjustments reach or pass zero require additional rules and are outside this example. The displayed per-unit values are rounded; calculations retain full precision rather than rebuilding the total cost from a rounded per-unit label. Subtract adjusted cost and selling expenses once The final sale redeems all 525 units at CAD 22, producing gross proceeds of CAD 11,550. A separately entered CAD 20 selling expense leaves net proceeds of CAD 11,530. The capital gain before any inclusion-rate calculation is CAD 11,550 − CAD 20 − CAD 10,300 = CAD 1,230 . The selling expense is subtracted once from proceeds. It is not also deducted from ACB as another adjustment. Using only the original CAD 10,000 purchase cost would produce a CAD 1,530 gain on the same net proceeds. That shortcut overstates the result by CAD 300, which equals the net cost-base increase from CAD 500 reinvested less CAD 200 returned. The signed comparison shows both calculations and their difference. Depending on the entered adjustments, ignoring later cost changes can either overstate or understate a gain. A negative calculated sale result is simply a loss amount here; the tool does not determine whether or how it can be used for tax purposes. Do not confuse sale gain with all cash and value received The retained CAD 200 return of capital is outside the fund before the final sale. Adding it to CAD 11,530 of net sale proceeds gives CAD 11,730 of remaining resources before any tax, compared with CAD 10,000 originally supplied. That CAD 1,730 resource increase is different from the CAD 1,230 sale gain because the illustration also included the earlier CAD 500 distribution. The distribution and later sale gain are different events. Their tax treatment is not calculated by adding the two as though every income category had the same rules. The return of capital itself is not new investment profit added on top of all other returns. It transferred value into outside cash and reduced the cost base. Counting it again as extra profit while ignoring that adjustment would disconnect the cash and cost records. The matrix varies sale NAV and the cash return-of-capital amount. Each cell is a separate complete ledger, with the same opening purchase, reinvested distribution and selling expense. It is not a prediction of prices or a sequence of additional payments. Use complete transaction records before turning the illustration into a filing number The calculation assumes no other identical holdings, purchases, partial sales, transfers, foreign-currency amounts or adjustments. Real records can be more involved. The CRA guidance discusses average cost for identical units in the same fund class or series, rather than treating every purchase as an isolated lot selected after the fact. Reconcile the relevant transaction history, distribution records and cost-base adjustments. A quoted market value, the first bank transfer or one sale slip may not supply every amount needed. Confirm the applicable scope of identical holdings when records span more than one account. This article stops at the gain or loss before any inclusion-rate calculation. It supplies no personal tax rate, allowable-loss assessment, refund or after-tax spending amount. Its purpose is to make the cost record inspectable before those separate tax and planning questions are answered.

documents.title: Charitable-donation statistics: a claimant count, a median and a total tell different stories
documents.description: Explore official 2022 and 2023 donation-claim data, separate claimant counts from participation rates, and compare reported medians with approximate means derived from published totals.
documents.body: Check who is counted and what the denominator means. A tax-return claim is not a complete record of giving, and a national average is not a personal donation target. Identify the people and the event being measured Statistics Canada’s Charitable donors, 2023 release uses the preliminary T1 Family File. It describes charitable donations reported on tax returns, rather than every act of giving. This article retains its published 2022 and 2023 observations and was reviewed on 25 October 2026. The source covers claims supported by official receipts for charities and approved organizations. It does not capture every small gift, unclaimed receipt or donation to an individual through crowdfunding. Nor does it count volunteering as a dollar donation. The year control selects a tax year in this dated extract. It does not forecast giving or estimate a family’s tax credit. Keep the source population visible before comparing a chart with a household’s records: claiming tax filers, residents and people who actually gave are different groups. A large claimant count does not establish a high participation rate The first chart shows counts for the provinces and territories. Larger jurisdictions can have more claimants simply because they contain more people. A count alone does not tell us the share of that jurisdiction’s tax filers who reported a donation. That share would require a matching denominator: all relevant tax filers in the same place and year. Dividing by a household count, a population estimate from another year or the Canada claimant total would answer a different question. This chart does not manufacture a denominator from unrelated data. The national total is displayed separately from the jurisdiction bars. Canada is not another region to add to its constituent parts. Published counts and amounts are rounded, so small differences between an aggregate and a sum of displayed components should not be interpreted as missing individual records. Keep units and claim timing beside the amount The source table reports total donations in thousands of dollars. The dollar charts multiply those entries by 1,000. This unit conversion is essential: a table entry of 2,172,850 represents CAD 2,172,850,000, rather than CAD 2,172,850. These are nominal amounts. The charts make no inflation adjustment and do not report a percentage of household income. A change in aggregate claims can reflect a change in claimant numbers, claimed amounts or their composition; the total alone cannot identify every driver. The date a donation is claimed can also differ from the date cash left a bank account. The release explains that claims can include earlier gifts carried forward and donations pooled between spouses. The extract therefore should not be read as a complete calendar of cash paid to charities during the selected year. Read a reported median separately from a derived mean The reported median is the middle amount among the claiming tax filers in the group. It is not a donation made by the average resident. A higher regional median does not, by itself, establish a higher participation rate, a larger total or greater generosity. A mean answers another question: total claimed dollars divided by claimant count. Using the published Canada totals gives an approximate mean of CAD 2,532 for 2023, compared with the reported median of CAD 390. The derived mean is rounded to the nearest dollar because the published inputs are themselves rounded. The age chart repeats that calculation within each reported age group and uses the source’s Both sexes section. A large mean–median difference does not reveal every individual amount or the exact shape of the distribution. Neither statistic is a suggested gift, and neither determines what a household can afford. Compare like groups without turning descriptions into causes The age groups remain in their published order. Each median and derived mean conditions on claiming tax filers in that age band. Comparing those values does not show what would happen to the same person’s donations as they became older. Income, wealth, family circumstances, tax-claim choices and other group differences can matter. The chart does not isolate those factors or estimate a causal age effect. It also supplies no confidence band or individual prediction. Do not average the group medians to recreate a national median. Likewise, an unweighted average of group means would give a small claimant group the same influence as a large one. A national mean requires the national total divided by the national claimant count, or an appropriately weighted calculation using compatible group data. Use the statistics as context for a separate giving plan For a household plan, keep a record of gifts paid, receipts received and amounts claimed in each tax year. Those records answer different questions. A cash budget needs the dates money leaves; a tax claim needs the applicable receipt and reporting treatment. The related giving-budget guide models personal payment timing separately. A published median cannot set an affordable commitment, and a tax-credit assumption does not supply cash before it is received. Begin with the household’s priorities and other obligations rather than treating a regional comparison as a target. This extract is dated. The release states that a redesign delayed the 2024 reference-year release to winter 2026/2027. Recheck the official publication schedule before calling these figures the latest available. No missing year is invented or interpolated here, and two annual observations are not extended into a long-term forecast.

documents.title: Bond duration: why yield is only part of the return
documents.description: Use five charts to price annual coupons and principal, compare exact yield sensitivity with duration, and reconcile a one-year coupon plus sale return.
documents.body: A quoted yield describes a set of cash flows and pricing assumptions. Your realized return also depends on price changes, reinvestment, credit and the date you sell. Name the yield before comparing it A bond with a 4% coupon pays 4 per year on 100 of face value under an annual-payment convention. If its market price is 95, its current yield is 4 ÷ 95 = 4.21%. That ratio describes coupon income relative to price. It leaves out the difference between the purchase price and the eventual repayment amount. Yield to maturity is the discount rate that equates price with promised coupons and principal. Realizing that annualized compound rate requires the relevant payment and reinvestment assumptions, including no default. A fund’s distribution yield, portfolio yield to maturity, and historical total return answer different questions. When reviewing two funds, write down the yield definition, observation date, currency, fee treatment, credit mix, and duration. A higher number can reflect a different calculation or more risk. It is not a sufficient basis for choosing the holding. Specify every cash flow before quoting a price The interactive example is an invented annual-pay, noncallable bond. Face value is CAD 1,000, its annual coupon rate is 5%, initial required annual yield is 5%, and ten full years remain. Purchase occurs just after a coupon date, so the first new coupon is one year away and no accrued-interest adjustment is needed at the selected boundaries. It promises CAD 50 at each annual date and an additional CAD 1,000 of principal at the final date. Discounting every promised payment at 5% gives a price of CAD 1,000. If the required yield instantly changes to 7% before any payment, the same ten-year payment schedule is worth approximately CAD 859.53 under this model. The coupon does not change when the discount yield changes. Price = sum of [promised cash flow at year t ÷ (1 + annual required yield) t ] The cash-flow chart shows future nominal payments, while the price curve shows their value at the purchase-date clock. Do not add the future coupons to the purchase price as extra wealth. Their present values are already inside that price. All promised payments are assumed to occur; the model does not establish an issuer’s creditworthiness or an executable market quotation. These annual payment and annual compounding conventions are chosen for teaching. They are not a statement that all Canadian bonds use this quotation convention. For an actual security, verify payment frequency, yield convention, accrued interest, call terms and trade costs. Translate a yield shock into a price estimate For a small parallel change in yield, a common first-order estimate uses modified duration: Approximate price return = −modified duration × change in yield Write the yield change as a decimal. A rise of one percentage point is 0.01; a rise from 4% to 5% is not entered as 25%. A portfolio with duration 6 would have an estimated price change of −6 × 0.01 = −6%. Fidelity’s duration guide explains interest-rate sensitivity and why the estimate becomes less accurate for larger changes. Effective duration is commonly used when embedded options affect cash flows; read which measure a fund reports. Duration is not a maturity date or a guarantee of recovery by a particular year. Derive duration from the specified payments Macaulay duration is the average payment time weighted by each payment’s present value. For the default bond it is approximately 8.1078 years. Under this annual convention, modified duration divides that number by 1 + 0.05, giving approximately 7.7217. The CFA Institute public duration overview distinguishes these measures and explains the limits of linear price estimates. A yield rise from 5% to 7% is a change of 0.02 in decimal form. The first-order price estimate is 1,000 × (1 − 7.7217 × 0.02), or about CAD 845.57. Exact discounted-cash-flow pricing gives about CAD 859.53. The approximation is therefore roughly CAD 13.96 below the exact result in this invented shock. The curved exact-price line and straight duration line meet at the initial yield and diverge away from it. With sufficiently large changes, the straight-line estimate can even become negative while the price of the promised positive payments remains positive. That negative approximation is displayed as a failure of a local estimate, not a valid bond value or a possible contractual payment. The duration comparison also distinguishes maturity from duration. A zero-coupon bond pays only at its final date, so Macaulay duration equals maturity. Modified duration is maturity divided by 1 + annual yield; it equals maturity only when that yield is zero. The coupon and maturity matrix separately reprices complete payment schedules rather than treating one duration number as an exact formula for every bond. Keep the separate first-order portfolio illustration in its own scope Assume a hypothetical portfolio worth 10,000, modified duration of 6, and cash income of 400 over the next year. Hold duration fixed, apply one parallel yield shock, and ignore convexity, defaults, fees, reinvestment, currency, and all other price effects. These are mechanical illustrations, not bond-fund forecasts. The last row deliberately stretches a linear approximation. A proper repricing would discount each cash flow at the new curve and account for changing duration and convexity. The table shows why income does not eliminate mark-to-market losses; it cannot tell you the exact year-end value of a real fund. This original portfolio table keeps its independently assumed duration of 6 and cash income of 400. Those are not the calculated duration and coupon of the single bond in the interactive controls. The table is retained to illustrate a simple first-order portfolio stress; it does not calibrate or reconcile the new cash-flow model. Move the payment clock before calculating a one-year return An immediate price shock and a sale one year later use different remaining cash flows. At the default changed yield of 7%, the immediate ten-year price is CAD 859.53. One year later, just after the first CAD 50 coupon is paid, the bond has nine remaining annual payments. At the same 7% required yield, its modeled sale value is approximately CAD 869.70. The year-one cash is the coupon plus that sale value: 50 + 869.695355 = approximately CAD 919.70. Relative to the original CAD 1,000 purchase, the one-year total return is about −8.0305%. Using the ten-year shocked price as the year-one sale price would retain a payment date that has already passed. The waterfall starts with purchase cost, replaces it with the correctly aged sale or redemption value, then adds the first coupon once. It is a reconciliation of ending cash, not an assumption that purchase cost itself earns an additional payment. No reinvestment rate is required because the only received coupon arrives at the endpoint. With exactly one year remaining at purchase, the final coupon and principal are both paid at year-end. No bond remains to sell, so changing the exit-yield control cannot change that assumed redemption cash. With unchanged required yield under the stated conventions, the one-year coupon-plus-exit return equals the initial annual yield; this does not make the same return certain when default, costs or other payment terms are possible. Distinguish an individual bond from a rolling portfolio An individual noncallable bond has a specified principal repayment date, subject to the issuer meeting its obligations. A conventional open-ended bond fund typically replaces maturing or sold holdings. Its duration exposure can remain substantial even after you have held the fund for several years. For a spending goal on a known date, compare the cash-flow schedule with the liability rather than assuming the word “bond” supplies a maturity match. A target-maturity fund has its own termination and distribution terms, which require separate inspection. Holding an individual bond to maturity does not make its interim economic value stable. It can remove the need to realize a market loss through sale if the cash flows meet your needs and the issuer pays. It does not remove default, inflation, reinvestment, or opportunity-cost risk. Separate government yields from credit spreads A corporate bond’s yield can rise because the government yield curve rises, because its credit spread widens, or both. A single duration number cannot explain the cause. Credit deterioration can hurt a corporate portfolio even while government yields fall. As an additional hypothetical stress, a spread duration of 4 and a 0.50-percentage-point spread widening imply approximately −2% from that spread move, before interactions and other effects. Do not add this to an all-in yield shock if the all-in shock already includes the same widening. The Investor.gov bond overview identifies credit, interest-rate, inflation, liquidity, and call risks. In practice, ask which of these risks the holding is meant to carry and which could interfere with its role in the portfolio. A useful bond-fund review Record the fund’s role: near-term spending, diversification, income, or a deliberate rate exposure. Match yield definitions and check whether fees have already been deducted. Inspect duration, maturity distribution, credit quality, sector weights, and currency policy. Stress parallel yields, curve shape, spreads, and liquidity separately. Compare the resulting drawdown with the date and flexibility of the spending need. Higher reinvestment yields may help over time after rates rise, while lower reinvestment yields can reduce future income after rates fall. The realized path depends on when the moves occur and how the portfolio changes. A duration-only stress is an exposure estimate, not a complete reinvestment model or a promise about long-term recovery.

documents.title: When higher yields hurt the price but help later cash: chart a bond’s investment horizon
documents.description: Follow sale value, coupons and reinvestment growth across time, reconcile the offsetting effects and test cash dates against constant yield scenarios in four charts.
documents.body: A bond’s immediate price reaction and the cash available years later answer different questions. The comparison date and the reinvestment assumptions determine how the two effects combine. Begin with the same bond and two different yield paths The example buys a hypothetical bond with CAD 100,000 face value, a fixed 5% annual coupon and ten years to maturity. Its purchase yield is 5% effective annually, so the purchase price is CAD 100,000. The purchase occurs immediately after a coupon boundary, with no accrued interest or dealing cost. Immediately afterward, the selected scenario changes the yield to 7%. It then keeps that yield constant for pricing every remaining payment and reinvesting every receipt. The comparison leaves the yield at 5%. Both own the same contractual cash flows and begin with the same purchase outlay. The SEC’s fixed-income bulletin explains the inverse relationship between fixed-rate bond prices and market yields. This article adds an explicit cash ledger so that the immediate price effect can be read beside the later reinvestment effect. The first plotted value comes after the yield change The line chart starts at time zero immediately after the hypothetical rate change. In the changed-yield scenario, the remaining payments are discounted at 7%, so the bond’s value is below the original CAD 100,000 purchase price. The 5% comparison begins at the original price. A lower initial point is not a new deposit or a withdrawal. It is a change in the model sale value. The two scenarios still receive the same CAD 5,000 coupon at the end of each year and the same CAD 100,000 face amount at maturity. Each subsequent point falls immediately after that year’s payment. Before maturity, plotted wealth combines the assumed sale value of unpaid bond cash flows with cash already received and reinvested. At and after maturity, there is no outstanding bond: the model replaces it with received principal, which also earns the selected reinvestment rate. An early cash date can be dominated by the price effect At the end of year one, the 7% scenario has CAD 86,969.54 of remaining bond sale value and the just-paid CAD 5,000 coupon. The coupon has had no time to earn additional interest. Together they give CAD 91,969.54. The unchanged-yield comparison has CAD 100,000 of bond value plus the same CAD 5,000 coupon, totaling CAD 105,000. The changed-yield result is CAD 13,030.46 lower. It is also CAD 8,030.46 below the original purchase outlay. Those are different comparisons and should be labelled separately. The chart assumes that the remaining bond can be sold immediately at its calculated value. A real household cash goal also needs a buyer, settlement time and usable proceeds. The model includes no bid–ask spread, liquidity restriction or credit deterioration, so it cannot establish the actual amount available from a sale. Read the year-eight offset in its original units At the default eight-year horizon, the changed-yield sale value is CAD 96,383.96. Eight coupons originally contributed CAD 40,000 of cash. Reinvesting those coupons at 7% grows their combined value to CAD 51,299.01, including CAD 11,299.01 of growth. Total modeled wealth is CAD 147,682.98 . The 5% comparison has CAD 100,000 of sale value and CAD 47,745.54 of accumulated coupon cash, for CAD 147,745.54 . The changed-yield result is only about CAD 62.57 lower at this date, despite its much larger early price disadvantage. The waterfall explains the reconciliation: sale value is CAD 3,616.04 lower, while growth on received cash is CAD 3,553.47 higher. The original coupon amounts cancel because the contracts are identical. Adding a separate coupon difference would count a change that never occurred. Duration explains a local balance, rather than a guaranteed finish Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average payment time. For this example, calculate the present value of each annual cash flow at the original 5% yield, multiply each by its payment year, add those weighted amounts and divide by the purchase price. The result is approximately 8.10782 model years . The CFA Institute’s public interest-rate-risk overview connects investment horizon with price and coupon-reinvestment effects. In this constant-yield model, choosing a horizon equal to the original duration makes the first-order effect of a small immediate yield change zero. That is a local mathematical result. The selected eight-year horizon is close to, rather than exactly equal to, 8.10782 years. A two-percentage-point change is also a finite change. Do not expect identical wealth for every large rate movement, or treat an originally matched duration as a permanent hedge against later changes in the yield curve. Use a cash-flow identity to check the result Let CF t be the coupon plus any principal due at year t, H the comparison date and y the constant post-purchase annual yield as a fraction. Each received payment grows forward to H; each unpaid payment is discounted back to H. The combined value is W(y,H) = Σ CF t (1+y) H−t . The same expression equals P(y) × (1+y) H , where P(y) is the value at time zero of all remaining payments discounted at y. This identity checks the complete cash ledger; it does not mean the investor originally paid the changed-yield price P(y). The actual purchase price remains the value calculated using the original yield. For a positive horizon, annualized wealth return is (horizon wealth ÷ actual purchase price) 1/H − 1. The unchanged 5% case produces 5% under these reinvestment assumptions. The default changed-yield eight-year case produces about 4.99444%. A coupon percentage alone would not supply either complete result. Maturity removes the outstanding bond, but not every reinvestment question At year ten, both cases have received the same CAD 100,000 principal and CAD 50,000 of original coupons. The 7% case has accumulated CAD 19,082.24 of coupon-reinvestment growth; the 5% case has CAD 12,889.46. Their wealth totals are CAD 169,082.24 and CAD 162,889.46, a difference of CAD 6,192.78. There is no remaining sale-price difference at this point because the assumed principal payment has occurred in both cases. For later dates, the model reinvests that principal too. It does not leave principal inside an already matured bond or add it a second time to an outstanding bond value. If the household instead spends each coupon, those amounts are unavailable to compound toward this cash goal. If principal is needed immediately at maturity, no later principal-reinvestment income belongs in that goal. Use the actual intended treatment of receipts when interpreting the chart. Use the matrix to expose the date assumption The matrix changes the cash date and the constant post-purchase yield. Each cell subtracts the unchanged-yield wealth at that same date. A negative value describes a disadvantage against that comparison, while a positive value describes an advantage. Neither is a probability or a statement that the household’s required payment is funded. This model deliberately excludes default, calls, changing credit spreads, taxes, fees, inflation, foreign currency and later rate changes. Its annual coupons and flat discount rate are teaching conventions. Actual securities may have different payment schedules and contractual options. For a real goal, begin with its required cash date, verify the security’s payment schedule and consider what happens if a sale is required earlier. Then document the treatment of each coupon and maturity receipt. The four charts help reveal those assumptions before an attractive yield is treated as a complete financial plan.

documents.title: Where Canadians seek financial advice, and how to budget for the service
documents.description: Four charts pair selected official survey observations with a separate, editable comparison of an initial planning project, periodic reviews and an annual retainer.
documents.body: Survey popularity does not measure advice quality. Define the service you need, verify its scope and price, and draw the payment calendar before judging the cost. Use the survey to understand reported behaviour FCAC’s advice spotlight reports professional-advisor use of 20% among people aged 18–34, 26% among those aged 35–54, and 27% among those aged 55 or older. Its data come from the 2024 Canadian Financial Capability Survey. The spotlight was issued on 17 November 2025 and modified on 21 November; the observations remain tied to the survey period. The first chart uses a different denominator for each age group. Adding the percentages would not produce a national share. The gaps describe reported use; the displayed source does not supply uncertainty intervals for these comparisons, and this guide makes no significance or causal claim. The second chart selects three sources among the 18–34 group: family or friends, professional advisors and social media. People can use more than one channel, and other channels are omitted. The bars are therefore not a complete allocation of one common pool. A pie chart would suggest a partition that these selected figures do not establish. Define the work before comparing a fee A statement about where people obtain advice does not tell you whether an individual source can answer your specific question. A tax calculation, an investment implementation task and an ongoing household plan can require different work and qualifications. FCAC’s guidance on choosing an advisor recommends examining the services, cost, compensation and relevant experience. For a real engagement, clarify the deliverables, the assumptions to be reviewed, who performs the work and which follow-up is included. Check the current qualifications and applicable authorizations for the actual services needed. The calculator below assumes two hypothetical fee packages. It does not assume that their services are equivalent, that one arrangement produces better outcomes, or that a survey respondent used either package. The figures are entered prices for a budgeting exercise, not evidence of typical Canadian fees. An initial project and an annual retainer have different dates The project schedule pays one initial planning fee immediately. It then pays a separate review fee after each selected number of complete years, provided that payment falls inside the chosen service window. The annual-retainer schedule pays at the start of every service year, including an immediate first payment. In the original example, the initial project costs CAD 1,500. A CAD 500 review in starting-date dollars is scheduled every three years, and the competing first annual retainer is CAD 1,800. Future quoted review and retainer fees increase at an assumed 2% per year. A review after three years is paid at time three, the start of service year four. A window containing only the first three service years does not include that later payment. Over ten service years, the original project schedule includes reviews at times three, six and nine, with nominal amounts of approximately CAD 530.60, CAD 563.08 and CAD 597.55. The annual-fee chart connects the amounts charged at successive year starts. The connecting line is a reading aid; it does not add charges between those payment dates. Keep total cash outlay separate from the value of payment timing The final chart accumulates the nominal fees. In the original ten-year example, the project and scheduled reviews total approximately CAD 3,191.23. The growing annual retainer totals approximately CAD 19,709.50. Both totals include their immediate first payment. The present-cost metric answers a different question. It discounts each dated payment back to the start using the selected effective annual discount assumption. A payment at time t has present cost payment ÷ (1 + discount rate) t . An immediate payment has t = 0 and is not discounted. At the original 3% discount assumption, the present costs are approximately CAD 2,915.12 and CAD 17,233.61, a difference of CAD 14,318.49. These are timing calculations, not investment returns or the value of advice. A higher nominal total paid over many years need not have the same present cost as the same nominal amount paid immediately. The discount input is independent of the fee-growth assumption. Setting it equal to fee growth makes every annual-retainer payment have the same starting-date present cost under this model; that is an arithmetic identity, not a forecast about prices or markets. Use the cost schedule as one part of a service decision Before implementing a fee budget, obtain the actual terms. A quote may exclude implementation, additional meetings, specialized work, sales tax, investment-product expenses or a change in circumstances. An annual arrangement may include services that a one-time project does not, and the reverse can also be true. The tool calculates neither the cash available to pay the bill nor any benefit from the service. A low total does not establish that a plan can be implemented or maintained; a high total does not establish that the work creates enough value. Service scope, competence, incentives and the ability to act on recommendations need their own review. Write the question or decision for which help is needed. Confirm the deliverables and the relevant expertise. List the initial, recurring and event-triggered charges separately. Place each charge at its payment date and budget the cash. Review the arrangement when circumstances or the work required change. The survey panels provide context for how people report seeking help. The fee panels provide an inspectable cost calendar. Keeping those roles separate allows the article to explain both without treating popularity as a quality score or a quoted fee as a promised financial result.

documents.title: Reading pension statistics: count the plans, count the members and check the dates
documents.description: Explore four charts from an official Canadian pension-table snapshot, with a reference-year selector, separate count scales and a reconciled funding-instrument breakdown.
documents.body: Plan counts and active-member counts describe different quantities. Their dates, units and classifications must be clear before the numbers can inform a planning question. Start with the two things being counted Statistics Canada’s Table 11-10-0099-01 reports registered pension plans, active members and asset measures across several dimensions. This article selects Canada, total registered pension plans and the count statistics for plans and active members, both sexes. It does not select the table’s percentage or asset-value measures. For the 2025 table reference, the selected plan count is 15,762 and the reported active-member count is 7,352,686. Those figures have different units. They cannot be added to form a meaningful total, and one should not be labelled as the other. A reported member count also is not a dollar amount or an annual pension quote. It cannot show how much a particular household will receive in retirement. The charts provide context for understanding the pension system, while an individual plan statement supplies a different kind of evidence. The January reference date does not put every measure on the same day The source metadata distinguishes its reporting clocks. The number of plans and their terms refer to 1 January. Membership relates to the plan’s year-end in the preceding calendar year, normally 31 December. A column headed 2025 therefore does not make every membership observation a live count on 1 January 2025. The charts retain the publisher’s table reference years from 2021 through 2025. Their titles and notes identify the membership timing, rather than silently relabelling it as a current 2026 observation. The snapshot was released on 28 July 2026 and checked on 25 October 2026. The reference-year control changes which columns of that fixed snapshot are displayed. It does not request fresh observations or extend the data into later years. Starting the control at 2022 retains at least two reference points for the comparisons, while every index continues to use the same 2021 baseline. Compare changes on an index, then return to the absolute counts The 2021 reference contains 16,359 plans and 6,593,256 reported active members. By the 2025 reference, the plan count is lower by 597 while the reported membership is higher by 759,430. The direction of one quantity does not determine the direction of the other. The first chart divides each series by its own 2021 value and multiplies by 100. Both begin at 100, allowing their proportional changes to be read on one index scale. An index of 110 means that a series is 10% above its own starting value. It does not mean 110% of employees are covered. The index chart uses a declared 95–115 vertical range to make the proportional movements visible. The second and third charts keep the original counts on separate scales. This avoids plotting roughly sixteen thousand plans and several million members on the same absolute axis, which would make one series visually disappear. The zero-based plan bars also keep modest differences in plan counts in proportion. The pattern alone does not establish why counts changed. A change in the organisation or composition of plans could matter, but attributing the observed difference to a specific cause would require further evidence. These figures do not follow one worker through a career. Read a funding category as a classification, not a benefit promise The final chart groups reported members by funding instrument for the selected reference year. The metadata describes the funding instrument through the legal or contractual arrangement used to hold and invest contributions. There are six direct categories below the total in the selected hierarchy. The insurance-company-contract total has more detailed subcategories of its own. Adding those children again alongside their parent would count the same category membership twice, so the graphic uses only the six direct categories. The curated extract checks that those six values sum to the published active-member total for every displayed reference year. For the 2025 reference, the trust-agreement category reports 4,276,098 active members; that is a category count, not a personal account balance. This classification answers a different question from defined-benefit versus defined-contribution design. It also does not describe an equity/bond allocation or the quality of a provider. A funding label cannot replace the actual plan terms when you need to understand investment responsibility, benefit calculation or access to money. Translate the statistical question into the personal records you need Before using a national figure in a personal plan, identify the missing information. To measure a share of employed people, you would need a suitable employment denominator and matching definitions and periods. Dividing these counts by an unrelated population figure would not establish that coverage rate. To estimate retirement cash, obtain the administrator’s actual benefit statement or account information, expected payment dates, applicable options and a separate tax assessment. Keep a capital balance distinct from an annual pension payment. No national member count supplies those details. Write down the measure, unit, reference date and population. Use the original count scale for magnitudes and a declared baseline for proportional changes. Check whether category totals and subcategories overlap. Identify what additional evidence is needed for the household decision. Recheck the public table for revisions before treating a snapshot as current. The four graphics support this reading process. They do not estimate a personal entitlement, forecast future membership, calculate a worker-coverage probability or recommend a pension option.

documents.title: A one-year GIC rate does not lock in five years: chart the renewal assumption
documents.description: Compare five consecutive one-year deposits with one five-year deposit, trace annual interest differences and solve the later renewal rate that equates their final values.
documents.body: A fixed rate applies to the term purchased. Reinvesting at maturity creates a new rate decision, so a higher first-year rate does not establish the better five-year outcome. Separate the deposit term from the planning horizon A household may have a five-year goal while comparing deposits with different terms. A one-year rate describes the first purchase. It does not by itself specify the return earned in years two through five, when another deposit would need to be purchased. The OSC Investor Office’s GIC overview explains that a maturity creates choices, including reinvesting or taking the money in cash. This guide treats each reinvestment as a new purchase with an explicitly assumed rate. It does not assume the original rate will still be available. The comparison starts each alternative with CAD 50,000 and ends both after five years. One buys successive one-year deposits and reinvests all proceeds at each maturity. The other buys one five-year deposit that compounds annually and pays everything at its final maturity. There are no extra contributions or spending withdrawals. Read the rate calendar before the ending balances Restore the example to give the first one-year deposit a hypothetical 4% rate and the five-year deposit a hypothetical 3.5% annual compound rate. The first-year interest amounts are therefore CAD 2,000 and CAD 1,750 respectively. The one-year case finishes its first term at CAD 52,000 and appears ahead by CAD 250. The selected later renewal rate is 2%, however, and applies separately in each of the following four years. The five-year deposit keeps its original 3.5% compound rate under the assumed agreement. The rate bars show that difference directly. This is an invented rate structure, not a statement about the current yield curve or the best available product. A real comparison needs dated quotes for the initial purchases and a clearly identified assumption for any future rates that cannot yet be locked in. Reinvest the returned principal and interest exactly once The rolling case’s five-year endpoint is CAD 50,000 × 1.04 × 1.02 4 , or about CAD 56,286.47. Every annual maturity returns both principal and interest. All of that money buys the next one-year deposit, rather than being counted as an additional contribution from the household. The five-year endpoint is CAD 50,000 × 1.035 5 , or about CAD 59,384.32. Under these inputs, rolling the shorter terms finishes about CAD 3,097.84 behind despite the higher first-year rate. The value chart uses matching year-ends. The rolling balance is available at each annual maturity immediately before the assumed reinvestment. The intermediate five-year figures are accrued values under the compound formula. They are not promises of accessible cash or early-redemption proceeds. Comparing their heights alone does not establish that both choices provide the same liquidity. Explain the final gap through annual interest differences The waterfall compares interest earned in each year. It starts with the rolling case’s CAD 250 first-year advantage, then adds the later annual differences. The later figures use each alternative’s own accumulated opening balance, so they preserve the consequences of earlier compounding. Adding those annual differences reconciles to the same negative CAD 3,097.84 endpoint. No separate deduction for original principal belongs in that bridge because both alternatives began with the same principal. Likewise, a maturity proceeds amount is not all interest: it includes capital already invested. This decomposition helps locate the assumption driving the result. The first-year quote is not irrelevant, but it is only one part of a five-year sequence. If later renewal rates were higher instead, the outcome could change. The model isolates that possibility without claiming to know which future rate path will occur. Find the constant later rate that makes the endpoints equal The break-even calculation solves for one constant rate applied to each of the four renewals after year one. Its equation is (1 + first-year rate) × (1 + later rate) 4 = (1 + five-year rate) 5 . At the default inputs, the later rate is about 3.38% annually. A common later rate above that mathematical threshold makes rolling finish larger; one below it makes the five-year case finish larger, under the stated assumptions. The threshold is not a rate offer or a prediction of what an institution will pay. The matrix replaces the first-year and later renewal rates while holding initial capital and the five-year rate selected. It retains signed final differences. A negative mathematical break-even rate can occur when the first-year advantage is already sufficient under the comparison; that does not imply a negative rate is available. With no principal invested, the two values are zero and the displayed break-even rate is unavailable. Bring cash access and taxes back into the actual plan A rate comparison should follow a cash-needs review. Annual maturities create decision points, but this tool assumes every dollar is reinvested immediately. Spending part of the proceeds would reduce later invested capital and require another schedule. An actual lock-in, redemption condition or renewal instruction also needs to be read from the agreement. The calculations are before tax and fees. A taxable account can need tax cash before a compound deposit pays out; a registered account can have separate contribution or withdrawal rules. Those questions are outside this comparison. The illustration also assumes repayment as agreed and does not establish deposit-insurance coverage. Use the four views to distinguish the term purchased, the rate assumed at each renewal, the accrued value and the cash actually released. The practical decision record should identify the initial quote, the future rate assumptions, the common comparison date and any earlier spending need. A higher rate on one short term is only one input to that record.

documents.title: A later pension quote needs a price year: compare future payments with today’s purchasing power
documents.description: Identify whether a retirement-income amount is quoted in today’s dollars or its future payment year, then map the income components and spending on consistent dates.
documents.body: A future payment and its value in today’s purchasing power are different amounts. Record a quote’s price year and payment date before applying indexing or comparing it with a current spending budget. Record the quote’s price year as well as its payment date A retirement-income quote can describe a future payment amount or express that future benefit in today’s purchasing power. Those descriptions use different units. Entering the same numeral without recording its price year can make a plan appear better funded than the underlying quote supports. A pension deposit can also contain a lifetime part and a temporary part. As a specific plan example, the federal public-service pension explanation distinguishes lifetime pension from a bridge benefit, with its stated normal age-65 end and an earlier disability-related exception. Those are that plan’s provisions, not universal employer-pension rules. This tool combines the two planning questions: what amount is payable in each period, and what price year does the amount represent? It uses independent net-cash inputs rather than that plan’s pension formula or a CPP, QPP or OAS entitlement calculation. Real quotes must supply their own gross/net basis, start date, indexing and price-year convention. Give each stream its own start or stop date The default starts at age 60 with CAD 24,000 of annual net lifetime pension and a CAD 12,000 annual net temporary supplement. Together they provide CAD 36,000 in the first modeled year. The temporary amount is absent from the full year labelled age 65 onward. A separate CAD 9,000 annual net income begins at age 67. This is an independently entered amount in its first payment year. It is not calculated from the lost supplement or a government-benefit formula. The model therefore includes two annual periods, ages 65 and 66, after the supplement ends and before that later income begins. The selected 2% annual increase applies separately to each income stream while payable. Lifetime and temporary amounts grow from their first modeled amounts; later income grows from its own first payment year. These are original indexing assumptions, not a claim that real sources all receive the same increases or have the same after-tax treatment. Compare net resources with spending on the same basis The initial spending basket is CAD 36,000 and rises by an assumed 2% annually. Before the supplement ends, the default income and spending assumptions move together. This is a controlled reference, not evidence that a particular household’s expenses and pension will match. At the full-year age-65 point, lifetime net pension is about CAD 26,497.94. The temporary component and later income are both zero. The annual spending basket is about CAD 39,746.91, leaving an annual gap of about CAD 13,248.97. At age 66, the gap is about CAD 13,513.95, the largest annual gap in the default schedule. Later income begins at age 67 and reduces the difference, but it does not automatically eliminate it. The net-cash inputs have already assumed tax and deductions; the chart does not calculate them or subtract a second flat tax amount from those same inputs. Convert future dollars once, and index only from the correct date The CAD 9,000 later-income input is an amount in its first payment year, age 67. With the model beginning at age 60 and assumed spending inflation of 2%, that payment represents about CAD 7,835.04 in the first modeled year’s purchasing power: CAD 9,000 ÷ 1.02 7 . A quote of CAD 9,000 in age-60 purchasing power would imply a different nominal age-67 amount under that same price assumption: about CAD 10,338.17. The quotation-basis bars compare those two interpretations of the same numeral. They do not calculate two available benefits or recommend a claiming age. If the quote already means CAD 9,000 actually payable in the future first year, increasing it by seven years of inflation again would overstate that annual amount by about CAD 1,338.17. The model therefore begins the later stream at its entered first-payment-year amount and applies its separate income-growth assumption only after payments start. The lifetime and temporary inputs instead begin in the first modeled year. Those different starting bases are stated beside the controls. An annual gap total is not a required investment balance The matrix changes the first-payment-year later-income amount and its start age while retaining the other selected assumptions. A repeated nominal amount at a later start is not a repeated amount of starting-year purchasing power. Each cell sums positive annual spending gaps through age 90. The default total is about CAD 172,308.05 across the full schedule. That figure is undiscounted and does not carry a surplus from one year to another. It is neither an opening capital requirement nor a recommended portfolio withdrawal. Converting a sequence of gaps into a funded asset plan requires starting assets, returns, costs, withdrawal timing, taxes and a rule for handling any surplus. The tool assumes the person remains alive and the described payments remain available through the selected age range. It does not attach a survival probability, measure lifetime value or compare pension elections. Its narrower task is to reveal the income calendar and the years that need another supported funding source. Replace the annual illustration with actual plan evidence Request the lifetime and temporary amounts separately, along with the exact month in which each component begins or ends. Record whether each quoted amount is already expressed in its future payment year or in a stated current price year. The annual age labels used here omit partial-year payments. They are not a monthly implementation of a plan’s birthday rule, processing lag or disability provision. The federal source illustrates why that precision matters: it describes the bridge ending in the month after the 65th birthday, and explains how early or later CPP/QPP retirement timing interacts with the temporary payment. This calculator applies none of those individual eligibility or adjustment calculations. Its later income must be independently supported for the age entered. Then reconcile the amounts to household spending and the rest of the retirement plan. Keep survivor changes, tax estimates, health costs and indexing conditions visible rather than hiding them inside a single annual growth rate. A current total pension deposit is useful evidence about today’s cash; a component-by-component schedule is needed to understand what may change.

documents.title: DIY or hired work: separate actual cash savings from the value of personal time
documents.description: Compare all-in task costs, genuine earnings forgone and non-work hours. Keep a subjective value for personal time visible without turning it into an extra bill.
documents.body: Only hours that actually remove paid work create the modeled earnings loss. Non-work time can still matter to the decision, but its subjective value belongs in a separate comparison from cash outlays. Compare the same completed task before comparing prices A decision to complete a task yourself can change both money and personal time. A lower materials bill alone does not describe the full cash effect, and assigning a wage to every free hour can misstate it in the other direction. Begin with a comparable scope. The federal Office of Consumer Affairs renovation guide emphasizes detailed work and contract information. Here, the hired quote and the DIY alternative are assumed to deliver the same defined task. The model does not assess quality, qualifications or whether a particular job is appropriate for DIY. Restore the example to use a CAD 3,000 all-in hired price, CAD 1,200 of DIY materials and CAD 300 of new tools and other upfront costs. All known taxes and fees are already included. The tools receive no resale or future-use credit in this example, so the entire initial outlay remains in the cash comparison. Identify paid work that would actually be lost The DIY task takes fifty personal hours. The selected 40% share means twenty of those hours genuinely displace paid work that would otherwise be available. At independently entered after-tax earnings of CAD 30 per displaced hour, the household forgoes CAD 600 of take-home income. The other thirty hours come from non-work time. They may be valuable, but the model does not assume those hours could automatically have been sold at the person’s wage. A fixed-salary employee doing a task on a free weekend might enter a zero displaced-work share even if their usual hourly-equivalent salary is high. The distinction depends on the actual alternative, not simply an employment contract’s headline pay. A reduction in overtime, a cancelled paid shift or foregone billable work can create a cash effect. Free time that would not have produced earnings does not create the same missing cash inflow. Tax and work-related costs should already be reflected in the independently entered net earnings amount. Reconcile the cash saving without pricing leisure twice The DIY cash-resource cost is CAD 1,200 of materials plus CAD 300 of new tools plus CAD 600 of earnings actually forgone, for CAD 2,100. Compared with the CAD 3,000 hired price, this produces a CAD 900 cash-resource saving. The waterfall retains the distinction between cash spent and cash not earned. The CAD 600 is not another invoice from a supplier; it is a reduction in household inflow. Both effects matter to how much money remains available after the task. No charge for the remaining thirty DIY hours appears in this cash bridge. Adding a subjective leisure value here and then adding it again in a broader comparison would count it twice. Likewise, a work hour already valued through lost after-tax earnings should not receive a second charge as a non-work hour. Add a subjective time value as a separate layer The example independently values each non-work hour at CAD 40. Thirty DIY non-work hours then have a subjective value of CAD 1,200. Hiring the task uses five non-work coordination hours, valued at CAD 200. Adding those separate time values to cash-resource costs gives CAD 3,300 for DIY and CAD 3,200 for hiring. The broader comparison therefore favors hiring by CAD 100 under that preference, even though DIY saves CAD 900 in cash resources. The stacked bars show which part of each total is cash and which part is a non-cash valuation. Those combined amounts are decision aids, not bank balances, invoices or investment returns. The CAD 40 input can reflect how strongly a person values time for rest, family or other activities. Another household can reasonably enter a different amount, including zero. The tool does not claim to discover an objective price for personal time. Read the relevant time difference before dividing the cash saving DIY uses forty-five more personal hours overall than the five-hour coordination alternative. However, twenty DIY hours have already been charged through the CAD 600 of lost earnings. The remaining non-work-time difference is thirty DIY hours minus five coordination hours, or twenty-five hours. At the default cash saving, a subjective value of CAD 900 ÷ 25 = CAD 36 per additional non-work hour makes the broader totals equal. That threshold is a preference comparison after accounting for actual lost pay. It is not an hourly wage offer or a statement that the person can earn CAD 36 for every free hour. The matrix instead stays cash-only. It changes task hours and the share that actually displaces paid work, holding the quote, materials, tools and after-tax earnings selected. Subjective time value does not affect those cells. This keeps an affordability question separate from how a household chooses to value its time. Record what could change the comparison Confirm comparable scope, materials, completion standard and included costs before using the result. A quote with cleanup or warranty provisions cannot be compared fairly with a DIY budget that silently omits the relevant work or cost. The model does not assign a warranty value or estimate the cost of redoing a failed task. Check the time estimate against the household calendar. Hired-task coordination is assumed to use non-work time only; if it also displaces paid work, another earnings-loss entry is needed. New tool resale, later reuse, borrowing costs and differences in completion dates can also change the analysis. They should be added explicitly rather than treated as invisible benefits or expenses. The four views support a transparent decision: the hours split, the cash bridge, the separate time valuation and the displaced-work sensitivity. A household can then see whether DIY is affordable, how much cash it would preserve, and what personal time it requires. The calculation does not decide how much that time should matter to the person making the choice.

documents.title: A callable bond can return principal early and stop the coupons your plan expected
documents.description: Use four charts to compare coupon dates, early redemption, reinvested receipts and the value difference at one common original maturity date.
documents.body: An early return of principal changes the income calendar. Test what happens to later coupons and what return the received money can earn afterward. The maturity date is not the only date to read A bond’s coupon and original maturity can suggest a long stream of income. A call provision can change that stream. The issuer may have the right to redeem the bond before its stated maturity under the contract’s terms. Investor.gov’s callable-bond explanation describes the issuer paying the call price and stopping future interest payments. It also highlights the risk of reinvesting the returned money at a less attractive rate. The issuer’s call right is different from an investor’s right to demand an early cash-out. This tool uses original hypothetical cash flows rather than an actual bond quote. It assumes a purchase at face value, annual coupons and a call at face value immediately after a selected coupon. Actual contracts may have different call prices, premiums, protection periods and payment details. Separate principal returned from coupons no longer paid The default face amount is CAD 10,000 with a 6% annual coupon, so each full coupon is CAD 600. The original maturity is ten years. The no-call case pays ten coupons totalling CAD 6,000 and returns CAD 10,000 at the end of year 10. The selected early-call case pays coupons in years 1, 2 and 3, then returns CAD 10,000 immediately after the third coupon. Its issuer coupons total CAD 1,800. It pays no coupons in years 4–10. The difference in issuer coupons is CAD 4,200, but that is not a CAD 4,200 principal loss. Principal has arrived seven years earlier and can be used or reinvested. A complete cash comparison needs to account for that earlier receipt rather than comparing coupon totals alone. Use one common endpoint and state what happens to every receipt The example retains all coupons and principal receipts in a separate reinvestment pool. At each year-end, money already in the pool earns the selected annual return, then the new coupon or redemption arrives. The default return is 2% as an independent assumption. The line chart begins at zero because the opening CAD 10,000 has bought the bond. The large jump at a redemption date represents principal entering the pool. Before original maturity, the chart omits any bond still outstanding, so it is not a comparison of complete interim portfolios. At year 10, both cases have redeemed. The no-call pool is about CAD 16,569.83 and the early-call pool about CAD 13,596.12 under the default assumptions. The common-date difference is approximately negative CAD 2,973.71. These endpoints assume the receipts were retained, rather than spent on household bills. Reconcile missing coupons with the benefit of earlier principal The waterfall begins with the negative CAD 4,200 difference in coupons received from the issuer. It then adds the extra growth on principal that arrived at year 3 rather than year 10. Finally, it includes the difference in growth on the two coupon streams. These components reconcile the gap between the terminal pools. The common principal amount cancels, because both scenarios ultimately return the same face value. The gap is not a quoted bond price, a mark-to-market loss or a guarantee of what a replacement investment will earn. Set reinvestment to zero to isolate nominal receipts. With no growth after receipt, the gap is exactly the CAD 4,200 of issuer coupons no longer paid. Increasing the reinvestment assumption changes the contribution made by the earlier principal. Test the replacement return without predicting the issuer’s decision The matrix changes the call year and reinvestment return while preserving the same face amount, coupon and original maturity. Each cell compares the two cases at the original maturity date. A later call preserves more issuer coupons but leaves less time for early principal to compound. At a 6% reinvestment assumption matching the default 6% coupon, the two terminal pools coincide in this par-purchase example. Both payment schedules can then compound to the same endpoint. With a reinvestment return above the coupon rate, an early principal receipt can even produce a larger modeled terminal pool. That arithmetic does not forecast a favourable call or show when an issuer would rationally exercise its option. The call date and reinvestment return are independent scenario inputs. No option value, probability, credit risk or market pricing is estimated. Build the income plan around the payment terms and the use of cash If coupons are intended to pay ongoing expenses, the relevant question includes how that spending will be replaced after an early call. The reinvested-pool example deliberately retains every receipt, so it does not calculate a household withdrawal plan. Review the actual call schedule and redemption terms before relying on a coupon calendar. Distinguish the annual coupon amount, cash paid at redemption and any replacement-income assumption. For a premium-price purchase or different call amount, the par-value illustration would need a different initial and redemption cash-flow comparison. The related bond-goal guide examines a different timing issue: needing cash before a bond matures. Here the timing changes because the issuer returns principal earlier than the plan expected. Both situations show why an income plan needs dates and cash-flow terms alongside a headline percentage.
