documents.title: A vacation membership has ongoing bills: compare dues, actual use and the reporting window
documents.description: Use five charts to compare an upfront vacation commitment with renting the nights actually used, including rising dues, an assessment, cost per night and discounted cash costs.
documents.body: A low annual usage charge can hide a substantial upfront payment and continuing fees. Divide the complete cost by nights actually used, and keep the model’s finish date separate from the contract’s obligations. Identify the commitment before comparing the nightly price A vacation ownership, right-to-use arrangement or points membership can combine an upfront purchase with recurring charges. Its value to a household depends on the rights obtained, the dates available, how often those rights are used and the costs that continue even in a year without travel. The Government of Canada’s consumer guide to timeshares distinguishes different arrangements and recommends examining availability, additional fees, ongoing costs and resale conditions. The examples here do not reproduce any provider’s contract. They assume a cash purchase and enough availability for the entered usage. Begin with comparable accommodation: similar dates, location, room type, taxes and included services. A membership entitlement is not evidence that a desired booking can be made. A rental price observed for a quiet week is also not a reliable comparison for a peak holiday stay. The model keeps those qualitative questions outside its arithmetic rather than pretending the costs settle them. The first annual bill does not include the purchase already paid The default case pays CAD 30,000 at the start, then CAD 1,300 of first-year dues and a CAD 100 booking charge in each year with use. It uses seven nights per year for a fifteen-year reporting window. Dues rise by an assumed 4% annually, and a hypothetical CAD 5,000 assessment arrives in year eight. First-year recurring costs are CAD 1,400, compared with CAD 1,750 for seven rental nights at CAD 250 each. The annual-cost bars could therefore make the ownership case look cheaper if the upfront purchase were ignored. The cumulative cash chart begins at CAD 30,000 precisely to prevent that omission. Across the full window, dues total about CAD 26,030.66. Adding the purchase, CAD 1,500 of booking charges and the CAD 5,000 assessment brings ownership cash paid to about CAD 62,530.66. The rental alternative, with a separate 3% annual price-growth assumption, totals about CAD 32,548.10. Those are original scenario results, not market prices or a forecast for a particular resort. Divide by nights used, not nights advertised Seven nights per year across fifteen years produce 105 nights actually used. Dividing the complete nominal ownership cost by that usage gives about CAD 595.53 per night. This is an allocation of the reporting-window cost, not an additional charge paid when checking in. Unused entitlement does not become free accommodation in the model. If no nights are used, booking fees disappear under the stated assumption, but the purchase, dues and any included assessment remain. The cost-per-used-night metric then says that no nights were used instead of dividing by zero or reporting a misleading zero cost. The sensitivity matrix shows why actual use matters. More nights spread the same assumed purchase and fixed annual charges across more consumption. That does not prove more nights are available or desirable, and travelling more can create costs excluded here. Also avoid comparing the ownership average directly with today’s rental quote: rental prices change across the window too. Compare the same period and cost basis on both sides. Recurring increases and occasional assessments have different effects Dues grow on an increasing base. At the default 4% assumption, year-eight dues are about CAD 1,710.71, before the booking charge and the entered assessment. That assessment lifts the ownership cash cost in year eight to about CAD 6,810.71. A smooth average annual amount would conceal the year when the larger payment is due. The annual bars include the first year, the finish, each fifth year within the window and any included assessment year. The waterfall then reconciles all purchase, dues, booking and assessment dollars. Together they show both the accumulation of recurring costs and the concentration of a selected extra bill. The assessment is a stress input. It is not a reserve study, an estimate of a property’s condition or a probability-weighted forecast. A bill assigned after the reporting finish is excluded from the current total; it has not been forgiven. Real contracts can contain other charges or different collection dates, which need to be added to an actual cash plan. Discounting future charges does not make the invoice smaller The final comparison places undiscounted cash costs beside present values. The purchase is at time zero. Annual costs are placed at year-end and divided by (1 + discount rate) year . At the default 3% discount assumption, ownership costs have a present value of about CAD 55,415.26 and rental costs about CAD 25,485.44. These present values express the timing difference on a common comparison date. They are not balances in an investment account, additional costs to add to the nominal totals or an estimate of the membership’s resale price. The selected discount rate is a valuation assumption, not an offered investment return. A future CAD 5,000 assessment still requires CAD 5,000 when it falls due even though its present value is smaller today. Actual annual dues can also be collected earlier than the model’s year-end convention. For liquidity planning, replace the annual aggregate with actual payment dates; a discounted cost comparison does not establish how much cash must be available before each invoice. The reporting finish is not a promised exit The fifteen-year default is a measurement window. It does not establish that a deed, lease-like arrangement or membership ends then, that a buyer will appear, or that a provider will release the household from further charges. No resale receipt, exit payment or rental income from unused rights is included. If a real arrangement continues beyond the window, the omitted costs remain relevant to the decision. Extending the model includes more years of the assumed dues and usage, but it still cannot determine legal obligations or saleability. An expected resale amount needs its own evidence about the net receipt, timing and costs rather than being inserted simply to make a comparison look favourable. Read the actual contract and the applicable local requirements independently of the charts. For a foreign-currency obligation, convert dues and other payments on a consistent basis and stress the exchange rate separately. The Government of Canada guide was last modified in June 2024; it is useful consumer context, while current contract terms and jurisdiction-specific questions require fresh checking. Build the comparison from use, costs and commitments you can verify Record the rights, booking limits and dates the household can realistically use. List the cash purchase, all recurring fees and possible additional charges. Choose the same accommodation and usage basis for the rental comparison. Test lower use and higher dues without assuming either is a forecast. Keep cash due dates, reporting-window costs and actual exit conditions separate. The result is a structured cost comparison, not a recommendation for or against a product. Enjoyment, flexibility, booking risk, travel costs and the household’s willingness to accept a long commitment remain part of the decision alongside the numbers.

documents.title: A construction-price index is not your renovation quote: build the budget from its actual parts
documents.description: Read official construction-price changes, compare an earlier estimate with a detailed quote, reconcile project cash and test a separate contingency in four charts.
documents.body: A market index describes its defined construction population and period. A workable household project still needs a current scope, a complete quote and cash for commitments outside that quote. Read what the index measures before using its percentage Statistics Canada’s 24 July 2026 release reported a 0.5% quarterly rise in the residential Building Construction Price Index for its 15-CMA composite. The first chart also displays six selected local changes, including positive and negative values. It is not a complete ranking. The index measures contractor prices for new buildings. It excludes land and specified development, design, tax and real-estate costs. It is not seasonally adjusted, and prior-quarter values may be revised. It is neither a renovation quote nor a rebuilding appraisal. The composite is not the simple average of the six local observations shown. Those scope distinctions explain why a household cannot turn the headline into a complete project budget. A statistic can supply useful background while leaving the particular work, quantities, condition and contractual inclusions unresolved. The model therefore keeps the official chart fixed and asks for a separate quote. Give the earlier estimate and the current quote a clear scope The example starts with an earlier contract budget of CAD 80,000: CAD 40,000 for materials, CAD 30,000 for labour and CAD 10,000 for other contract costs. The current quote allocates CAD 44,000, CAD 34,500 and CAD 10,000 to the same three headings, totaling CAD 88,500. The category chart makes the changes visible. Materials are CAD 4,000 higher, labour CAD 4,500 higher and other costs unchanged. Together these add CAD 8,500 to the earlier estimate, a 10.625% difference. That calculation does not establish a market inflation rate. The original estimate may have been incomplete, and the specification or quantity of work may have changed. The Canadian Home Builders’ Association’s contract guide recommends comparing quotes against the same plans and specifications. It distinguishes an early rough estimate from a detailed quote and discusses scope, payment terms, taxes and written changes. Use that checklist to establish what is actually being compared before attributing a difference to prices. Allocate the quoted taxes and costs once The calculator’s categories are bookkeeping allocations of the current contract total. They need not match every invoice line. Each amount belongs in one category only, and the three amounts together should reconcile to the quote being reviewed. Include the applicable quoted taxes consistently in those entries. If a contractor’s tax line applies across the job, allocate it across the categories or include it once within the other-cost entry. Do not add it again outside the quote. The tool does not calculate a tax rate or decide whether a supply is taxable. Known outside costs have a separate input. They might include independently obtained design services, temporary accommodation or another item that the particular contract leaves to the household. Enter only costs that are actually outside the entered quote. A service already included by the contractor must not be budgeted a second time. A CAD 88,500 quote can exceed a CAD 100,000 cash plan At first glance, a CAD 88,500 quote appears to fit within CAD 100,000 of assigned cash. The example also has CAD 5,000 of known costs outside the quote and a separately selected contingency equal to 10% of the quote. The contingency earmark is CAD 8,850, so the full selected commitment is CAD 88,500 + CAD 5,000 + CAD 8,850 = CAD 102,350 . The waterfall ends at −CAD 2,350 . The household needs that much additional funding, or a change in the work or other commitments, to support this particular plan. The starting cash must already be available for this project after other household commitments. Money required for the next mortgage payment cannot also fund the renovation. The tool creates no credit line, grant, insurance payment or investment-sale proceeds to fill a negative result. A contingency is reserved money, not a certain extra invoice A contingency holds capacity for an uncertain requirement. It is not automatically paid to a contractor, an investment loss or a prediction that costs will rise by the entered percentage. If unused, it remains household cash. The chart subtracts the earmark when calculating unassigned project cash because that amount has a job in the plan. This treatment does not reduce net worth at the time of budgeting. It prevents the same cash being presented both as a contingency and as money available for another purpose. The percentage applies to the current contract quote alone. It does not apply to the original budget or to known outside costs. At the default quote, a 5% reserve is CAD 4,425; at 10% it is CAD 8,850. Neither setting is presented as a universal professional standard or a probability-based estimate of the project’s risks. Let a quote change affect its reserve as well as its price The matrix scales the current quote by −10%, 0%, +10% and +20%, and separately tests contingency rates of 0%, 5%, 10% and 20%. Known outside costs and available cash remain selected. Every cell reports additional cash needed beyond the amount already assigned. A 10% quote increase raises the example’s contract total to CAD 97,350. With a 10% contingency, the new reserve is CAD 9,735. Adding CAD 5,000 outside costs produces CAD 112,085 of commitments and a CAD 12,085 funding need. The extra need is CAD 9,735 larger than the original CAD 2,350 gap: CAD 8,850 of quote change plus CAD 885 of additional contingency. Holding the reserve fixed while calling it 10% of a larger quote would fail to preserve the stated rule. The matrix recalculates both parts. Finish the scope review, then build the payment calendar A funded total still does not prove that every deposit or progress payment can be made on its date. This calculator assumes all entered cash is already available and does not model dates. Use the separate renovation-payment article to map actual milestones against saving receipts and other obligations. The index also cannot establish an insurer’s replacement-cost estimate, an accepted claim or a coverage limit. Those questions belong in a separate property and policy review. A lower quarterly construction-price change does not by itself justify lowering a particular policy amount. Define the work and compare consistent specifications. Reconcile the current quote, inclusions and taxes. Add verified costs that sit outside that quote. Assign a separate contingency and test changes in both amounts. Match the resulting commitments to actual cash and payment dates. Keep the source period beside the statistic and the quotation date beside the project amount. The two pieces of evidence can inform the same review while answering different questions.

documents.title: ETF tracking: the gap between the index and your return
documents.description: Use four charts to compare matched NAV and index returns, separate annual and cumulative gaps, and distinguish tracking difference from tracking error.
documents.body: Compare the exact benchmark with fund NAV total return first. Then account for the price, spread and conversion costs of your own transaction. Keep three return records separate An index return describes a calculation maintained by an index provider. A fund’s NAV total return describes the performance of its net assets with the stated distribution-reinvestment convention. Your account return additionally reflects the prices and dates of your trades, your cash flows, and any investor-level costs. Write all three on separate lines. Comparing your brokerage account gain with a headline price index can mix distributions, purchase timing, and fund implementation in one unexplained difference. A reliable comparison starts with matching dates, currency, benchmark version, and return definition. The CFA Institute’s ETF overview discusses tracking, trading costs, and premiums or discounts. Those are related dimensions, but they require different measurements. Tracking difference measures the return gap On this page, tracking difference means fund NAV total return minus benchmark total return over the same interval. Some publishers reverse the sign, so check the stated convention. If the benchmark returns 8.00% and the fund returns 7.72%, the difference is −0.28 percentage points, or −28 basis points. Tracking difference = fund NAV total return − matching benchmark total return Do not subtract the fund’s expense ratio again from a published return that is already net of those expenses. Doing so would charge the same cost twice. Similarly, if the benchmark has a net-dividend convention, do not assume the resulting gap is entirely caused by withholding tax. For a multi-year comparison, state whether you subtract annualized returns or compare cumulative wealth. These produce different-looking numbers. An eight-year cumulative shortfall cannot be labelled an annual cost without a suitable annualization. Vanguard Canada’s index-tracking explanation uses this fund-minus-index convention and distinguishes the gap from its standard-deviation measure. The OSC Investor Office’s ETF Facts sample describes displayed performance as net of expenses, supporting the check against deducting an embedded expense twice. Read the actual return definition before applying that check to a real statement. A small annual gap compounds into a different cumulative comparison The controls start both references at CAD 10,000. The benchmark’s hypothetical annual total return is 8.00%, and the fund’s annual NAV total return is 7.72%. The annual fund-minus-benchmark tracking difference is therefore −0.28 percentage points. These are assumed net NAV results; no separate expense-ratio subtraction follows. After ten identical annual factors, benchmark reference wealth is about CAD 21,589.25 and fund NAV wealth is about CAD 21,036.01. The signed fund-minus-benchmark wealth difference is approximately negative CAD 553.24. Relative to the same initial CAD 10,000, that is a −5.5324 percentage-point difference between the two cumulative returns . That cumulative return gap is neither the annual −0.28 percentage-point gap nor the percentage by which ending fund wealth is below ending benchmark wealth. Each comparison uses a different denominator or horizon. Dividing −5.5324 by ten would not recover the annual rate difference. The signed bars state each horizon explicitly. Changing the annual gap to a positive value lets the hypothetical fund exceed the benchmark; this is a sensitivity, not evidence that a real fund can repeatedly achieve that result. The benchmark wealth reference is also a calculation, rather than a directly investable account with no implementation costs. Tracking error measures how variable the gap is Tracking error is commonly the annualized standard deviation of periodic fund-minus-benchmark returns. It asks how much the gap fluctuates. It does not directly measure how much return the investor lost over the whole period. Both series have an arithmetic mean gap of −0.02 percentage points per month. Fund A has zero variability in this deliberately artificial sample; Fund B does not. This is a demonstration of the distinction, not enough history for a useful tracking-error estimate. Equal arithmetic mean gaps also do not guarantee equal compounded wealth. In a real study, record daily or monthly frequency, the sample period, the standard-deviation convention, and the annualization factor. Compare like with like rather than ranking incompatible published statistics. The monthly chart uses the exact four observations in this table, independent of the annual controls. The two artificial series have the same simple mean and different dispersion, but the page does not present their annualized standard deviations as useful estimates. A four-observation pattern illustrates a definition; it does not establish a fund’s likely future tracking error. Do not compound the active-return differences by themselves to reconstruct fund wealth. You would also need the benchmark’s return for each matching month, then compound the fund and benchmark series separately. The monthly pattern and the annual wealth path are deliberately separate examples. Build an explanation instead of guessing from the fee Suppose a hypothetical one-year gap is −0.28 percentage points. An analyst’s illustrative reconciliation might assign −0.15 to operating expenses, −0.06 to portfolio trading, −0.08 to unrecovered taxes, +0.03 to net lending revenue, and −0.02 to other implementation effects. The sum is −0.28. This is an invented attribution, not a claim that public reports reveal each component exactly. In actual research, label observed expenses separately from inferred residuals. Sampling, cash balances, valuation timing, index changes, and the treatment of corporate actions can also require investigation. A one-year favorable residual is not automatically a repeatable skill. Read the fund’s reports, benchmark methodology, replication policy, and lending disclosures before extrapolating it. Avoid choosing a fund because of a tiny return advantage that cannot be explained or survives only over one chosen interval. Your entry and exit add another layer The SEC ETF bulletin explains that exchange prices can differ from NAV and that the bid–ask spread affects investor costs. These trading effects sit outside a clean NAV-to-index comparison. Imagine an unchanged order book with a bid of 49.95 and ask of 50.05. Buying 200 units at the ask costs 10,010. An immediate sale at the bid returns 9,990, a loss of 20 before commissions. Relative to the 50 midpoint, the initial purchase costs 10 and the sale another 10. This full round-trip spread is 0.20% of the 10,000 midpoint value. A limit order controls the worst price you accept, but it can remain unfilled. Compare the quote with current underlying-market conditions; yesterday’s closing NAV may be a poor intraday fair-value reference when the underlying market is closed or moving quickly. The separate ETF bid–ask spread and order-cost guide diagrams investor execution cash. Those costs belong to your trade record. They must not be inserted into fund NAV tracking difference as though every investor incurred the same execution price or commission. Read the four figures as two controlled and two fixed examples The first two figures share the controls: they compare annual NAV and benchmark growth factors, then show their cumulative return differences at stated horizons. The final two figures retain the original article’s independent examples: four monthly active returns and a one-year attribution that sums to −0.28 percentage points. A change to the annual-gap input does not rewrite the fixed monthly pattern or scale the invented attribution components. That would imply a relationship which the example has not established. Their purpose is to show the difference between a measured gap, its variation and a proposed explanation. The attribution waterfall uses percentage points throughout. A positive lending-revenue entry offsets part of the negative entries; it is not a separate return to add again to the ending wealth line. Real disclosures may support some components better than others. Leave an unexplained residual visible instead of presenting an exact-looking invented explanation as measured evidence. A comparison sheet that can be checked Identify the legal fund, exact share class, benchmark, and hedging policy. Compare fund NAV and matching benchmark total returns over identical periods. Record operating expenses and realized tracking differences without subtracting costs twice. Inspect spread, premium or discount history, brokerage charges, and currency-conversion costs. Check holdings, replication, lending, and the explanation for persistent residuals. For a long holding period, a persistent annual gap can outweigh a modest one-time trading cost. For frequent transactions, spreads and commissions can matter much more. Estimate both using the intended behavior, and keep that estimate separate from the fund’s published performance record.

documents.title: RDSP withdrawals: separate the beneficiary’s payment from assistance repaid to government
documents.description: Follow a hypothetical permitted RDSP payment through the ordinary proportional repayment rule, then reconcile the cash leaving the plan and the value that remains.
documents.body: A beneficiary payment and a government assistance repayment are different outflows. Read each destination separately before interpreting the reduction in the RDSP balance. Identify where each dollar leaving the plan goes A withdrawal-related reduction in a Registered Disability Savings Plan (RDSP) balance need not equal the money directed to the beneficiary. A permitted payment can be accompanied by a separate repayment of government grants and bonds. Those two destinations should remain visible in the household’s cash plan. Employment and Social Development Canada’s withdrawal guidance explains that certain withdrawals can trigger assistance repayment. The illustration here isolates an ordinary proportional-repayment case for a beneficiary who remains eligible for the Disability Tax Credit (DTC), before the calendar year in which they turn sixty. It assumes that the issuer has separately confirmed the proposed payment is permitted. It does not decide whether someone can withdraw, establish an annual payment limit or cover specified disability savings plans, loss of DTC eligibility, closure or death. Those conditions can change the applicable treatment and need their own review. Use the applicable assistance holdback amount rather than lifetime grants The assistance holdback amount, or AHA, is a defined measure of recent government assistance, reduced by relevant amounts already repaid. It is not simply every grant and bond ever received, and it is not automatically the entire RDSP balance. The default example enters an assumed issuer-confirmed AHA of CAD 10,000 and a plan fair market value of CAD 100,000. These are invented records for teaching. The calculator does not derive the holdback from account age, contribution history or a presumed final grant date. Payment dates and prior repayments matter when an issuer determines the applicable amount. The ordinary definition refers to the preceding ten-year period, while special circumstances require separate treatment. A single balance field cannot establish that a particular assistance payment has aged out. The controls’ limits are illustration boundaries, rather than RDSP program limits. They keep sufficient plan assets in every displayed case so that the selected gross payment and assistance repayment can be reconciled without a negative plan value. Apply the ordinary repayment calculation to the hypothetical payment For the scoped ordinary case, section 5.3 of the Canada Disability Savings Regulations sets repayment as the least of three amounts: three dollars per dollar of the disability assistance payment, pre-payment plan fair market value and the applicable AHA. The gross beneficiary payment is CAD 2,500. Three times that amount is CAD 7,500, below both the CAD 10,000 entered AHA and CAD 100,000 opening value. The modeled assistance repayment is consequently CAD 7,500 . The beneficiary payment and assistance repayment together remove CAD 10,000 from the plan. Subtracting those two outflows leaves CAD 90,000 in the RDSP. The waterfall traces each destination rather than presenting the whole CAD 10,000 reduction as cash paid to the beneficiary. This calculation assumes the ordinary rule applies. It does not convert an entered request into an authorized payment or replace the issuer’s application of other payment conditions. Read the cap without treating several scenarios as repeated payments The line chart varies a single gross beneficiary payment against the same hypothetical starting record. Assistance repayment initially rises at three times the gross payment, until the entered AHA caps it. The combined plan outflow includes both the payment and repayment. With the default CAD 10,000 AHA, the cap is reached at a gross payment of CAD 10,000 divided by three. The plot includes that exact turning point, rather than drawing a smoothed curve that obscures the change in slope. Each point is an alternative single transaction. It is not a sequence of withdrawals that each starts again with CAD 10,000 of holdback. In the selected CAD 2,500 example, repaying CAD 7,500 reduces the entered AHA to CAD 2,500 immediately after the modeled repayment, assuming no intervening changes. The grouped bars compare different hypothetical starting AHAs while holding the selected payment constant. Actual subsequent payments require an updated issuer record, including any new assistance, aging or other relevant event. Distinguish plan outflow from household wealth lost For a small payment while the three-for-one rule is uncapped, CAD 1 directed to the beneficiary can be accompanied by CAD 3 repaid to government. The matrix describes this as CAD 4 leaving the RDSP for each CAD 1 of gross beneficiary payment. That is a measure of plan outflow, rather than CAD 4 of household wealth automatically disappearing. If the beneficiary retains the CAD 1 outside the RDSP, it remains a household asset. In the default example, CAD 90,000 remains in the plan and CAD 2,500 is directed outside it, totaling CAD 92,500 before any tax or other cost. The separate CAD 7,500 government repayment explains the reduction from the original CAD 100,000 combined resources under that retained-cash assumption. Spending the beneficiary payment would create a further change outside this plan-only ledger. A lower outflow ratio after the cap binds is not a reason to request more money. A larger payment can lower that ratio while still removing more dollars from the plan. The actual cash need and the permitted payment are separate decisions. Confirm the permitted payment and spendable cash separately A gross beneficiary payment does not establish after-tax spending cash. The payment’s composition and applicable tax treatment require separate calculation. This tool does not divide it into taxable and non-taxable portions, estimate withholding or assess effects on benefits. The CRA’s RDSP guide discusses payment conditions and exceptions beyond the simplified ordinary case. Confirm the applicable AHA, permitted payment, repayment amount and net cash treatment with the issuer before using real amounts in a plan. The legal consolidation consulted was current to 30 September 2026 and last amended on 29 June 2021; the sources were reviewed on 25 October 2026. Recheck the current rules and the account record for an actual transaction. The four charts explain a narrow reconciliation while keeping those unresolved eligibility and payment details outside the arithmetic.

documents.title: GST/HST in the bank is not all business income: keep the tax reserve beside the cash ledger
documents.description: Use four interactive charts to separate sales receipts, GST/HST received, eligible input-tax assumptions, a modeled remittance and cash remaining after the tax reserve.
documents.body: Track sales-tax money separately from the customer payment total. A bank balance can include tax still owed, while a potential refund may not yet be cash. Separate the sale from the tax within the same deposit A customer payment can contain both the price of a sale and GST/HST charged on it. Both amounts may reach the same bank account, but the full deposit is not automatically business income available for an owner’s household spending. CRA’s collection guidance states that collected GST/HST is held in trust until remitted. The first chart therefore splits the hypothetical monthly customer receipt into CAD 10,000 excluding tax and CAD 1,300 of separately entered GST/HST. The example assumes a registrant and uses independently supported tax amounts as inputs. It does not choose a place-of-supply rate, decide whether a sale is taxable or test whether registration is required. These are management-ledger illustrations, not completed GST/HST returns. Keep the input-tax assumption explicit CRA’s net-tax guidance describes the regular method using tax collected or collectible and eligible input tax credits, with applicable adjustments. A business cannot assume every tax-looking payment qualifies for the same credit. The default operating cash payment is CAD 6,000 excluding tax. Another CAD 400 is paid as GST/HST and assumed fully eligible, documented and claimed as an input tax credit in the relevant model period. The simplified monthly net-tax amount is CAD 1,300 − CAD 400 = CAD 900. No adjustment or special method is modeled. If the entered tax paid would be only partly recoverable, or if the business uses a different calculation method, this simplified ledger does not establish the correct filing amount. Use the applicable records and method before treating the illustrated reserve as a real liability estimate. Follow the bank movement before treating the balance as free cash Each default month brings CAD 11,300 of customer cash and pays CAD 6,400 of operating costs including the separately entered input tax. The bank position increases by CAD 4,900. Of that increase, CAD 900 represents positive unsettled net tax in the illustration. The other CAD 4,000 is the difference between receipts and operating cash payments excluding GST/HST. It is a narrow operating cash subtotal, not a calculation of taxable income or an owner’s after-tax pay. Income tax, payroll, capital purchases, debt payments and other commitments are outside this tool. After three months, opening cash of CAD 5,000 has become CAD 19,700. The positive tax reserve is CAD 2,700, leaving a cash position of CAD 17,000 after that reserve. The two lines show these different readings of the same bank resources. Paying an amount already reserved is not a second operating cost The model groups months 1–3 into a first period and months 4–6 into a second. At the start of month 4, it pays the first period’s positive CAD 2,700 net-tax amount. This is an explicitly selected planning event, not a statutory deadline calculated from a reporting frequency. The later bank position includes that payment once. By the end of month 6, the bank funding position is CAD 31,700. A new CAD 2,700 reserve has accumulated for the second period, so the position after that reserve is CAD 29,000. The waterfall reconciles opening cash, receipts and payments. The closing reserve remains inside the bank amount; deducting it as a bank payment and then subtracting it again from closing cash would double-count the same obligation. The after-reserve metric performs the planning subtraction separately. A potential refund needs a separate receipt assumption Change the eligible input-tax assumption above the tax charged and received. The simplified net-tax result then becomes negative. The illustration tracks that amount as a potential receivable and reserves no negative amount from the bank. At the first period boundary, a negative amount remains a separate potential receivable awaiting cash. The tool does not deposit it automatically in month 4. The second period’s negative amount also remains outside the bank total. This makes the cash needed to wait for a possible refund visible without promising an approval or payment date. The eligibility assumption is still essential. A mathematical negative result does not establish that CRA owes the amount or when it will arrive. The cash ledger contains only the receipts actually assumed to have occurred, while the chart preserves the potential amount awaiting cash. Connect the tax record to the business and household plan CRA’s collection guidance notes that tax charged belongs in the reporting period covering the invoice date even if the customer has not yet paid. This model deliberately assumes invoices and related cash are received in the same month. It therefore does not solve the additional funding need created by unpaid invoices. For an actual plan, keep the invoice record, collection date, eligible purchase-tax record and remittance calendar distinct. A tax reserve is also separate from the provision for personal or corporate income tax. The related self-employment guide addresses how business cash connects to an owner’s household draw. The position after the GST/HST reserve is a useful intermediate number. Apply the other business obligations and household commitments before deciding what can leave the account. If the modeled position is negative, it identifies missing funding; it does not assume a bank will supply credit.

documents.title: A term-life premium needs a renewal budget: today’s payment is only one part of the schedule
documents.description: Follow two independently entered premium periods, reconcile a dedicated household reserve and test whether early saving can fund a later increase.
documents.body: A low current premium creates a future resource only if the household keeps the unused budget. That cash belongs to the household reserve, not to the term policy. Separate the current payment from the renewal conditions The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s life-insurance guide explains that certain term policies may be renewed and premiums may increase at renewal. It also distinguishes term insurance from policies with cash value. Those general points do not establish the terms of a particular contract. The illustration takes two monthly premium amounts as independent inputs. It does not estimate premiums from age, health, occupation or an insurer’s pricing. Nor does it establish that renewal or conversion is available, that a new application will be accepted, or that both periods provide the same benefits. Begin a real review with the policy’s actual premium schedule, renewal conditions and coverage details. Confirm whether a future amount is specified by the contract or depends on a new quote. A comparison of cash payments is not a recommendation to cancel or replace existing coverage. Give the two periods an explicit length and boundary The default has two ten-year periods. A selected CAD 50 monthly premium applies in months one through 120. An independently selected CAD 250 monthly premium applies in months 121 through 240. The equal lengths and fixed premium within each block are simplifying assumptions. An actual renewal schedule with annual changes or different term lengths needs its own dates and amounts. This calculator does not extend either selected premium indefinitely beyond its stated block. The household assigns CAD 150 each month to the dedicated premium budget. That assignment arrives before the modeled premium payment. It is a transfer from other household resources, not additional household income. The remaining regular budget must be able to support the full assignment throughout the twenty-year example. Keep the early difference if it is meant to fund the later bill During the first period, each CAD 150 assignment pays a CAD 50 premium and retains CAD 100. With no interest and no withdrawals, 120 monthly differences build a CAD 12,000 cash reserve. During the second period, the CAD 250 premium exceeds the ongoing CAD 150 assignment by CAD 100 per month. The reserve supplies that difference for 120 months and finishes at zero. The path chart shows the accumulation and later use of the same separately held cash. If the first-period CAD 100 difference is spent elsewhere, it is not available for the later premiums. The household would need a different funding plan, such as more cash assigned during the second period or a separately funded reserve. The illustration does not assume an emergency fund can be used twice or automatically restore cash spent on another goal. Premium totals and a reserve balance are different quantities First-period premiums total CAD 6,000. Second-period premiums total CAD 30,000. The combined CAD 36,000 equals 240 household assignments of CAD 150, so the dedicated budget reconciles to zero in the default. The waterfall records those assignments and premium outflows. It does not turn CAD 36,000 of payments into an investment balance. The CAD 12,000 peak reserve is cash the household retained before paying later premiums; it is not cash accumulated inside the term policy. Likewise, cumulative premiums do not measure the value of protection received or a refund payable on cancellation. The model calculates no death benefit, claim probability, surrender value, tax outcome or return on premiums. Use the related coverage-needs guide to examine the household funding gap that insurance is intended to address. Test the future premium beside the ongoing assignment The matrix varies the second-period premium and monthly household assignment while keeping the first premium, period lengths and selected opening reserve fixed. Each cell reports extra cash needed at the beginning to prevent any modeled negative balance. A zero cell means the selected cash assignments and reserve cover that particular payment schedule. It does not confirm that the assignment is affordable, the premium is available or the coverage is sufficient. A positive cell is an unfunded requirement, rather than an automatic loan. A larger opening reserve shifts the whole path upward. A larger monthly assignment changes the path over time. They are different commitments to household cash, so check both the amount tied up initially and the recurring amount no longer available for other priorities. The lowest balance matters alongside the final reconciliation. Review coverage and funding when the actual schedule changes Review the plan before a confirmed renewal or other premium change. Compare the payment dates with actual income receipts and other commitments. The monthly assignment-before-premium convention must match the real cash calendar; a later transfer cannot fund an earlier debit. Keep the dedicated reserve visible in the household balance sheet and avoid counting it simultaneously toward another goal. If the reserve earns interest, incurs tax or is used for another purpose, record those cash flows explicitly rather than assuming the zero-return path still applies. This example assumes every selected premium is paid and models no death, claim, cancellation or lapse. It also assumes no further renewal after the second block. Its purpose is to make the funding schedule reviewable while leaving policy rights, underwriting, coverage suitability and actual premium commitments to separately verified information.

documents.title: A higher deposit rate can meet an earlier bill only through a separate funding plan
documents.description: Compare hypothetical cashable and locked deposits at the same end date, fund the same earlier bill and reconcile the interest cost of a separately assumed bridge loan.
documents.body: A maturity amount cannot fund an earlier bill by itself. Compare the cash available after the bill and all loan settlement, using the actual withdrawal and credit terms. Confirm access before comparing a quoted rate The FCAC’s GIC and term-deposit disclosure guide identifies principal and interest payment terms, charges, and whether early cashing is possible. It also describes disclosure of net proceeds and charges before an allowed early redemption. That information requirement does not establish that a locked product can be broken. The two contracts in this model are independently authored assumptions. No bank’s withdrawal permission, minimum balance, interest treatment or product rate is imported. Both routes begin with CAD 20,000 and must fund the same CAD 5,000 bill after ninety completed days. They finish at day 365. The comparison includes only these defined cash flows. It cannot replace checking the actual contract or deciding how much accessible cash the household needs for other purposes. Apply the cashable rate to the principal that remains The hypothetical cashable contract pays 3% simple annual interest on daily principal. It permits a principal-only partial withdrawal after thirty completed days. The model assumes all accrued interest is paid at day 365, with no withdrawal fee or change in the selected rate. The first ninety days earn interest on CAD 20,000. The CAD 5,000 withdrawal then pays the bill, leaving CAD 15,000 to earn interest for the remaining 275 days. Interest across those two intervals totals approximately CAD 486.99. Ending cash is therefore approximately CAD 15,486.99: remaining principal plus the modeled interest. The interest had not been received when the earlier bill was due, so it is not counted as part of that bill’s funding. Actual cashable products can have different withdrawal and interest rules; these particular assumptions need independent confirmation before use. Treat the bridge as a separate prerequisite and liability The locked contract pays 4.5% simple interest for the full year and releases nothing earlier. It returns CAD 20,900 at day 365. That larger maturity amount alone cannot pay the day-ninety bill. The second route assumes a separately available CAD 5,000 bridge advance funds that bill. At an assumed 8% simple annual rate over 275 days, bridge interest is approximately CAD 301.37. Both loan principal and interest become payable at day 365. After repaying CAD 5,301.37 from maturity proceeds, approximately CAD 15,598.63 remains. The waterfall deducts the loan settlement once. It does not deduct the earlier bill again because the bridge advance already funded it. If the assumed credit is unavailable, this locked-deposit route cannot fund the earlier bill as modeled. Compare the actual interest paths, not two untouched deposits The locked-plus-bridge route finishes approximately CAD 111.64 ahead in the default, before fees and taxes. The shared initial principal and shared bill cancel when the two ending balances are compared. The interest bridge explains the remainder: CAD 900 of locked interest less approximately CAD 486.99 of cashable interest gives about CAD 413.01. Subtract approximately CAD 301.37 of bridge interest, leaving the CAD 111.64 difference. Using CAD 600 as cashable interest would be inconsistent with this scenario. That would assume the entire CAD 20,000 stayed invested for the full year, even though CAD 5,000 funded the earlier bill. Likewise, comparing only the two deposit rates would omit the separate borrowing cost. Keep the amount invested, withdrawal date and funding route consistent throughout the comparison. Test timing and borrowing cost while holding the bill constant The matrix varies the completed days before the bill and the simple bridge rate. Initial principal, the bill percentage and both deposit rates stay selected. Each signed cell is locked-plus-bridge ending cash minus cashable ending cash at the common day-365 endpoint. A later bill shortens the borrowing interval but also leaves more principal earning the cashable rate before withdrawal. The calculation includes both effects. Changing the bill’s percentage changes how much principal leaves the cashable deposit and how much the bridge must advance. A positive cell is an arithmetic advantage under the chosen assumptions, not proof of an available or suitable strategy. Fees, taxes, changing rates or repayment conditions can change the result. A negative locked-route endpoint means additional outside cash is required at settlement; the model does not create further borrowing to fill it. Build the payment plan from confirmed net amounts and dates For an actual decision, confirm whether partial withdrawal is permitted, how it changes interest, when interest is paid, and what charges or minimum balances apply. Obtain the expected net amount rather than assuming the headline deposit rate determines the withdrawal proceeds. Confirm any separate funding source before relying on it. Its amount, fees, interest convention, payment dates and maturity need to match the bill and deposit dates. Paying interest regularly or repaying principal earlier would require different cash flows from the single settlement modeled here. The example uses a fixed 365-day year, simple interest, no fees and no tax. It does not model rollovers, emergency access rights or lending approval. Its purpose is to compare equal starting resources, the same expense and a common finish date while making the cost and availability of the earlier funding explicit.

documents.title: Why two investments do not make a simple average of risk: five views of diversification
documents.description: Explore allocation curves, a risk–return scatter plot, a variance waterfall, signed risk contributions and a correlation matrix with editable two-asset assumptions.
documents.body: Portfolio return is a weighted arithmetic mean in this one-year model. Portfolio standard deviation also depends on how the two returns move together. Neither number establishes the right investment plan. Define the returns before drawing the portfolio Two portfolios with identical capital weights can have different risk when their investments behave differently together. This article isolates that relationship using two hypothetical assets, A and B. Neither name represents a fund, a security, a country or an asset-class forecast. The example assigns 60% to A and 40% to B at the start of one year. A has an assumed arithmetic mean return of 4% and a return standard deviation of 6%. B has corresponding assumptions of 8% and 18%. Their assumed correlation is 0.2. These are chosen inputs for an explanation, rather than estimates extracted from market data. The public CFA Institute portfolio-risk overview identifies individual risk, return and correlation as determinants of portfolio risk. The calculations below apply those general relationships to this independent example. They do not reproduce a historical portfolio or select an allocation for the reader. Read the arithmetic mean separately from a growth forecast The one-year portfolio return is 0.6 times A’s realized return plus 0.4 times B’s realized return. Taking its arithmetic mean gives 0.6 × 4% + 0.4 × 8% = 5.6% . Changing correlation leaves this mean unchanged when the weights and both asset means stay fixed. An arithmetic mean describes a distribution’s average one-period return. It is not a promised return, a compound annual growth rate or a complete retirement projection. A multiyear calculation would need further assumptions about the sequence of returns, changing weights, contributions, withdrawals and costs. This calculator supplies none of those assumptions. The capital input translates standard deviation into Canadian dollars. It does not change either asset’s return characteristics. Doubling the portfolio from CAD 100,000 to CAD 200,000 doubles the dollar translation while leaving the percentage mean and standard deviation unchanged. Use the allocation curves to see the missing relationship The first chart varies A’s weight from 0% to 100%, assigning the remainder to B. It compares the selected correlation with −0.5 and +1. At each endpoint only one asset remains, so all curves meet at that asset’s standalone standard deviation. For nonnegative weights and correlation +1, portfolio standard deviation equals the weighted sum of the two standalone standard deviations. At the default weights, that sum is 0.6 × 6% + 0.4 × 18% = 10.8% . At correlation 0.2, the calculated standard deviation is about 8.67% . The difference comes from covariance, with the standalone risks held fixed. Reducing correlation cannot increase variance in this particular two-asset, long-only comparison. It need not reduce risk below the risk of the safer individual asset at every weight. Nor does the result mean that adding any second holding improves every plan. The quantities and their relationship both matter. A point on the scatter plot is an allocation The horizontal coordinate of each point is calculated annual standard deviation. Its vertical coordinate is the assumed arithmetic mean return. Hollow points represent allocations at ten-percentage-point intervals; the larger filled point identifies the exact selected weight, including an intermediate weight if entered. The default selected point is therefore approximately (8.67%, 5.60%). It is not an observed year, a simulated future outcome or an investor’s survey response. The chart plots alternative portfolios derived from the same inputs. The table identifies every allocation and both coordinates. A point with a lower mean and at least as much standard deviation as another point has an unattractive comparison on those two selected measures. That observation does not establish a universally optimal investment. This small opportunity set omits taxes, liquidity, inflation exposure, downside asymmetry, restrictions and the household’s required payment dates. Add variance terms before taking the square root Write the weights as fractions wA and wB, standalone standard deviations as σA and σB, and correlation as ρ. Portfolio variance is wA²σA² + wB²σB² + 2wAwBρσAσB . Portfolio standard deviation is the square root of that total. The waterfall uses squared percentage points to make the arithmetic readable. Its default first term is (0.6 × 6)² = 12.96. The second is (0.4 × 18)² = 51.84. The covariance cross term is 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 × 0.2 × 6 × 18 = 10.368. Together they produce variance of 75.168 squared percentage points . Its square root is approximately 8.66995 percentage points. The chart labels round displayed values, while the calculation retains precision. These three variance components cannot be added as if they were three percentage returns. A negative covariance term reduces the variance total; it does not represent a payment, investment profit or negative standalone variance. State a convention before calling something a risk contribution The signed bars assign half of the weighted covariance cross term to A and half to B. On that stated convention, A receives 12.96 + 5.184 = 18.144 squared percentage points. B receives 51.84 + 5.184 = 57.024. Their sum reconciles to 75.168. These figures describe contributions to variance. They are neither capital weights nor additive contributions to standard deviation. Reporting 18.144 as A’s percentage allocation would confuse the measurement unit and the question being answered. A contribution can become negative. For example, keep the default weights and standalone risks but change correlation to −0.5. A’s attributed variance becomes 12.96 − 12.96 = 0; at correlation −1 it becomes −12.96. The other contribution offsets it so total variance stays nonnegative. This describes the model’s covariance relationship and does not establish a reliable real-world hedge. Test the relationship instead of treating one estimate as permanent The matrix varies both correlation and allocation. It holds the two standalone standard deviations fixed. At correlation −1, A’s 75% weight and B’s 25% weight give equal weighted standard deviations of 4.5 percentage points with perfectly opposite movements. Their modeled portfolio standard deviation is zero. That cancellation requires an exact relationship in this idealized model. It is not evidence that an available pair of investments is risk-free. Estimated correlations depend on the observations, frequency, currency and measurement period; future relationships can differ. Zero correlation also does not generally establish statistical independence. Standard deviation alone cannot specify the probability of losing money or the worst loss. Without a distributional assumption, “one standard deviation” is not a stated confidence interval. The default CAD 8,669.95 dollar translation is a dispersion measure for CAD 100,000, rather than a maximum loss, a reserve target or a guaranteed band around the mean. Bring the chart back to the goal and payment calendar Investor.gov’s asset-allocation overview connects allocation choices with investing horizon and risk tolerance. It also explains diversification across and within investment categories. Counting account names or fund wrappers does not by itself establish different underlying exposures. For a real planning exercise, record the goal’s amount and date, identify money needed before a market recovery could be tolerated, and inspect the underlying investments. Then document how actual risk estimates were obtained and test plausible changes in the relationships. This article’s adjustable inputs illustrate those questions without answering them for a particular household. The model has no leverage, short positions, taxes, fees, exchange-rate conversion, cash flows or trading constraints. Its calculations are a transparent starting point for understanding diversification. A complete plan must still fund the actual obligations and fit the investor’s capacity and willingness to bear losses.

documents.title: The same ten-year inflation total can require different retirement capital
documents.description: Five charts reverse the order of two invented inflation blocks, then trace spending requests, portfolio balances, funding requirements and any unmet spending.
documents.body: A closing price level does not reveal when the price increases arrived. Earlier increases can affect more withdrawals, even when the investment return and final price level match. Hold the inflation factors constant and change only their order The first chart draws two price paths. In the original example, one has three years of 8% inflation followed by seven years of 2%. The other reverses exactly those ten annual factors. Both finish with the same price level: approximately 144.7 when the starting index is 100. The rates are invented. They are not a replay of Canadian CPI, an estimate of future prices or probabilities assigned to a retirement scenario. Their purpose is to hold the total compounded increase constant while changing when it occurs. The two blocks remain labelled A and B when inputs change. If block A is entered below block B, the first path no longer represents higher inflation arriving early. If both rates are equal, the paths coincide. The labels describe order rather than promising which sequence is more difficult. Every spending request needs a price observation and a payment date The first annual withdrawal request is made immediately at the start of year one, before any modeled inflation or investment return. The next year’s request follows the price level after year one. Each later request uses the preceding year-end price index to maintain the same selected spending basket. The second chart shows these requested nominal amounts. A price increase early in the horizon affects several later requests. A price increase at the very end cannot change an earlier bill that has already been requested. This convention also explains the tenth inflation update. It determines the closing year-ten price level and purchasing power, but an eleventh withdrawal is outside the ten-year horizon. The year-ten request uses the first nine price increases. Matching closing indices therefore does not require the ten withdrawal amounts or their sum to match. Keep returns identical to isolate the inflation-spending channel The third chart gives both withdrawal paths the same initial capital and the same constant nominal investment return. The original example starts with CAD 500,000, requests CAD 25,000 immediately, and uses an assumed 5% effective nominal return every year. Each request first uses the capital available at the start of that year. The remaining capital then earns the selected return. The tool records any amount that cannot be funded; it does not borrow automatically or show a negative investment account. Under the original assumptions, the A-first path requests about CAD 315,286 across the decade and ends with about CAD 403,919. The reversed path requests about CAD 279,084 and ends with about CAD 450,086. Both original examples fund all ten requests. The difference combines extra spending with the growth forgone on earlier withdrawals; it is not an investment-performance difference. The no-spending line is a control. It removes all withdrawal requests and therefore produces one common investment path. It is not a retirement lifestyle that a household can adopt without a separate source of income. Discount every requested withdrawal from its actual timing The fourth chart calculates the opening capital required to fund the ten requests under the selected constant return, ending with no capital requirement beyond the horizon. The first request is immediate and is not discounted. The request at the start of year two is discounted one year, and so on. The equation is required opening capital = Σ requested spending in year t ÷ (1 + nominal return) t − 1 for years one through ten. These cash-flow dates must agree with the portfolio recurrence; using year-end discounting would answer a different question. In the original example, the requirements are approximately CAD 252,029 with block A first and CAD 223,686 with block B first. The difference is approximately CAD 28,342. A third bar holds the initial spending request and nominal return constant while removing all price increases, providing a separate inflation control. This is an arithmetic funding identity for ten known requests and one certain return assumption. It is not a recommended reserve, a safe withdrawal rate or a statement that retirement ends after ten years. Read unmet spending beside the remaining portfolio The final chart separates requested spending into amounts funded and left unfunded. A lower funded total can mean that the household could not meet its needs. It should not be praised as a more efficient spending strategy without reading the unfunded segment. Try reducing initial capital. The opening-capital requirement bars do not change because they depend on the requested spending path and return. The actual portfolio path and unmet requests do change. Later returns cannot retroactively finance an earlier request that lacked capital. A real retirement plan would also include pensions, tax, fees, changing spending quantities, benefit indexation, cash timing and uncertain returns. Price increases may differ by category, and households may adjust discretionary spending. This example isolates one channel to make its effect visible. Keep a record of whether values are nominal or in today’s purchasing power. Specify when each withdrawal happens. Test earlier as well as later inflation pressure. Show any spending cuts or unmet requests beside capital balances. Extend the horizon and add other resources before treating the exercise as a retirement plan. The useful question is how price changes reach the budget through time, rather than only which index value appears at the finish.

documents.title: The rate says 5%. Which compounding convention turns it into a monthly payment?
documents.description: Four graphics compare nominal rate conventions with an already-effective annual interpretation, then follow the converted rate through interest and principal repayment.
documents.body: The number and the convention belong together. Convert them to a common annual growth factor and a matching payment-period rate before comparing the payment. Read the convention before dividing the rate by twelve An annual percentage printed beside the word interest does not tell you every detail needed for a payment calculation. The quotation needs a compounding convention, and the payment schedule needs a rate for its own period. FCAC’s sample fixed-mortgage information box illustrates interest compounded twice a year but charged monthly. It also presents annual percentage rate separately, including applicable fees. The example is useful for understanding the labels; its figures are not a current mortgage offer. This tool places three interpretations of one entered number side by side: a nominal quote with the selected compounding count, a nominal quote compounded monthly, and a number treated as already effective for one year. They share a principal and complete repayment horizon, with no fees. None is asserted to be the convention used by every lender or product. Build the annual growth factor, then translate to a payment month For a nominal annual rate j compounded m times a year, the annual growth factor is (1 + j ÷ m) m . Subtract one to obtain the effective annual interest rate. Rates in this equation are decimals, so 5% is entered as 0.05. The equivalent monthly rate is (1 + j ÷ m) m ÷ 12 − 1 . This preserves the same annual growth factor across twelve equal model months. A nominal rate compounded twice yearly is therefore converted with an exponent of one-sixth after dividing the quote by two. If the entered number is already an effective annual rate, the monthly conversion is (1 + j) 1/12 − 1 . Dividing by twelve instead would make a different assumption. The tool retains unrounded rates for calculations; rounding an intermediate rate can change a long amortization schedule. Compare the same rate number without assuming the same interest With the original 5% input, nominal twice-yearly compounding implies an effective annual rate of 5.0625%. Nominal monthly compounding implies approximately 5.11619%. The already-effective annual interpretation is exactly 5%. The first chart displays the conversions on the same effective annual basis. For an original CAD 300,000 principal repaid through three hundred monthly payments, the corresponding payments are approximately CAD 1,744.81, CAD 1,753.77 and CAD 1,734.41. These are original mathematical results, not three borrowing offers. The same-number comparison deliberately changes economic rates. It should not be read as a claim that compounding creates extra cost when effective annual rates are held equal. If two quotes are first converted to the same annual growth factor, they also produce the same equivalent monthly rate and payment under the remaining common assumptions. Carry the converted rate through the actual interest and principal split The second chart shows additional cumulative interest relative to treating the entered number as an already-effective annual rate. Subtracting the same baseline makes a small convention difference easier to see. A zero line means equal cost to that baseline, not that the loan charges no interest. Each case solves its own payment to repay the same principal over the same number of months, with no rate renewal. The third chart examines payment one. Interest is opening principal times the converted monthly rate. The remainder of the payment reduces principal. The final payment is capped at the amount still owed so that a small rounding residual is not treated as a new debt. The fourth chart translates selected nominal annual quotes across annual, twice-yearly, monthly and 365-period compounding. It shows effective annual percentages to two decimal places, with more precision retained inside the calculation. The 365-period row is a mathematical count, not a dated daily-accrual contract; it does not address leap years or an actual day-count rule. An effective interest conversion still does not include every borrowing cost Converting interest conventions is one part of comparing borrowing. A real offer can also have fees, required conditions, optional products, repayment restrictions, early-exit costs or a rate that changes before the debt is fully repaid. Those are outside this exercise. The complete repayment horizon in the tool is not a promise that a mortgage rate remains fixed for its whole amortization. Actual contractual terms and renewals must be checked separately. The calculated effective annual interest rate is also not an all-in APR disclosure: no fee has been included in its cash flows. Record the quoted number and whether it is nominal or effective. Record the compounding and payment frequencies separately. Translate to a common annual growth factor. Use the matching payment-period rate for the repayment calculation. Add actual fees and contractual terms before assessing a live offer. These steps explain why two calculators can disagree while displaying the same annual number. Before changing the principal or repayment budget to force agreement, check whether they used the same rate convention.

documents.title: An RDSP withdrawal has two outflows: the beneficiary payment and the grant repayment
documents.description: Four graphics explain an ordinary proportional repayment, the remaining assistance holdback and the difference between cash requested, cash paid and value removed from the plan.
documents.body: A gross payment to the beneficiary can trigger a separate government repayment. Check both outflows and the issuer’s payment capacity before treating an account balance as available cash. Start with a confirmed payment type and holdback snapshot An RDSP supports long-term saving for a person with a disability. A spending decision needs more than an account value: the issuer must establish the payment rules, the assistance holdback amount and any annual payment capacity that applies. The CRA’s payment guide distinguishes disability assistance payments from lifetime disability assistance payments, and explains that payment limits depend on the plan’s situation. An entered capacity in this tool means a remaining amount already confirmed by the issuer. The calculator does not establish that capacity itself. This example isolates an ordinary proportional-repayment case: a beneficiary under 60 with continuing Disability Tax Credit eligibility. It excludes specified disability savings plans, specified-year exceptions, DTC-loss cases, closure and death. Those situations can require different treatment. A result here cannot substitute for the issuer’s assessment of a real request. Trace a CAD 5,000 request through both outflows The hypothetical plan starts at CAD 100,000. Its confirmed assistance holdback amount is CAD 21,000, and independently confirmed remaining annual payment capacity is CAD 10,000. The beneficiary requests a gross payment of CAD 5,000. For the ordinary case, the CRA’s RDSP guide describes a proportional repayment of CAD 3 of grants and bonds for each CAD 1 withdrawn, capped at the assistance holdback amount. The example therefore repays min(3 × 5,000, 21,000) = CAD 15,000 . Two outflows reduce the account: CAD 5,000 for the beneficiary and CAD 15,000 for the government. Remaining plan value is 100,000 − 5,000 − 15,000 = CAD 80,000 . The government repayment is additional to the gross beneficiary payment. It is not taken a second time from that CAD 5,000. The payment may contain taxable amounts. This illustration does not calculate that composition, tax payable, benefit interactions or the beneficiary’s after-tax spending money. “Gross beneficiary payment” is deliberately the label used in the charts. Read the bend where the holdback cap is reached The curve compares independent payment alternatives from the same opening snapshot. With a CAD 21,000 holdback, the three-to-one repayment reaches its cap at a CAD 7,000 gross payment. Below that point, an extra CAD 1 of payment increases total plan depletion by CAD 4 in this narrow example: CAD 1 to the beneficiary and CAD 3 repaid. Above the cap, the repayment remains CAD 21,000. A CAD 10,000 permitted payment would therefore remove CAD 31,000 in total. This is arithmetic for one event under the stated conditions. It does not describe investment performance, an annual expense ratio or a tax rate. Nor is the curve a series of withdrawals: every point starts with the same original assets and holdback. The formula matrix keeps this distinction visible. Each cell shows only the capped repayment formula. A displayed number does not confirm that its hypothetical withdrawal satisfies annual limits or leaves adequate assets. Keep the remaining restriction separate from remaining assets After the default event, repaying CAD 15,000 also reduces the entered holdback from CAD 21,000 to CAD 6,000. The second comparison chart shows that amount alongside CAD 80,000 of remaining assets. The two quantities must not be added. Holdback identifies a repayment-related amount within the plan’s circumstances; it is not another investment account. ESDC’s technical guidance explains that the applicable period and repayment obligation depend on the event, age and DTC status, and that earlier repayments must be considered. The calculator conservatively caps the beneficiary payment at both the entered annual capacity and plan value above the confirmed opening holdback. It then applies the separate repayment. If the entered holdback already exceeds plan value, the tool illustrates no payment and leaves the discrepancy for issuer review. For example, with CAD 25,000 of assets and CAD 21,000 of holdback, only CAD 4,000 lies above that opening restriction. Even an entered annual capacity of CAD 10,000 does not make the full request fundable in this illustration. Use the actual assistance history before making a date decision A recent contribution date, a recent grant date and an account-opening date are different facts. The assistance calculation needs the issuer’s grant, bond and repayment history and the applicable event rules. A blanket instruction to wait ten years from the latest personal deposit can answer the wrong question. This tool accepts a confirmed holdback snapshot. It does not age individual grants, reconstruct past repayments, predict new grants or roll a future date forward. Lowering the holdback control means testing another assumed snapshot; it does not establish that the lower number will apply on a chosen date. Confirm the payment type and gross amount with the issuer. Obtain the assistance holdback and remaining annual capacity for the actual request. Separate beneficiary cash, government repayment and remaining assets. Check the payment’s tax composition and any benefit interactions separately. Place the confirmed spendable amount in the household’s spending calendar. The purpose is to understand the two outflows before committing the money. It does not recommend a withdrawal, determine program eligibility or calculate a personalized disability-savings strategy.
