documents.title: When a pension bridge ends: chart the income drop before the next source begins
documents.description: Four graphics map temporary and ongoing pension income, independently timed later income, spending and the annual cash reserve needed between the changes.
documents.body: The date a temporary benefit ends and the date another income source begins are separate inputs. Put both on the calendar before relying on the first pension payment. Identify which part of the pension is temporary A quoted pension payment can contain components with different durations. A household that spends the first total indefinitely may miss a scheduled reduction even when the plan pays exactly what it promised. The federal public service pension explanation distinguishes a lifetime pension from a temporary bridge benefit. Under the described plan, the bridge normally ends after the member reaches 65, with an earlier end possible on entitlement to CPP/QPP disability benefits. The page also explains why starting a reduced CPP/QPP pension early can leave a lower combined income after the bridge ends. Those are features of the named plan, rather than rules for every employer pension. The amounts and annual bands in this tool are independent hypothetical inputs. Obtain the actual statement, net-payment estimate and end date from the relevant administrator before applying them to a household. Map three income components in the same price basis The worked example begins with the whole-year period at age 60. Ongoing pension income is CAD 32,000 a year after tax, and a temporary bridge supplies another CAD 8,000. Spending begins at CAD 45,000, leaving a CAD 5,000 annual gap before savings. The first whole-year band without the bridge is age 65. A separate CAD 14,000 annual income source starts at age 67. Each amount is entered in year-1 dollars, then increased by the same 2% assumption. At the original price level, income therefore moves from CAD 40,000 to CAD 32,000 and later to CAD 46,000. The composition chart selects the first and last bands plus the bands around the two changes. The income-and-spending chart retains every annual observation. Neither treats the later source as an automatic continuation of the bridge. Changing the later start age changes the calendar only. It does not increase that source’s annual amount as a real CPP deferral calculation might. A different start-age quotation must be assessed separately. Budget the years after the bridge stops The initial CAD 5,000 gap is manageable only if resources are assigned to it. When the bridge ends before later income starts, the first-year-price gap becomes CAD 13,000 a year. The chart then applies the common annual increase to the actual nominal amounts in each band. The selected opening cash reserve is CAD 30,000. Across the whole fifteen-year schedule, the minimum required opening cash is about CAD 55,013.36. The additional requirement above the selected reserve is therefore about CAD 25,013.36. This calculation looks for the deepest cumulative annual deficit. It does not simply sum every shortfall while ignoring a surplus elsewhere. The model saves any annual surplus in the same zero-interest cash ledger, and allows it to fund subsequent obligations. A later surplus still cannot pay an earlier bill on its original due date. That is why the largest earlier deficit determines the required opening amount even when the ending position improves. Read negative cash as an unfunded position The cash chart begins immediately before the first modeled age band. Each following point adds that year’s income and subtracts spending. At the defaults, the position ends the fifteenth year at about negative CAD 15,154.23. That is a funding need, not an approved overdraft or an actual negative savings account. The tool calculates no borrowing interest, asset sale or government support to fill it. A real plan would need to change resources, spending or timing before the payment became due. The extra-starting-cash result is conditional on the modeled ordering: annual receipts are available before the annual spending settlement. Monthly rent, bill dates and a birthday-month pension change can require a different buffer. The federal plan’s actual monthly bridge-end rule is not reproduced by these whole-year bands. A larger reserve can fund the illustrated calendar, but this horizon omits later care needs, survivor changes and spending after the final year. It is an annual transition exercise, not a lifetime adequacy assessment. Separate a timing sensitivity from an available pension choice The matrix varies the first year without the bridge and the later-income start age. Each cell reports additional opening cash after the selected reserve, holding all entered amounts fixed. A lower cell does not mean an administrator offers that end age or that a government pension can be moved without changing its amount. Some cells may move a transition outside the selected horizon, in which case that transition has not been tested. Read the horizon with the result. OSFI’s Pension Members’ Guide emphasizes checking the details of the particular plan with its administrator. For a practical review, request a breakdown of ongoing and temporary components, identify each end date, obtain independent estimates of other income, and compare the resulting net receipts with essential and flexible spending. Use exact monthly dates for an implemented budget. Keep any decision about CPP/QPP start age, pension options, tax, disability benefits or survivor protection separate from this deliberately simplified cash comparison.

documents.title: Insuring a home: separate market value, rebuilding cost and the cash gap
documents.description: Four graphics compare three property values, independent cost and limit increases, an explicit teaching payout formula and the owner’s remaining cash need.
documents.body: A property’s sale value does not measure the rebuilding bill. Review the rebuilding estimate, policy terms and available cash together. Give each property figure the right job A home’s market value, estimated rebuilding cost and policy coverage limit can be three different amounts. The first describes a possible sale; the second estimates a construction task; the third is part of an insurance contract. Intact’s Canadian replacement-cost explanation , published on 2 July 2026, distinguishes rebuilding from market value and describes the role of construction characteristics and current costs. It also notes that some policies have replacement provisions subject to their own conditions. The hypothetical comparison starts with CAD 1.2 million of market value, CAD 650,000 of covered rebuilding cost and a CAD 600,000 dwelling limit. Market value supplies context but does not enter the calculator’s claim arithmetic. Changing only that number leaves the modeled payout and cash need unchanged. This is not an appraisal or a quote for a particular insurer. The selected figures are teaching assumptions, and a broker or insurer must confirm what the actual contract covers. Write the payout assumption before using the number The model assumes a total covered dwelling loss. Its teaching contract first caps the covered rebuilding cost at the dwelling limit, then subtracts a fixed deductible, with the payout floored at zero: Assumed payout = max[0, min(covered rebuilding cost, dwelling limit) − deductible] . With the starting figures and a CAD 2,500 deductible, the modeled payout is CAD 597,500. The owner’s share is CAD 52,500. Against CAD 50,000 of assigned cash, that leaves CAD 2,500 to fund. The order in the formula matters. An actual contract may apply limits, deductibles, replacement provisions or other adjustments differently. This illustration applies no coinsurance percentage and does not generalize a foreign jurisdiction’s underinsurance rule. It provides a transparent assumed cash calculation rather than determining an actual claim. Watch rebuilding costs and the stated limit separately The default cost increase is 5% annually, while the coverage limit grows by 2%. After five years, the rebuilding estimate is about CAD 829,583.02 and the assumed limit is about CAD 662,448.48. Applying the same fixed deductible gives a modeled insurer payment of about CAD 659,948.48. The owner’s share reaches about CAD 169,634.53, of which about CAD 119,634.53 exceeds the selected cash reserve. These are compounded sensitivities. They are not a construction-price forecast, a probability of a loss or a statement that an insurer will increase a particular limit by 2%. The lines make visible what happens when two independently entered quantities grow at different rates. A policy review can change the relevant inputs. Updated measurements, renovations, materials, local labour conditions and the contract’s actual replacement provisions need to be reflected in a fresh assessment rather than assumed away by a smooth curve. Reconcile the owner’s share without counting the deductible twice The funding waterfall begins with the covered rebuilding bill. It subtracts the assumed insurer payment and then the cash assigned to the owner’s share. A positive endpoint identifies additional funding; a negative endpoint identifies assigned cash left over. The deductible is already incorporated in the payout formula. Adding it again to the waterfall would overstate the funding need. Similarly, an insurance payment cannot be counted both as a reduction in the rebuilding bill and as a separate cash receipt a second time. The illustration assumes the modeled payout and cash are available when the bill is due. Actual claim advances, contractor deposits and reimbursement dates can produce an additional timing need. The separate reimbursement guide explains that kind of calendar without assuming an eventual payment can finance an earlier bill. No home sale, borrowing or investment liquidation is created automatically. The reported additional amount is a problem to plan for, rather than evidence that a loan is available. Read the parts of protection this dwelling example leaves out FCAC’s home-insurance guide describes protection that may include belongings, liability and additional living expenses when a home cannot be occupied. Those categories have their own terms and are not added to this dwelling-only estimate. The model also excludes land, contents, exclusions, bylaw and demolition provisions, extended or guaranteed replacement coverage, premium changes and claim-handling delays. A positive cash result for one assumed rebuilding bill says nothing about these other needs. The matrix changes the construction-cost increase and the hypothetical loss date while keeping the limit-growth assumption, deductible and cash fixed. A cell is a conditional funding calculation. None is a risk rating or an estimate of which year a loss will occur. Confirm the current rebuilding estimate and the property details behind it. Read the applicable dwelling limit, deductible and replacement conditions. List related living and other costs separately. Check when funds would be available against likely payment stages. Review the policy after material changes to the home or its use. The calculation helps organize that review. Actual coverage and claim outcomes depend on the insurer’s assessment and policy wording.

documents.title: Federal pension bridge expiry and CPP: build a monthly reserve calendar
documents.description: Four charts map the federal public-service bridge expiry and independently entered CPP cash, with a December birthday and a monthly reserve ledger.
documents.body: A later income increase cannot fund an earlier shortfall. Put the temporary benefit’s last payment and the replacement income’s first payment on the same calendar. Separate the lifetime pension from the temporary payment The annual pension-bridge guide explores whole-year bands and a common increase in income and spending. This page adds a monthly cash ledger tied to a stated December-birthday convention, with independently entered CPP cash and spending growth separated from flat income. A pension statement can contain more than one income component. A total received this month should not automatically become the amount entered for every future year. The first graphic separates ongoing income, a temporary bridge and independently entered CPP cash. For the federal public service plan, Treasury Board’s age-65 guide distinguishes a lifetime pension from a bridge ending on the first of the month after the sixty-fifth birthday. Entitlement to CPP or QPP disability benefits can end the bridge earlier. This illustration excludes that disability case and does not establish eligibility. The example uses independently entered net cash amounts rather than a service-and-salary pension formula. No tax withholding rule is applied. A real statement’s gross components must be reconciled with actual spendable receipts before using them in a household cash plan. Make the birthday and payment convention explicit The model begins in January after an assumed December sixtieth birthday. Its first five calendar years cover January ages sixty through sixty-four. The bridge pays through the December turning sixty-five, then stops the following January. This selected convention places the first month without bridge cash at month 61, five years after the start. The tool is not asking for a birth date and cannot produce a personal final-payment date. Use the administrator’s actual statement to map a real birthday and processing calendar. CPP starts in January at the selected whole age. Choosing sixty-seven therefore starts its first modeled payment in month 85. Income arrives before that month’s spending. Application delays, arrears, retroactive payments and spending before the monthly deposit are outside this simplified schedule. Do not assume the bridge amount equals the later CPP amount The federal guide explains that taking CPP retirement benefits earlier or later does not move the ordinary age-65 end of its bridge. The two plans’ amounts should not be treated as interchangeable. A household may lose one amount and later receive a different one. The current CPP start-age guide also makes clear that timing affects actual monthly benefits. Here the CPP amount is independently entered for the chosen start. The tool does not apply start-age percentages or convert a quotation at one age into a quotation at another. The matrix intentionally holds the entered CPP cash unchanged while varying its start date. It isolates a timing question. It is not a complete comparison of claiming ages, a lifetime-income ranking or a recommendation to claim at the earliest displayed date. Follow the default budget before and after the bridge stops The default ongoing lifetime pension is CAD 2,200 per month, with CAD 500 of other net income. Before the bridge ends, another CAD 700 brings monthly resources to CAD 3,400. Spending is CAD 3,500, leaving a CAD 100 monthly gap. After sixty months, CAD 6,000 has been drawn from the initial CAD 20,000 reserve, leaving CAD 14,000. In the next twenty-four months, the bridge has ended and CPP has not begun. Income is only CAD 2,700, so the gap grows to CAD 800 per month. Immediately before CPP starts, the cumulative funding need reaches CAD 25,200. The entered reserve is CAD 5,200 short. Negative cash on the chart represents that unmet need; the tool does not open an overdraft, sell an investment or supply the missing money. A recovered ending balance does not repair a missed payment At the selected CPP start, CAD 1,000 of new monthly cash raises resources to CAD 3,700. With unchanged spending, the monthly difference becomes positive CAD 200. The reserve path then rises. At the end of the fifteen-year schedule, modeled cash is again positive CAD 14,000. That endpoint does not remove the earlier CAD 5,200 shortage. The required starting reserve comes from the deepest cumulative deficit across the whole ledger, not from the final balance. For this particular calendar, CAD 25,200 of starting cash would keep all modeled month-end balances nonnegative. It is a scenario result, not a universal emergency-fund recommendation. Payments within a month could still require a separate daily calendar. Test spending growth separately from pension indexing All income inputs remain fixed nominal cash amounts. The spending-growth control raises costs each January. It does not apply statutory indexation to the pension or CPP. This deliberately separates a spending stress from a benefit calculation. Try increasing spending growth or moving the assumed CPP receipt to age seventy. Read the reserve trough and the full starting reserve requirement as well as the endpoint. The matrix replaces temporary bridge cash and start age while retaining the other inputs. For an actual retirement plan, add the verified payment dates, indexing provisions, tax effects and other benefits or assets that apply. This tool includes no OAS, GIS, investment growth, mortality or account withdrawal rules. Its purpose is narrower: make the temporary-income expiry visible before committing the same cash to future spending.

documents.title: Rebalancing while taking money out: choose the sale source before adding another trade
documents.description: Four charts compare proportional and target-directed withdrawals, showing the cash taken out, the remaining asset weights and any separate exchange still needed.
documents.body: A withdrawal can move an allocation toward a target, but the target applies to the smaller portfolio left behind. Taking cash out does not always complete the rebalance. Ask where the same withdrawal will come from Two portfolios can begin with the same holdings, provide the same spending cash and finish with different asset weights. The difference can come entirely from the choice of assets sold, even before any market movement. Investor.gov defines rebalancing as bringing a portfolio back toward its original allocation. This article considers a related cash-flow question: when money already needs to leave, how much of that allocation adjustment can the required sale accomplish? The example has only equity and bond buckets. It does not select securities or judge the entered target’s suitability. The SEC’s allocation guide places asset mix in the context of investment horizon and risk tolerance. A mechanically achievable percentage is not automatically the right percentage for a household. Reconcile the starting holdings and the cash leaving The default portfolio is CAD 300,000 with 70% in equity and 30% in bonds. That means CAD 210,000 of equity and CAD 90,000 of bonds. The requested withdrawal is CAD 30,000 before tax and transaction costs. Both illustrated rules supply exactly that CAD 30,000. Both leave a CAD 270,000 investment portfolio. The first stacked comparison therefore has the same ending total under either rule, making it possible to inspect composition without confusing it with a difference in wealth. The cash withdrawn is outside the remaining portfolio. It is not shown as another investment asset, and no return is applied to it. The tool also does not claim that a gross withdrawal is the same as a household’s after-tax spending amount. A proportional sale preserves the existing weight The proportional rule uses the starting 70/30 mix to fund the withdrawal. It sells CAD 21,000 of equity and CAD 9,000 of bonds, leaving CAD 189,000 and CAD 81,000 respectively. CAD 189,000 divided by CAD 270,000 is still 70%. Selling both buckets in proportion does not by itself correct the original allocation drift. It simply scales the portfolio down under the model’s no-price-change assumptions. This is a useful control case. If a proposed withdrawal strategy claims to change risk exposure, check the weights of what remains rather than the percentage of the withdrawal that came from each asset. Those are different denominators. Apply the target to the portfolio remaining after the withdrawal The entered target is 60% equity. After CAD 30,000 leaves, that target would mean CAD 162,000 of equity in the CAD 270,000 remaining portfolio. Starting from CAD 210,000, reaching it would require CAD 48,000 of equity sales. The spending withdrawal is only CAD 30,000. The directed rule is not allowed to sell CAD 48,000 and silently reinvest CAD 18,000 in bonds. It can sell only enough assets to provide the requested spending cash. It therefore takes all CAD 30,000 from equity in the default example. The remaining holdings are CAD 180,000 of equity and CAD 90,000 of bonds. Equity falls to about 66.67%: closer to 60%, but not at the target. Make the extra exchange visible rather than hiding it inside the withdrawal The default directed portfolio still has CAD 18,000 more equity than the 60% target permits. Reaching the target would require a separate exchange: sell another CAD 18,000 of equity and buy CAD 18,000 of bonds. That exchange is not executed in the model. The matrix reports this residual in dollars. Positive means equity still above target; negative means equity below target. A negative cell would require an equity purchase, funded by an equal bond reduction, if the target were to be reached with a separate trade. Rows replace the target equity percentage. Columns replace the withdrawal with a percentage of starting assets. The original equity weight remains selected. This lets the reader see when a cash withdrawal can finish the adjustment and when it cannot. Respect the assets available and the amount actually needed The directed rule cannot sell a negative amount or more than the holding available. Within those limits, it chooses the source split closest to the entered equity target after funding the withdrawal. It does not use leverage or buy an asset during the spending transaction. With a CAD 75,000 withdrawal under the default starting mix, taking all of it from equity leaves CAD 135,000 of equity and CAD 90,000 of bonds, exactly a 60/40 mix. A larger withdrawal can require sales from both buckets. If the entire portfolio is spent, there is no remaining allocation to measure. Requests above available assets are capped, with the unfunded amount displayed separately. Tax, dealing charges, spreads, settlement dates, registered-account rules and future market changes need another layer of planning. The charts compare sale sources for a single hypothetical transaction; they do not establish a withdrawal order that is best for every account.

documents.title: Compare the same starting assets and the same cash leaving

documents.title: Mortgage life or a level life benefit: chart the declining debt, premiums and payout destination
documents.description: Four charts compare two hypothetical protection contracts over the same mortgage schedule, separating premium cash, conditional death benefits and the amount left after debt repayment.
documents.body: Compare what the contract covers and who receives an accepted claim, alongside its premium. A declining debt benefit and a level personal benefit are not the same promise. Begin with the type of insurance, not just the word “mortgage” FCAC’s mortgage-life rights guide distinguishes optional mortgage life insurance from mortgage default insurance. They address different events and should not be treated as interchangeable products. This article compares two hypothetical death-benefit contracts: a mortgage-life limit tied to the remaining debt and an individual policy with an entered level benefit. It does not model default, disability, critical illness or unemployment coverage. All insurance amounts and premiums are assumptions. The tool cannot determine whether a person qualifies, whether a claim will be accepted or which contract is suitable. The graphics assume both contracts remain in force and any illustrated death claim is fully eligible and accepted. A debt-linked benefit can shrink as the mortgage is repaid FCAC’s comparison of optional mortgage products describes mortgage-life benefits paid to the lender and decreasing with the mortgage balance. Its comparison with individual life insurance also identifies the different beneficiary and coverage structure. The first chart uses those two structures as selected contract assumptions. The mortgage-life limit follows the scheduled debt after each payment. The individual policy’s entered benefit remains fixed throughout the chosen comparison period. Neither curve is a probability-weighted payout. A level benefit above the debt does not mean that extra money will necessarily be received; an insured event and a valid claim are still required. A benefit below the debt leaves a funding gap in this deliberately limited comparison. Use the same loan schedule under both insurance alternatives The default begins with CAD 400,000 of mortgage principal, a 25-year amortization and a nominal 5% rate compounded semiannually. The model converts that quote to an equivalent monthly rate and calculates a level month-end payment. The mortgage assumptions are identical under both insurance alternatives. Selecting a different premium does not change the loan’s interest rate or accelerate its repayment. Insurance premiums are separate cash expenses and are not treated as additional principal payments. The comparison keeps the mortgage rate unchanged for the full displayed horizon. It therefore does not reproduce a real sequence of mortgage renewals. Fees, refinancing, extra payments, arrears and changes in the debt contract are excluded. A personal review should use the actual projected balance at the date being considered. Follow the premium cash separately from the conditional benefit The default mortgage-life premium is CAD 60 per month and the individual-policy premium is CAD 40. Over ten years, with the default mortgage still outstanding, those assumed cash commitments total CAD 7,200 and CAD 4,800. The second chart accumulates the premiums as payments. They are not contributions to an investment account and do not create an accessible reserve. The illustration includes no savings component, surrender value or investment return. Both premiums are assumed flat within the selected horizon. The mortgage-life premium stops after the month the debt reaches zero; the individual policy continues for the full comparison period. Those are model conventions. Actual renewal prices, expiry dates and termination conditions must come from the written policies. Trace who receives an accepted claim and how cash is used The third graphic assumes death immediately after the final scheduled mortgage payment shown in the selected horizon. For the mortgage-life example, the accepted benefit equals the remaining debt and is paid to the lender. For the individual-policy example, the named beneficiary receives the fixed benefit and is assumed to choose mortgage repayment first. The chart separates the amount applied to debt from any residual. This use of the individual benefit is an illustration, not an automatic instruction imposed on the beneficiary. If the entered individual benefit is too small, residual family cash is zero and the remaining debt is reported in the figure note. The waterfall shows benefit less outstanding mortgage. A negative endpoint means a debt-funding shortfall, not a negative insurance payout or a new loan. Compare the actual promises before making a protection change Price is one part of the comparison. Confirm the insured person, policy term, beneficiary, coverage limit, exclusions, evidence requirements and whether the contract continues when a mortgage is refinanced or moved. The calculator does not verify any of those terms. FCAC’s rights guide calls for charges, express consent and cancellation information for applicable optional products, with a separate disclosure from a bank. Use that disclosure and the policy wording to ask questions about the actual contract, rather than treating this generic curve as a quote. A family’s protection need may also include other debts, replacement income and near-term expenses. Conversely, other verified coverage or resources may already fund part of the need. This narrow two-contract illustration is not a complete insurance-needs analysis and does not recommend replacing or cancelling an existing policy.

documents.title: Debt statistics: a holder’s median and a population’s average answer different questions
documents.description: Read official Canadian debt-holding shares and conditional median balances with their confidence intervals, then explore an independent invented population that includes zero-debt units.
documents.body: Ask which units are included before comparing a debt balance. A median among borrowers excludes nonborrowers, and multiplying it by a holding share does not generally produce the population mean. Ask whether the statistic describes everyone or only debt holders A headline about how much debt families owe can conceal an important filtering step. Some statistics include all family units, while others describe only units that hold a particular debt. A dollar balance without its population definition can therefore be easy to misread. The first two charts use Statistics Canada’s Survey of Financial Security table 11-10-0016-01 . One measures the share holding each selected debt type. The other gives the median balance among holders of that debt, excluding units with no holding of it. The reference population combines economic families with persons outside an economic family. It is not simply a count of individual adults or occupied dwellings. The 2023 survey covers the ten provinces and excludes Indigenous communities and collective dwellings. Its observations are context for understanding a population, rather than amounts a particular household ought to borrow. Keep the holding share beside the holder-only balance In 2023, the estimated holding shares were 39.0% for mortgage debt, 18.7% for lines of credit, 36.0% for credit-card and instalment debt, 12.0% for student loans and 27.1% for vehicle loans. Mortgage debt includes principal-residence mortgages and mortgages on other real estate. The corresponding holder-only median balances were CAD 205,000, CAD 20,000, CAD 4,500, CAD 14,000 and CAD 20,000. These amounts use 2023 constant dollars. The survey reference year is 2023 and the release date is 29 October 2024; they are not current borrowing offers or a snapshot of today’s accounts. A relatively common debt can have a comparatively small median balance among its holders. Conversely, a less common category can still matter greatly to the units that owe it. Neither the percentage alone nor the median alone supplies the full distribution of balances, interest rates or required payments. The categories overlap. One family unit can have a mortgage, a vehicle loan and a credit-card balance. The holding shares are therefore not slices of one mutually exclusive pie and should not be added to find the share with any debt. Read confidence intervals as uncertainty about an estimate The official table supplies lower and upper 95% confidence bounds. The charts show them as whiskers and repeat both endpoints in the data tables. These are published survey intervals, rather than uncertainty ranges invented by this website. For example, mortgage holding has an estimate of 39.0% with bounds of 38.0% and 39.9%. The holder-only mortgage median is CAD 205,000 with bounds of CAD 200,000 and CAD 215,000. The first interval concerns an estimated share; the second concerns an estimated median. Neither means individual mortgage balances mostly fall between CAD 200,000 and CAD 215,000. A confidence interval around a summary statistic is different from the spread of people’s actual balances. The selected charts do not show percentiles or individual-level data. Sampling, coverage and published rounding limit what can be concluded. The bars are descriptive; the page does not perform a significance test, infer a causal relationship between debt categories or place a reader at a national debt percentile. Build a separate population where every value is known The interactive illustration is independent of the survey. It creates exactly 100 unweighted family units. At the default, forty hold an invented debt balance of CAD 10,000 each and sixty owe zero of that debt. Neither control starts from an official observation. The median among the forty positive-debt units is CAD 10,000 because every one owes that amount. The median across all 100 units is zero: after sorting all balances, both the fiftieth and fifty-first observations are zero. The population mean is different again. Total debt is forty times CAD 10,000, or CAD 400,000. Dividing by 100 gives CAD 4,000 per invented family unit . This is an average over everyone, including the sixty zero balances. All three results are internally consistent. They answer different questions about an explicitly specified dataset. The example does not imply that real borrowers have equal debts or that the actual survey can be reconstructed from one percentage and one median. Watch the median respond differently when more units hold debt The final chart changes the whole number of holders from zero to one hundred while retaining the selected positive balance. Every point represents a different invented population, not the same families moving through time. With fewer than fifty holders, both middle observations in this particular population remain zero. At exactly fifty holders, the ordinary even-sample median averages a zero balance and a CAD 10,000 balance, producing CAD 5,000. At fifty-one holders, both middle observations are CAD 10,000. The mean rises gradually with the holder count because total debt rises by the same amount for each added identical borrower. The holder-only median stays CAD 10,000 whenever at least one holder exists. With no holders, that conditional median is unavailable; assigning it zero would hide the empty subset. This unweighted teaching rule is not a reproduction of the survey’s weighting or estimation procedure. It isolates the effect of including zero balances before interpreting a summary statistic. Use population context without turning a median into a personal limit In the invented population, multiplying the holder share by the identical holder balance gives the all-unit mean because every positive balance is known and equal. That shortcut does not generally work with a real conditional median. The population mean requires the conditional mean, alongside the holding share, rather than the middle holder’s balance. Likewise, adding several holder-only medians does not create the debt of one typical family. Each category can describe a different subset, and medians do not generally add even when measurements come from the same population. For a household plan, list its actual balances, contractual rates, payment amounts and due dates. Consider available cash and repayment capacity separately from national comparisons. The official charts clarify who and what was measured; the independent illustration makes the arithmetic consequences of changing that denominator visible.

documents.title: Currency and CAD returns: understand what you actually own
documents.description: Use four interactive charts to distinguish trading currency from exposure, invert currency quotes correctly, and find a conditional CAD break-even rate.
documents.body: The currency on the trading screen tells you how you pay. The assets and hedge policy determine the currency exposure you carry. Separate the different currency labels A Canadian investor can purchase a CAD-listed fund that owns foreign assets. Paying in Canadian dollars does not by itself eliminate the effect of exchange rates. A USD trading line likewise does not tell you the full economic currency exposure of the companies inside it. Record four fields: the currency in which you trade, the currency used to report fund values, the currencies of the underlying assets, and the fund’s hedge target. For multinational businesses, revenues, costs, and financing can introduce additional economic exposures beyond the currency of a share listing. Investor.gov’s international-investing overview identifies exchange-rate changes as one source of international investment risk. The CAD calculations below apply that general mechanism to an invented Canadian-dollar example; they do not forecast an exchange rate. The State Street issuer explanation distinguishes an ETF’s trading currency from its underlying currency exposure. Its publication is international context; no product, domicile or tax comparison from that article is modeled here. A fund return measured in USD may already reflect several underlying currency moves. Translating that USD performance into CAD is a measurement conversion, not proof that all holdings have one economic USD exposure. Use an exchange-rate quote with explicit units Define S as Canadian dollars per one US dollar. An increase in S means one US dollar buys more Canadian dollars. If R USD is the investment’s USD total return and all wealth is measured at the beginning and end, the unhedged CAD return is: 1 + R CAD = (1 + R USD ) × (S end ÷ S start ) This convention assumes any distributions remain within the USD investment and are reflected in its total return. If dividends are converted into CAD on their payment dates, translate those cash flows separately. A single ending exchange rate would otherwise misstate their timing. If your data source instead quotes US dollars per Canadian dollar, invert the relevant ratio. Writing the units beside both exchange rates is an inexpensive way to prevent a sign error. The controls use FCU for one selected foreign-currency unit. The worked USD example is one instance of that convention. A foreign-unit ledger begins with CAD wealth divided by the starting CAD-per-FCU quote. Apply the foreign-currency total return to those units, then multiply by the ending CAD-per-FCU quote to obtain ending CAD wealth. Never add CAD and FCU amounts or translate a performance number already reported in CAD a second time. Work through a gain, a headwind and a break-even point Begin with CAD 10,000 at CAD 1.25 per USD. Ignoring conversion costs, you acquire USD 8,000 of assets. Assume the USD investment earns 8% with distributions reinvested, leaving USD 8,640. Translate the ending wealth under three hypothetical exchange rates. In the first row, the foreign asset rises while the USD buys fewer Canadian dollars. The currency move is −8%, but 8% + (−8%) is not the final return. Multiplication produces −0.64% because the translation also affects the investment gain. The break-even ending rate is 1.25 ÷ 1.08 = approximately 1.1574 CAD per USD. This threshold is conditional on the assumed 8% investment return and zero costs. It is a sensitivity result, not an estimate of where the currency should trade. An 8% move does not become the opposite 8% when you invert it The default quote falls from 1.25 to 1.15 CAD per FCU, a decline of 8%. The reciprocal rises from 0.80 to approximately 0.869565 FCU per CAD, an increase of about 8.70%. The two percentage denominators differ. They describe the same conversion in different units, not independent gains and losses. Reciprocal quote change = 1 ÷ (1 + original quote change) − 1 When Q is quoted in FCU per CAD, the correct CAD growth factor is (1 + foreign asset return) × (Q start ÷ Q end ). Using Q end ÷ Q start would reverse the economic direction. Put units beside every input before comparing performance statements. The reciprocal bars isolate this quote-reading issue. The separate foreign-investment return guide shows the asset–currency interaction in a waterfall and compares repeated annual scenarios. This page’s ending-quote curve holds the foreign wealth fixed instead of extending a repeated annual forecast. A break-even quote is conditional on the asset result The final curve solves for the quote change that makes ending nominal CAD wealth equal starting CAD wealth. Its formula is 1 ÷ (1 + foreign asset return) − 1. At an 8% asset gain, a 7.4074% quote decline reaches break-even; an 8% decline goes further and produces the default 0.64% CAD loss. After a 20% foreign asset loss, a 20% quote increase is insufficient: 0.80 × 1.20 − 1 equals −4%. A 25% increase is required to restore the starting nominal CAD amount. The resulting curve is asymmetric because the percentage base changes, not because an assumed market relationship has been discovered. The curve spans foreign asset returns from −50% to +50%. A −50% asset result requires a 100% quote increase, which exceeds the quote-change control’s maximum; it remains visible on the curve rather than being clipped to the control range. A complete 100% unlevered asset loss cannot be repaired by any finite positive exchange rate. That boundary is excluded from the controls and curve. All thresholds exclude costs, taxes and inflation. They also assume no contributions, withdrawals or interim CAD conversion of distributions. None is a forecast, a likelihood, a trading signal or a hedge recommendation. What a hedge attempts to change A currency hedge takes an offsetting position intended to reduce specified exchange-rate movements. Funds commonly use foreign-exchange forwards and reset positions periodically. The actual coverage can differ from the target as asset values and cash flows change. Read the current prospectus for the hedge target, reset frequency, instruments, and residual exposure. Hedging one reporting currency is not automatically the same as hedging all of the currencies associated with the underlying holdings. A hedged return is not simply the local-market return less a fixed fee. CME’s FX pricing explanation connects forward and futures pricing with interest-rate differences. Implementation, trading, collateral, and imperfect coverage can also affect results. A hedge can remove a favorable currency contribution as well as an unfavorable one. It does not remove the market risk of the assets. Vanguard Canada’s FAQ describes extra expenses, an imperfect offset and the loss of favorable currency benefits as possible implications of hedging. An unchanged exchange-rate reference in an illustration is therefore not the performance of a real hedge. The charts here calculate unhedged translation only; they do not evaluate a forward contract, a hedge ratio or a hedged fund’s return. Connect currency exposure with the spending liability Start with what the portfolio must eventually pay. A CAD expense due soon and a flexible foreign-currency expense decades away create different problems. Evaluate the asset’s role, the size of its currency sensitivity, and how much uncertainty the spending plan can absorb. For a hypothetical 20,000 allocation, an isolated 10% translation move is about 2,000 before interactions with the asset return. Write that amount beside the relevant spending goal. Then test a joint scenario in which the asset falls and the currency moves against the investor. Partial hedging can leave part of the translation exposure in place, but its implementation still needs a stated policy. There is no universal hedge ratio on this page. Select and review a policy against the portfolio’s actual obligations instead of treating a recent currency trend as a complete investment thesis. Checks before comparing hedged and unhedged funds Confirm that the funds hold comparable assets and follow comparable benchmarks. Identify the target currency, hedge policy, fees, and distribution conventions. Compare returns in the same investor currency over the same dates. Separate fund hedge implementation from your brokerage conversion cost. Model both favorable and adverse currency outcomes with the spending goal in view. The index workbench on TickerLantern uses normalized currency-neutral scenarios. Its result is not automatically a CAD forecast. To build one, translate the modeled wealth or each dated cash flow under explicit exchange-rate assumptions and include the chosen hedge implementation consistently.

documents.title: A financed insurance premium becomes debt: follow the premium, interest and cash payments
documents.description: Use five charts to separate a loan’s usable proceeds from an optional insurance premium, compare payment schedules and trace the interest charged when the premium is financed.
documents.body: Financing a premium can reduce the cash needed at the start while increasing the debt and total payments. Compare that cost schedule separately from what a policy actually covers. Separate the protection decision from the payment decision Choosing whether a policy meets a household need and choosing how to pay for it are related decisions, but they answer different questions. A premium can look small when folded into a monthly loan payment, even though it creates a larger borrowing obligation. The example begins with CAD 25,000 needed for a purchase or another loan purpose. An optional policy has a hypothetical one-time premium of CAD 1,800. If that premium is financed, the starting debt is CAD 26,800, while usable cash for the purchase remains CAD 25,000. The additional CAD 1,800 goes to the insurer rather than becoming extra spending money. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada describes credit or loan insurance as optional and discusses recurring and one-time premiums. The charts here are original cost illustrations, not quotes from a lender or insurer. They do not determine whether a particular policy, applicant or claim qualifies. The payment increase includes principal and interest With a five-year term and an 8% nominal annual rate compounded monthly, the base CAD 25,000 loan requires about CAD 506.91 each month. Adding the CAD 1,800 premium raises the modeled payment to about CAD 543.41. The difference is about CAD 36.50 per month. Over sixty payments, the financed premium generates about CAD 2,189.85 of additional repayments. That consists of the CAD 1,800 premium and about CAD 389.85 of financing interest. The waterfall makes the two parts visible. Treating the monthly increase as though it were merely CAD 1,800 divided by sixty would leave out the interest. The loan uses a fixed monthly interest rate equal to the nominal annual rate divided by twelve. Payments occur at month-end and the final payment clears the remaining balance. The model does not round each month’s interest to cents, so an actual lender schedule can differ slightly. Fees, taxes, changing rates and early repayment would require further adjustments. A lower first payment does not settle the full cost comparison Paying CAD 1,800 from separate cash uses the entire premium before the first loan payment. Financing it spreads premium-related repayments over the loan term. A separate hypothetical recurring-premium quote of CAD 35 per month uses CAD 35 at the end of each covered month. The calendar chart isolates those insurance-related outlays. Through month twelve, the cash-premium case has used CAD 1,800, the financed-premium case about CAD 437.97, and the recurring case CAD 420. The ordinary base-loan repayment is excluded from this chart because it is common to all three cases. That earlier cash retention can matter to a household with a tight reserve. It also comes with a continuing payment obligation and, for the financed case, interest. This tool does not assign a return to retained cash or decide how much liquidity is appropriate. Read the early cash need and the full-term cost together rather than treating either number alone as the answer. The cheapest premium schedule may describe different protection The recurring-premium example totals CAD 2,100 across sixty months. The cash one-time premium totals CAD 1,800, and the financed premium totals about CAD 2,189.85. Those are cost figures under entered assumptions. They do not establish an ordering of insurance value. Actual policies can differ in eligibility, insured events, maximum benefits, definitions, exclusions and claim timing. A recurring premium may also depend on a balance or another contractual measure instead of remaining flat. The entered monthly quote therefore needs independent confirmation; the tool does not derive it from the one-time premium or assume the policies are equivalent. FCAC recommends reviewing the insurance certificate and comparing the protection with other coverage already held. A cost analysis can help identify the payment commitment, but it cannot replace that coverage review. No claim probability or claim payment is included here, and the loan-only baseline contains no insurance benefit. Count the premium once when reconciling total payments The stacked bars contain three parts: repayment of the cash advanced for the loan purpose, loan interest, and insurance premiums. In the financed case, the interest segment includes interest attributable to the premium. The premium itself is included in the premium segment even though it is repaid through the loan. Adding both the full insured-loan principal and another CAD 1,800 premium to the same bar would count the premium twice. Omitting the premium because it was financed would understate the amount being repaid. The chart instead keeps usable loan-purpose cash fixed and reconciles the complete payment total. The balance chart shows the other side of that ledger. Both loans decline to zero over the same term, but the financed-premium loan starts higher and requires a higher payment. A payment history can therefore look similar in shape while representing a different starting debt and a different monthly commitment. A longer term and a policy change need separate treatment The matrix keeps the one-time premium fixed and changes only the rate and financing term. Its cells show total premium-related repayments, including interest. A longer term can reduce the payment per month while increasing the sum paid. At zero interest, every cell equals the entered premium. The illustration keeps the loan and premium schedule in place for the full selected term. It does not estimate a refund when coverage is cancelled, calculate a lender’s payout statement or assume that cancelling a policy automatically removes the premium from an outstanding loan. A changed contract or early payoff needs a revised cash ledger using the actual terms. FCAC directs readers to the certificate and insurer for cancellation steps. Keep any actual refund, its date and its destination separate from the remaining loan balance. A refund expected later is not cash already available for today’s bill, and a balance shown on a policy illustration is not a confirmed loan payout amount. Collect the figures that make a comparison usable Confirm the net cash needed for the purchase and the total amount borrowed. Identify whether the premium is paid from cash, added to debt or charged separately. Get the rate, term, monthly payment and total scheduled repayments on a consistent basis. Read the policy’s eligibility, benefit and limitation terms independently of its price. Check actual cancellation, refund and loan-payoff terms before changing either agreement. The five charts are designed to keep each part of that conversation visible. They explain the cost mechanics without choosing a policy, valuing a potential claim, or replacing the household’s wider protection and cash-flow plan.

documents.title: The investment rose in its own currency: why your CAD return can still fall
documents.description: Use four graphics to translate a foreign-currency asset return into CAD, reconcile the interaction term and compare matched currency scenarios.
documents.body: The CAD growth factor combines the asset’s local growth factor with the change in CAD per foreign unit. Adding the two percentage changes omits their interaction. State the currency in which you measure the result An investment can rise in its own currency while declining in the currency used for the household budget. Its local value and the amount of CAD represented by each foreign unit are separate factors. Both affect the CAD value of an unhedged position. The SEC’s international-investing bulletin explains this general currency risk using a U.S.-dollar perspective. This article applies the same translation principle to original hypothetical CAD examples. It does not reproduce a market return series or assess a particular investment. The model holds one foreign-currency exposure without additions or withdrawals. Its asset-return assumption includes any distributions reinvested in the foreign currency. It assumes that the exposure is unhedged and excludes taxes, trading charges and conversion fees. Read the exchange-rate quote in the stated direction The currency control always means the percentage change in CAD per one foreign currency unit . If it is positive, each foreign unit translates into more CAD. If it is negative, each foreign unit translates into fewer CAD. The Bank of Canada’s daily exchange-rate page expresses one foreign unit converted into CAD and identifies its published rates as indicative. No rate from that page is used in this tool. The controls and examples are independent assumptions, not executable conversion quotes. For a fictional quote moving from 1.35 CAD per foreign unit to 1.215, the CAD value of each foreign unit falls by 10%. The reciprocal quote rises by about 11.11%, rather than exactly 10%. Reversing the quote changes the denominator as well as the direction, so simply reversing a percentage sign can give the wrong input. Multiply the two growth factors The one-year CAD return is (1 + local asset return) × (1 + currency change) − 1 . In the default case, the asset gains 10% in its foreign currency while CAD per foreign unit falls 10%. The CAD factor is 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, producing a 1% decline. A CAD 10,000 opening position therefore becomes CAD 9,900 after one year, before the excluded costs and taxes. The two percentages do not cancel because the currency translation applies to the ending foreign-currency value, which already includes the asset’s gain. The one-year waterfall expands the calculation into the opening CAD 10,000, a CAD 1,000 asset effect, a negative CAD 1,000 currency effect on the opening amount and a negative CAD 100 interaction. These four entries reconcile CAD 9,900 without mixing units. Distinguish an unchanged result from opposite percentage signs For a 10% local asset gain to translate into exactly zero CAD return, the currency factor would need to be 1 ÷ 1.10. That is a decline in CAD per foreign unit of about 9.09%. A 10% decline is slightly larger and produces the default loss. The fixed matrix shows other one-year combinations. A negative asset return and a positive currency change can partly offset each other, while a negative currency change can deepen an asset loss. The result depends on the pair of factors, not on the asset direction alone. The matrix assigns no probability to its scenarios. It also does not say that asset and currency returns are independent in observed markets. It isolates the translation arithmetic without estimating their joint behaviour. Use a repeated scenario without mistaking it for an observed path The default path repeats the same two annual assumptions for five years. The combined CAD factor of 0.99 repeats five times, so CAD 10,000 becomes about CAD 9,509.90. If the currency quote instead remained unchanged, the same hypothetical local asset return would produce about CAD 16,105.10. The grouped bars keep the entered asset return and starting amount fixed while replacing only the annual currency assumption. Each row has its own stated horizon. This makes the currency sensitivity visible without crediting one scenario with extra deposits or a different local asset performance. Real annual returns and exchange rates do not need to repeat. These lines connect modeled annual endpoints and contain no historical observations. The unchanged-quote comparison is a counterfactual with a constant exchange rate, not a simulated currency hedge with its own costs and mechanics. Connect the measurement currency to the household goal A household that will spend CAD needs to understand the position’s CAD value. A household with a future bill in the same foreign currency has a different currency-matching question. The foreign-goal guide separates the bill’s own price from the CAD amount required to fund it. For an actual account, identify the relevant exposure and the currency in which performance is reported before using a return number in a plan. This tool does not infer the underlying exposures of a fund, measure a company’s operating currencies or choose a hedge. Finally, allow for the costs and dates of making funds spendable. The illustrated investment values are translated reference amounts. Actual sale proceeds and conversion cash require the applicable prices, charges, taxes and settlement arrangements.

documents.title: When the goal price keeps rising: compare the saving balance with the bill you will actually pay
documents.description: Follow two growing paths, solve the monthly contribution and test how a later deadline changes both the time available and the price of the goal.
documents.body: A larger saving balance does not by itself establish progress toward an affordable goal. Compare the account and the goal price at the same future date, using separately stated assumptions. A target amount needs a date as well as a number A saving plan can pass an old target while still falling short of the purchase it was meant to fund. The account may have grown, but the cost of the same goal may have changed too. A comparison with the original price answers a different question from a comparison with the bill due at the planned purchase date. The FCAC’s goal-setting guidance pairs an amount with a timeframe and recommends reviewing the plan. This guide extends that planning structure by giving the goal price and the saving account separate growth assumptions. The goal is a fixed quantity: the same underlying purchase throughout the illustration. Its price increases at a constant assumed rate. An actual family may instead reduce the scope, choose another supplier or change the purchase. Those are useful decisions, but they should be recorded as changes to the goal rather than silently hidden inside an assumed investment return. Read the price and saving paths together Restore the example to start with a CAD 50,000 goal, CAD 10,000 already assigned to it and CAD 500 added at every month-end for eight years. The goal price is assumed to increase by 5% annually. The saving account earns a separate assumed 3% effective annual return. At the deadline, the account holds about CAD 66,751.42. That is more than the original CAD 50,000 target, but the modeled goal now costs about CAD 73,872.77. The shortfall is about CAD 7,121.35. Using today’s price as the future target would incorrectly describe this particular plan as fully funded. The line chart places both amounts on one nominal-CAD scale and the same calendar. The account receives monthly contributions after that month’s growth. The goal price uses proportional monthly compounding of its annual assumption. Neither line is a forecast or a quotation. Their purpose is to make the consequences of the chosen assumptions visible. Solve the contribution without treating it as an investment return The required-transfer calculation first grows the starting balance to the deadline. It then asks how much of the future goal remains to be funded by new monthly contributions. Each earlier contribution has more months to grow than a later one. With monthly account rate r and n contributions, the accumulated value of one dollar contributed at each month-end is ((1 + r) n − 1) ÷ r . The required monthly transfer is the remaining future funding need divided by that factor. When the account return is zero, the factor is simply n. If starting funds alone already cover the modeled goal, the required new contribution is zero. At the default settings, the solved monthly amount is about CAD 565.84, rather than CAD 500. The calculation uses unrounded values internally; displayed cents can leave a small rounding difference if used as an actual standing instruction. A transfer also needs to fit the household budget and the rules of the chosen account. The solver does not establish either affordability or available registered-account contribution room. A longer wait changes both sides of the plan The deadline bars solve separate two-, five-, eight- and twelve-year plans. Every case starts with the same assigned savings and the same current goal price. Each future date receives its own accumulated account value and its own repriced goal. Extra time creates more contribution dates and more opportunity for account growth. It also exposes the goal to more assumed price increases. The resulting required monthly amount reflects both effects. It should not be interpreted as a comparison that keeps the future purchase price fixed while only adding saving years. Under some combinations of a fast-growing price and a lower account return, extending a sufficiently distant deadline may stop reducing the required monthly amount. This is a property of those assumptions, not a prediction that waiting is always harmful. The appropriate response is to review the goal, saving capacity and timing together. Raising the return assumption solely to make an unaffordable plan appear funded leaves the underlying uncertainty unresolved. Reconcile the gap before deciding how to close it The waterfall starts with today’s CAD 50,000 goal and adds about CAD 23,872.77 of modeled price increase. It subtracts the CAD 10,000 starting balance, CAD 48,000 of new contributions and about CAD 8,751.42 of account growth. The endpoint is the same CAD 7,121.35 shortfall shown above. This separates the household’s contribution effort from the account’s return. The CAD 48,000 is not a gain earned by the investment; it is new money the household supplied. Similarly, the increase in the target is not a loss inside the account. It is a change in the price of the separate goal. If accumulated funds exceed the target, the waterfall retains a negative endpoint to show the surplus. The headline instead reports zero unfunded amount. Those displays use different sign conventions for different purposes, so the surplus should not be added back to the account a second time. Keep the plan tied to supported prices and usable cash The matrix changes goal-price growth and the account return independently. It holds the starting price, starting balance and deadline selected in the tool. Every cell solves the full monthly transfer under that combination. The cells are scenarios, not confidence intervals, success rates or recommendations for particular investments. For an actual plan, replace the starting cost with a dated, relevant estimate and record what it includes. Check whether deposits are due before the final purchase date; a single deadline cannot represent an earlier payment schedule. Confirm which savings are exclusively assigned to this goal rather than also required for an emergency reserve or another bill. Review the price and the account at consistent intervals. A real target can change abruptly, while account returns can be uneven or negative. This simple tool excludes those paths, taxes and fees. Its practical contribution is a repeatable funding question: at the date the money is needed, how much does the goal cost, how much is actually assigned to it, and what saving commitment closes the supported gap?

documents.title: One bank balance, several promises: stop counting the same savings more than once
documents.description: Compare requested earmarks with money actually available, then use a payment calendar to find whether future deposits arrive before the cash is needed.
documents.body: Naming a bank balance an emergency fund, a tax reserve and a purchase fund does not create three balances. Reconcile all claims to the same cash and then check the payment dates. Separate a purpose label from an additional asset Suppose a household sees CAD 30,000 in a bank account and mentally describes it as enough for a CAD 12,000 emergency reserve. Later, the same statement seems sufficient for a CAD 9,000 bill. A planned CAD 14,000 purchase also looks smaller than the displayed balance. Each statement can appear reasonable in isolation while the three claims together exceed the cash. The combined requirement is CAD 35,000. Only CAD 30,000 exists at the start, so the full claims are overcommitted by CAD 5,000. Repeating the balance beside each goal does not make the difference available. The FCAC’s budgeting guidance treats saving goals as part of the same plan as income and expenses. This article applies that idea to money already accumulated. It does not prescribe a reserve size or decide which personal goal should receive priority. Allocate existing money once, in an explicit order The opening-allocation bars use a stated illustrative order: assign cash to the protected floor, then the required bill, then the planned purchase. This is an accounting convention for the example, not a legal priority rule or an optimized recommendation. The first CAD 12,000 is assigned to the floor, leaving CAD 18,000. The required bill receives CAD 9,000, leaving CAD 9,000. The purchase requests CAD 14,000 but can be assigned only the remaining CAD 9,000. Its opening funding gap is therefore CAD 5,000. The three assigned amounts add to CAD 30,000, exactly the actual balance. Another order could move the unfunded amount to a different purpose; it would not eliminate the total shortage. A dedicated bank subaccount can make an assignment easier to track, but a transfer between a household’s own accounts does not create new resources. Reconcile the combined balances and assignments once. Understand what the opening waterfall subtracts The opening waterfall begins with the real bank balance and subtracts all requested claims. Its negative CAD 5,000 endpoint describes unassigned capacity after those full requests. It is not the bank’s actual closing balance, because no bill has been paid merely by writing down the earmarks. This distinction matters when reviewing a household balance sheet. Earmarked cash remains an asset. A planned expense is a future use of that asset. Subtracting the cash from net worth when it is labelled, and then subtracting the later bill again, would count the same use twice. The allocation test deliberately ignores future income. It answers whether all the purposes can be funded immediately from current cash. The next chart adds a separate calendar to answer whether new money can close the gap before each bill. Passing that second test does not mean the opening claims were fully funded at the start. Future saving helps only before the relevant payment The default calendar adds CAD 500 of new money before each month’s bills. It pays the required CAD 9,000 bill in month four and the CAD 14,000 purchase in month eight. The CAD 12,000 protected floor is a reference amount retained as cash throughout, not a third bill paid away. After the required bill, the account holds CAD 23,000. By month eight, new saving and the purchase payment leave CAD 11,000. That is still a positive bank balance, but it is CAD 1,000 below the selected protected floor. At year-end, the account has recovered to CAD 13,000. A year-end review would therefore miss the earlier use of the protected money. The calendar needs CAD 1,000 of extra starting cash to stay at or above the floor at every modeled date. That is different from the CAD 5,000 opening allocation shortage: four thousand dollars of new saving has arrived by the purchase date, reducing the funding problem before the bill is paid. Test the floor, purchase size and new-money assumption The matrix changes the planned-purchase amount and monthly new money. Starting cash, the selected floor, the required bill and both payment months stay fixed. Each cell measures additional starting cash needed to preserve the floor at every date, including time zero. If both bills fall in the same month, the ledger adds them before testing the remaining cash. If a bill actually arrives before that month’s income, a more detailed daily calendar may require additional accessible cash. The modeled order of receipts before bills should therefore be checked against real dates. The tool pays entered bills in full even if the balance becomes negative. That negative amount identifies an unfunded need; it is not an assumed overdraft approval, credit line or permission to miss another payment. No borrowing interest is hidden in the chart. Changing or postponing a purchase would require an explicit new scenario. Keep one source of truth for cash assigned to goals Start with a dated statement balance for money that is actually accessible. List every purpose already claiming part of it. Confirm bill amounts and dates independently; the field labelled required bill can represent a tax payment, but this tool neither determines tax owed nor establishes its due date. Record an amount as assigned, still unfunded or paid. When a bill is paid, reduce both bank cash and its outstanding claim so that a completed expense does not remain in the future budget. When new saving arrives, assign it once. Interest, refunds or transfers should be added only when the plan has supported amounts and receipt dates. Use the four views together: requested versus assigned money, total opening capacity, the real cash calendar and alternative funding assumptions. A reserve is useful only to the extent that the cash remains available when needed. A good set of labels helps reveal that availability; the labels themselves cannot supply it.

documents.title: Leverage and drawdowns: why a 20% asset loss can halve the money you own
documents.description: Follow own capital through a leveraged loss. Separate the asset move, unchanged loan principal and interest already paid, then compare household resources across four stress charts.
documents.body: A lender’s principal remains owed when an investment falls. Measure the remaining own capital and the interest cash already paid, rather than interpreting the asset’s percentage change as the household’s full result. Write down the asset and the liability separately Borrowing can make an investment account larger without adding the same amount to household net worth. A CAD 30,000 loan adds CAD 30,000 of purchasing power and a CAD 30,000 liability. The account statement shows the investment; a complete plan also needs the debt. The Autorité des marchés financiers explains the risks of borrowing to invest , including that the loan and interest remain payable when investments lose value. The charts isolate that arithmetic with original inputs. They do not determine whether a lender will approve a loan or whether borrowing is appropriate for a particular household. The example invests CAD 20,000 of own capital with CAD 30,000 of borrowed principal, creating a CAD 50,000 investment. Interest is paid from new outside household money. The investment is sold at the selected final date and the original loan principal is repaid then. There is no assumption that the investment pays distributions to cover the monthly bill. A 20% asset loss can remove half the original own capital The default asset-change input is a cumulative negative 20% over the entire three-year horizon. It is not negative 20% in each year. The CAD 50,000 investment therefore falls by CAD 10,000 and is sold for CAD 40,000. Repaying the unchanged CAD 30,000 loan leaves CAD 10,000. Relative to the original CAD 20,000 of own capital, half remains before considering outside interest payments. The asset’s 20% decline and the own-capital reduction use different denominators. The sale waterfall makes the distinction explicit: own money plus the borrowed principal, plus the investment-value change, less the loan repaid. If sale proceeds are below the loan, the arithmetic endpoint becomes negative. The chart retains that gap rather than flooring it at zero. It does not determine the borrower’s legal liability, the availability of other collateral or contractual guarantees. Paying the interest elsewhere does not remove its cost At the assumed nominal annual loan rate of 8%, the unchanged CAD 30,000 principal requires CAD 200 of interest each month. Across three years, the household supplies CAD 7,200 of outside cash. The model pays it as it arises, so it is not added to the loan balance. The account’s sale residual is CAD 10,000, but the complete investment result also subtracts the CAD 20,000 initially supplied and the CAD 7,200 interest paid along the way. That leaves a negative CAD 17,200 result. It is an amount of money lost across the modeled cash flows, not an annualized return or a statement that the whole loss occurred at the final sale. The annual-interest bars show alternative assumed loan rates on the same principal. These cash commitments exist even when the asset supplies no cash income. A principal repayment schedule, loan fees, changing interest rates or capitalized interest would require another ledger. None is silently included here. Compare equal household resources, not a free interest budget A no-loan alternative invests only the same CAD 20,000 of own capital. To keep the household-resource comparison consistent, it also receives the same CAD 200 of outside money each month. It retains that money in zero-return cash because it has no loan-interest bill to pay. After the same cumulative 20% investment decline, the unborrowed investment is CAD 16,000. Adding CAD 7,200 of retained cash gives CAD 23,200 of ending resources. The borrowed alternative has CAD 10,000 after repaying principal. The difference is negative CAD 13,200. That difference consists of the CAD 6,000 loss on the borrowed investment portion and CAD 7,200 of interest paid instead of retained. The extra monthly money is not treated as an investment gain in the no-loan case. Both households received it; one kept it and the other used it to service debt. This is why the ending-resource lines and the net-investment-result headline answer related but different questions. A positive result does not establish that borrowing helped Change the cumulative investment move to positive 20% while leaving the three-year horizon and 8% nominal loan rate unchanged. The CAD 50,000 investment becomes CAD 60,000, leaving CAD 30,000 after loan repayment. Subtracting own starting capital and outside interest produces a positive CAD 2,800 investment result. The no-loan alternative has a CAD 24,000 investment plus CAD 7,200 of retained outside cash, or CAD 31,200. The borrowed choice is still CAD 1,200 behind on the same household-resource basis. Making money overall and benefiting from the borrowing are therefore separate tests. In this simple zero-fee, zero-tax, zero-cash-return setup, the incremental borrowed portion needs a cumulative asset gain greater than the loan rate multiplied by the number of years to finish ahead. At the defaults that threshold is 24% over three years. It is not a guaranteed return, a quoted loan hurdle, or a sufficient assessment of risk. The asset path may also create cash or contractual problems before the endpoint. Use the stress views to identify obligations outside the investment The signed matrix changes cumulative asset moves and loan sizes. It deducts the original own capital and every outside interest payment from sale proceeds after repaying principal. More borrowing increases both market exposure and required interest cash. Negative cells remain visible; the matrix does not attach a probability to them. Real borrowing can add collateral requirements, early demands for repayment, trading restrictions, fees and tax questions. The illustration intentionally calculates none of those. Its fixed principal, fixed interest rate and ability to wait until the endpoint are assumptions that would need to be supported by an actual agreement. In particular, these charts must not be used to estimate a margin call or a permitted brokerage borrowing limit. Begin a household review with the money required for bills, reserves and debt service independently of investment performance. Then record the actual liability beside the asset and trace interest payments from their real cash source. The useful lesson is the reconciliation: asset value, loan principal, remaining own capital and cash already paid are different quantities, and a plan needs all of them.
