documents.title: A rental move on a daily cash calendar: include full rent, pay dates and the deposit refund
documents.description: Follow a fictional sixty-day rental move in four charts, with overlapping rent, deposits, pay dates and an independently assumed refund arrival.
documents.body: An expected deposit refund is different from cash already available. Find the lowest balance on the calendar before using a positive final balance to judge the move’s funding. Start with accessible cash and a separate refund assumption The fictional household allocates CAD 4,000 before the first model day. That amount excludes the old deposit still held elsewhere and money already reserved for other bills. Four CAD 2,000 net pay deposits arrive on days ten, twenty-five, forty and fifty-five. The household separately expects CAD 900 back from its old-home deposit, with actual cash availability assumed on day thirty-five. The refund is entered as an amount expected to arrive, rather than inferred from the original deposit, interest rules or a claim against a landlord. The first chart follows daily cash. A second line begins with the minimum opening amount that funds every listed day. It changes the starting reserve, while keeping every receipt, cost and date the same. It does not automatically borrow the difference or move a required rent payment. List the old rent, new rent, deposit and moving payment separately The assumed cash obligations are CAD 1,800 of final old-home rent and CAD 1,000 of new deposit cash on day one, CAD 600 of moving costs on day fourteen, and CAD 2,000 of new-home rent on days fifteen and forty-five. Four CAD 900 living-cost payments occur on days seven, twenty-two, thirty-seven and fifty-two. These are entered cash dates, not a determination of when a lease ends or how rent must be prorated. Some rent paid within the sixty-day window can cover occupancy beyond it. The calendar therefore measures payments, rather than accrued housing expense for an exactly matched occupancy period. At the starting inputs, cash falls to negative CAD 300 after the first new-rent payment on day fifteen. It reaches negative CAD 1,200 after the living-cost payment on day twenty-two. The day-thirty-five refund cannot pay either earlier obligation without another identified source. Distinguish the required reserve from the final cash balance Funding all listed events requires CAD 5,200 before day one. With CAD 4,000 already allocated, the additional opening requirement is CAD 1,200. The fully funded line reaches zero at its lowest point; it does not represent income earned or a loan approved by the model. The originally allocated path nevertheless ends day sixty with positive CAD 1,900. That endpoint can coexist with the earlier shortfall because later receipts restore the cash balance. A positive final total alone does not establish that every payment was fundable when due. The second figure provides thirty-day receipt and payment summaries. In the first thirty days, cash received is CAD 4,000 and cash paid is CAD 7,200. Opening cash leaves a day-thirty balance of CAD 800, even though the daily balance previously fell below zero. The summary cannot replace the dated check. Reconcile money paid without treating every deposit as consumption The waterfall begins with CAD 4,000, adds CAD 8,000 of pay and the CAD 900 refund received, then subtracts CAD 5,800 of rent, CAD 1,000 of new deposit cash, CAD 600 of moving costs and CAD 3,600 of living payments. The endpoint is CAD 1,900. The new deposit uses cash but is not automatically a permanently lost expense. The old refund returns money previously held elsewhere; it is not a second paycheque in this ledger. Any eventual deduction, deposit interest or dispute needs its own evidence and treatment. Do not include the old deposit in starting bank cash and add its refund again later. Conversely, a deposit still held can represent a separate expected claim without being available to pay the next bill. The model does not value or adjudicate that claim. Test arrival dates and amounts without predicting a legal result The grid changes opening cash and the assumed arrival of the same CAD 900 refund. With the starting costs, a receipt on day ten or twenty reduces the required opening fund to CAD 4,300. The CAD 4,000 allocation would then need another CAD 300. A receipt on day thirty-five requires CAD 5,200 because the worst funding point has already occurred. Moving the receipt to day sixty-one leaves that same peak requirement in this example, while reducing day-sixty cash to CAD 1,000. Every delay does not mechanically increase the worst shortfall; its position relative to other events matters. An earlier cell assumes an actual earlier payment. It does not create a right to demand that timing. A day after sixty means no refund has arrived within the plotted window, not that the claim has vanished. For a disputed or uncertain receipt, reducing the assumed amount or setting it to zero tests funding without deciding what is legally owed. Keep BC deposit rules separate from the cash-arrival control For ordinary tenancies covered by BC’s Residential Tenancy Act, RTB guidance describes a security deposit capped at half the first month’s rent and a separate pet damage deposit capped at half a month’s rent. The calculator accepts assumed cash amounts and does not determine whether a specific requested charge is lawful. Section 38 of the Act generally requires repayment with applicable interest or an application claiming against a deposit within fifteen days after the later of tenancy end and the landlord’s receipt of the tenant’s written forwarding address. Inspection rights, written retention consent, orders and statutory exceptions can affect the result. That process is different from a promise that spendable bank funds arrive fifteen days after moving. The RTB return calculator addresses process dates and initiation. This guide does not calculate service, legal deadlines, interest, permitted deductions, penalties or entitlement, and the BC context should not be applied automatically to another jurisdiction. Replace the fictional calendar with confirmed obligations and evidence Confirm the old tenancy’s actual end and rent obligation, the new agreement’s payment dates and deposit amounts, and the moving quote. Keep any overlap or proration agreement separate from the day on which keys physically change hands. For the old deposit, retain receipts, condition reports, inspection communications and the written forwarding-address record. Identify any agreed deduction, application or order and the amount actually returned. The RTB moving-out guidance provides context; these graphs do not resolve a disputed settlement. Finally, use the date money becomes available, including the payment method’s processing time, rather than only a cheque or transfer instruction date. Same-day receipts are assumed available before outflows in this example. If that cannot be verified, separate the events and retain enough cash for the earlier obligation. The reserve is a timing requirement alongside the move’s eventual costs.

documents.title: An upfront loan fee can shrink the cash you receive without shrinking the debt you repay
documents.description: Reconcile a fee withheld from a loan advance, follow monthly amortization and calculate an explicitly defined annual cash-flow rate without calling it statutory APR.
documents.body: Compare the cash actually received with every repayment. A quoted interest rate and a payment amount do not, by themselves, explain the effect of an upfront fee. Separate contract principal from net cash advanced The hypothetical loan has CAD 10,000 of contract principal and a 5% upfront fee withheld from its proceeds. The fee is CAD 500, so the borrower receives CAD 9,500. The repayment schedule still amortizes CAD 10,000. The first waterfall makes that difference visible. This is one particular fee arrangement. A charge paid separately from other cash or added to financed principal would require a different opening ledger. Do not combine those treatments by withholding the fee and also adding it to the loan balance. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s personal-loan guide identifies interest, fees and term as elements of borrowing cost. The amounts and rate conventions here are independently authored examples. They are not a lender quote, an eligibility assessment or a recommendation to borrow. State the rate and payment conventions before comparing schedules The default uses an 8% nominal annual interest rate divided by twelve, with 36 payments at month-end. The full term is also the full amortization period. There is no unpaid balloon at the end and no rate renewal during the schedule. The unrounded monthly payment is approximately CAD 313.36. Interest for each month applies to the principal outstanding before that payment. The remainder of the payment reduces principal. As principal falls, monthly interest falls and more of the same payment reduces the balance. The path chart separates outstanding principal, cumulative principal repaid and cumulative interest paid. Changing only the withheld fee leaves these contractual paths unchanged. It changes the initial cash received. Actual agreements may use different dates, interest conventions, rounding or charges, all of which need to be reconciled before using an illustration as a payment plan. Subtract net proceeds from payments without charging the fee twice The modeled 36 payments total approximately CAD 11,281.09. Of that amount, CAD 10,000 repays contract principal and approximately CAD 1,281.09 is interest. The initial proceeds, however, were only CAD 9,500. Payments less net proceeds therefore equal approximately CAD 1,781.09. That difference reconciles to CAD 1,281.09 of interest plus the CAD 500 withheld fee. The stacked chart shows these two cost components, rather than describing every repayment dollar as a borrowing expense. Once the fee has reduced initial proceeds, do not add it again to the payment-minus-proceeds difference. Conversely, subtracting the full CAD 10,000 contract principal from payments and stopping there would omit the withheld fee’s cost. Keep the opening cash event and the repayment ledger beside one another. Define the annualized cash-flow measure precisely The calculator finds the monthly discount rate at which the scheduled equal payments have a present value equal to the CAD 9,500 actually received. It then compounds that monthly rate over twelve periods. In the default, this effective annual cash-flow rate is approximately 12.15%. With no withheld fee, the same calculation gives approximately 8.30% effectively per year. That differs from the stated 8% nominal annual rate because the example converts a monthly rate into an annually compounded measure. The fee then creates an additional difference by reducing the proceeds supporting the same payment stream. This explicitly defined measure is not a calculation of statutory disclosed APR. FCAC’s disclosure guide lists annual interest, APR when different, payment details and other charges for federally regulated fixed-rate loans. Use the actual disclosure and applicable calculation rules for a regulated comparison. A longer term can lower one rate measure while increasing total interest The matrix varies the fee percentage and the number of monthly repayments while retaining the contract principal and nominal annual interest rate. Every cell recalculates both the payment and the net-advance discount rate. Spreading an upfront fee over more months can reduce its annualized impact. That does not mean the longer loan necessarily costs fewer dollars. A longer repayment schedule usually leaves principal outstanding for more time, creating additional interest under this fixed-rate model. Read the monthly commitment, full payment total, fee and effective cash-flow measure together. A lower payment can help a monthly budget while extending indebtedness. A lower annualized measure can coexist with a larger full-term dollar cost. None of those measures alone decides whether the loan meets a household’s needs. Reconcile the offer with the household’s payment calendar Begin with the amount that will actually arrive, the amount owed, every required charge and the date of each repayment. Confirm whether optional services are included, how interest accrues and what changes if the loan is repaid early. This calculator assumes the full schedule is completed. Then place the payments beside actual take-home receipts and existing commitments. A mathematical payment does not establish that cash will be available on the withdrawal date. Avoid treating a fee-financed or fee-withheld offer as interchangeable with an offer that delivers a different usable amount. The illustration excludes loan insurance, other fees, missed payments, extra payments, refinancing and tax. Calculations retain full precision and reconcile a tiny numerical residual in the last payment. They explain the relationship among principal, proceeds and cost without determining legal compliance, qualifying terms or a personal borrowing decision.

documents.title: Child-benefit cash needs a payment calendar: a July change and a year-end surplus do not fund an earlier bill
documents.description: Use the official 2026 CCB schedule beside independently entered half-year receipt amounts, then trace first-of-month bills, dedicated funding and a hypothetical receipt delay.
documents.body: Confirm the benefit amount and payment pattern independently. A benefit assigned to a later date can support the annual budget while leaving an earlier bill unfunded. Keep the benefit period separate from the calendar year The CRA’s CCB payment page , updated 22 October 2026 and reviewed here on 25 October, provides twelve scheduled 2026 dates. Its mapping uses the 2024 tax year for January–June payments and the 2025 tax year for July–December payments. A calendar-year budget can therefore contain portions of two benefit periods. The CRA amount guide explains the annual July recalculation using prior-year adjusted family net income. This is a reference-year relationship, not a calculation of the amount an individual family will receive. The model takes two independently entered monthly receipt amounts. It does not calculate eligibility, adjusted family net income, child-age effects, custody arrangements or combined provincial benefits. An actual family’s notice and expected payment details must establish the receipt amounts and pattern before they belong in a working cash plan. Enter known receipts rather than inferring an entitlement The authored default assigns CAD 450 to each scheduled January–June receipt and CAD 600 to each scheduled July–December receipt. Those six-month amounts total CAD 6,300 across the 2026 schedule. They are hypothetical inputs, not published maximum CCB amounts. Each half-year remains constant solely to make the calendar readable. A reassessment, changed family circumstances, stopped payment or other adjustment may require a more detailed schedule. Entering zero does not decide whether a benefit is payable; it simply removes that assumed receipt from the arithmetic. Use the monthly model only where a recurring monthly pattern has been independently established. CRA also describes a lump-sum arrangement for low annual entitlements. The calculator does not create that arrangement or transform a small entered amount into a monthly entitlement. No future-year payment schedule is inferred from the 2026 dates. Place the bill before the benefit when that matches the budget The dedicated budget begins with no opening cash. On every month’s first day, the household assigns CAD 150 from its other resources and then pays a selected CAD 600 child-related bill. The month initially reaches negative CAD 450. Under the default timing, the first CAD 450 benefit receipt later returns January’s balance to zero. The same pattern repeats through June. A later receipt does not retroactively provide the cash needed on the first day, so the required extra opening reserve is CAD 450. From July, the selected CAD 600 receipt exceeds that month’s CAD 450 gap by CAD 150. The dedicated balance gradually improves. Other household funding is an allocation from resources outside this sub-budget; it is not a newly created source of total household wealth. Confirm that the allocation is affordable alongside the rest of the family’s commitments. Reconcile the annual surplus separately from the interim reserve Twelve assignments of CAD 150 provide CAD 1,800. Add CAD 6,300 of benefit receipts and subtract twelve CAD 600 bills, or CAD 7,200. The calendar-year reconciliation leaves CAD 900. That positive ending amount coexists with the earlier CAD 450 funding requirement. The opening reserve shifts the cash path upward; it does not change the benefit entitlement or make the selected expense cheaper. Looking only at the annual surplus would miss the need to fund the first bill before its later receipt. The waterfall stops on 31 December. It includes only receipts that the selected timing places inside 2026. A delayed receipt arriving after that date belongs in the later collection segment, not in the year-end cash balance. The chart data retains the full dates of each funding assignment, bill and receipt. Test a receipt delay without presenting it as a forecast The lag control adds a hypothetical number of calendar days after every scheduled date. It does not alter CRA’s published schedule, predict a processing delay or guarantee that a bank balance will be available at a particular time. With a 14-day lag in the default, all selected receipts still arrive during 2026, and the final balance remains CAD 900. The required opening cash increases to CAD 900 because another first-of-month bill can arrive before the delayed receipt. At 35 days, the selected December receipt moves to 15 January 2027. The 2026 balance becomes CAD 300; the later CAD 600 receipt brings the collection-only endpoint to CAD 900. No 2027 bill or additional household funding is modeled during that runoff segment, so it is not a complete forecast of the following year. Keep the dedicated reserve connected to actual family cash flow The matrix changes the opening reserve and other monthly household funding while retaining the benefit inputs, selected bill and lag. Each cell reports extra starting cash required to keep every modeled bill funded. It does not report extra benefits, a tax saving or a probability of a shortfall. For implementation, confirm the actual expected receipts, list the relevant bills and place both on a calendar with other income. Keep costs entered here separate from costs already included elsewhere, and count each reserved dollar once. A bill already paid from another budget should not be deducted again without transferring its funding too. Review the plan after a confirmed payment or cost change. This is a fixed-year cash illustration, not an application tool or an entitlement calculator. Its purpose is to show when supported resources arrive, how much cash is needed beforehand and why the timing question remains important even when the annual total looks comfortable.

documents.title: Compound GIC interest: plan for tax cash before the investment pays out
documents.description: Separate a locked compound investment from an outside tax reserve, then identify a pre-maturity cash gap that a large final payout can conceal.
documents.body: Interest reporting, access to investment cash and the date tax must be funded are separate questions. A growing locked balance cannot automatically pay a bill due before maturity. Separate interest income from accessible cash A compound investment can earn interest without delivering that interest to a chequing account. The balance grows inside the product, while the household’s available cash may remain unchanged. That difference matters if an income-related payment must be funded before the investment matures. The CRA’s line 12100 guidance explains that interest on term deposits, GICs and similar investments may need to be reported for each complete investment year even when cash is paid later and no T5 slip has been received. Waiting for maturity does not automatically postpone reporting all the interest. This article illustrates the resulting cash-planning question for a non-registered compound investment. It does not calculate a return or deadline for a particular taxpayer. Registered accounts, ownership attribution, other income, credits and benefit effects require their own rules and records. Keep the investment and the outside reserve in separate ledgers The example invests CAD 100,000 for five years at a hypothetical 4% effective annual rate, compounded annually. It assumes that neither principal nor interest can be withdrawn before maturity. The first completed investment year adds CAD 4,000 of interest, leaving CAD 104,000 inside the locked investment. An independently assumed tax rate of 30% produces CAD 1,200 of modeled tax funding for that year. The tax money comes from outside the investment. Deducting it from the GIC would contradict the selected no-access assumption and would also change subsequent compound interest. The outside ledger starts with CAD 2,000 and receives CAD 50 at every month-end. Those transfers are new household saving, rather than investment profit. Outside cash earns zero interest in this simplified exercise. The graph labels any negative outside balance as a provisional funding gap. It does not create an overdraft, loan or hidden injection of money. A plan with such a gap needs an additional supported funding source before it can be implemented. State the funding dates without mistaking them for tax law For transparency, the model funds the assumed tax at the end of each completed investment year, after that month’s reserve transfer. At the end of the final investment year, it first receives the maturity proceeds and then funds the last modeled tax amount. Those are deliberately chosen arithmetic dates. A completed investment year, a calendar tax year, a filing deadline and a tax-payment deadline are not interchangeable. Actual reporting and payment requirements must be checked separately, including any instalment obligation. The CRA page reviewed on 25 October 2026 is dated 20 January 2026 and includes 2025-return examples. It supports the distinction between accrued interest and cash received; it does not supply the calculator’s funding calendar or its 30% input. For a real account, identify the investment’s issue and maturity dates, actual interest records and applicable tax requirements before mapping cash transfers to payment dates. The tool’s investment-year labels intentionally avoid claiming to be a calendar-year filing schedule. Find the shortage before looking at the final payout The first four years add interest of CAD 4,000, CAD 4,160, CAD 4,326.40 and CAD 4,499.46, with calculations retaining unrounded precision. Their modeled tax funding totals approximately CAD 5,095.76 . By the fourth year-end, the outside ledger has received the CAD 2,000 opening reserve plus forty-eight CAD 50 transfers, or CAD 4,400. After the accumulated modeled tax payments, its provisional balance is negative CAD 695.76. This is the largest pre-maturity shortage in the default scenario. The household would need approximately CAD 695.76 of additional opening cash, rounded up to cents, to cover those simplified dates without a negative balance. The exact underlying requirement is calculated before display rounding. It is additional to the CAD 2,000 already assigned. The investment itself is still growing at that point. Its larger balance does not solve the cash shortage when access is unavailable. The first chart focuses on outside cash before maturity, keeping the earlier shortage visible instead of compressing it beside the much larger future payout. Annual interest is shown separately. Reconcile the maturity endpoint without ignoring external saving After five years, gross interest totals CAD 21,665.29 and the maturity proceeds are CAD 121,665.29. The modeled final-year tax funding is about CAD 1,403.83, bringing all five years’ modeled tax to CAD 6,499.59. The final waterfall begins with the CAD 100,000 investment, adds the CAD 2,000 opening outside reserve, CAD 3,000 of new monthly saving and CAD 21,665.29 of gross interest, then subtracts all modeled tax. The arithmetic cash endpoint is approximately CAD 120,165.70. That endpoint includes the new household resources and cannot be read as the investment alone earning CAD 20,165.70 after tax. The return contribution is the gross interest less modeled tax; the opening reserve and monthly transfers have different origins. A positive endpoint also does not prove that the earlier plan worked. The calculation carries a provisional funding deficit through time to reveal it. Maturity proceeds arriving later cannot retroactively settle a payment that lacked cash before maturity. Use the reserve matrix to test a funding plan The matrix varies the assumed tax rate and the monthly outside allocation, holding the selected principal, interest rate, horizon and opening reserve fixed. Every cell recalculates the greatest pre-maturity shortage. A zero cell means the entered resources cover this simplified schedule, rather than proving no tax is payable. A larger monthly allocation requires room in the household budget. An increased opening reserve also needs a supported source and should not be counted as simultaneously available for another goal. Neither change modifies the locked investment’s gross compound return in this example. Use actual statements and issuer information to reconcile reportable interest, and check current tax guidance before filing or paying. Then build a dated outside-cash plan. The practical lesson is a reconciliation: what has been earned, what is accessible, what must be paid, and which resources can reach the payment date.

documents.title: Claim an RRSP deduction now or later: compare the tax savings at the same date
documents.description: Use four interactive graphics to compare an earlier tax saving with a larger later one, including cash availability, opportunity growth and the break-even saving rate.
documents.body: A higher later tax-saving rate is only part of the comparison. Earlier cash has a use during the wait, so value both alternatives at the same date. Separate making a contribution from claiming its deduction An RRSP contribution and an RRSP deduction are related records with different roles. A contribution places money into the plan. A deduction is claimed on a tax return within the applicable limit. An amount reported as contributed does not have to be fully deducted on the same return. CRA’s contribution questions and answers explains that unused contributions can be deducted in a future return up to the deduction limit. Its unused-contribution guidance describes reporting the contributions and locating the recorded unused amount. This article examines a narrow timing choice: the same eligible, already-funded contribution and the same deduction amount in both alternatives. It does not compare contributing now with contributing later, or RRSPs with another account. The common RRSP assets are held identical so the charts can isolate the tax-saving cash. Estimate the tax reduction over the whole deduction The default amount is CAD 10,000. A current assumed tax reduction of CAD 25 per CAD 100 deducted produces CAD 2,500. The later assumption of CAD 35 per CAD 100 produces CAD 3,500. These are independently chosen teaching inputs rather than federal or provincial tax brackets. A deduction may cross several tax brackets. Its total income-tax reduction divided by the deduction amount can therefore differ from the marginal rate on the next dollar of income. A real comparison should estimate the return with and without the deduction and review any other affected items separately. No benefit or credit interaction is calculated here. Nor does a tax saving necessarily mean a cheque of that amount: it may reduce an outstanding tax balance. The cash comparison requires an amount that is actually available for the modeled use. Place both amounts at the later cash-availability date Time 0 is the date when the current alternative’s tax-saving cash becomes available. The later amount becomes available four full model years afterward in the default example. These dates are abstractions for cash timing, not a claim that filing a return releases money immediately or that the waiting period equals a particular number of tax returns. If the CAD 2,500 current saving is retained outside the RRSP and earns a constant 5% annually after assumed tax and costs, its value after four years is CAD 2,500 × 1.05⁴ = CAD 3,038.77 . The later CAD 3,500 receipt is therefore CAD 461.23 larger at that same date under the selected assumptions. Comparing CAD 2,500 today directly with CAD 3,500 later omits the use of the earlier cash. Conversely, applying four years of growth to both amounts would give the deferred alternative growth before its cash exists. The line chart compounds only the earlier receipt and shows the later receipt as a final jump. Calculate the later rate needed to cover the wait With a positive deduction amount, equal cash values occur when the later saving rate equals the current saving rate × (1 + opportunity return) raised to the waiting years . The common deduction amount cancels from that comparison. At the defaults, 25% × 1.05⁴ is about 30.39%. A later assumed rate of 30% is higher than 25%, yet its CAD 3,000 saving would be slightly below CAD 3,038.77 at the comparison date. A higher rate by itself does not establish that waiting wins. Change the return to zero to remove this particular opportunity cost. Try a negative return to see the effect of a loss on the retained saving. The constant return is a scenario, not a promise that an investment will provide it. If the earlier saving would be used differently, choose an appropriate comparison rather than assuming this cash account describes the household. Stress the rate and the delay as separate uncertainties The matrix replaces the later assumed tax-saving rate and the waiting period while retaining the other inputs. Each cell compares the two alternatives at that row’s later receipt date. A negative amount favours the current saving’s opportunity value; a positive amount favours the later receipt in this limited calculation. The rows end in different years, so they are not four wealth amounts measured on one common calendar date. They show how each proposed wait changes its own comparison. The matrix assigns no probability to an income rise or a future tax-saving rate. The waterfall explains the selected case: later saving, less the current saving forgone, less the growth on that current saving. This reconciliation helps identify whether an apparent advantage comes from the assumed tax reduction or the treatment of time. Check the deduction record and the household use of the cash CRA identifies unused contributions on the RRSP Deduction Limit Statement and related records. Keep contribution receipts, reported unused amounts and the amount actually deducted distinct. A decision to claim less this year does not create additional contribution room or make an otherwise excessive contribution permissible. Confirm that the chosen deduction is available in the relevant year before applying a timing comparison. The calculator assumes eligibility in both alternatives and does not test room, excess-contribution tax, transfers or repayment designations. It also does not value different future withdrawals because the contribution and RRSP path are common to both cases. Finally, connect the cash choice to the household plan. If the earlier saving is spent, used to repay debt or needed for an upcoming bill, its use differs from the retained account drawn here. Compare that actual use and its dates with the later saving before treating an illustrative dollar difference as a decision.

documents.title: Moving between rentals: fund the new deposit before the old one comes back
documents.description: Follow four interactive charts through a six-month move budget, separating upfront cash, extra overlap rent, refund timing and the buffer you want to preserve.
documents.body: A refundable deposit can still create a cash shortage. Match payments and expected receipts to dates, then fund the lowest point rather than relying on the final total. A move has both a cost budget and a cash calendar A move can look affordable when you subtract an expected deposit refund from the total bill. The payment calendar may tell a different story. Your next landlord may need a deposit while your previous landlord still holds the old one. Movers and extra rent may also be payable before the next amount you can save from income. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s renting guide includes account setup charges, moving services and supplies among the costs to consider. Those categories help build a complete budget. This article adds a second step: assign the cash movements to dates. All amounts in the tool are hypothetical CAD inputs. They are not estimates of local rent, typical moving charges or legally permitted deposits. The six-month window begins when the new deposit is paid; it is not a legal notice or refund period. Keep the regular household budget outside the move ledger The default scenario starts with CAD 2,500 already available for the move. It adds CAD 400 at each month-end. That monthly amount is what remains after regular rent, groceries, utilities, debt payments and other continuing commitments. It is not gross salary or the whole bank deposit from a paycheque. Extra overlap rent is the additional rent caused by carrying both places beyond the regular rent already allowed for in your household budget. Entering both full rental payments here after also deducting regular rent elsewhere would count part of the cost twice. If the new ongoing rent is higher, update your regular budget before choosing the monthly surplus. The assumed old-deposit refund is also separate from the opening cash. Money still held by someone else is not part of the amount available today. If it has already arrived and is included in your opening cash, set the future refund input to zero. Find the low point before counting later receipts The model pays a CAD 1,200 new deposit at the start of month 1. The move pool falls from CAD 2,500 to CAD 1,300, then the month-end surplus raises it to CAD 1,700. At the start of month 2, CAD 2,000 of extra rent and CAD 1,500 of moving/setup costs create a funding position of minus CAD 1,800. That negative number is an unmet need using the selected resources. The model has not arranged a loan or assumed a bank will honour an overdraft. A CAD 1,000 refund at the end of month 3 improves the later arithmetic but cannot pay a bill due at the start of month 2. The line chart shows both the position after bills and the position after receipts. Its default low point is minus CAD 1,800, even though the six-month endpoint is positive CAD 1,200. Looking only at the final balance would miss the earlier financing problem. Calculate the initial amount needed to preserve your selected buffer Choose the cash amount you want to keep available throughout the move. The default is CAD 500 as an illustration, not a prescribed reserve. The required additional initial cash equals the greater of zero and the selected buffer minus the lowest before-receipt funding position . At the defaults, CAD 500 minus negative CAD 1,800 is CAD 2,300. Adding that amount before month 1 would shift every point upward by CAD 2,300 and leave CAD 500 at the modeled low point. The chart continues to show the entered resources so that the original shortfall remains visible; it does not quietly assume you have found the extra money. Possible changes include saving more before committing, reducing quoted moving costs or changing the assumed overlap. Test changes separately to see which payment date they affect. If borrowing is considered, its availability, fees and repayments need a separate household cash plan. Stress the refund without treating a scenario as a legal deadline Move the refund from month 3 to month 5, then choose 7 to put it outside the six-month window. Try a smaller refund as a separate test. These assumptions show how much the plan depends on a receipt whose timing or amount still needs confirmation. A refund outside the chart is not assumed to be permanently lost. Deposit rules and processes depend on the jurisdiction and tenancy. As one local example, British Columbia’s deposit guidance describes condition inspections, a written forwarding address and procedures for returning or retaining deposits. Check the applicable process and actual records before treating a refund as available cash. This calculator determines no entitlement, lawful deposit cap or statutory deadline. The sensitivity matrix counts months when the position before receipts is below your chosen buffer. It does not measure the size of the shortage: two scenarios can have the same count and very different dollar gaps. Read it alongside the low-point metric and the payment chart. Use the endpoint as a reconciliation after checking the dates The waterfall adds opening cash, six monthly transfers and the refund actually scheduled within the window. It subtracts the new deposit, extra rent and moving/setup costs. At the defaults, CAD 2,500 + CAD 2,400 + CAD 1,000 − CAD 1,200 − CAD 2,000 − CAD 1,500 equals CAD 1,200. The new deposit remains tied up throughout these six months. The tool does not assume that it returns on a convenient date, earns interest or can be substituted for a rent payment. Its eventual treatment belongs in the applicable agreement and local rules. Keep a simple dated record of quotations, deposit payments, receipts and expected refunds. Update the plan as amounts become confirmed, while preserving enough cash for payments that arrive first. The useful result is a move schedule you can fund at each step.

documents.title: Mortgage default insurance: separate the premium, its interest and the cash needed at closing
documents.description: Read selected published CMHC premium bands, calculate an illustrative financed premium, and reconcile the added monthly payment with a separate closing-cash ledger.
documents.body: A financed insurance premium becomes mortgage principal and carries interest. The down payment, applicable premium tax and other closing costs still require their own cash funding. Identify what is insured and who receives the protection Mortgage default insurance and insurance that pays a household after a death or disability address different risks. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada explains that mortgage loan insurance protects the lender if the borrower cannot make the mortgage payments. Paying its premium does not create equivalent income protection for the borrower. This distinction matters when building a home-purchase budget. The premium can be part of the borrowing transaction while the household still needs a plan for payments, emergency cash and other risks. Combining all of those protections under one insurance label can obscure what has actually been purchased. The illustration assumes an approved owner-occupied purchase with a traditional down payment. It does not assess a property, borrower, credit record, income qualification or required minimum cash. Its purpose is to reconcile a selected premium with debt and cash, after eligibility has been considered separately. Read the premium percentage against the base loan The fixed reference chart uses three selected rows from CMHC’s published premium table , reviewed on 25 October 2026. Its premium-on-total-loan rates are 2.80% for the published 80.01%–85% loan-to-value band, 3.10% for 85.01%–90%, and 4.00% for 90.01%–95%. These are pricing bands, not average premiums paid by a population or a personalized quote. The chart uses the premium-on-total-loan column; CMHC’s separate portability column is not interchangeable with it. The non-traditional-down-payment row is also outside this illustration. The numerical controls keep the price between CAD 100,000 and CAD 500,000, the down payment between 5% and 19.99%, and amortization at no more than twenty-five years. Those boundaries define the example’s scope rather than a full lending rule. Refunds, surcharges, credits and product-specific adjustments are not modeled. Add the premium once to the opening mortgage The default purchase price is CAD 500,000 and the down payment is 10%, or CAD 50,000. The base loan is consequently CAD 450,000. Its pre-premium loan-to-value ratio is 90%, which selects the 3.10% rate in this simplified schedule. The premium is CAD 450,000 × 3.10% = CAD 13,950 . With the full premium financed, the opening mortgage is CAD 463,950. Applying the rate to the CAD 500,000 property price would use the wrong denominator. Repeatedly applying insurance to the premium-inclusive loan would also misstate this calculation. The stacked bars repeat the calculation at several down-payment percentages while holding the selected price fixed. Each total consists of the base loan plus financed premium. The down payment remains cash supplied by the purchaser and is not added as a third component of mortgage debt. These bars do not establish which down payment creates the best whole-household outcome. Different down payments use different amounts of cash, and real financing offers can also carry different rates or conditions. Isolate the payment and interest attributable to financing the premium The rate assumption is a nominal 5% annually, compounded semi-annually, converted to an equivalent monthly rate. The illustration holds that rate unchanged for a twenty-five-year, 300-payment amortization. There are no prepayments, later charges or renewal-rate changes. At that convention, the mathematical payment on CAD 450,000 of principal is approximately CAD 2,617.22 monthly. Adding the financed premium raises the modeled payment to about CAD 2,698.36, an increment of CAD 81.13 before display rounding. The base-only amount is a calculation reference, not an offer of an otherwise identical uninsured loan. At a common rate and amortization, the payment formula is linear in principal. That lets the tool isolate how much of the full payment corresponds to the additional CAD 13,950. Across 300 unchanged payments, approximately CAD 24,340.17 is attributable to that financed component: CAD 13,950 of premium principal and CAD 10,390.17 of interest. The line chart tracks the remaining premium principal and cumulative interest separately. Neither line should be added again to the original premium as a new opening charge. Build the closing-cash ledger alongside the loan ledger The example begins with CAD 65,000 of available closing cash. It uses CAD 50,000 for the down payment and CAD 5,000 for independently entered other closing costs. The premium-tax input initially equals zero, leaving CAD 10,000 after those modeled payments. Zero is a placeholder rather than a conclusion that no tax applies. Where an independently verified tax on the premium is payable outside the loan, enter its applicable percentage. The calculator multiplies that assumption by the CAD 13,950 premium and deducts the resulting cash payment. Financing the premium means it is already included in mortgage debt. Deducting CAD 13,950 again from this closing-cash ledger would describe paying it twice. By contrast, a tax paid outside the loan or other closing expense needs separate cash funding. A negative waterfall endpoint remains a funding gap; the tool does not repair it with an overdraft or another loan. Other closing costs must exclude the down payment, financed premium and separately entered premium tax to prevent overlap. Check the approved premium and future payment conditions The official premium chart stays fixed while hypothetical price, down payment and financing inputs change. This preserves the difference between a checked public schedule and a scenario built from it. The lender’s actual approved premium and financing details remain the relevant amounts for a live purchase. Confirm which costs are paid at closing, which are financed, and whether any credit, refund or adjustment applies. Verify applicable tax independently; this page supplies no province-specific tax determination. Keep a supported cash reserve separate from funds already committed to completion. Finally, distinguish amortization from the term over which an actual rate is fixed. The twenty-five-year interest total assumes no rate changes merely to make the arithmetic inspectable. Use a separate renewal and household-payment plan for real future obligations. A clear purchase ledger should show the cash used now, the principal borrowed now and the assumptions behind payments made later.

documents.title: Reverse-mortgage cash at closing: deduct old debt and fees before budgeting the advance
documents.description: Reconcile net cash after fees and an old mortgage payout, follow hypothetical capitalized interest and inspect a property-sale remainder before contractual protections.
documents.body: Read the usable cash, growing loan balance and property scenario together. A future arithmetic gap is not a calculation of the liability payable under an actual reverse-mortgage contract. Start with the cash that remains after the initial deductions A reverse mortgage is a loan secured against home equity. The FCAC’s consumer guide describes it for homeowners usually aged fifty-five or older, with eligibility and borrowing amounts depending on the property, owners and lender. These charts do not calculate that eligibility. The first figure starts with a fictional CAD 200,000 gross advance. It deducts CAD 4,000 of upfront costs and CAD 40,000 required to settle an existing secured loan. The result is CAD 156,000 of cash available from this particular funding arrangement. The new debt starts at CAD 200,000. It does not start at CAD 156,000, and the model does not add the fees or old payout to the gross advance again. The deductions explain how the borrowed money is used. If they exceed the advance, the chart shows an initial cash requirement that needs another source; it does not increase approved borrowing automatically. Follow interest added to the balance For this illustration, the nominal annual rate stays at 7%, divided by twelve, and no regular payment or further advance occurs. Each month, interest is added to the modeled balance. The formula after m months is 200,000 × (1 + 0.07/12) m . After fifteen years, the calculated balance is about CAD 569,789.35. Of that amount, CAD 200,000 is the original gross advance and CAD 369,789.35 is accumulated interest. The stacked chart keeps those two components visible over independent elapsed-time scenarios. The interest grows with the balance on which it is charged. It is therefore different from multiplying the original amount by 7% and fifteen years. Monthly capitalization is an explicit teaching convention here, rather than a claim about every lender’s contract. A real rate can change, compounding can differ and additional advances or repayments would alter the path. Give the property its own assumption The home starts at a hypothetical CAD 750,000. With the selected 2% annual value increase, its modeled value after fifteen years is CAD 1,009,401.25. That calculation is independent of the loan’s interest rate. The second chart places home value beside the loan balance. The property is an asset; its assumed appreciation does not itself make a cash payment to the lender. A different value path can leave more or less equity even when the advance and interest terms are unchanged. The smooth line is not a property appraisal, an observed house-price series or a forecast for a neighbourhood. The model also excludes upkeep, insurance, property taxes and the way the household uses its advance. It cannot establish the complete cost of staying in the home or the change in total household wealth. Reconcile a sale before interpreting the remainder At the selected fifteen-year date, assumed selling costs of 4% reduce the CAD 1,009,401.25 modeled sale value by about CAD 40,376.05. That leaves CAD 969,025.20 before settling the loan in this partial reconciliation. Subtracting the uncapped calculated balance of CAD 569,789.35 gives a raw property remainder of about CAD 399,235.86. The fourth figure displays those steps. It excludes other claims, actual closing adjustments, taxes and any contractual repayment charge. This property-only remainder does not add back the initial CAD 156,000 of net proceeds. That money may have been spent, retained or used for another purpose, none of which is tracked here. Counting it as an asset at the future date would require a separate cash and investment ledger. Treat a negative cell as arithmetic before contract protections The final grid changes the constant loan rate and annual home-value assumption independently while preserving the selected gross advance, horizon and selling-cost percentage. Negative cells mean that modeled net sale value is below the uncapped mathematical balance. That difference does not establish that a borrower or estate must pay the shortfall from other assets. For a specifically attributed example, HomeEquity Bank describes a conditional No Negative Equity Guarantee for CHIP . Its stated conditions include maintaining the property, paying property taxes and insurance, and meeting mortgage obligations. It excludes administrative expenses and interest accumulated after the due date. The chart does not reproduce that guarantee or extend it to every product. Simply replacing debt with the smaller of the calculated balance and the modeled sale value would also fail to represent all of those conditions. Actual protections, valuation terms, sale costs, obligations and repayment dates need the signed contract and a lender statement. Put the repayment event and household obligations on a calendar The FCAC’s home-equity borrowing overview identifies sale, moving out, the last borrower’s death and default as repayment events for a reverse mortgage. The actual timing and consequences depend on the agreement. The selected sale year is only a scenario; it is not permission to leave the balance outstanding until that date. Retaining ownership comes with ongoing costs and contractual responsibilities. The absence of a regular mortgage payment in these charts does not fund property taxes, repairs, insurance or a later move. Those obligations belong in the household cash budget alongside any use of the advance. An estate may also face a repayment deadline before every other administrative step is complete. The graphs calculate neither estate administration nor a bridge facility. Record the relevant repayment trigger, required evidence, settlement window and other housing commitments separately from the interest calculation. Bring the complete quote back to the planning question A reviewable quote needs the approved gross advance, any existing secured-debt payout, itemized fees, net proceeds, rate and compounding method, future-advance terms, repayment conditions and available protections. Confirm how any guarantee treats property obligations, due dates and excluded amounts. The personal planning question then needs its own dates and dollars. How much usable cash is required, when is it needed, what recurring housing costs continue, and what cash would be available if the household moves earlier? The model’s one-advance structure cannot answer a plan that needs later borrowing without adding those future cash flows. Keep the fictional sensitivities as a way to inspect the mechanics. Compare actual alternatives with matched cash needs, expenses and ending assets and debts. Neither a large initial advance nor a positive modeled property remainder alone determines whether a reverse mortgage suits a particular retirement plan.

documents.title: ETF trading costs: follow the spread and commissions through a complete purchase and sale
documents.description: Reconcile hypothetical ETF purchase cash and sale proceeds, distinguish a full quote spread from a one-sided cost, and test how fixed commissions affect different order sizes.
documents.body: The ask and bid already incorporate the assumed spread. Reconcile the actual cash paid and received before adding costs, and keep trading costs separate from fund expenses and market returns. Define the quote and its denominator An ETF’s displayed price is not a complete trading budget. A buyer may face an ask quote, a seller a bid quote, and either may incur a broker commission. Understanding how those pieces fit together helps distinguish a transaction’s cash cost from the investment’s later performance. This illustration starts with a hypothetical CAD 25 quote midpoint and a full bid–ask spread of 20 basis points of that midpoint. One basis point is 0.01 percentage point, so the full spread is 0.20%. The assumed quotes are symmetric: the ask is CAD 25.025 and the bid is CAD 24.975. Each side is 10 basis points from the midpoint, rather than 20. The full CAD 0.05 spread separates the ask from the bid. The midpoint is just the average of those two quotes; the calculator does not identify it as NAV, an executable price or independently verified fair value. Reconcile the dollars paid and received The example buys 400 whole units at the assumed ask and pays a CAD 5 commission. The units cost CAD 10,010 and the total purchase cash is CAD 10,015 . At this point, the CAD 10 concession relative to midpoint is already embedded in the executed price. Suppose the midpoint remains CAD 25 until a later sale, and the full spread remains 20 basis points. Selling 400 units at the assumed bid produces CAD 9,990 before commission. Deducting the CAD 5 exit commission leaves CAD 9,985 of sale cash. The completed round trip therefore loses CAD 30: CAD 9,985 received less CAD 10,015 paid. The waterfall explains the same result as zero midpoint movement, less CAD 10 of entry spread concession, CAD 10 of exit spread concession and CAD 10 of combined commissions. Do not deduct another full spread from those cash figures. Buying at the ask and selling at the bid has already included it under these assumptions. A commission is an additional charge; a spread concession is a difference between execution price and the chosen reference quote. Separate proportional costs from fixed ticket charges The grouped bars compare independent trades of different unit quantities. Spreads remain the same percentage of the respective quote midpoints. At unchanged midpoint, doubling units doubles the dollar spread concession while keeping its share of entry midpoint notional unchanged. The selected flat commissions behave differently. With one executed order on each side, their combined CAD 10 cost is spread across more units in a larger transaction. The chart expresses both cost components relative to units multiplied by entry midpoint, before commissions, so the denominator is consistent across the bars. This comparison does not recommend increasing a purchase beyond the financial plan. It isolates a fee schedule’s arithmetic. A smaller suitable purchase and a larger unsuitable purchase cannot be ranked by transaction-cost percentage alone. The model permits at least 24 whole units and at most 24 executed orders per side. The same total units can therefore be divided into whole-unit orders without requiring fractional-share trading. It assumes each order receives the same respective quote and incurs the selected flat charge. Read more orders as the same capital divided differently The matrix holds the selected total units fixed while changing the number of executed orders and the spread. Four orders per side do not mean four times as many units or four times the invested capital. They divide the same total quantity into smaller pieces. At the default 400 units, unchanged midpoint and 20-basis-point spreads, four CAD 5 commissions on entry and four on exit total CAD 40. Spread concessions still total CAD 20, producing a CAD 60 net loss. With a zero commission input, splitting the same quantity adds no modeled commission cost. Each matrix row replaces both the entry and exit full spreads with its labelled value. Outside the matrix, the controls allow those two spreads to differ. Real prices and depth may change between orders, so neither view predicts what splitting a live order will cost. Solve the movement needed to recover the modeled costs A small increase in midpoint does not automatically make the completed trade profitable. Under the default assumptions, net sale proceeds equal purchase cash only after the midpoint rises by approximately 0.3003%. The calculation includes both commissions and the exit bid discount from its new midpoint. That threshold is slightly different from dividing CAD 30 by CAD 10,000, because the exit spread concession also grows with the exit midpoint. The tool solves the cash equality directly rather than treating every cost as a fixed opening-dollar amount. The final chart varies midpoint movement and displays net gain or loss after the assumed execution costs. It omits fund distributions, management expenses, taxes, foreign exchange and other account charges. It is therefore a narrow trading reconciliation rather than an ETF’s complete holding-period total return. Treat price protection and execution certainty as separate questions Vanguard Canada’s trading guidance explains that a limit order sets an acceptable execution price but can remain partly or entirely unfilled. It also notes that market conditions and the tradability of underlying holdings can affect ETF spreads. This calculator assumes a complete fill at the selected ask and bid, with enough quoted depth and no market impact. It does not model a limit order’s fill probability, guarantee that a displayed quote remains available, or assume that a limit order eliminates spread costs. For an actual transaction, check the current quote, quantity, broker charges and order terms alongside the investment plan. Keep the quote time and denominator visible when comparing spreads. A clear reconciliation of paid and received cash is useful precisely because it leaves the uncertain execution outcome and the separate investment decision open to proper review.

documents.title: Reverse-mortgage planning: cash received, interest accumulated and home value left at sale
documents.description: Track a hypothetical loan with capitalized interest, separate advances from fees, and test the home-value residual after assumed future sale costs and debt repayment.
documents.body: Borrowed cash can support today’s spending while the repayment balance grows. Keep the amount received, the debt owed and the uncertain home-sale value in separate parts of the plan. Put the loan proceeds and the liability in different columns A home can be valuable while supplying little cash for monthly bills. Borrowing against it can convert some financing capacity into spendable money, but the cash arrives with a liability. A useful plan therefore tracks both the money delivered and the amount that will eventually need to be addressed. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s reverse-mortgage guide explains that interest is added to the loan and that fees may be financed or paid separately. It also describes different ways of receiving funds. Actual availability and terms depend on the agreement. This calculator isolates those mechanics. It begins with an opening advance, adds specified fees to the loan, then assumes additional month-end advances without regular repayments. These entries are independent assumptions. The tool does not establish that a borrower qualifies or that a lender would authorize the selected cash schedule. Reconcile the opening advance with financed fees The default home value is CAD 750,000. The borrower receives CAD 150,000 at the start, while CAD 5,000 of costs are added to the opening loan. The initial liability is consequently CAD 155,000 , even though the borrower receives only CAD 150,000 of cash. Those financed fees are not an additional cash advance available for household spending. They nevertheless become part of the balance on which the hypothetical loan interest accumulates. Paying them separately would require a different opening cash plan and a smaller financed balance. The illustration then adds CAD 500 of borrowed cash at each month-end for fifteen years. Those 180 advances total CAD 90,000. Combined with the initial cash, the borrower receives CAD 240,000 over the full period. The amounts are nominal CAD and have not been adjusted for purchasing power. A fixed CAD 500 advance may buy less in later years. The calculator also does not assume those advances are savings: their later spending, retention or investment is outside this loan ledger. Follow the compounding debt separately from cumulative cash The selected interest assumption is a constant 7% effective annual rate. It is converted to an equivalent monthly rate using 1.07 to the power of one-twelfth, less one. Each month, interest first accrues on the opening balance; the new CAD 500 advance is then added. After fifteen years, the modeled loan reaches approximately CAD 583,202.27. Its components are CAD 150,000 of opening cash borrowed, CAD 5,000 of financed fees, CAD 90,000 of later advances and CAD 338,202.27 of accrued interest. The first chart compares that debt balance with cumulative cash received. The widening gap is financed fees plus interest, rather than additional spending money. A month without a regular repayment can still add to the amount owed. The effective-rate convention is explicit so the arithmetic can be checked. A quoted product might use a different compounding convention, change rates, charge further fees or restrict advances. This model does not convert an advertisement into a contractual repayment schedule. Read the future sale bridge before calling an amount equity The independent home-value assumption is 2% growth each year. It takes CAD 750,000 to approximately CAD 1,009,401.25 after fifteen years. Hypothetical sale costs of 5% use about CAD 50,470.06, leaving CAD 958,931.19 before addressing the loan. Subtracting the modeled CAD 583,202.27 balance leaves an arithmetic sale-value residual of approximately CAD 375,728.92. The waterfall shows the same subtraction using each component of the debt, so financed fees and later cash advances do not disappear inside a single endpoint. This residual is not cash automatically available while the owner continues living in the home. It assumes a sale at the illustrated value and cost percentage. Other secured debts, tax, penalties, legal costs and estate obligations could require further adjustments. Nor is it a complete household-net-worth comparison. Previously advanced money may have been spent or may still exist elsewhere. Without tracking those uses and assets, comparing only the home residual with an unborrowed home would leave out part of the household’s financial history. Vary the loan rate and home-value path independently The matrix keeps the opening home, advances, fees, horizon and sale-cost assumption fixed. Rows change annual home-value growth and columns change the effective annual loan rate. Each cell is a separate possible arithmetic path, with no probability assigned to it. A home-value assumption does not change the loan’s compounding rate. Likewise, slower home appreciation does not automatically reduce the amount owed in the model. Keeping these assumptions independent makes the effect of each visible. Negative residuals remain negative rather than being hidden at zero. They identify a gap between hypothetical sale proceeds and the modeled balance. They do not determine a borrower’s legal shortfall obligation or apply any contractual no-negative-equity protection. Those questions require the actual agreement and applicable rules. Try a zero loan rate as an accounting check: the closing balance equals total cash advanced plus financed fees. That scenario isolates principal accumulation; it is not presented as an available loan offer. Connect the debt projection with a dated housing and cash plan FCAC describes repayment events including selling, moving out, the last borrower’s death and default, with timing and conditions governed by the agreement. A chosen fifteen-year chart horizon therefore cannot be treated as a guaranteed period before repayment is required. For an actual plan, identify what could change the living arrangement, what continuing home costs remain, and how a repayment event would be funded. Confirm draw availability, interest conventions, fees and relevant conditions rather than assuming that today’s terms extend unchanged for decades. Compare the resulting cash plan with supported alternatives, including different housing arrangements or other suitable financing. The graphs do not select an option. They make today’s borrowing and its later balance visible together, so the decision can be assessed alongside future housing needs and the resources that remain available.

documents.title: Taxable savings: a higher dollar balance does not always mean more purchasing power
documents.description: Follow gross interest through a simplified annual tax payment, calculate the exact real rate and separate nominal cash reconciliation from purchasing-power adjustments.
documents.body: Compare the interest retained after tax with price growth. Keep tax-payment timing and inflation adjustments separate before interpreting an account’s growth. Start with the interest that stays in the account A hypothetical CAD 50,000 accessible savings balance earns 4% gross interest during its first year. That is CAD 2,000 before tax. With an independently assumed 40% combined tax rate on each dollar of interest, the model pays CAD 800 of tax from the same account and retains CAD 1,200. The ending balance is CAD 51,200. Its nominal increase is 2.4%, rather than the 4% gross rate. The tax assumption is deliberately simple: it does not calculate federal or provincial brackets, credits, deductions or benefit reductions for a particular household. The CRA’s interest-income guidance explains reporting interest paid or credited on bank accounts, including income for which no information slip is received. The source supplies reporting context; the calculator’s rate and payment timing remain original assumptions. Divide by price growth to measure purchasing power Under a constant 3% inflation assumption, an amount that bought CAD 50,000 of goods at the start would require CAD 51,500 after one year. The modeled CAD 51,200 balance is higher in dollars but falls short of that purchasing-power benchmark. The exact annual real rate is one plus the after-tax nominal rate, divided by one plus inflation, minus one. Here that is 1.024 divided by 1.03, minus one: approximately negative 0.58%. Simply subtracting 3% from 2.4% gives a nearby approximation, rather than the exact compound relationship. The Bank of Canada’s investment calculator also distinguishes interest and inflation effects when illustrating savings values. This article uses its own model and inputs. Neither the 4% interest assumption nor 3% inflation is a current market observation, a product quote or a forecast. State where the tax money comes from and when it leaves Every modeled year credits interest to the opening balance, then pays tax immediately from that balance. The next year earns interest only on what remains. This convention makes the compounding effect of retained net interest inspectable. Real tax payments follow the applicable reporting and payment requirements. A bank does not necessarily withhold the assumed amount merely because this example subtracts tax at year-end. A household paying tax from employment income would also need to record that outside cash contribution before comparing total household resources. Keep this accessible-savings example separate from a locked investment whose interest is taxable before cash can be withdrawn. The CRA page discusses term deposits and similar investments separately. Use confirmed account terms and actual tax dates when building a funding calendar; the related instalment guide explains why reserving money and paying tax are different events. Compare nominal growth with the same amount of starting-date buying power The line chart shows three labelled paths: a before-tax reference balance, the balance after the modeled annual tax payments, and that after-tax balance expressed in starting-date purchasing power. No path receives new deposits or spending withdrawals. The before-tax reference leaves every gross interest dollar invested. It is a mathematical reference, not an assertion that a registered account is available, appropriate or able to provide the assumed rate. Its extra ending value includes the compounding effect of interest that the taxed account could no longer retain. The real path divides the after-tax balance by the cumulative price-growth factor. Inflation is not a separate invoice deducted from the account. A gap between nominal and real values is a difference in valuation units. Compare the real path with the original principal when asking whether buying power has increased. Reconcile the actual interest ledger before attributing the gap The waterfall begins with initial cash, adds the gross interest actually earned by the taxed account and subtracts the modeled tax actually paid from it. Those steps reconcile exactly to its ending nominal balance. Use that account’s own annual interest amounts. Subtracting its tax from the untouched reference account’s much larger interest total would combine two different balance paths. The tax also changes later interest, so the ending-value difference between paths is not generally equal to the simple sum of tax payments. The chart excludes fees and all personal tax interactions. Its interest and tax totals are cash-model components, not a completed tax return or an amount to copy onto a reporting slip. Reconcile real income to the actual statements and applicable tax guidance before filing. A required break-even rate is a threshold, not an available offer With the model’s assumptions, preserving buying power requires gross interest times one minus the assumed tax rate to equal inflation. At 40% tax and 3% inflation, that implies a 5% gross annual rate. The threshold covers no fee, withdrawal or other cost. The matrix varies the tax and inflation assumptions while retaining the selected gross interest rate. Its cells are annual real rates; principal and the number of years do not change that annual relationship. Those controls do change how many dollars the balance path gains or loses over time. Do not turn the required rate into a reason to accept a product’s risk or restrictions. The household may need accessible cash for near-term payments even when its modeled real return is negative. This example clarifies the trade-off and the cash assumptions without selecting an account, recommending an investment or promising a return.

These are different rate definitions, not additive portions of a single return. Negative real values mean less purchasing power.

documents.title: The spousal RRSP withdrawal calendar: review the year of withdrawal and the two before it
documents.description: Use four graphics to organize a contributor’s annual record, follow a moving calendar window and distinguish elapsed months from income-reporting decisions.
documents.body: Calendar dates help identify which contribution records need review. Determining who reports a withdrawal also requires the applicable tax process and the full relevant history. Identify the contributor and the annuitant before drawing the calendar A spousal or common-law partner RRSP involves two roles. The contributor makes deposits for the other person’s plan, while the annuitant is the person entitled to receive the plan amounts. A useful withdrawal review keeps those roles and the relevant records clear before discussing a tax result. The annual inputs in this tool represent one contributor’s deposits to the same annuitant’s RRSPs across calendar years. They are hypothetical totals, not contribution-room estimates or instructions to make deposits. The annuitant’s own contributions are a separate history and are not silently added to this contributor’s ledger. CRA’s spousal-RRSP withdrawal guidance describes circumstances in which a contributor may report some or all of a withdrawal. The article explains the calendar component of that review without calculating anyone’s income allocation. Build the window from calendar-year labels The reviewed CRA framework considers the withdrawal year and the two preceding calendar years. If the hypothetical withdrawal is in 2029, the displayed review covers 2027, 2028 and 2029. For a 2028 withdrawal, the three labels become 2026, 2027 and 2028. The stacked bars apply that arithmetic to the same entered annual record. Each colour shows one relative year in the review. The bar total is a sum of contribution records to examine. It is not a calculation of attributed income, because no withdrawal amount or full attribution history is supplied to this tool. The controls cover 2025–2031 so every displayed three-year window is complete within the illustration. For an actual review, gather the relevant records across plans rather than looking only at the account from which money will be withdrawn. Verify the applicable rules and tax-year process before acting on a future-date example. Read the month gap without replacing the calendar rule A deposit in December 2026 and an example withdrawal in January 2029 are 25 month labels apart. Yet the 2029 review labels are 2027, 2028 and 2029, which exclude 2026. Moving the example deposit to January 2026 makes the elapsed gap 36 months while leaving the same calendar-year membership. The reverse comparison also matters. A December 2026 deposit and a December 2028 withdrawal are 24 month labels apart, and 2026 remains inside the 2026–2028 review. The amount of time between two dates and the three calendar years selected by the rule should therefore be recorded as separate facts. The calculation is 12 × (withdrawal year − contribution year) + withdrawal month − contribution month . It uses month labels rather than exact days. The fixed matrix compares several 2026 deposit months with several 2029 withdrawal months, while the bar chart uses the months selected in the controls. A later contribution can change the relevant record set The default ledger has CAD 5,000 in 2026 and zero in the other years. The 2027 and 2028 windows include that recorded amount. The 2029 window does not. This is an example of selecting records by year; a zero bar should not be interpreted as a complete tax conclusion. Now enter CAD 2,000 for 2028. The 2029 window includes that later amount even though it still excludes 2026. Focusing on the date of the earliest deposit would miss the newer record. The graph keeps each year separate so that the later contribution is visible. These future annual amounts are planning assumptions. A real review uses deposits actually made and the complete relevant history. The calendar-year ledger is also separate from the year for which a contribution deduction may be claimed. Keep the deposit receipt date rather than inferring it from a deduction on a return. Use the calendar as the start of the income-reporting review CRA provides Form T2205 for determining the income amounts the contributor and annuitant must report in the applicable circumstances. Its published worked example considers a withdrawal and contribution history together. A window total on its own is therefore insufficient to allocate a withdrawal between people. This tool does not model earlier withdrawals or attribution, relationship or residency exceptions, RRIF minimums, specified pension plans or FHSA transfers. It also calculates no withholding or final tax. Those matters should be checked in the applicable current process rather than inferred from the date graphics. For the household cash plan, separately record the gross withdrawal, immediate proceeds, any tax allowance and when the money is required. Read the withholding guide for that distinction. The calendar can improve the record review while the withdrawal’s legal, reporting and cash consequences remain distinct planning questions.
