documents.title: Selling investments for a cash goal: separate proceeds, cost base and money available to spend
documents.description: Use a sale-proceeds bridge, cash curve and price stresses to distinguish a holding’s market value from the cash left after selling costs and an assumed tax earmark.
documents.body: The amount sold, the realized gain and the cash available for a bill are different numbers. Cost base helps calculate the gain; it is not another cash deduction from the sale. Give market value, cost base and the cash goal separate jobs A statement can show enough market value to cover an upcoming expense without telling you how much must be sold to leave that expense funded. Selling costs and tax-related cash needs can make the required gross sale larger than the bill. A price change before the sale can change the calculation again. The default uses one hypothetical holding worth CAD 100,000 with a total adjusted cost base of CAD 60,000. The spending goal is CAD 20,000 after a flat CAD 100 selling cost and a separate tax earmark. Fractional units are allowed, so the model can solve a continuous sale amount rather than rounding to a whole number of units. The CRA describes a capital gain using proceeds, adjusted cost base and selling expenses . This article uses that calculation structure for a capital-property example in a non-registered account. It does not determine whether a real transaction is on capital or income account, and it does not apply to every account wrapper. Allocate cost base to the portion sold At the selected market value, each dollar of the holding has sixty cents of allocated cost base. Selling 20% of the units would produce CAD 20,000 before costs and allocate CAD 12,000 of cost base to the sold units. The remaining units would retain CAD 48,000 of cost base. After the CAD 100 selling cost, that particular CAD 20,000 sale has a modeled gain of CAD 7,900: CAD 20,000 minus CAD 12,000 minus CAD 100. The tool then earmarks the entered 25% of that full positive gain, or CAD 1,975. Only CAD 17,925 remains available for the spending goal. The 25% is an invented effective cash allowance on the full gain. It is neither the statutory inclusion rate nor a personal marginal income-tax rate. Entering a marginal rate directly could misstate the allowance. Actual tax requires the relevant year’s rules, other income and losses, account treatment and the taxpayer’s circumstances. Solve for the sale that leaves the requested cash Because the first CAD 20,000 sale does not leave CAD 20,000 to spend, the model solves for a larger gross sale. Under the defaults, approximately CAD 22,305.56 must be sold. The allocated cost base is about CAD 13,383.33 and the gain is about CAD 8,822.22. The separate tax earmark is approximately CAD 2,205.56. The cash reconciliation is CAD 22,305.56 − CAD 100 − CAD 2,205.56 = CAD 20,000 , allowing for displayed rounding. The holding retains about CAD 77,694.44 of market value at the unchanged assumed price. The waterfall does not subtract the CAD 13,383.33 cost base as a cash outflow. That amount represents allocated investment cost used in calculating the gain; it is not another payment made during the sale. Subtracting both cost base and the tax allowance from proceeds would confuse the gain calculation with the cash ledger. Keep the tax cash separate without pretending it has been assessed The model reserves the assumed tax amount immediately, making it unavailable for the goal. It does not assert that a broker withholds that amount or that the tax is due on the trade date. An earmark is a household planning choice, while an actual payment date belongs on a separate tax cash calendar. If the selected sale has a loss, the tax earmark is zero. The calculator creates no immediate tax refund and does not apply a loss against another gain. It also excludes loss carryovers, superficial-loss treatment, other account activity, benefits affected by income and any additional consequences of the transaction. A zero cash goal makes no sale and incurs no fee. A positive sale incurs the flat selling cost, capped at its proceeds. A tiny sale can therefore produce little or no usable cash. Actual trading spreads, percentage commissions or redemption charges would require a different cost function and must not be assumed covered by the single flat input. Hold unit count and cost base fixed when stressing the price The price-stress bars change the market value by minus 40%, minus 20%, zero and plus 20%, while keeping the same units and total cost base. Each case then solves for the same CAD 20,000 cash goal using the selected fee and tax-earmark percentage. After a 40% decline, the holding is worth CAD 60,000 and its cost base remains CAD 60,000. The model needs a CAD 20,100 sale, with no positive gain after the selling cost and no tax earmark. That smaller sale amount does not mean the household is wealthier: the price decline has already reduced the whole holding’s market value by CAD 40,000. For a larger goal, selling the entire holding may still leave a shortage. The main metric reports that shortfall, and the proceeds curve shows when the horizontal goal lies above all achievable cash amounts. The matrix marks a fully funded required sale as unavailable when the holding cannot produce it, instead of displaying a sale larger than the assets owned. Use supported records and a dated funding plan Replace the market value with a relevant observation and reconcile adjusted cost base from appropriate records. Acquisition costs, reinvestments, returns of capital and other adjustments can make cost base different from the amount originally transferred to an account. The tool accepts an independently established total; it does not reconstruct those records. All amounts here are CAD and assume one proportionately sold holding. Foreign-currency transactions require their own currency calculations, and a portfolio with several securities requires a decision about which assets are sold. The model does not rank holdings, select tax lots or recommend a security to sell. Finally, match the expense deadline with the time needed to execute, settle and transfer an actual sale. The calculator assumes cash is available once the sale and earmark are recorded. Its four charts explain the amount reconciliation; a complete plan also needs supported tax assumptions, execution details and a calendar that puts usable cash in place before the bill.

documents.title: Canadian wealth statistics: read the median, the population and the cash you can use
documents.description: Four graphics connect dated Canadian wealth observations with the difference between a statistical benchmark, net worth and immediately spendable money.
documents.body: A wealth statistic describes a defined population. Your plan needs a consistent personal balance sheet and a separate measure of the cash available for upcoming bills. A median is a middle observation, not an average or a target The word “typical” can conceal several different statistics. The median places observations in order and identifies the middle. The arithmetic mean adds them together and divides by their number. Neither is automatically the amount a household needs for its own goals. The third graphic uses five entirely invented families with net worth of CAD 40,000, 80,000, 120,000, 160,000 and 1,100,000. Their combined wealth is CAD 1,500,000. Divide by five and the mean is CAD 300,000; the middle observation is CAD 120,000. Increase only the last invented family’s wealth by CAD 1,000,000. The mean becomes CAD 500,000 while the median remains CAD 120,000. The example shows sensitivity to a large observation. It does not show how Canadian wealth is distributed or establish that one statistic answers every planning question. Read the date, unit and family definition before the number Statistics Canada’s October 2024 release table reports a 2023 national median net worth of CAD 519,700 for economic families and persons not in an economic family. The survey covers the ten provinces and excludes Indigenous communities and collective dwellings. The first chart uses the major income recipient’s age and compares 2019 with 2023. Both sets of dollar values are already expressed in constant 2023 dollars. Do not apply another inflation adjustment to the earlier column. These are dated survey observations, not current 2026 account values. Comparing a single individual with a family aggregate can create a misleading scorecard. Before making a comparison, define whose assets and debts belong together, which date is being measured and how pension assets are valued. A statistic cannot repair an inconsistent balance sheet. Age-group comparisons are not a personal growth path The age chart shows separate groups at two survey dates. It does not follow the same families through time. A line joining different age groups could suggest a life trajectory that the displayed data do not establish; grouped bars preserve the separate comparisons. A younger reader cannot infer a future balance by moving from one age bar to another. Differences in housing, family structure, pension access and the people entering or leaving a group may matter. The displayed medians do not isolate the effect of saving behaviour. The cited release tables do not provide confidence intervals. The graphics therefore report observations without error bars and make no statistical-significance claim. A visible difference is not evidence that a particular household should change its allocation or take more investment risk. Regional context helps explain why a national number is incomplete The second chart uses Statistics Canada’s 2023 provincial medians , sorted for readability. Provincial populations differ in age, housing and family composition. The bars are not adjusted for those differences or local living costs. Do not average the provincial medians to reconstruct the national median. Medians are not additive. Similarly, adding a median home value, median pension value and median bank balance would not construct a representative family: those middle values may belong to different families. These distinctions are practical. A home-rich household with little accessible cash and a renting household with more financial assets may have different immediate constraints even if a broad wealth comparison places them close together. Build one coherent balance sheet, then measure the available cash The fourth graphic changes with the inputs. Its default home value is CAD 600,000, pension asset value CAD 200,000 and uncommitted cash CAD 15,000. Subtract CAD 350,000 of debt and hypothetical net worth is CAD 465,000. Only CAD 15,000 is treated as immediately spendable. With CAD 3,000 of essential monthly cash spending, that covers five months under the model’s no-income, no-interest assumptions. Home equity and pension value do not enter this coverage calculation. Neither is automatically a bank balance available next week. Try increasing the home value without changing cash. Net worth rises while cash coverage stays the same. Then raise cash instead. Both measures rise. This experiment explains why a net-worth target cannot replace a reserve calendar. Turn the comparison into questions you can actually answer For a personal review, record valuation dates, include all relevant debts, distinguish pension capital values from annual pension payments and identify cash already promised to taxes or other bills. The tool’s deliberately short balance sheet excludes other assets, transaction costs and taxes. Use wealth statistics as context for questions, not as a pass mark. Can the next twelve months of commitments be funded? How much depends on one property? Which assets can be accessed without a sale, restriction or tax consequence? Those questions need your own records. Do not compare the hypothetical current balance sheet directly with constant-2023-dollar observations as if they shared a valuation date. The tool does not calculate a ranking, recommended saving rate or retirement funding requirement. Its purpose is to keep the statistical comparison and the household decision clearly defined.

documents.title: Paying for a career change: chart the training cost, lost income and recovery time
documents.description: Four interactive charts compare retraining with staying in the current job, including foregone take-home income, a search delay and ten-year present value.
documents.body: The course invoice is only part of the investment. Compare the same calendar, include income you give up and test a smaller income uplift or longer search. Define what you are comparing with A career-change calculation needs a comparison path. This tool uses continuing in the current job at unchanged monthly take-home income for ten years. It measures only the cash differences caused by training and the assumed new job. This is a deliberately limited baseline. The current role might also change, and a new career might improve health, flexibility or job satisfaction. Those outcomes matter, but the charts do not assign them invented dollar values. Job Bank’s career-planning guidance recommends researching requirements, wages and job prospects. Use that research to challenge the inputs. A posted occupation-wide wage is not a personal offer, and a course’s marketing claim does not establish a future take-home pay increase. Add the income you give up to the money you pay out The default upfront course and equipment cost is CAD 12,000. Current take-home income is CAD 4,000 per month, but only 50% continues during six months of training and a further three months of job search. The monthly income difference is therefore CAD 2,000. Six training months create CAD 12,000 of foregone income, and three search months add CAD 6,000. Together with the upfront cost, the incremental investment reaches CAD 30,000. The first waterfall makes these components add visibly to the total. The CAD 18,000 foregone income is not another invoice. It is income available in the comparison path but absent in the training path. Adding it again to actual tuition payments would misstate the amount owed to the school. An opportunity-cost calculation is not the reserve needed to live Rent, groceries and other spending common to both paths cancel from an incremental comparison. They still have to be paid. A positive long-term result therefore does not establish that the training period is affordable. WorkBC’s student-budgeting guide separates expected income and expenses, including fixed, variable and one-time costs. Build that full cash calendar alongside this comparison, using actual payment dates and only confirmed support. If reduced work still brings in CAD 2,000 but essential household bills are CAD 3,000, a monthly cash gap remains before tuition. That example is separate from the tool: its controls do not calculate living expenses, grants, student debt or financing charges. Loan proceeds would fund a gap while creating an obligation, rather than reducing the economic training cost by themselves. Use the extra take-home pay after the new job’s extra costs The default new role adds CAD 700 of monthly take-home income once the transition is complete. Additional work expenses are CAD 150 per month, leaving a CAD 550 monthly improvement compared with staying in the current job. The new income begins in month ten. Recovering CAD 30,000 requires 55 of those CAD 550 months, so the cumulative line first moves above zero in month 64 from the start. It is still CAD 300 below zero at month 63 and CAD 250 above at month 64. Gross salary growth and take-home cash growth are different inputs. Here the income uplift is already net of payroll deductions; the tool does not calculate tax, benefits or pension contributions. Recurring commuting, child-care or licensing costs belong in the additional-cost input when they differ between the two paths. Keep the same finish date when the transition takes longer Every scenario ends 120 months after training begins. The default nine-month transition leaves 111 months of extra earnings. CAD 77,700 of extra take-home pay, less CAD 16,650 of new work costs and CAD 30,000 of incremental investment, produces CAD 31,050 of undiscounted incremental cash. The third waterfall reconciles that total. It does not restart a new ten-year clock at graduation. Delaying the new job both extends reduced earnings and removes higher-income months from the common horizon. Try increasing the search delay and reducing the income uplift. If the monthly uplift fails to exceed additional work costs, there is no ongoing cash gain to recover the earlier cost. “Not within 120 months” means the selected window does not contain recovery; it does not mean recovery is guaranteed immediately afterward. Present value asks a different question from nominal payback Nominal payback counts undiscounted dollars. Present value brings each cash difference back to the start using the selected annual discount rate converted to an equivalent monthly rate. The upfront payment is already at that date. At a zero discount rate, present value equals the final undiscounted total. At a positive rate, a later positive dollar carries less weight. The scenario matrix replaces the search delay and income uplift while preserving the remaining inputs, so each cell describes a consistent ten-year comparison. The cells are assumptions, not employment probabilities or confidence intervals. The discount rate is a comparison convention, not a promised investment return. No inflation, pay progression, course failure, career interruption or promotion beyond the selected uplift is modeled. Use the charts to improve the decision before committing Obtain the complete course price, refund terms, credential requirements and timetable. Investigate local job demand and realistic entry roles rather than relying only on experienced-worker salaries. Confirm whether the current job, hours and benefits can actually be retained during study. Then prepare a weaker-income case and a longer-search case, alongside a household reserve plan. Part-time training may cost less foregone income but take longer; comparing it properly requires entering its own duration, retained earnings and costs. A career decision can still be worthwhile for reasons beyond financial payback. These charts make the cash trade-off inspectable. They do not decide whether a program is suitable, certify its employment outcomes or recommend borrowing to enroll.

documents.title: Buying back pension service: compare the payment calendar with the additional pension
documents.description: Four charts compare an upfront payment with quoted monthly deductions, the wait before pension receipt and the effect of different receipt horizons.
documents.body: The buyback price, payment timing and additional pension answer different questions. Use matched plan quotes, then examine the cash commitment and conditional benefit stream. Start with the plan’s quote, not a generic pension formula A service buyback purchases recognition of eligible prior service under a particular pension plan. Whether it is available, what it costs and how it changes benefits must come from that plan. The model does not infer eligibility or turn years worked into a pension amount. For the federal public service plan, Treasury Board’s explanation describes a legally binding agreement and payment choices including a lump sum, monthly deductions or a combination. These rules do not establish the terms of another employer’s plan. Ask for a comparison of benefits with and without the proposed buyback, at the same retirement date. Confirm the effect on eligibility, temporary benefits, indexing and survivor provisions. Enter only an independently quoted incremental monthly pension; this tool assumes it can be represented by one starting amount and an annual increase. A smaller monthly deduction can add up to a larger nominal payment The default alternatives are CAD 30,000 paid immediately or CAD 350 deducted monthly for ten years. The latter totals CAD 42,000 across 120 deductions. The first chart makes that total visible. The federal explanation says its monthly deductions include principal, interest and life-insurance amounts. It also describes protection associated with life-insured instalments. A real quote’s additional charges and protections need to be assessed together; a comparison of payment totals alone cannot value them. The tool accepts the monthly quote directly. It does not calculate an interest rate, insurance premium, outstanding buyback loan or death settlement. Both options are assumed to buy the same additional pension after their commitments are fulfilled. A quote offering different service or benefits would need a different comparison. Draw the years when you pay but do not yet receive the increase The example waits ten years before the first pension receipt year begins. Monthly pension payments then start at the end of month 121. The first twelve are CAD 250 each, a gross CAD 3,000 over that first receipt year. The upfront line begins at negative CAD 30,000 at year zero. The instalment line begins at zero and falls as deductions are paid. Both later receive the same modeled pension increase. Annual points summarize a monthly ledger, with no hidden return on the money retained under either option. Shorten the wait while keeping the deduction term unchanged and payments can overlap pension receipts. The ledger continues subtracting them. An annual positive change does not establish that all intra-year household bills can be funded; this is incremental buyback cash, not a full bank-account schedule. Specify when indexing begins and what the pension amount includes The default pension increase grows by an assumed 2% after every twelve payments. The second receipt year therefore pays CAD 255 per month. No increase is applied during the ten-year wait because the input is explicitly the quoted amount for the first receipt year. If a plan quote is expressed in today’s dollars or already incorporates an indexing estimate, reconcile that basis before entering it. Applying an extra increase to a quote that already includes it would double count. Likewise, a temporary bridge component cannot be assumed to continue indefinitely. All benefits and payment costs here are gross cash amounts. The illustration excludes deductions, tax relief, changes to contribution room, past service pension adjustments and transfers from registered savings. A tax deduction or direct transfer should not be assumed to be freely available cash. Bring both payment schedules and the pension receipts to the election date The third chart discounts each monthly amount to the date of the decision. Its payment bars differ because CAD 30,000 now and CAD 350 spread over ten years have different timing. Its benefit bars match because both options receive the same pension stream by assumption. Subtract the payment present value from the pension present value to reconcile each headline result. At a zero discount rate, this is simply total gross pension receipts less the relevant nominal payment total. With a positive rate, a later receipt has less present weight. A positive conditional present value is not an actuarial valuation or an instruction to buy. The tool does not compare an invested portfolio, attach probabilities to future payments or value protection on death. The appropriate comparison rate itself requires judgment and cannot turn contingent income into certain cash. Test the receipt horizon without pretending it predicts survival The main comparison shows thirty pension receipt years after the selected wait. The matrix separately tests ten, twenty and thirty receipt years for the upfront option, alongside three starting monthly increases. Those are chosen horizons, not life-expectancy estimates or probability bands. A shorter receipt horizon reduces the modeled benefit stream while leaving the upfront cost unchanged. A longer wait also places the same future receipts farther from the election date. These two timing effects are distinct and can be explored separately. The model assumes the member survives throughout the selected receipt period, then ends the calculation. It does not model a death event, refund, survivor pension or estate payment. Those omissions make a personal plan quote and its protection terms essential before interpreting the result as a complete economic comparison. Check the agreement and the household cash capacity together Before acting, obtain the current written cost, expiry date, eligible service, payment schedule and benefit comparison from the administrator. Resolve any medical conditions, tax certification, deadlines and cancellation restrictions with the plan. The charts do not confirm any of them. Separately, check how an upfront payment affects emergency cash and nearer goals, and how payroll deductions fit the working-year budget. A pension increase later cannot pay an unrelated bill today. Registered money transferred to a pension is also money no longer available in its former account. A useful decision combines verified plan terms, an affordable funding method and a retirement-income plan. This article provides a transparent gross cash comparison; it does not replace the plan’s calculations or recommend electing an agreement.

documents.title: After a job loss: chart the settlement date, the income gap and the cash runway
documents.description: Use four interactive graphics to map eighteen months of receipts and spending, compare a temporary budget reduction and expose cash gaps before later money arrives.
documents.body: A settlement amount needs a receipt date. Build the transition reserve from the lowest cash point, then review the budget again when temporary support ends or new earnings begin. Start with accessible cash and confirmed net receipts The first number in a job-loss budget is the cash that can actually pay the next bill. Separate accessible savings from locked deposits, securities that would have to be sold, an expected settlement and unused borrowing capacity. They have different receipt dates, conditions and consequences. Do not add an undrawn credit limit to savings without also modeling the resulting debt. This example starts with CAD 18,000 of accessible cash and pays CAD 1,000 of transition costs before month one. Its opening chart point is therefore CAD 17,000. A separately entered CAD 12,000 settlement arrives at the start of month two. It is not available at time zero. Use amounts expected to reach the bank account after relevant deductions and any independently assessed obligations. Keep the gross settlement document beside a separate receipt estimate. The FCAC job-loss guide provides general context for reviewing compensation, spending and available savings. The calculator determines none of those entitlements. Put each recurring receipt on its own timeline The default household retains CAD 1,500 of other monthly net income. Temporary support of CAD 1,800 begins in month three, after two full months without it, and lasts for six payments. New earnings of CAD 4,200 begin in month ten, in addition to the continuing CAD 1,500. That creates three distinct income windows. Months one and two have CAD 1,500 of recurring income; months three through eight have CAD 3,300; month nine falls back to CAD 1,500. From month ten, recurring receipts become CAD 5,700. The one-off settlement stays outside these recurring-income bars. The assumed support schedule is an independent net cash input. It is not an EI calculation, a promise of approval or a statutory payment window. Delaying its start moves the entire modeled payment window; it does not create an arrears cheque. If new earnings begin sooner, the example stops support at that point. Real arrangements may behave differently and need a separately confirmed schedule. Give the spending reduction a start and an end Normal spending is CAD 4,500 per month. The selected CAD 600 reduction lowers it to CAD 3,900 before new earnings begin. The model restores normal spending from month ten. This avoids quietly assuming that an emergency budget will remain achievable for the next eighteen months. During the first two months, recurring income is CAD 2,400 below the reduced budget. During the six support months, the gap is CAD 600 per month. Month nine returns to a CAD 2,400 gap. From month ten onward, the normal budget has a CAD 1,200 monthly surplus under the chosen receipts. A workable reduction needs named expenses and realistic cancellation dates. Required loan payments, insurance and basic housing costs may be less flexible than travel or optional subscriptions. The control caps spending at zero if the entered reduction exceeds the normal budget; it does not treat an unused reduction as new income. New work-related expenses should be included in the normal budget or assessed separately. A positive ending balance can hide an earlier shortage The default reduced-budget path ends month eighteen with CAD 29,000 and stays funded throughout. That result depends on receiving the settlement in month two. Change accessible cash to CAD 3,000 and the settlement month to six while retaining the other defaults. The ending balance is still positive, but the cash position falls below zero before the settlement arrives. In that timing stress, cash after the immediate cost is CAD 2,000. It falls to negative CAD 400 after month one and reaches negative CAD 4,600 after month five. The additional starting reserve needed to prevent every modeled shortage is CAD 4,600. The later CAD 12,000 receipt cannot retroactively pay an earlier bill. The reserve calculation takes the largest cumulative deficit, including the immediate cost at time zero. Negative values identify funding that has not been arranged. The line does not approve an overdraft, assume a creditor will wait or calculate interest on borrowing that might bridge the gap. Use the four graphics together The income bars explain recurring receipts. The cash lines show what happens after the entire receipt and spending calendar, with and without the temporary reduction. The waterfall reconciles the final balance by counting the settlement once, eighteen months of continuing income, support actually received, new earnings actually received and all modeled costs. The matrix changes the first new-earnings month and settlement month. It holds the existing reserve and other assumptions fixed, then recalculates the extra starting cash needed for each timing combination. Its rows are job-search stresses, without probabilities. A later job start can also extend the period with reduced spending, so each cell must rerun the whole ledger. All monthly receipts are assumed to arrive before that month’s spending. Rent due before a late-month receipt could require more cash than these month-end balances show. For an immediate decision, replace the monthly calendar with actual paydays, bill dates and confirmed processing times. Build a review calendar for the transition Reconcile current accessible balances and immediate transition bills. Confirm the amount and expected receipt date of every one-off payment. Record support as a separate schedule, with an end date and any conditions. Identify feasible spending changes and when normal spending resumes. Stress a later first paycheque and check the lowest cash point. After employment resumes, review reserve rebuilding and any remaining debt. The official EI regular-benefits page is the starting point for current application and qualification information. Consult the relevant authority about how actual earnings and settlement terms affect a claim. This tool excludes benefit coordination, tax reconciliation, investment sales and employment-law advice. Update the ledger as dates become confirmed rather than using a large final settlement to dismiss a near-term cash gap.

documents.title: Retirement spending in phases: separate everyday costs, discretionary plans and later care
documents.description: Explore four charts that separate changing spending quantities from rising prices, then compare the annual budget with independently indexed net income.
documents.body: A smaller travel budget does not automatically make later retirement cheaper. Separate essentials, discretionary choices and added care, give each a time basis, and compare the resulting cash needs with income. Build a retirement budget from categories and dates A single retirement spending number is convenient but can hide several different assumptions. Housing and basic food may continue. Travel may change. Additional care may begin later. A category budget lets each event have its own amount, price assumption and date instead of assuming one smooth total describes every year. The worked example begins at retirement with CAD 36,000 of annual essentials and CAD 18,000 of annual discretionary spending. Its first annual budget is CAD 54,000. Discretionary quantity falls to 60% of the initial level from retirement year eleven. An additional care budget begins in year twenty-one. These are authored choices for exploring a household plan. They are not survey averages, typical retirement phases or evidence that every retiree spends less on leisure with age. The FCAC retirement-planning guide encourages comparing current expenses with expected retirement needs. The detailed paths here remain independent scenarios. Separate buying less from paying a higher price Everyday and discretionary prices rise by an assumed 2% a year in the default. Year one uses the starting prices; year eleven has ten increases. The year-eleven discretionary expense is therefore CAD 18,000 × 60% × 1.02 10 , about CAD 13,165. The 40% quantity reduction does not mean the nominal amount falls 40% from CAD 18,000. Prices have also changed. Essentials in that same year are about CAD 43,884, making total spending about CAD 57,049 before any added care. In retirement-start purchasing-power terms, the two categories sum to CAD 46,800. The stacked bars show selected years around the transitions. The nominal-versus-real chart displays all thirty annual budgets and a simple comparison that only inflates the original CAD 54,000. That comparison has no change in discretionary quantity and no additional care. It is a reference path, rather than a recommended spending rule. Give the care assumption an explicit dollar basis The default additional care input is CAD 18,000 per year in retirement-start dollars. Its assumed price increase is 4% per year from the beginning of retirement, including the years before care starts. When it begins in year twenty-one, the nominal allowance is CAD 18,000 × 1.04 20 , about CAD 39,440. Inflating only from the year care starts would use a different meaning: a price quoted at that future date. Mixing those two bases can materially understate a late-life budget. The controls and chart notes specify which meaning applies so the delay does not silently remove twenty years of assumed price increases. This is an additional, non-overlapping allowance. If paid care replaces housing, food or a family service already in essentials, remove or revise the displaced expense in a personal plan. The calculator leaves essentials intact and therefore does not calculate the net cost of moving into a care facility. It also supplies no care-price quotation, public subsidy estimate or probability of needing care. Deflate consistently when the categories have different price paths The real spending line divides each nominal annual total by cumulative general inflation. Before added care, the default real budget drops from CAD 54,000 to CAD 46,800 in year eleven. Once care begins, its contribution in those same general purchasing-power units can keep rising because the assumed care price rate exceeds general inflation. For example, year-twenty-one nominal spending is approximately CAD 108,983. Dividing by 1.02 20 gives approximately CAD 73,342 in retirement-start dollars. That number combines the reduced real everyday budget with care whose price has grown faster than the general basket. The Bank of Canada’s inflation overview explains the role of a broad consumer price measure. A household category assumption is a separate modeling choice. These 2% and 4% paths are constant hypothetical rates, not current CPI observations or an official forecast of personal care costs. Compare spending with the income that reaches the household Non-portfolio income starts at CAD 36,000 net and rises at an independently entered 2% a year. With the defaults, it matches the essential-spending path. The positive annual gap therefore begins at CAD 18,000, falls when discretionary quantity changes and rises when added care begins. In year thirty, the annual gap is about CAD 75,315. This is an after-tax household cash need. It is not automatically the gross amount to withdraw from an RRSP or RRIF. The gross withdrawal needed to supply it depends on the accounts, other income, tax and benefit interactions, which this budget model does not calculate. The sum of positive annual gaps is about CAD 990,497. That is an undiscounted thirty-year cash-flow total, not a required starting portfolio. It assumes no return and does not carry an earlier income surplus into a later year. Estimating starting capital requires an additional model with investment risk, tax, withdrawal timing and the intended horizon. Stress the category that could change the plan The matrix changes the additional annual care allowance in retirement-start dollars and its price increase, then displays the largest annual spending gap. The care start year and all other selected inputs remain fixed. A darker cell means a larger cash need; it does not describe how likely that need is. Try reducing the income growth rate while leaving general inflation unchanged. Then move care earlier and test retaining more discretionary activity. Each change answers a different question: income purchasing power, duration of an added expense, or the amount of optional spending. Do not treat an assumed late start as insurance against an earlier event. Review the plan with actual household spending and confirmed income terms. Identify which costs overlap, what can be adjusted, who would provide support and how receipts might change after a death or health event. Use the related longevity guide for the horizon and the income-bridge guide for the years before later income begins. This article organizes the spending side without claiming a safe withdrawal rate or a universal retirement pattern.

documents.title: A wedding or event budget needs payment dates: fund the deposit before the final bill
documents.description: Explore four charts that split fixed and guest costs, separate the booking deposit from the final bill and count only savings that arrive before each deadline.
documents.body: The total event budget and the cash available on a payment date answer different questions. Check the booking deposit immediately, then fund the final bill from transfers that arrive before it is due. Separate fixed costs from the costs that depend on attendance Start with a fully inclusive quote rather than an attractive per-person headline. This example separates CAD 6,000 of fixed event costs, CAD 100 per guest and CAD 4,000 of other fixed costs. At eighty guests, the base quote is CAD 18,000. These are hypothetical teaching amounts, not a survey of wedding prices or a supplier offer. Reducing attendance changes the guest-based part of this model. It does not automatically reduce the venue, photography or other fixed amounts. For example, forty fewer guests remove CAD 4,000 at the selected unit price while the CAD 10,000 combined fixed amount remains. The first chart exposes that distinction. Every input is assumed already to include applicable taxes and fees. Check whether a real quote includes staffing, rentals, service charges, transport, required insurance and other costs before entering its amount. The calculator supplies no tax rate and does not infer a missing fee from the type of event. Keep the contingency separate from the quoted cost The default adds an allowance equal to 10% of the entire CAD 18,000 base quote, or CAD 1,800. That makes the fully funded stress budget CAD 19,800. The allowance is an additional modeled expense at the final payment date; it is not an observed price increase or a probability-based estimate. Keeping it separate helps prevent two different mistakes. A reserve for uncertain extras should not be mistaken for a supplier’s confirmed invoice. Equally, a quote that already includes a named extra should not have that same expense added again under the contingency label. This illustration spends the full allowance so the cash path tests a definite amount. If the event costs less, the unused amount would remain available in a real account. The calculator does not allocate that possible remainder to another goal in advance. For a detailed budget, replace a broad allowance with named costs as they become known and retain a separate reserve for genuinely uncertain items. The deposit is part of the bill and an immediate cash requirement The selected booking deposit is 30% of the base quote, paid at time zero. With a CAD 18,000 base, it is CAD 5,400. The remaining base cost is CAD 12,600. Adding the CAD 1,800 allowance produces a final cash call of CAD 14,400. The deposit and final cash call sum to CAD 19,800. Adding the full base quote again after the deposit would count the deposit twice. The payment bars show the two actual outflows rather than a deposit beside an already inclusive total. Existing allocated cash is CAD 6,000, so booking leaves CAD 600. This first check happens before any future saving transfer. If allocated cash is changed to CAD 1,000, the deposit alone creates a CAD 4,400 gap. A large monthly saving assumption can improve the eventual balance without repairing that immediate shortage. The headline then explicitly says to fund the booking deposit first. Count saving dates before dividing the remaining target The final bill is due at the beginning of month twelve. Monthly saving arrives at each earlier month-end, so there are eleven qualifying transfers: the ends of months one through eleven. A paycheque at the end of month twelve arrives after this bill and is excluded. At CAD 1,000 per transfer, those eleven contributions add CAD 11,000. Together with CAD 6,000 of starting cash, they provide CAD 17,000 against CAD 19,800 of spending. The final cash gap is CAD 2,800. The modeled extra cash required at booking is therefore CAD 2,800, larger than the zero deposit gap in this default. When the booking deposit is already covered, the monthly target is maximum of zero and (total budget minus existing allocated cash) divided by (event month minus one) . Here it is CAD 13,800 divided by eleven, or about CAD 1,254.55. Rounding a practical standing order upward avoids relying on a fraction of a cent. Read remaining cash and cumulative contributions as different ledgers The cash-path chart starts after the booking deposit. It rises as earlier month-end transfers arrive, then falls when the final bill is paid. The second line shows only cumulative new saving transfers. It excludes starting cash and does not subtract event bills, so it is not another estimate of the amount left in the account. The matrix changes guest counts and monthly saving amounts. Each cell rebuilds the quote, deposit, allowance and payment calendar, then measures additional starting cash needed to keep every modeled date funded. Darker cells indicate a larger gap, without assigning likelihood to attendance or spending. The model holds all quotes fixed after booking, earns no interest and assumes no gifts or reimbursements. Expected gifts are not automatically cash available before a supplier deadline. If another person has committed support, include it only when both the amount and receipt timing are confirmed in a more detailed calendar. Do not count the same shared money twice. Reconcile the payment calendar before making commitments Collect fully inclusive quotations and separate fixed from guest-based costs. List every deposit, instalment and final-payment date. Confirm how much existing cash is actually assigned to this event. Count only saving transfers that precede each bill. Test a larger guest count or cost allowance while retaining the deadlines. Check the saving amount against the rest of the household budget. The FCAC budget guide provides a general framework for reconciling income, saving and expenses. This event calculator uses one immediate deposit and one final bill; a real event can have several earlier instalments. It does not determine whether a deposit is refundable, interpret cancellation rights, assess a supplier or calculate borrowing costs. Review those terms separately and preserve a distinct emergency reserve instead of assigning every accessible dollar to the event.

documents.title: HELOC payments in four charts: interest paid, debt remaining and a rate change
documents.description: Compare paying interest alone with adding fixed principal repayments, then trace how a different rate changes the monthly cash commitment and cumulative interest.
documents.body: Paying the interest can keep a balance from growing while leaving the original debt intact. Track the cash payment, principal remaining and interest cost separately. Separate the payment from the progress A debt statement contains several different planning questions. How much cash leaves the household this month? How much of that cash reduces what is owed? How much interest has been paid to use the borrowed money? A small required payment does not answer all three. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s HELOC guide describes a revolving credit product secured by the home. Depending on the agreement, regular payments may cover interest alone or include principal. The agency also explains that interest-only payments do not repay the borrowing. The charts start after a hypothetical CAD 60,000 has already been borrowed. They compare two repayment habits on that same debt. This is not a recommendation to borrow, a comparison with investing the borrowed funds, or a calculation of available home equity. There is no new spending financed from the line during the illustration. Read the first month in dollars The initial nominal annual rate is an assumed 7%. Under the monthly simplification used here, first-month interest is CAD 60,000 × 7% ÷ 12 = CAD 350 . The interest-only case pays that CAD 350 and still owes CAD 60,000. The second case pays the same CAD 350 interest plus CAD 300 of principal, for a CAD 650 cash payment. Debt falls to CAD 59,700. Next month, interest is calculated on that smaller opening debt. The extra CAD 300 is a reduction of a liability, rather than another interest expense. This distinction explains why the payment bars and cost curves tell different stories. The principal-repayment case uses more household cash now but pays less interest as its balance falls. The comparison does not invest the cash retained by the interest-only case or calculate a complete net-worth advantage. That would require another account and its own return, cost and risk assumptions. A lower balance can still have a higher interest bill The selected rate changes after twelve completed months, so month thirteen uses the assumed 9% rate. In the interest-only case, debt remains CAD 60,000 and the monthly interest payment rises from CAD 350 to CAD 450. After twelve CAD 300 principal repayments, the other case opens month thirteen owing CAD 56,400. Its interest is CAD 423, and its total payment is CAD 723 after adding the CAD 300 principal amount. Interest has risen from the opening month despite the reduction in debt. The FCAC describes most HELOC rates as variable and notes that changing rates can increase payment requirements. The two rates and the change date here are invented stresses. They are neither a lender quote nor a prediction about prime rates. Use an actual agreement to confirm how its rate, daily accrual, minimum payment and notice provisions work. Reconcile the ten-year totals and the unpaid endpoint Over the selected ten years, the interest-only case pays CAD 52,800 of interest and finishes with the original CAD 60,000 still outstanding. The total is CAD 4,200 for the first year plus CAD 48,600 for the next nine years at the higher assumed rate. The principal-repayment case pays CAD 36,000 toward principal and CAD 36,768 in interest. Its total cash payments are CAD 72,768, and its ending debt is CAD 24,000. The liability check is CAD 60,000 − CAD 36,000 = CAD 24,000 . The cash-payment check is principal repaid plus interest. The modeled interest difference is CAD 16,032 within this window. It is not a lifetime interest saving: neither default path has fully repaid the line by the endpoint. Future rates, later repayments and new draws could change the eventual total. Extend the horizon or increase principal payments to see when the second balance reaches zero; the tool then stops collecting payments. Use the matrix to test a repayment habit The matrix replaces the later rate and the monthly principal repayment. Each cell totals interest over the selected horizon while retaining the opening balance, first rate and change timing. Read across one row to isolate principal repayment; read down a column to isolate the later rate. Because principal is a fixed amount above interest, its repayment schedule does not slow automatically when rates rise. Instead, the required cash payment rises. A real household with a fixed total payment budget would need a different model: more interest would leave less room for principal. Do not confuse these two payment rules. No redraw is assumed. If CAD 300 is repaid and then borrowed again to cover another expense, debt will not follow the declining line shown here. An effective review therefore checks both the repayment transfer and subsequent use of the facility. Connect the schedule to the household budget Start with a supported opening balance and the actual rate formula. Choose a principal amount that fits the budget alongside required housing payments, other debt and a cash reserve. Then test a higher interest rate without silently reducing that principal target. List any setup, administration, legal or discharge charges separately; the charts exclude them. Interest is modeled as a nominal annual rate divided by twelve on the opening monthly balance, rather than an actual daily lender ledger. No interest deduction or other tax benefit is assumed. The home secures a HELOC, so a manageable-looking monthly payment should not be read as proof that the borrowing is suitable. The practical output of these charts is a set of explicit commitments: the monthly cash needed under a rate stress, the intended pace of principal reduction, and the date at which the remaining liability must be reconsidered.

documents.title: An indexed pension can still lose purchasing power: chart the cap and the spending gap
documents.description: Use four graphics to compare fixed, capped and fully inflation-matched annual income in future dollars and starting-year purchasing power.
documents.body: An annual pension increase and preservation of purchasing power are different measures. Compare the increase formula with the spending basket it needs to support. Read the adjustment formula, not just the word indexed Two pensions with the same opening payment can develop very different purchasing power. One might remain fixed; another might receive annual increases subject to a ceiling. The word “indexed” alone does not identify the amount, timing or conditions of an adjustment. The FCAC’s employer-pension overview explains that a defined benefit pension may increase to help cover rising living costs and directs members to their administrator to confirm indexing. This guide does not apply a particular pension plan’s rules. The tool creates three original comparison paths. Fixed income receives no annual increase. Capped income increases by the lower of the selected inflation assumption and the entered cap. The full-match reference increases at the selected inflation rate. Real plans can use different reference periods, partial indexing, conditional increases or other formulas; replace the illustration with confirmed plan terms before relying on a projection. Start all three income paths at the same amount The default starts with CAD 36,000 of gross annual pension income and a separate CAD 36,000 annual spending basket. Inflation is assumed constant at 3%, while the capped path has a 2% annual ceiling. Every path starts at index zero with the same income amount. After twenty-five completed annual increases, fixed income remains CAD 36,000. Capped income reaches about CAD 59,061.82, while the full-match reference reaches CAD 75,376.01. The first chart shows those nominal annual amounts, rather than cumulative lifetime payments. The capped amount is visibly larger than its starting amount. That is useful information about the number of dollars received, but it does not establish that the pension buys more. The spending basket has also risen. The index convention matters: the point labelled twenty-five includes twenty-five increases; it is not the twenty-fifth payment with only twenty-four increases. Translate the income back into starting-year dollars The second chart divides each future annual income by the assumed price-level increase. Its rule is real income at year t = nominal income at year t ÷ (1 + inflation) t . Both income and prices use the same completed-year count. At the default horizon, CAD 36,000 of fixed annual income buys about what CAD 17,193.80 bought at the start. The capped path’s CAD 59,061.82 buys about CAD 28,208.25 in starting-year terms. Its purchasing power has fallen by about 21.64%, even though the nominal payment has increased. The full-match reference retains CAD 36,000 of starting-year purchasing power because its assumed income growth exactly matches the modeled price increase. This is a mathematical control, rather than a promise about a plan or the household’s actual inflation experience. Do not reduce the real amounts by inflation a second time. Measure an annual funding gap without inventing a portfolio The selected spending basket reaches about CAD 75,376.01 after twenty-five increases. Against the capped annual pension, this creates a positive annual difference of about CAD 16,314.19 in that future year’s dollars. The third chart compares spending, income and that difference side by side. The gap calculation is max(spending − income, zero) . When entered income exceeds spending, the reported positive gap is zero. The model does not assume that any excess is saved, invested or carried forward to meet later costs. These are gross pension amounts and an independently entered spending basket. They are not a complete after-tax retirement cash plan. Income tax can widen the resources needed for spending, while other pensions, savings or work income could help fund it. The chart also does not convert one future annual shortfall into a required lump sum; that calculation needs the full sequence of withdrawals, returns, costs and available resources. Read the inflation-and-cap matrix as a sensitivity test The matrix holds starting pension income and the horizon fixed. Its rows replace constant inflation and its columns replace the annual cap. Each cell shows the capped income at the horizon in starting-year dollars, allowing different nominal paths to be compared on one purchasing-power basis. A cap at or above assumed inflation preserves starting purchasing power in this formula. Raising the cap further has no additional effect because the modeled annual increase cannot exceed inflation. A zero cap reproduces the fixed-income case. These cells are alternatives, not probabilities or official inflation forecasts. The Bank of Canada’s inflation explanation provides context for price measurement. A household’s mix of housing, care, travel and other expenses can differ from an aggregate index. The scenario deliberately keeps quantities fixed to isolate prices; a change in lifestyle or care needs belongs in a separate spending adjustment. Put the purchasing-power question into the retirement review Request the pension’s actual indexing formula, its first adjustment date and any cap or conditions. Check whether a quoted benefit includes a temporary component that later ends. A payment reduction or survivor change should not be hidden inside an inflation assumption. Build a starting spending basket from the household’s own records and state whether it is before or after tax. Compare major expenses that may evolve differently. Then add separately verified income sources on their actual schedules rather than applying one indexing assumption to the whole household. This tool excludes mortality and assumes the selected annual amount remains payable throughout the horizon. It does not value the pension, estimate a transfer value or compare a lump sum with pension payments. Its narrower purpose is to show why a rising nominal payment can coexist with falling purchasing power and a growing annual spending gap.

documents.title: Biweekly pay and monthly bills: draw the dates before spending the average
documents.description: Follow a full daily calendar to compare monthly salary receipts, bill dates, the required opening reserve and the year-end cash reconciliation.
documents.body: An annual surplus does not tell you whether the next bill is funded. A dated cash calendar reveals the gap between average income and money already available. A monthly average is not a deposit date Dividing annual take-home pay by twelve is useful for comparing a year’s resources with a year’s costs. It does not tell you which day the money reaches an account. If bills arrive before salary, the household needs accessible opening cash even when the annual budget has a surplus. The FCAC’s budgeting guide emphasizes recording money received and spent. This article adds an explicit date to every modeled flow. Its purpose is to make payment timing visible alongside the annual total. The calendar is an invented 2027 example. It starts salary receipts on the selected January day and repeats them every fourteen days. It does not reproduce an employer’s payroll calendar, calculate wages earned or determine net pay from a salary. The same-day order is conservative: fixed bills and daily spending leave before that day’s salary arrives. Read two-payday and three-payday months on the actual calendar The default pays CAD 2,000 net on 8 January 2027, then every fourteen days. There are twenty-six receipts in this selected year, totaling CAD 52,000. April and October each contain three receipts, while the other ten months contain two. Annual receipts divided by twelve are about CAD 4,333.33 per month. Actual monthly receipts are CAD 4,000 or CAD 6,000 in this example. A monthly commitment based on the average therefore uses cash from the larger-receipt months to support the smaller ones. The first chart also shows outgoings: CAD 1,800 of fixed bills once each month plus CAD 60 on every calendar day. January costs CAD 3,660; February costs CAD 3,480. The daily allowance is intentionally calendar-based, including weekends. Do not multiply a workday-only allowance by every day of the year when adapting the example. Follow the account before the first payday The opening accessible reserve is CAD 500. Fixed bills of CAD 1,800 are due on 1 January, before any receipt. The same day also uses CAD 60 of other spending. By the moment immediately before the 8 January salary receipt, eight daily amounts have been paid. The total cost before that receipt is CAD 1,800 + 8 × CAD 60 = CAD 2,280 . Against CAD 500 already available, the unfunded amount is CAD 1,780. The CAD 2,000 receipt then takes the modeled account to positive CAD 220 at the end of that day. Looking only at the payday’s closing balance would miss the earlier shortage. The second chart therefore retains both points for every date: cash after costs but before salary, and cash after any salary. Negative values mark a funding requirement; the tool does not assume an authorized overdraft, delayed bill or available loan. Keep the annual surplus and the opening reserve in the same view Annual fixed bills total CAD 21,600 and other spending totals CAD 21,900. Combined outgoings are CAD 43,500. Against CAD 52,000 of salary receipts, the selected year generates CAD 8,500 of net cash before counting the opening reserve. The waterfall reconciles the endpoint: CAD 500 + CAD 52,000 − CAD 21,600 − CAD 21,900 = CAD 9,000 . That positive year-end amount coexists with the CAD 1,780 initial shortage. A later surplus cannot make an earlier payment on its own. The required-opening-cash metric is CAD 2,280, the amount which would keep this entire default schedule funded if it were accessible at the start. It includes cash already selected, so the additional amount is CAD 1,780. Increasing opening cash changes the funding gap and ending account amount dollar for dollar; it does not change salary, bills or the cash generated during the year. Use the date matrix without assuming equal annual receipts The matrix moves the first January receipt and the recurring monthly bill day. Each cell runs the full daily ledger again and finds the minimum opening reserve needed before any same-day salary receipt. Pay per receipt and all cost amounts stay fixed. A fourteen-day sequence can place twenty-six or twenty-seven paydays inside a calendar year, depending on the first date. Starting on 1 January 2027 produces twenty-seven in this mathematical schedule. The cells therefore do not all represent equal annual salary. They answer a cash-calendar question using the actual in-year receipts created by each selected date. Use the employer’s confirmed dates in practice, including holiday shifts. For example, the federal public-service calendar shows a specific employer schedule and explains its holiday adjustments and payment in arrears. Those employer-specific dates and rules are not applied to this invented calendar. Assign the next receipt before treating it as spendable List the bills due before the following payday, including automatic transfers and irregular commitments. Compare that dated list with cash that is already accessible. A three-payday month may provide room to build the opening buffer or fund another goal, but the next month’s obligations still need to be reserved. Keep genuinely unexpected costs separate from this known timing requirement. The opening amount here covers only the modeled bills and daily allowance. It is not a complete emergency reserve, and it includes no annual insurance payment, tax instalment, interest, service charge or unlisted purchase. The model fixes bills to a day from one through twenty-eight, so every selected day exists in every month. It has no business-day adjustments, leap-year logic beyond its fixed 2027 calendar or automatic rollover into another year. Before adopting the schedule, replace grouped bills with actual due dates and verify that receipts are settled and usable when needed.

documents.title: The credit-card minimum-payment trap: a smaller bill can hide a longer repayment
documents.description: Follow the changing payment, remaining debt and interest through four charts comparing a shrinking minimum with a maintained repayment amount.
documents.body: A lower required payment can ease this month’s budget while extending the debt. Track the balance, payoff date and total interest together. Why a shrinking payment deserves a second look Imagine opening a card statement and seeing that the required payment has fallen. That can be welcome cash-flow relief. It does not tell you how quickly the remaining debt will disappear. When the payment is a percentage of a falling balance, less money may go toward repayment every month, creating a long tail of small payments. The first chart follows that mechanism. It starts with an existing balance, charges one month of interest and then applies a hypothetical minimum. The comparison preserves a chosen payment amount whenever it exceeds the minimum. Both paths assume no new purchases and payments made on time. FCAC explains that minimum formulas vary and that paying more can reduce repayment time and interest. Use the agreement for an actual account. The selected percentage and dollar floor here are teaching inputs, not a statement of the rule that applies to every Canadian card. Read the two lines as different household commitments The maintained strategy is not simply a faster investment return on the same cash flow. It usually requires more money to leave the household earlier. The benefit comes from reducing the balance exposed to future interest; the cost is less cash available for other needs while the larger payments continue. The payment chart makes that trade-off visible. A chosen CAD 300 amount is treated as a floor, and a higher modeled minimum still takes priority. The final payment is reduced to the amount actually owed. This avoids overpaying the account or treating a selected amount below the minimum as acceptable. Check that the commitment fits after housing, food, required debt payments and other essential bills. If it does not, a mathematically short payoff schedule has not solved the cash-flow problem. Consider the budget and available assistance before relying on a path that cannot be funded. See exactly what the model calls interest and principal For an opening balance B and a nominal annual percentage rate a, the simplified monthly interest charge is B × a ÷ 12 , with a expressed as a decimal. The amount due becomes B plus that charge. The model then takes the larger of the entered dollar floor and the chosen percentage of that amount, capped at the amount due. For the maintained strategy, the actual payment is the larger of this modeled minimum and the chosen maintained amount, again capped at the amount due. The new balance is amount due minus actual payment. The following month starts from that balance, so paying principal earlier reduces later interest. Real cards can use daily calculations and several balance categories. Fees, grace periods, cash advances, promotional terms and payment dates can change results. This example deliberately uses one rate bucket. It does not reproduce a statement, determine a legally required minimum or model the consequences of a missed payment. An unfinished balance is still an obligation The stacked bars show payments already made alongside the balance still owed at each path’s stopping date. Together they equal the original principal plus the interest charged through that date. If a path has finished, the remaining-balance segment is zero. If it has not, treating payments already made as the full repayment cost would hide debt. The calculation stops after 600 months. An NR cell means the balance has not been repaid within that window. It does not mean the debt has vanished or that the remaining interest is zero. Low percentage payments at a sufficiently high rate can even allow the balance to grow. The bars can cover different lengths of time because each path stops when it finishes. They measure nominal cash and debt through those endpoints, without reinvesting payments released after payoff. They are not a comparison of investment wealth at a common future date. Turn the matrix into a payment decision Read across one rate row to test several maintained amounts. Then read down a payment column to see what a different interest assumption does. The starting balance and minimum rule stay fixed. In every cell, the modeled minimum overrides a smaller maintained amount; the column heading is not a promise that payments never exceed it. Start with a payment that can be sustained and note its modeled finish date. Next test a modest increase, then a higher rate. If the plan depends on a promotional rate staying low, include the period after it expires using the separate balance-transfer guide. Review the actual statements as you go. New spending, changed rates and fees can move the endpoint. Once the debt is repaid, make a fresh decision about the cash that becomes available: rebuilding a reserve or funding another goal requires a new instruction, not an assumption hidden inside this calculator.

documents.title: Give each pay rise a job: chart the split between saving and lifestyle spending
documents.description: Use four graphics to trace repeated take-home increases into extra contributions, extra spending and a long-term savings balance.
documents.body: A repeatable saving rule can make a series of small pay increases meaningful. The larger balance requires real contributions and less spending along the way. Begin with the increase that actually reaches the budget A raise expressed as a percentage of gross salary does not directly tell you how much more can be spent or saved. Deductions, benefit costs and payroll contributions can change the amount reaching the bank account. Start with an independently checked increase in take-home pay, then decide which new expenses that money must cover. This example uses a fixed dollar increase in monthly take-home pay at each annual anniversary. Year one has no increase. The first step arrives at the start of year two and continues thereafter. Another equal step begins in year three. This is a hypothetical income path, not a forecast of wages or a promise of annual raises. FCAC’s budgeting guidance brings income, spending, saving and changing circumstances into the same review. The tool starts after that review: its original monthly saving must already be affordable, and the entered increases must be available after any separately planned rise in essential costs. A small recurring increase accumulates into a larger pool Suppose the assumed monthly take-home increase is CAD 150 each year. Monthly income in year two is CAD 150 higher than at the start; in year three it is CAD 300 higher. By year ten, nine increases make the monthly difference CAD 1,350. These are accumulated additions to recurring income, not a single annual bonus. The selected saving share applies to that accumulated pool. With a 50% rule, half of each increase adds to monthly saving and half adds to spending. Earlier saving increases continue when the next increase arrives. The first chart annualizes both parts, so each bar equals twelve times that year’s monthly pool. The chart excludes original spending and original saving to keep the new-money decision visible. A larger bar later in the period comes from the assumed sequence of increases. It is not evidence that investments generated additional salary or that spending has automatically remained affordable. Compare saving rules with the income path held constant The three curves share starting savings, original monthly contributions, the pay-rise schedule, the assumed return and the finish date. They differ only in how much of each raise is saved. Saving none of the raises preserves only the original saving habit. Saving all assigns the entire increase to the account. The selected rule sits between those endpoints. These are different consumption choices. A household on the all-saving path has less additional spending during the period. Calling its larger endpoint better investment performance would confuse effort with return. The same assumed investment return applies to every path. Try a zero return first. The difference between endpoints then equals the additional cash contributed. Next test a lower or negative return to see how the investment assumption changes the outcome without changing the pay-rise commitment. Separate the saving effort from the investment effect The waterfall subtracts the zero-capture path from the selected path. Common starting savings and original deposits cancel. The first step is the total extra contributions funded by the rule. The second is the difference between the resulting extra wealth and those contributions: growth when positive, an investment loss when negative. The monthly return is (1 + annual return) 1/12 − 1 . Each month, the existing account grows at that rate before the month-end deposit arrives. Every deposit therefore gets only the remaining months of growth; the calculation does not give a late deposit the return earned by the initial balance. For N whole years and a fixed monthly pay-rise step S, the cumulative extra contributions are 12 × S × saving share × N(N − 1) ÷ 2 . This formula checks the saving effort independently of any investment return. All amounts are nominal CAD before account taxes and fees. Choose a rule that survives changing circumstances The matrix varies the saved percentage and planning horizon. It shows additional ending savings relative to saving none of the raises over the same number of years. A thirty-year case contains more assumed pay increases than a ten-year case, so the gap combines more contributions with more time for investment growth. A household might first assign part of an observed increase to essentials, then divide what remains between saving and optional spending. That real-world sequence is separate from this simplified tool. Inflation, caregiving, changing hours and a missed raise can all reduce the amount available. Write the rule in monthly dollars and review it when actual pay changes. An automatic transfer can implement a feasible decision, but it should follow the cash-flow check. Use the multiple-goal guide to decide where the extra saving goes; this article does not choose an account, set contribution room or rank goals for you.

documents.title: After the emergency: rebuild the reserve before the next cash shock
documents.description: Follow two unexpected bills through four charts showing cash available at the due date, actual rebuilding deposits and remaining funding gaps.
documents.body: An emergency reserve is a repeating cash-flow process. A later contribution can rebuild the balance, but it cannot fund a bill that was already due. Using the reserve changes the next planning decision A reserve can do its job successfully and still leave a household exposed afterward. Paying an urgent bill reduces the cash available for the next one. The useful follow-up is not just whether the original target was sensible; it is how much remains, how quickly it can be rebuilt and what happens if another need arrives sooner. FCAC distinguishes unexpected expenses from occasional expenses that can be planned in the ordinary budget. This article concentrates on rebuilding after an unexpected use. Recurring annual bills belong in a separate calendar so they do not repeatedly consume money intended for surprises. The two bills in the tool are deliberately hypothetical. Their amounts and dates do not describe observed Canadian household losses, an insurance forecast or the chance of a second event. The scenario makes a timing problem visible before a more detailed plan is built. Check the money available when the bill arrives The ledger begins with the selected reserve and runs for 24 months. At the start of a bill month, the unexpected expense arrives before the next contribution. The bill can use only the reserve cash already present. At month-end, the affordable contribution rebuilds the reserve toward the selected target. For example, if CAD 500 remains when a CAD 1,000 bill arrives, the ledger funds CAD 500 and records CAD 500 as unmet. A CAD 400 deposit later that month improves the ending reserve. It does not make the earlier CAD 500 gap disappear. This is why the chart shows both cash after bills and cash after the contribution. The account is never allowed to become negative. A shortfall is recorded outside it, without assuming an overdraft, credit-card balance, delayed payment or help from another person. Each of those would require its own terms and cash-flow consequences. Rebuilding is limited by both the budget and the target The entered monthly contribution is money available after ordinary commitments. The model transfers only what is needed to reach the target, up to that contribution. Once the target is reached, further transfers pause until another bill reduces the reserve. Money not transferred stays outside this ledger. This distinction matters when comparing the contribution setting with actual deposits. A CAD 400 setting over 24 months does not necessarily create CAD 9,600 of deposits. Some months may need less, and some may need none. The waterfall uses the actual transferred amounts to reconcile starting cash, funded bills and ending cash. If starting cash is already above the target, the model retains it. It does not force a withdrawal merely to match the chosen line. The target is an assumption for rebuilding, not a maximum balance, an assessed personal reserve requirement or an account contribution limit. The second bill tests the recovery period Read the matrix across one monthly-saving row. Moving the second bill later may allow more rebuilding before it arrives. If the reserve reaches its target first, waiting longer adds no further reserve under this rule. A target smaller than a later bill can therefore leave a gap even after a long recovery period. Read down one date column to compare affordable contribution amounts. Faster rebuilding can reduce exposure, but only if the household can actually make those transfers. Raising a number in the tool does not create surplus in the ordinary budget. If both bills share a month, they are combined before that month’s deposit. Changing dates can also place the second labelled bill before the first. The model follows chronological cash movements rather than assuming the labels establish an order. Every matrix cell reports total unmet bills at their actual modeled due dates. Track the balance and the unresolved need separately The recovery metric counts months from the last positive bill until the reserve is at or above target at a month-end. Zero means it reaches the target in that same month, or is already there when there are no positive bills. NR means the target is not reached within the 24-month window; it is not a forecast of permanent failure. A restored reserve does not prove every bill was funded. The headline shortfall remains visible even after later contributions rebuild the account. Before treating the scenario as workable, identify how an earlier gap would be paid and whether that would create repayments that reduce future saving. A practical review records the remaining reserve, the next affordable transfer, known upcoming bills and any unresolved expense. Add separately confirmed reimbursements only when their timing is known. Use the insurance-reimbursement guide for that extension, and revisit the target when essential spending or household responsibilities change.
