documents.title: A charitable giving budget needs gift dates as well as tax assumptions
documents.description: Four charts compare equal annual gift commitments, the cash required before payments and an independently entered usable tax saving.
documents.body: Fund the gross gift when it is paid. Count a tax saving only when it can actually free cash for the budget, and keep it separate from the gift itself. Start with the cash commitment to the recipient A donation pledge belongs in the household budget at its gross amount. A later tax saving can affect household cash, but it does not reduce the amount the recipient needs to receive on the gift date. The CRA’s donor guidance explains the role of registered charities, other qualified donees and official donation receipts. A payment to an organization does not automatically establish an individual’s usable credit. The CRA’s Gifts and Income Tax guide for 2025 describes donation credits as non-refundable and based on eligible gifts. This article uses that general context without applying 2025 rates to a later year. It calculates no federal or provincial credit, eligibility limit or actual tax refund. Compare three schedules with the same annual gift total The default monthly gift is CAD 200. Over one year that is CAD 2,400, and over the full twenty-four months the recipient receives CAD 4,800. Three schedules preserve those annual totals. The monthly schedule pays CAD 200 at each month’s start. The year-start alternative pays CAD 2,400 at the start of months one and thirteen. The year-end alternative pays CAD 2,400 at the start of months twelve and twenty-four, the final month of each modeled year. Other household budget surplus contributes CAD 150 at each month-end. That amount is available after the household’s other commitments. It must not already include the tax saving entered in the separate control, or the same resource would be counted twice. Enter a usable saving and its arrival date independently The default assumes CAD 600 attributable to first-year gifts becomes usable at the end of month sixteen. This amount is an independent scenario input, rather than a tax calculation or a promise that a refund arrives then. A non-refundable credit may reduce tax otherwise payable. Depending on the broader return and payments already made, the household effect can be a smaller payment rather than a cash refund. Include only the amount that can actually become available to this giving budget, at the appropriate time. The illustration caps the entered saving at first-year gifts and sets it to zero when there are no gifts. That is a modeling convention, not a statutory credit limit. No tax benefit from second-year gifts is received within the horizon, and no carryforward or gift of appreciated property is modeled. Measure the lowest cash point before later resources arrive With monthly gifts, the plan needs CAD 950 of starting cash under the default assumptions. Starting cash is CAD 1,000, leaving a lowest modeled balance of CAD 50. Gifts are paid before that month’s budget surplus and any assumed tax saving. The year-start schedule needs CAD 3,000 at the start because its second annual gift falls before the assumed saving arrives. The year-end schedule needs CAD 750 because more monthly budget contributions accumulate before each gift. These are timing comparisons, not rankings of generosity or impact. The cash lines show the point just after month-start gifts. Month-end resources have not yet arrived at each plotted point. After all month-twenty-four resources, every schedule ends at CAD 400: CAD 1,000 starting cash plus CAD 3,600 of budget contributions and CAD 600 of usable saving, less CAD 4,800 of gifts. Keep the two-year cash measure separate from lifetime cost The waterfall shows CAD 4,800 of gifts less the one CAD 600 saving realized inside the horizon, giving CAD 4,200 of net gift cash outflow. It is not the lifetime after-tax cost of both years’ donations, because any later second-year benefit is outside the schedule. The matrix varies the usable saving and when it arrives in year two. It shows total starting cash required for monthly gifts. An earlier or larger usable saving can ease later cash needs, but it cannot pay an earlier gift retroactively. Before committing, confirm the recipient, the intended amount, gift dates, receipt treatment and a conservative usable tax assumption. Retain the gross commitment in the budget even if the saving is uncertain. The charts organize those cash decisions while leaving actual tax calculations and the choice of recipient outside the model.

documents.title: Buying a home: build the cash plan beyond the down payment
documents.description: Four graphics separate the basic down-payment rule, a credited deposit, closing allowances and cash retained after the purchase.
documents.body: Start with the full purchase cash requirement, subtract the credited deposit once, then compare the remaining amount with cash actually available now. Use the price-based minimum as a starting point The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s down-payment table sets out a basic price-based minimum: 5% for a home costing CAD 500,000 or less. Above that price and below CAD 1.5 million, the calculation is CAD 25,000 plus 10% of the portion over CAD 500,000. At CAD 1.5 million or more, the basic minimum becomes 20% of the entire purchase price. The first chart uses separate price examples to show that threshold. Immediately below CAD 1.5 million the basic amount is about CAD 125,000; at CAD 1.5 million it is CAD 300,000. This is a narrow rule illustration. A lender can require more, and the cash calculation does not assess income, credit, the property, or mortgage qualification. The selected down payment cannot fall below the basic minimum in this model. Treat the deposit as part of the price already funded The hypothetical home costs CAD 700,000. A requested 10% down payment is CAD 70,000, above the basic CAD 45,000 minimum. A CAD 20,000 deposit has already been paid and is assumed credited toward that same purchase price. The down payment still due is therefore CAD 50,000. Adding the deposit to CAD 70,000 again would count the same purchase funding twice. The waterfall first shows the complete cash requirement and then subtracts the credited deposit once. The tool assumes the whole deposit is credited without a refund. If it exceeds the requested down payment, the modeled down payment increases to include it; a deposit above the price is capped at the price. Real contract terms and adjustments need confirmation. A deposit’s due date also matters: money needed before closing must already be accessible then. Give closing costs their own budget lines The default uses a 3% closing-cost allowance, or CAD 21,000, plus CAD 2,000 of additional fixed closing costs and CAD 5,000 for moving and setup. These are hypothetical placeholders. The percentage does not calculate a provincial transfer tax or establish the actual legal bill. Replace allowances with quotes and a closing statement as those become available. Ensure the fixed-cost line excludes items already covered by the percentage allowance. A practical ledger records the description, amount, due date and source of each charge. CMHC explains mortgage loan insurance and the possibility of paying a premium upfront or financing it. This tool calculates neither premiums nor taxes on them. Add confirmed cash charges once to the appropriate allowance; a financed amount needs a separate mortgage analysis. Retained cash is still part of the funding requirement The example deliberately retains CAD 10,000 after closing. That money remains an asset, but it must be funded if the purchase is to leave the intended reserve intact. Calling it a closing fee would misdescribe it; leaving it out would hide the desired cash cushion. The total requirement is CAD 108,000: CAD 70,000 down, CAD 21,000 closing allowance, CAD 2,000 fixed costs, CAD 5,000 setup and CAD 10,000 reserve. Subtracting the CAD 20,000 credited deposit leaves CAD 88,000 to cover. Cash available now is CAD 80,000 after the deposit has been paid. The additional amount to arrange is CAD 8,000. Entering the pre-deposit bank balance would wrongly make the paid deposit appear available a second time. Test the price and down payment before committing the cash The remaining-requirement bars show where the CAD 88,000 goes. The matrix then varies price and the requested down-payment percentage. The basic rule and deposit floor continue to apply, so requesting a smaller percentage does not bypass them. A higher down payment increases cash committed to the property, while a price increase can also raise the percentage-based closing allowance. The matrix keeps fixed costs and current available cash unchanged. It does not estimate local taxes, future selling costs or investment returns. Review the payment calendar alongside this total. Funds tied up in another property, a pending withdrawal or an investment sale may arrive after a deposit or closing obligation. A zero modeled shortfall means the entered cash lines balance; it does not establish borrowing capacity or the affordability of ongoing ownership.

documents.title: Splitting household bills: compare the rule and the cash left over
documents.description: Four charts compare equal and income-based assignments while keeping shared costs, savings commitments and individual constraints visible.
documents.body: Agree on the shared budget first. Then compare how each assignment rule fits both people’s resources and separate commitments. Define what belongs in the shared commitment A household can agree on a percentage split and still disagree about what that percentage covers. Start with a common list of bills, then decide which savings transfers are also shared commitments. Keep separate personal obligations visible alongside that list. The FCAC’s guide to managing money as a couple describes different arrangements for sharing expenses and suggests discussing transfer timing, contribution percentages and a potential loss of income. The right arrangement depends on the people and their circumstances. This example focuses on monthly allocation arithmetic. Shared bills are CAD 4,000 and the agreed shared savings transfer is CAD 800. Together they require CAD 4,800 each month. The transfer remains an asset, but it is committed cash for this budget rather than money available for another bill. Compare equal amounts with shares of take-home income Person A has CAD 5,000 of monthly take-home income; Person B has CAD 3,000. Under equal shares, each is assigned CAD 2,400 of the shared total. Under the income rule, A earns 62.5% of the combined CAD 8,000 and B earns 37.5%. Applying those weights to CAD 4,800 assigns A CAD 3,000 and B CAD 1,800. The formula uses take-home income before separate personal commitments. Both rules assign exactly CAD 4,800. The grouped bars show who is assigned the money, not a saving produced by the rule. Neither rule is automatically fair in every household: unpaid work, income stability, personal obligations and the agreed purpose of savings can all matter to the discussion. Check each person after their separate commitments The default separate commitments are CAD 500 for A and CAD 300 for B. After those amounts and equal shared assignments, A has CAD 2,100 left and B has CAD 300. Under income shares, A has CAD 1,500 and B has CAD 900. Those individual remainders explain why the same shared total can feel different under two rules. Equal amounts consume 48% of A’s take-home income and 80% of B’s; income shares consume 60% of each income in this particular example, before separate obligations. The income-check chart deliberately compares amounts rather than percentages. If an income becomes zero, a percentage burden would be undefined. An assignment above the income bar is clearly unfunded even before separate commitments. A smaller assignment can still be unaffordable once those other commitments are deducted. Keep the household balance separate from the allocation Combined take-home income is CAD 8,000. Subtracting CAD 800 of separate commitments leaves CAD 7,200. After CAD 4,000 of shared bills and the CAD 800 savings transfer, CAD 2,400 remains unassigned. The waterfall gives the same endpoint under both rules. Reassigning a bill between people cannot create household income or reduce the amount paid to a landlord, utility or savings account. If the endpoint is negative, the entered plan has an unmet household need. A positive household endpoint can coexist with one person’s shortage. Resolving that situation requires an explicit agreement about contributions, transfers or commitments. The model does not assume that one person automatically covers the other’s obligations or that money in an account is legally shared. Use the matrix to discuss changes before they happen The matrix replaces A’s income and scales the shared total while holding B’s income selected. Each cell shows A’s income-based assignment minus an equal half. A positive number assigns A more than half; a negative number assigns less. Neither sign measures whether a household is better off. If both entered incomes are zero, the current income-weighted comparison is omitted because there is no income share to calculate. Equal assignment remains visible, with the household cash shortage shown separately. The matrix still describes its explicitly hypothetical positive A-income cases. Agree when to revisit the arrangement: a job change, leave, irregular pay or a changed savings goal may alter what is workable. Match transfers to actual bill dates as well as monthly totals. This tool does not determine taxes, benefits, joint borrowing liability, property ownership or account access; those questions need their own facts and applicable rules.

documents.title: Interest-free student loans still need a repayment cash plan
documents.description: Four graphics separate a zero-interest Canada Student Loan from other education debt, then compare repayment terms and the monthly budget.
documents.body: Separate each balance, rate and payment obligation. A zero future-interest rate reduces borrowing costs but does not make the opening amount disappear. Separate the federal rule from other education borrowing The National Student Loans Service Centre’s current-interest-rate explanation states that accumulation of interest on Canada Student Loans was permanently eliminated effective 1 April 2023. That rule concerns federal student loans, not every debt used to pay for education. Provincial or territorial loans and private borrowing can have different terms. The model therefore keeps the Canada Student Loan amount at zero new interest and gives a second education-debt balance its own hypothetical rate. The default 6% for that second balance is an assumption, not a quoted provincial or bank rate. Enter current amounts owed. Any earlier accrued amount still payable must remain in the opening ledger. This illustration calculates future interest and payments; it does not decide how a servicer applies payments between historical interest, principal or portions of an integrated loan. Put the first payment date into the post-study budget Canada’s repayment-start guide describes a six-month non-repayment period after leaving school and directs borrowers to their loan terms and the relevant servicer. That interval is different from a permanent absence of payment obligations. The charts begin when repayment starts. They do not simulate the study period, a waiting-period interest convention or the date a specific person’s payment is due. Confirm the opening balance, required payment, first due date and payment channel from the actual account. A new graduate’s monthly plan may also need housing deposits, work transport and irregular setup costs. Enter the amount available for loan payments after those other commitments, rather than treating the full first paycheque as disposable cash. Turn each opening balance into an illustrative payment The default has CAD 20,000 of Canada Student Loan debt and CAD 10,000 of other education debt. Both use 120 illustrative monthly repayment periods. That selected term is a modeling choice, not a statement of the official default schedule or an approved repayment option. At zero new interest, CAD 20,000 divided by 120 is CAD 166.666… per month. Rounding the scheduled payment up to cents gives CAD 166.67, with a smaller final payment. The other balance at a hypothetical 6% nominal annual rate requires CAD 111.03 under the model’s monthly-interest convention. The combined scheduled amount is CAD 277.70. Against the default CAD 300 monthly budget, the model shows no shortfall and CAD 22.30 remains outside these scheduled payments. Changing the budget control does not change an obligation or authorize a lower payment; it only changes the comparison. Read principal repayment and borrowing cost separately The stacked bars show opening amounts and new modeled interest. The federal bar has no new-interest segment, but the CAD 20,000 still needs to be repaid. Removing interest reduces the cost above that opening amount rather than removing the balance itself. The balance paths use the same selected horizon. The zero-rate component declines in equal scheduled amounts until the capped final payment. On the interest-bearing component, part of each early payment covers interest, so the principal reduction grows as the outstanding balance falls. The calculation charges the selected nominal annual rate divided by 12 before each month-end payment. Actual loan statements may use daily interest, different payment dates, changing rates or integrated payment-allocation rules. The paths are transparent comparisons, not a reproduction of a servicer’s statement. Compare a lower monthly payment with a longer commitment The matrix varies the other-debt rate and the illustrative term for both balances. Federal new interest stays zero. A longer term spreads its opening amount over more payments without adding new federal interest under the selected rule. For interest-bearing debt, a longer term can reduce the scheduled monthly amount while increasing total interest. A smaller payment is therefore only one part of the choice. Compare total cost, the length of the commitment and the budget’s ability to absorb changes. The tool excludes repayment assistance, forgiveness, tax credits, missed payments and future policy changes. If the actual payment does not fit the budget, review the servicer’s available options and eligibility before changing payments. Keep this modeled schedule separate from an approved arrangement and refresh it when actual balances or terms change.

documents.title: Tuition statistics are a starting point, not the full student budget
documents.description: Two official tuition graphics and two budget scenarios separate preliminary 2026/2027 averages from the costs and funding of an individual study plan.
documents.body: Use an average to frame the question, then replace it with the actual tuition quote and add the other costs. A tuition figure alone cannot establish how much cash a student needs. Read the official numbers with their population and period Statistics Canada’s Table 37-10-0045-01 reports preliminary 2026/2027 national undergraduate tuition averages of CAD 8,021 for Canadian students and CAD 42,062 for international students. The first graphic presents those published observations, rather than values calculated from the budget controls. These are weighted averages for full-time students at public degree-granting institutions, expressed in current dollars. They are tuition amounts, not complete living budgets or individual program quotations. The difference between the groups can reflect different program and institution mixes. The ten-province graphic shows the Canadian undergraduate observations from the same release. It includes no territory. A province’s bar is not the price every student pays there, and a lower average does not rank the quality or overall affordability of a particular program. Keep a weighted average separate from a personal quote The survey methodology explains how institutions report fees and how enrolment weights are used to combine them. The current table uses 2023/2024 enrolment weights. The national estimate is not a simple average of the provincial bars. A weighted mean is also different from a median. These bars do not say that half of students pay less than the displayed amount, and they provide no price range for a particular program. Program mix and residency treatment also affect comparisons. Some provincial averages incorporate different fees for in-province and out-of-province Canadian students. The source marks the current academic year preliminary, even though the selected CSV status cells are blank. The data were released on 16 September 2026 and retrieved for this article on 25 October 2026. The two observation charts remain fixed when the controls change. For a personal plan, replace the editable tuition value with the institution’s quote and confirm which fees that quote includes. Add the costs that tuition does not cover The default budget starts at the published CAD 8,021 Canadian undergraduate national average. The remaining amounts are hypothetical: CAD 1,000 of additional compulsory fees, CAD 1,000 of books and equipment, and CAD 1,000 of travel and setup. Living and local transport are budgeted at CAD 1,400 a month for eight months, adding CAD 11,200. The resulting modeled total is CAD 22,221. Tuition is about 36.10% of this particular example; that share is not a population estimate of what students generally spend. The waterfall expresses all the cost lines and confirmed funding in CAD. Check for overlap when entering real amounts: a residence package might already include food, or a quoted fee might already include a compulsory charge. Each actual cost belongs in the ledger once. Subtract confirmed resources without treating borrowing as a price reduction The example enters CAD 12,000 of confirmed funding, leaving CAD 10,221 to arrange under the selected budget. The funding input does not calculate grants, scholarships, tax benefits, family support or loan approval. A loan can supply cash for a bill while creating a separate repayment obligation. If borrowing is included in confirmed funding, the budget gap may close without the underlying education cost becoming smaller. Record that repayment plan separately. A negative waterfall endpoint means entered funding exceeds this budget; the additional-funding metric is then floored at zero. The tool assigns no destination to the surplus. A zero-cost example reports that no modeled cost share is available rather than dividing by zero. Test the living-cost calendar and revise the plan The matrix varies monthly living costs and the number of months to cover. Tuition, fees, books, setup and confirmed funding remain selected. A twelve-month living plan therefore adds summer costs without automatically changing the tuition entry. The model does not prorate tuition when the living-cost duration changes. Tuition schedules can depend on programs, credits, terms and status, so the quote needs its own review. The matrix contains hypothetical allowances and is not an accommodation-price survey. Use the observed averages as context, then build a dated personal cost and funding list. The charts distinguish an official statistical benchmark from the cash a particular plan needs, while leaving enrolment choices, funding approval and account-withdrawal rules to their own evidence.

documents.title: A balance-transfer promotion has a deadline, a fee and a remaining balance
documents.description: Four graphics compare promotional and later rates, debt paths, full repayment charges and the payment needed to finish during the promotion.
documents.body: A low starting rate is one input. Include the transfer fee, the amount left when the promotion ends and the payment schedule before comparing borrowing costs. Read what the offer applies to and when it ends The FCAC’s credit-card guide explains balance-transfer fees and promotions that apply for a specified period. It also distinguishes purchase grace periods from balance transfers, which do not receive that purchase grace period. This model isolates one transferred debt. There are no new purchases, cash advances or competing rate buckets. The transfer fee is added to the opening balance and receives the same modeled rate. An actual agreement can treat fees and payments differently. The promotional rate applies for a selected number of monthly cycles. The follow-on rate then applies to remaining debt prospectively. The model includes neither retroactive interest nor the consequences of losing a promotion through a missed payment. All rates and terms are hypothetical. Include the fee in the amount that needs repayment The default current balance is CAD 10,000 at a 20% nominal annual rate. A transfer fee of 3% adds CAD 300, so the alternative starts with CAD 10,300 of debt. A zero promotional rate does not remove that fee. The selected payment is CAD 400 at each month-end. With twelve promotional cycles at 0%, those payments reduce the transferred balance by CAD 4,800. CAD 5,500 therefore remains when the promotion ends. From the next cycle, the example charges a 22% nominal annual rate divided by twelve on remaining debt before the payment. Actual cards can calculate daily interest and use different payment allocation rules. The illustration uses one explicit monthly convention so the schedule can be inspected. Solve the payment needed to clear during the promotion The second metric calculates a constant monthly amount that would repay the fee-inclusive balance within the promotional cycles. At 0%, CAD 10,300 divided by twelve is CAD 858.333… per month. The tool rounds up to CAD 858.34, with the final payment capped at the remaining amount. Rounding down to CAD 858.33 would leave four cents after twelve payments. That amount is more than the selected CAD 400 payment. The difference explains why the default schedule continues beyond the promotion. At a positive promotional rate, the tool uses the fixed-payment amortization formula rather than simply dividing principal by months. If zero promotional cycles are selected, the new balance begins at the follow-on rate and no within-promotion payment is reported. A zero original debt creates no transfer fee in the model. The metric does not determine affordability or replace actual minimum-payment requirements. Compare the complete schedule when it is available Under the defaults, the current balance clears in month thirty-three and incurs approximately CAD 3,044.21 of interest. The transferred balance clears in month twenty-eight, with approximately CAD 895.35 of interest and the CAD 300 fee. The transfer’s modeled borrowing cost is therefore CAD 1,195.35, about CAD 1,848.86 below the current-card cost under these assumptions. Original principal is excluded from both cost bars because it must be repaid either way. Interest on the financed fee is already included in the interest component. The charts stop at payoff or 120 months. A “Not repaid” metric means the model did not clear that balance within the limit. Charges for an incomplete schedule are partial and cannot be called a full repayment cost. The matrix uses NR instead of reporting a full-life cost for such cases. Test the payment and the time available The matrix changes monthly payments and promotional cycles while holding the original balance, fee and rates fixed. Each completed cell shows total interest plus the fee. A larger promotional window helps only within the entered repayment schedule and assumptions. The comparison keeps the same fixed payment while each balance remains outstanding. It does not invest money released after earlier payoff, add an annual card fee or simulate new spending. Those effects belong in a wider household comparison if they apply. The FCAC notes that missed payments can cause the loss of promotional terms. Check the agreement, transaction types, fee treatment, minimum payments and expiry dates before relying on an actual offer. The four graphics explain a cost schedule without treating a headline rate as a complete borrowing decision.

documents.title: Insurance reimbursement and cash flow: a covered expense can still need money upfront
documents.description: Four graphics connect recognized claims, a remaining deductible, an insurer-payment maximum and the cash needed before receipts arrive.
documents.body: The eventual amount reimbursed and the cash needed to pay invoices answer different questions. Track both the benefit calculation and the timing of bills and receipts. Separate the invoice, recognized amount and insurer payment The FCAC’s health-insurance guide highlights that a policy may pay only a percentage of a claim or impose a maximum annual amount. The actual contract determines what is covered and how a claim is assessed. This illustration assumes approved private-benefit claims and uses an explicit calculation order: cap the recognized amount at the invoice, apply the remaining deductible, apply the insurer’s percentage, then apply the remaining insurer-payment maximum. Those are hypothetical contract conventions, not rules for every plan. The tool calculates neither eligibility nor a public dental or health-program benefit. The number and size of invoices are financial assumptions, rather than a recommendation about treatment or clinical need. Follow the remaining deductible and maximum through the claims The default schedule has a CAD 600 invoice at the start of each of six consecutive months in one benefit year. CAD 500 per invoice is recognized. The remaining deductible starts at CAD 100, the insurer percentage is 80%, and the remaining insurer-payment maximum is CAD 1,500. For the first claim, CAD 500 less CAD 100 leaves CAD 400 to which the 80% share applies. The modeled reimbursement is CAD 320. The next two claims reimburse CAD 400 each. Only CAD 380 remains under the payment maximum for the fourth claim. The fifth and sixth invoices still cost CAD 600 each, but the maximum has been exhausted and their modeled reimbursements are zero. Total invoices are CAD 3,600, total reimbursement is CAD 1,500, and the unreimbursed cost is CAD 2,100. The bars show why a headline 80% share does not mean 80% of every invoice is paid. Place cash receipts after the invoices that generate them Every invoice is paid at the start of its month. A two-month receipt delay means the first claim, from month one, is reimbursed at the end of month three. Even zero full-month delay means month-end payment in this model, rather than payment at the provider’s counter. The household also contributes CAD 150 of other budget surplus at each month-end. That amount is assumed available after regular household costs and premiums, before the invoices shown here. It must not include a reimbursement that is already entered elsewhere in the schedule. The default starts with CAD 1,500 allocated cash. After the month-three invoice, cash reaches zero before the later month-end resources arrive. After the month-four invoice it reaches negative CAD 130, although that month ends positive at CAD 420. A positive month-end observation can therefore hide an earlier funding need. Use the deepest shortage to measure starting cash needs The lowest default position after an invoice is negative CAD 230 in month six. The starting amount needed for the entire schedule is CAD 1,730, or CAD 230 beyond the selected reserve. A negative chart point represents an unfunded need, not an approved overdraft. The model continues through invoice months plus receipt delay, so all assumed claims have a receipt date within the horizon. With the selected monthly surplus, the default ledger ends month eight at positive CAD 600. That eventual balance does not remove the earlier shortage. The receipt-delay bars keep invoices and eventual reimbursement unchanged. Under the defaults, zero full-month delay requires CAD 1,350 at the start, while four months requires CAD 2,530. Timing can change liquidity needs without changing the eventual benefit amount. Check the timing assumption as well as the coverage percentage The matrix varies the insurer share and receipt delay. Recognized costs, deductible, payment maximum, invoice count, budget surplus and starting cash stay selected. Different percentages can produce the same eventual payment when the maximum binds. All invoices are assigned to one benefit year, with no maximum reset. The model excludes direct billing, a second plan, claim disputes, premiums, tax credits and borrowing costs. Actual reimbursement dates and contract ordering need confirmation before using a schedule for real payments. The four graphics keep ultimate cost and temporary cash needs visible together. A practical review records the invoice amount and due date, the confirmed benefit calculation, the expected receipt date and the source that funds the interval.

documents.title: TFSA withdrawals and recontributions: draw the calendar before replacing the money
documents.description: Four graphics separate account value, current contribution room, unplaced requests and the ordinary room restored when a new calendar year begins.
documents.body: An ordinary withdrawal reduces account value now and restores contribution room next calendar year. A same-year deposit still needs room that is already available. Keep account value separate from contribution room The CRA’s withdrawal guidance states that an ordinary TFSA withdrawal does not immediately create new available contribution room. The amount returns as room on January 1 of the next calendar year. Replacing money earlier requires unused room that is already available. This calendar models a holder eligible and resident in Canada throughout both illustrated years. Starting room is assumed already reconciled across all of the holder’s TFSAs. It is entered separately from combined account value because one amount cannot be inferred from the other. The model includes only the selected ordinary contributions and withdrawal, with no investment returns or other transactions. It excludes transfers, specified distributions, excess histories and non-resident periods. It is an explanation of one transaction sequence, rather than a statement of anyone’s actual room. Follow what changes during the withdrawal year The default starts with CAD 40,000 of combined account value and CAD 7,000 of unused room. The first requested CAD 5,000 contribution fits, raising value to CAD 45,000 and reducing available room to CAD 2,000. The next event is a CAD 10,000 ordinary withdrawal. Account value falls to CAD 35,000, while available room remains CAD 2,000. The value and room bars therefore move differently at exactly the same event. A later request to contribute CAD 10,000 is capped at the remaining CAD 2,000 in this model. That deposit raises value to CAD 37,000 and leaves no current-year room. The other CAD 8,000 of the request is marked unplaced; it never enters an account and is not modeled as an actual excess contribution. Build the next-year room calculation from its components When the new calendar year begins, the model adds unused room from the prior year, the ordinary withdrawal actually made, and a separate new-dollar-room assumption. Under the defaults, those components are zero, CAD 10,000 and CAD 7,000 respectively, producing CAD 17,000 before the next contribution. The requested CAD 15,000 year-two deposit fits. Combined account value then reaches CAD 52,000, and unused room is CAD 2,000. The account-value check is opening value plus the three deposits actually placed, less the withdrawal actually made. The new-year addition is an editable assumption, not an official future-year limit or a forecast. The CRA’s published table lists CAD 7,000 for 2026, but the applicable year, eligibility and transaction history must be checked for an actual calculation. Read requests and accepted transactions separately The contribution bars show the requested amount as a total, split between the deposit placed and the amount left out. This deliberately prevents the illustration from placing money beyond its simplified room calculation. The withdrawal is also capped at the account value available at that event. A request above that amount does not create extra cash or additional restored room. The new-year waterfall uses the withdrawal actually modeled, rather than the original request. The unplaced contribution amount is not a tax penalty, an investment loss or a balance in another account. The calendar assigns it no destination. A household budget needs its own record of where withdrawn or unplaced cash goes and whether a later contribution can be funded. Use the matrix to isolate the same-year constraint The matrix varies starting unused room and the later year-one contribution request. The first selected contribution still uses room before that later request. Each cell shows the amount of the later request that cannot be placed. Changing the ordinary withdrawal cannot change this same-year result. It changes account value and the following year’s restoration instead. That distinction is the reason a withdrawal confirmation alone is insufficient evidence that the same amount can be contributed again immediately. The CRA also explains that room applies collectively across a holder’s TFSAs and recommends reconciling records rather than relying only on a displayed account figure. Verify current room and transactions before making an actual deposit. These graphics make the ordinary timing visible without determining eligibility, calculating tax on excesses or replacing the holder’s full transaction ledger.

documents.title: Using an RESP for education: separate contribution refunds, EAPs and the net budget
documents.description: Four graphics connect two available RESP payment sources with outside funding, an illustrative tax allowance and education costs.
documents.body: The gross RESP withdrawal and the money available for education can differ. Keep contribution refunds, educational assistance payments and the student’s wider tax calculation separate. Identify the payment type before calling it income The CRA distinguishes contribution refunds from educational assistance payments , or EAPs. Contribution refunds are paid tax-free under the applicable plan conditions. EAPs include grants, bonds and earnings, and are included in the beneficiary student’s income. This example assumes a Canadian-resident beneficiary remains eligible in a qualifying full-time program beyond the first thirteen consecutive weeks. The promoter is assumed to have confirmed both the contribution amount and gross EAP amount available for the modeled budget after the applicable checks. The entered EAP capacity is not a calculation from an account’s headline value. It does not independently allocate grants and earnings, verify a beneficiary’s grant history or approve an expense. The source-use chart deliberately shows only the amounts assumed available for this scenario. Confirm capacity before choosing a withdrawal mix For a qualifying program, the ordinary EAP limit is CAD 8,000 during the first thirteen consecutive weeks. Different period limits apply to specified part-time programs. The model does not calculate those periods or approve an exception; its assumed eligible full-time case is beyond the initial period. The CRA’s EAP bulletin also describes an administrative review threshold of CAD 29,459 for 2026. That threshold is a promoter guideline, not an unconditional annual withdrawal entitlement. Reasonableness and other eligibility requirements still matter. The illustration calculates neither grant repayments nor the consequences of a beneficiary becoming ineligible. Those cases require their own review. Confirming payment types and available amounts with the promoter comes before relying on this budget arithmetic. Connect gross EAP, an allowance and contribution cash The default education budget is CAD 24,000, with CAD 4,000 of confirmed outside funding. The remaining net amount to fund is CAD 20,000. The example has CAD 20,000 of available contributions and CAD 15,000 of confirmed gross EAP capacity. The selected gross EAP request is CAD 10,000. With a hypothetical 10% tax budget allowance, CAD 1,000 is set aside and CAD 9,000 remains for the education budget. A contribution withdrawal of CAD 11,000 then fills the remaining net need, leaving no funding gap under these assumptions. Afterward, the model shows CAD 9,000 of contribution capacity and CAD 5,000 of EAP capacity unused. Those are scenario remainders, rather than a guarantee that the same amount will qualify for a later withdrawal. No return or future enrolment schedule is modeled. Keep the budget allowance separate from actual student tax The allowance percentage is a planning assumption applied only to the modeled EAP. It does not calculate withholding, tuition credits, final tax, benefit changes or the effect of other income. A zero allowance would be an assumption in the tool, not a determination that a student owes no tax. The model caps the gross EAP at the request, confirmed capacity and the remaining education budget after outside funding, before that allowance. The last cap is a voluntary cash-budget convention. It is not an additional legal EAP limit or a method for determining a promoter’s approval. Contribution cash fills any remaining need only up to its entered availability. If those two sources and outside funding are insufficient, the waterfall ends negative and the funding-gap metric is positive. Outside funding above the full budget can instead leave unassigned cash. Compare the sources left after funding the same budget The request curves hold the budget and available sources fixed while varying the gross EAP request. They show how the remaining contribution amount and unused EAP capacity change. The curves do not optimize tax across several study years or recommend one mix. The matrix changes education costs and confirmed outside funding. Each cell calculates the extra amount needed after the selected withdrawal assumptions. Its cost levels are hypothetical, rather than tuition statistics or a statement of expenses an RESP promoter will accept. A practical review needs actual eligible costs, proof of enrolment, confirmed payment capacity and a separate tax estimate. The four graphics connect those inputs to a net funding ledger while keeping the RESP’s payment rules and the household’s spending decision distinct.

documents.title: Mortgage prepayment or liquid savings? Compare debt, cash and the same monthly budget
documents.description: Four graphics reconcile a permitted lump-sum prepayment with keeping the same cash in savings, including unused payments after a mortgage is cleared.
documents.body: Interest avoided is only one part of the comparison. Track accessible savings and debt separately, and keep the monthly payment allocation identical in both choices. Confirm the prepayment terms before comparing the arithmetic The FCAC’s prepayment guide explains that a mortgage may permit extra payments or lump sums, with limits set by the contract. Paying more than the permitted amount can create a charge. The related rights page describes prepayment disclosures for federally regulated lenders. This comparison assumes the selected lump sum is permitted without a penalty. It does not calculate a privilege or verify a particular mortgage. A real prepayment charge, access restriction or change in contract terms would need to be added to the decision. Both choices start with the same mortgage and cash. One applies a lump sum immediately; the other retains that cash in savings. The original monthly mortgage payment is preserved in both, rather than automatically lowered after the prepayment. Match the starting resources and the monthly allocation The default mortgage is CAD 300,000, with twenty-five years of remaining amortization and a 4.5% quoted nominal annual rate. The example chooses semi-annual compounding converted to an equivalent monthly rate. It produces a scheduled payment of approximately CAD 1,660.42 a month. A CAD 20,000 prepayment reduces the initial mortgage to CAD 280,000 and leaves none of that selected cash liquid. Keeping the cash leaves the initial debt at CAD 300,000 and the CAD 20,000 available in savings. Home value is identical in both choices and is excluded from the comparison. Rates remain constant throughout the selected five-year horizon. The model does not predict renewal terms or assume every mortgage follows its chosen compounding convention. Use the actual disclosed calculation and payment schedule for a real contract. Read the cash path beside the mortgage path With the same scheduled payment applied to less opening debt, the prepayment path has a smaller mortgage throughout the default period. After five years, debt is approximately CAD 238,405.09 with prepayment and CAD 263,389.16 while keeping the cash. Under the selected 2% effective annual savings return after tax and costs, the retained CAD 20,000 grows to CAD 22,081.62. The prepayment choice has no liquid savings from that sum during the default horizon. The cash chart makes this difference visible instead of counting lower debt as cash on demand. If a modeled mortgage is cleared before the horizon, the unused part of its original monthly payment allocation moves into savings at month-end. The other choice receives the same treatment. This prevents the comparison from silently spending freed payments in one case while saving them in the other. Reconcile interest avoided with the savings-growth difference Net financial position in this limited comparison is liquid savings minus mortgage debt. The common home value cancels. Both options begin with the same net position and receive identical monthly payment allocations, so the difference can be reconciled through financing costs and savings growth. The default prepayment avoids approximately CAD 4,984.07 of mortgage interest over five years. It also gives up CAD 2,081.62 of modeled savings growth. The difference is approximately CAD 2,902.45 in favour of prepayment under these constant assumptions. The waterfall shows that reconciliation. It is an end-of-horizon nominal comparison, not an annual return, a present-value calculation or a valuation of liquidity. Positive arithmetic does not establish that allocating the selected cash to a mortgage fits the household’s other commitments. Test savings returns and cash amounts without losing the funding match The matrix supplies alternative initial cash amounts and after-tax savings returns. Each pair keeps the same mortgage, scheduled payment and horizon. Its signed cells show the prepayment choice’s cash-minus-debt position relative to keeping that cell’s cash liquid. Prepayment cannot exceed the debt in the model. If more cash is entered, the excess remains in savings, and any payment allocation no longer needed for debt also goes there. A zero mortgage or zero selected cash produces no advantage from a prepayment that does not occur. The savings return is a hypothetical constant net rate, with no investment-risk distribution. The model excludes charges, mortgage-interest deductions, actual account rules and future rate changes. Review the cash reserve needed for other purposes alongside the arithmetic, using confirmed contract terms and a budget that leaves each dollar assigned once.

documents.title: Debt avalanche or snowball? Change the repayment order while keeping the budget fixed
documents.description: Four graphics compare starting balances, repayment paths, interest and extra-payment scenarios across three hypothetical debts.
documents.body: A repayment comparison needs the same starting debts and total budget. Keep base payments in place, then show where released payments and extra cash go. Separate the priority rule from the amount you can pay The FCAC’s debt-repayment guide describes prioritizing either higher interest rates or smaller balances, while continuing required minimum payments on every debt. It also notes the importance of past-due accounts and the motivation a repayment approach may provide. This comparison isolates the order of extra payments. Both strategies use identical debts, rates, illustrative base payments and a fixed total monthly budget. It does not compare an aggressive budget for one strategy with a smaller budget for the other. The base-payment fields are modeling inputs, rather than calculations of contractual minimums. Actual obligations can follow different formulas or change over time. Reconcile those requirements before using an illustration to plan a payment. Build one budget and keep released payments working The default debts are CAD 5,000 at a 20% nominal annual rate, CAD 1,000 at 10%, and CAD 8,000 at 8%. Their base payments are CAD 125, CAD 50 and CAD 160 a month. Adding CAD 300 of extra monthly money produces one CAD 635 budget. Each month, the model charges interest at the nominal annual rate divided by twelve. It then pays each active debt’s base amount, capped at the amount owed. The remaining budget goes to the selected priority debt. If that debt is cleared, unused money reaches the next debt in the same month. When an account is repaid, its released base payment stays inside the CAD 635 total rather than disappearing from the plan. The final payment is capped at the total amount owed. The model does not assume any subsequent unused debt budget is invested elsewhere. Read the difference inside the repayment paths The highest-rate-first approach, often called an avalanche, directs remaining cash to debt A in the default example. The smallest-balance-first approach, often called a snowball, initially directs it to debt B. Both still make the other entered base payments. After the first payment cycle, total debt is CAD 13,510 in both cases. The allocation differs: highest-rate-first leaves approximately CAD 4,658.33 on A and CAD 958.33 on B, while smallest-balance-first leaves CAD 4,958.33 on A and CAD 658.33 on B. Debt C has the same balance in both. Later interest charges reflect where those balances remain. Under the defaults, both schedules clear during month twenty-five. The shared payoff month therefore hides a cost difference: interest totals about CAD 1,630.86 for highest-rate-first and CAD 1,712.87 for smallest-balance-first, a difference of approximately CAD 82.01. Distinguish a completed schedule from a partial one The charts stop after all debts are cleared or after 120 months. A “Not repaid” metric means the model did not clear the debt inside that limit. It does not mean repayment is mathematically impossible under every later schedule. Interest for an incomplete path is only the amount charged within those 120 months. It must not be read as a full-life repayment cost. The matrix reports NR instead of a full-cost figure for such a case. A rising balance indicates that the entered payments do not cover modeled interest. Balances are hypothetical and no credit limit, late fee, new purchase, rate change, promotional offer or lender intervention is modeled. The exercise cannot determine the effect of missed payments or predict a credit score. Compare payment capacity alongside the ordering choice The matrix changes debt A’s rate and the extra monthly amount while retaining the other selected inputs. Every cell uses the highest-rate-first rule and the same base-payment convention. It shows how the cost changes when the funding available to that rule changes. The smallest-balance rule is based on current balances after the month’s base payments. Rate and debt letter resolve ties. The highest-rate rule resolves ties by balance and then letter. These conventions keep an otherwise ambiguous comparison reproducible. A practical plan also needs a payment amount the household can maintain, funds for essential expenses and a review of actual account terms. Use the graphics to understand the cost of an ordering choice while keeping the budget, minimum obligations and ability to follow the schedule explicit.

documents.title: Several goals, one saving budget: deadlines can matter as much as the total
documents.description: Four graphics compare shared saving capacity, goal deadlines, two allocation rules and the effect of more time or a larger budget.
documents.body: A dollar earmarked for one goal cannot also fund another. Compare each deadline with cumulative saving capacity, and make the allocation rule visible. Write each remaining amount beside its own deadline The FCAC’s goal-setting guidance starts with priorities, amounts and timeframes. This illustration puts three remaining funding amounts on one calendar so their claims on the same monthly budget can be seen together. Enter only the money still to be raised for each goal. Existing earmarked savings have already been accounted for before these inputs. Amounts are fixed nominal CAD targets for their payment dates; the model applies no additional inflation or investment return. The default goals require CAD 6,000 by month twelve, CAD 12,000 by month twenty-four and CAD 18,000 by month thirty-six. Their labels remain A, C and B respectively because each input keeps its own identity when dates change. The shared month-end saving budget is CAD 900. Check cumulative obligations at every deadline At month twelve, cumulative funding due is CAD 6,000. At month twenty-four it is CAD 18,000, including the earlier goal. At month thirty-six it reaches CAD 36,000. The obligation chart steps up at those dates and compares the totals with the shared budget accumulated over time. A CAD 900 monthly budget supplies CAD 32,400 over thirty-six months. It cannot fully fund CAD 36,000 under this zero-return model. A positive final saving total is therefore not evidence that all goals fit the plan. The minimum constant budget for the deadline-first rule is the largest cumulative amount due divided by its deadline month. The default checks are CAD 500, CAD 750 and CAD 1,000 per month. The binding figure is CAD 1,000, assuming saving can begin now and funds can be earmarked early without restrictions. Compare two explicit allocation rules Deadline-first funding fills the earliest unfinished goal, then sends remaining cash to the next one. Under the default CAD 900 budget, A and C reach their full targets by their own deadlines. B receives CAD 14,400 by month thirty-six, leaving CAD 3,600 unfunded. The equal-share rule divides each month’s contribution among all active unfinished goals. If a share would exceed a goal’s remaining need, the excess is redistributed within the same month. A goal stops receiving money after its deadline, even when it was not fully funded. In the default equal-share case, A has CAD 3,600 at month twelve and C has CAD 9,000 at month twenty-four. B eventually reaches CAD 18,000. The shortfalls at A and C’s deadlines total CAD 5,400. Equal monthly amounts are not the same as equal progress toward different deadlines. Later unused cash cannot repair an earlier missed date The equal-share example leaves CAD 1,800 of the thirty-six-month contribution capacity unallocated after the remaining active goal has been funded. That later money is recorded separately. The model does not move it backward in time to make the missed deadlines appear successful. The cumulative-funding chart shows the amount earmarked in time under each rule. It is not a cash-account balance after purchases, and the model does not simulate the purchases themselves. Recorded goal funding remains committed once and is not reused for another goal. Deadline ties are resolved by goal letter in the deadline-first case. Both rules cap funding at a goal’s remaining target. A zero target needs no contributions, and a zero budget leaves every positive target unfunded. These conventions make the comparison reproducible. Test amounts, timing and priorities together The matrix supplies alternative monthly budgets and scales all selected deadlines, rounding to whole months with a one-month minimum. Goal amounts remain unchanged. Each cell totals shortfalls at the individual deadlines under the deadline-first rule. The minimum-budget metric is an arithmetic feasibility threshold for this model. It assumes no restricted accounts, no return, no opening funding and divisible month-end contributions. It does not establish affordability in the household budget or decide which goal should have priority. A real review may change an amount, postpone a flexible date or give a personally important goal precedence over another. The charts expose the consequence of a chosen rule; they do not rank the value of the goals. Record that judgment separately from the calculation so timing and personal priorities remain understandable.

documents.title: A RRIF minimum is a withdrawal rule, not a household spending target
documents.description: Four graphics separate an ordinary RRIF’s age-based minimum, a gross withdrawal request, a tax budget allowance and the spending assigned to that cash.
documents.body: Calculate the required gross withdrawal separately from the spending budget. Money leaving a RRIF is not automatically money spent, and a tax allowance is not a tax assessment. Establish which minimum calculation applies The CRA’s minimum-amount guidance calculates the ordinary minimum from the RRIF’s fair market value at the start of the year and an applicable prescribed factor. The annual minimum begins in the year after the RRIF is established. This tool assumes the account already exists before the illustrated year, uses the annuitant’s whole age at the beginning of that year, and applies the “All other RRIFs” factor column . It does not calculate an establishment-year minimum, a spouse-age election, legacy qualifying or pre-1986 treatment, or the special calculation for locked-in annuity contracts held inside a RRIF. Confirm the applicable account category, age basis and opening value with the carrier before using an actual withdrawal figure. The source table and Income Tax Regulations section 7308 were reviewed for this article on 25 October 2026. Apply the factor to opening assets For the stated ordinary case, the factor below age seventy-one is one divided by ninety minus the beginning-of-year age. The table supplies the later factors, including 5.28% at age seventy-one, 5.40% at seventy-two and 20% at ninety-five or older. The default opening value is CAD 500,000 and the year-start age is seventy-two. Multiplying by 5.40% produces a CAD 27,000 minimum for the illustrated year. The factor is a withdrawal rule; it does not describe an investment return or a personally sustainable spending rate. The factor graphic presents the rule table across ages, rather than projecting an account over those ages. The opening value is not assumed to remain CAD 500,000 for the rest of a person’s life. This is a single-year illustration with no future balance path. Compare the request with the modeled gross withdrawal The entered gross withdrawal request is CAD 30,000. Because it exceeds the CAD 27,000 minimum, the modeled gross withdrawal is CAD 30,000. A request below the minimum is lifted to that minimum in this ordinary example. The tool also caps the modeled withdrawal at the entered asset balance. That cap reflects its simplified assumption of no in-year change in asset value. It is not a calculation of account liquidity, a sale order or confirmation of how much an actual portfolio can produce on a particular date. The bars display all three amounts so the request is not silently confused with the modeled withdrawal. If opening assets are zero, both the minimum and available gross withdrawal are zero. The separate spending input can still show an unfunded requirement. Bridge gross cash to a separate spending assignment The default budget allowance is 25% of the modeled gross withdrawal, or CAD 7,500. Subtracting it from CAD 30,000 leaves CAD 22,500 for comparison with CAD 18,000 of assigned net spending. The ledger therefore shows CAD 4,500 of cash remaining unassigned. The 25% allowance is a hypothetical budgeting choice. It is not a prescribed withholding rate, an estimate of final income tax, a tax-credit calculation or a prediction of a refund. An actual tax calculation needs the wider household facts and applicable rules. The spending entry is the part of the household budget assigned to this RRIF cash, rather than necessarily the entire household’s expenses. A positive remainder is not automatically consumed or invested elsewhere. A negative remainder means the assigned spending needs another source under the selected allowance. Keep withdrawals, assets and spending distinct in the wider plan The matrix varies year-start ages and assigned spending while retaining opening assets, the requested gross amount and the assumed allowance percentage. Each cell is cash left or extra funding needed for one year. Gold negative cells and teal positive cells are signed cash positions. Where the minimum exceeds the gross request, the model increases the withdrawal. That may create cash beyond the assigned spending amount. A transfer out of a registered account and a household purchase are different events; the remainder needs its own destination rather than being counted twice. The tool does not calculate benefit interactions, pension splitting, restrictions on locked-in plans, actual withholding, final tax or lifetime sustainability. Review those separately using current rules and account information. The four graphics clarify the relationship between one year’s minimum and its budget without turning the minimum factor into a retirement withdrawal recommendation.

documents.title: Disability-income planning: fund the waiting period and the months after payments end
documents.description: Four graphics map temporary pay, a delayed net insurance benefit, payment duration and the cash reserve needed across an income interruption.
documents.body: A monthly benefit amount tells only part of the story. Put the first receipt, overlapping income and the final modeled payment on a calendar before assessing the cash reserve. Read the contract, then build the cash calendar The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s disability-insurance guide highlights waiting times, benefit amounts, tax treatment, definitions of disability and coordination with other benefits. Those details affect both eligibility and the cash a household can use. A policy’s headline payment should not automatically be treated as additional net income. This illustration assumes a selected benefit is approved and available after all taxes and offsets. It does not assess a claim or determine an entitlement. Continuing household income, temporary salary or sick pay, and the entered net insurance benefit are separate receipts in a monthly ledger. The waiting input counts full months with no insurance receipt. A three-month wait means the first modeled payment arrives at the end of month four. The payment-count input then specifies how many monthly receipts occur within the selected horizon. These are hypothetical timing assumptions, rather than a policy quotation or a prediction of recovery. The income gap can change more than once The default household spends CAD 4,500 each month and retains CAD 1,500 of continuing net income. Temporary salary or sick pay adds CAD 2,500 in each of the first two months. The remaining monthly gap is CAD 500 while that temporary payment is present. In month three, the temporary receipt has ended but insurance has not yet begun. The gap rises to CAD 3,000. In months four through nine, the entered CAD 2,200 insurance payment brings total net receipts to CAD 3,700, leaving CAD 800 a month to fund from cash. The six modeled insurance payments then finish. Months ten through twelve again have a CAD 3,000 monthly gap. The first graphic makes these phases visible. It does not assume that a policy necessarily stops after six payments; that count is an editable stress scenario for the example. Fund the deepest cash need, including the starting cost The example also includes CAD 1,000 of one-time costs before the first month. From CAD 10,000 allocated cash, the starting position after that payment is CAD 9,000. The reserve then pays each monthly difference between receipts and spending. Across the twelve-month schedule, the monthly gaps total CAD 17,800. Adding the initial CAD 1,000 gives a required starting amount of CAD 18,800. After the CAD 10,000 reserve already entered, another CAD 8,800 is needed under these assumptions. The path first goes negative in month ten. A negative point is an unfunded requirement, not a bank balance the household is allowed to maintain. The second cash curve removes insurance receipts while keeping everything else the same, providing a no-receipt stress comparison without assigning it a probability. Check overlaps and avoid counting the same support twice The income-source bars sum only receipts inside the selected horizon. The default totals are CAD 18,000 of continuing income, CAD 5,000 of temporary pay and CAD 13,200 of entered insurance benefits. Amounts scheduled after the horizon do not appear in those totals. The calculator adds inputs as entered. If temporary pay overlaps the insurance phase, the model does not reduce either amount automatically. Actual coordination needs to be resolved before using the figures: a payment already included in continuing income must not also be entered as a separate benefit. Use amounts available for household bills after the relevant deductions and offsets. A gross insurance amount or an expected reimbursement can differ from spendable cash on the date a bill arrives. This model calculates neither tax nor the contractual treatment of another source of support. Review waiting time, payment duration and the wider interruption The matrix varies full waiting months and the number of insurance payments. Each cell is additional starting cash after the selected reserve, calculated across the same household schedule. Temporary pay, ongoing income, spending and the initial cost remain unchanged. A longer wait and a shorter payment period affect different parts of the calendar. If payments begin after the illustrated horizon, none is counted. If income exceeds spending in a month, the surplus remains in the modeled cash reserve; the starting-cost requirement still exists before those receipts arrive. The schedule excludes inflation, interest, claim administration, premiums and changes in spending or work capacity. Replace the assumptions with supported dates and net amounts when reviewing an actual arrangement. The useful output is a dated cash requirement alongside the coverage terms, rather than a conclusion that a headline replacement percentage makes every month affordable.

documents.title: Saving for a foreign-currency bill: translate the goal before setting the CAD contribution
documents.description: Four graphics separate foreign-price changes, CAD exchange-rate assumptions, conversion charges and the monthly saving needed for one future payment.
documents.body: A foreign-currency goal has a price and a currency exposure. Keep both units explicit, then translate the future bill and its conversion costs into the currency being saved. Write the currency unit on both sides of the plan A tuition payment, family expense or planned purchase abroad may be priced in one currency while savings accumulate in Canadian dollars. The goal is the number of foreign units owed on the payment date, rather than a CAD amount that can remain unchanged regardless of exchange rates. This example uses the generic label foreign currency unit, or FCU . Define that unit consistently for the bill and the exchange-rate input. The rate is CAD paid per one FCU, so a higher number makes the same foreign bill more expensive in Canadian dollars. The Bank of Canada’s daily-rate page uses foreign units converted into CAD and explains that its published rates are indicative averages. They are not executable provider quotes. The default rate here is an independent hypothetical assumption; the calculator does not fetch or predict an exchange rate. Project the bill in its own currency first The default bill is 20,000 FCU at today’s price, payable in thirty-six months. At an assumed 3% annual price increase in that currency, the amount becomes 21,854.54 FCU after three years. That change is a foreign-price assumption, separate from the currency translation. Multiplying by the selected 1.40 CAD per FCU produces a CAD 30,596.36 reference cost, before rounding the intermediate calculation. The example then adds a 2% conversion charge, approximately CAD 611.93, and one CAD 25 fee. The full unrounded calculation gives a terminal funding target of CAD 31,233.28. The waterfall expresses every step in CAD, including the effect of the foreign-price increase. It does not add foreign units directly to Canadian dollars. The conversion percentage is an explicit markup on the reference CAD amount; actual providers may express their charges or offered rate differently. Match the saving schedule to the translated deadline amount The example starts with CAD 5,000 and adds CAD 500 at each month-end. A constant 2% effective annual CAD return is converted to its equivalent monthly rate. After thirty-six deposits, the modeled savings are CAD 23,836.16, leaving approximately CAD 7,397.12 below the translated bill. The required-contribution metric solves for the constant month-end CAD deposit that would reach the selected target from the selected starting amount. In the default case it is approximately CAD 699.60 a month. This result is an arithmetic funding amount, not evidence that the household budget can support it. The target line is flat because it shows the bill already projected to the deadline, translated at the selected terminal rate. It is not a claim that the bill costs that amount at every earlier date. All savings remain in CAD until one conversion at the end. Change the rate without changing the foreign bill The rate bars hold the foreign bill, payment date and charges constant while varying only CAD per FCU. If each foreign unit requires more CAD, the reference cost and percentage conversion charge both rise. A fixed fee remains the same. These alternatives are scenarios with no probabilities attached. They do not describe historical volatility or establish a likely future range. Reversing a quote also reverses the arithmetic: FCU per CAD would require division, whereas the convention used throughout this tool requires multiplication. If the real plan includes staged payments or savings already held in the foreign currency, one terminal conversion is an incomplete representation. Such a plan needs separate dated amounts and currency balances. This example isolates a single CAD-funded payment so the units remain easy to follow. Compare the deadline and the contribution together The matrix changes the terminal rate and the number of months available. Each cell reprojects the foreign price for that duration, translates it and solves for the necessary month-end CAD saving. Starting CAD assets, the selected savings return and charges remain fixed. More time gives contributions longer to accumulate, but it also allows the assumed foreign price to rise for longer. The result reflects both effects. If existing savings already fund the modeled bill, the required contribution is floored at zero. A zero foreign bill creates no conversion order and no flat fee in this illustration. A planning review can adjust the purchase amount, contribution, timing or currency arrangement. The graphs do not choose among those options or calculate a hedge. Their purpose is to show the foreign obligation, the CAD funding path and the exchange-rate assumption as three explicit parts of the same goal.

documents.title: Annuity income and liquid capital: read the cash flows before interpreting the payout
documents.description: Four graphics explain an illustrative premium allocation, conditional lifetime receipts, inflation and why a payout percentage is not an investment return.
documents.body: An income contract can replace part of a liquid portfolio with scheduled payments. Compare the payment, liquidity, inflation exposure and contract terms without treating cumulative receipts as an annual yield. Distinguish income from an accessible account balance The FCAC’s annuity guide distinguishes life income from fixed-term payments and describes options for survivors or beneficiaries. It also explains that payments can combine interest, returned capital and risk pooling. A payout amount therefore cannot be read as investment interest alone. This illustration assumes an immediate level-payment life-only contract. Every displayed receipt is conditional on the annuitant remaining alive. No guarantee period, survivor continuation, death benefit, tax calculation or contract surrender value is included. The entered payment per CAD 100,000 of premium is hypothetical, not an available insurer quote. The model scales it linearly with the selected premium allocation. Actual products, pricing and terms require separate verification. The graph does not estimate an expected lifetime payout or assign a probability to the selected payment horizon. See what remains liquid after the allocation The default illustration begins with CAD 500,000 of liquid capital and allocates 40%, or CAD 200,000, to the income contract. The waterfall leaves CAD 300,000 of liquid capital at the purchase date. The premium has been exchanged for contractual income. It is not labelled an immediate investment loss or a fee. Equally, it is not still available as cash for a separate purchase. The tool does not value the contract, so the waterfall endpoint is liquid capital rather than total wealth. The remaining liquid amount has no modeled return or withdrawal schedule here. A complete retirement budget would assign that money to reserves, future spending or other purposes, and compare those uses with the income supplied by the contract. A payout percentage does not isolate investment return The default hypothetical payment is CAD 550 a month for each CAD 100,000 of premium. On CAD 200,000, that produces CAD 1,100 a month, or CAD 13,200 over twelve payments. Annual cash paid divided by premium is 6.6%. That 6.6% is a cash-payout ratio. It does not separate interest from returned capital or pooling, and it assumes neither a redeemable principal balance nor a residual estate value. It is not directly comparable with a savings-account interest rate or a portfolio’s total return. The cumulative-receipts chart compares the original premium with payments actually assumed to occur. At CAD 1,100 per month, 181 receipts total CAD 199,100 and 182 total CAD 200,200. The nominal cash-receipt crossover is therefore 182 months, or fifteen years and two months, conditional on receiving every payment. Keep the receipt crossover separate from inflation and opportunity cost After thirty years of the selected payments, cumulative gross receipts total CAD 396,000. Comparing that sum with the CAD 200,000 premium does not account for when each receipt arrived, tax, inflation or returns that an alternative arrangement might have produced. The purchasing-power chart isolates one of those issues. The nominal monthly amount remains CAD 1,100. With 2% annual inflation, its purchasing power after thirty years is approximately CAD 607.28 in purchase-date dollars. The year-zero point is a comparison of payment amounts, not a payment received at purchase. An indexed payment would require its own terms and quote. This tool does not assume that an increasing payment can be purchased for the same premium and initial amount. The constant-payment illustration simply makes the price exposure visible. Compare contracts and household needs on the same basis The matrix shows cumulative gross payments as a percentage of a fixed CAD 100,000 premium at several hypothetical monthly amounts and durations. A cell above 100% means nominal cash received exceeds that premium, conditional on all the displayed payments occurring. It is not a gain after opportunity cost, an annual rate, an insurer offer or a survival probability. The fixed grid remains independent of the selected allocation. Choosing zero allocation leaves the selected payment at zero and reports no premium-receipt crossover. The FCAC guide also notes that contract options, tax treatment and the ability to change or cancel vary. Review those terms alongside other household income, the need for accessible cash and the treatment of a survivor or estate. The four graphics support that cash-flow discussion without deciding whether an annuity is suitable or ranking it against an investment portfolio.
