documents.title: Build a retirement-income bridge: map the years before later income begins
documents.description: Four graphics connect income start dates, temporary work, annual withdrawal requests and the capital needed over a defined retirement transition.
documents.body: A retirement plan needs a calendar as well as a total. Temporary earnings may end before another income source starts, leaving a larger withdrawal request in the intervening years. Draw the income calendar before choosing a withdrawal amount Retirement rarely replaces one paycheque with a single identical payment. An ongoing pension, temporary work, a later pension and personal savings can each follow a different schedule. The Government of Canada’s retirement-income overview describes public pensions, workplace plans and personal savings as separate sources. Actual benefits depend on their own rules and the individual’s history. This illustration starts with net amounts available to the household. It does not estimate pension entitlements or calculate tax. Enter a spending target, income already available, temporary work and an additional income source with its own starting year. All amounts use year-one purchasing power and then rise at the selected common annual rate. The first chart compares the resulting annual spending and income paths. It makes changes in the funding mix visible before a portfolio withdrawal rule is applied. The additional-income amount stays the same in year-one dollars when its start date changes; no delayed-pension enhancement is assumed. Notice the years between temporary work and later income The default target is CAD 60,000 a year, with CAD 18,000 of ongoing income and CAD 12,000 of temporary work for three years. Year one therefore asks savings to supply CAD 30,000. With the selected 2% annual cash-flow increase, the next two requests are CAD 30,600 and CAD 31,212. Temporary work then ends, while the additional income does not start until year six. The year-four withdrawal request rises to CAD 44,570.74 and year five to CAD 45,462.15. Those amounts reflect both the income interruption and the common annual increase. A flat average across the full horizon would hide the timing of the larger requests. In year six, the additional CAD 24,000 of annual income, stated in year-one dollars, becomes available. The nominal gap falls to CAD 19,873.45. It does not disappear because the combined ongoing sources still cover only CAD 42,000 of the CAD 60,000 base spending target. Separate the bridge subtotal from the full illustration The first metric adds withdrawal requests in the years before the additional source begins. In the default case, that is approximately CAD 181,844.89 over the first five years. It is an undiscounted nominal subtotal, rather than the capital needed on the starting date. The capital metric instead discounts every requested withdrawal across the selected twelve-year horizon. The formula is starting capital = sum of each year’s requested withdrawal divided by (1 + return) raised to that year . At the default constant 4% annual return, the result is approximately CAD 264,151.23. This amount funds only the displayed withdrawals under the selected timing. It requires no terminal reserve and includes no expenses after year twelve. Calling it a complete retirement target would overlook the rest of the person’s life, as well as uncertain returns, taxes and changing needs. Keep unfunded spending separate from portfolio assets The portfolio chart starts with CAD 200,000 in the default example. Each year, the balance earns the assumed return before the requested year-end withdrawal. The actual withdrawal cannot exceed available assets. Any difference is added to a separate cumulative unfunded-spending series. After depletion, the portfolio remains at zero; this model adds no new deposits. The unfunded curve is neither an investment account nor an available credit line. It records spending the assumed portfolio could not supply, without assuming that spending was financed elsewhere. If income exceeds spending, the withdrawal request is zero. That surplus is left unallocated rather than automatically saved. A real plan can assign it a destination, but doing so would introduce an additional decision about contributions, access and future use. Test the bridge without turning it into a pension recommendation The matrix changes the spending target and the later-income start year, keeping the selected return, horizon, temporary-work schedule and income amount. Its cells use the full-horizon present-value calculation. Changing a date can alter capital needs even when the annual income amount is unchanged. Actual CPP, OAS or workplace-pension timing may also change benefit amounts, tax, eligibility and household outcomes. Those effects are outside this generic calendar. Use current personal estimates and the relevant program rules before comparing an actual start-age choice. Review the bridge alongside the sequence-risk and longevity guides. This article explains the schedule of a transition; those additional questions concern uncertain return order and how long a wider plan must last. A useful review records both the dates that create the largest requests and the assumptions that could make those requests harder to fund.

documents.title: The cash cost of caregiving: combine support bills, lost earnings and available help
documents.description: A dated Canadian survey graphic and three interactive scenarios show how paid help, reduced earnings, setup costs and existing budget capacity affect cash needs.
documents.body: An unpaid care role can affect a budget through both extra bills and reduced earnings. Build one incremental cash ledger, then compare its timing with the money actually available. Use survey context without treating it as a personal forecast Statistics Canada’s 2022 survey , published in April 2024, reports mutually exclusive shares of 58.1% with no unpaid care, 14.4% providing adult care only, 21.9% child care only and 5.6% both. The target population was non-institutionalized people aged 15 or older living off-reserve in the ten provinces; the reference was care in the previous twelve months. The first graphic displays those rounded survey estimates. It remains fixed when scenario inputs change. The source provides confidence intervals; the chart does not estimate an individual’s future care needs or the price of paid help. The other three graphics are hypothetical cash calculations for a selected arrangement. Their hours, hourly cost, earnings reduction and support amounts are editable assumptions. They are not estimates derived from the survey. Add both sides of the household cash impact Start with the budget before the new arrangement. The model takes the monthly surplus already left after that budget, then calculates what the care arrangement changes. Paid support and additional transport or supplies add outflows. A reduction in net earnings removes receipts even though it is not a bill from a provider. The default eight hours of paid support each week at CAD 35 per hour becomes CAD 1,213.33 per average month, using 52 weeks divided by twelve. Add CAD 150 of transport and supplies and CAD 800 of lower monthly net earnings. The combined incremental burden is CAD 2,163.33. Confirmed net support of CAD 300 and the existing CAD 500 monthly budget surplus reduce the amount drawn from cash to CAD 1,363.33 per month. The waterfall makes these offsets visible so a source of help is not accidentally deducted twice or counted before it is available. Place one-time expenses at the start The default arrangement also requires CAD 2,000 at setup. That amount is paid before the recurring monthly flows begin. The reserve path therefore starts at CAD 10,000 after setup from the selected CAD 12,000 starting reserve. At the selected monthly draw, the illustrative cash position is still positive after month seven and negative after month eight. The negative section represents unfunded cash needs. It does not assume a bank permits an overdraft, a family member lends money, or a provider allows payment to be postponed. Across twenty-four months, setup plus recurring net draws requires CAD 34,720 of starting cash under the model. After counting the CAD 12,000 already allocated, the additional amount is CAD 22,720. These figures use the unrounded monthly arithmetic; displayed values may be rounded to cents. Use support amounts that can actually fund the schedule The support input is a net receipt that is assumed available every month. It does not calculate a tax credit, employer benefit, public program payment or reimbursement. A benefit paid later cannot fund an earlier invoice unless another source covers the interval. Keep the earnings reduction consistent with the starting budget. If the base budget already uses the lower earnings, adding the same reduction again would overstate the burden. Similarly, enter only additional travel and supplies, rather than costs already included in regular household spending. A negative monthly draw means entered resources exceed the incremental recurring burden. Even then, setup still needs funding at time zero. The required-starting-cash measure therefore cannot fall below the setup amount merely because later monthly receipts replenish cash. Vary the arrangement and revisit the wider plan The matrix compares paid support hours and durations while holding other selected inputs fixed. Each cell reports the additional starting cash after the chosen reserve. It is a funding comparison, rather than a determination of how many care hours are suitable. Different arrangements may also change the caregiver’s earnings, travel or support eligibility. The fixed-grid comparison isolates hours and duration, so those related effects must be considered separately. A new quote or confirmed work schedule provides a reason to update the inputs. The model does not put a monetary value on all unpaid work, calculate lost pension contributions, assess health needs or evaluate care quality. Those questions require their own information. The ledger’s purpose is narrower and practical: identify which receipts change, which bills arrive, when setup must be paid and whether available cash covers the selected schedule.

documents.title: Estate liquidity: a positive eventual balance can still hide an immediate cash gap
documents.description: Four graphics reconcile accessible cash, later asset-sale receipts, immediate obligations and dated payments without confusing a cash forecast with an estate distribution.
documents.body: List amounts and access dates separately. Assets expected to become cash later may leave immediate costs unfunded, even when the ledger ends with a positive balance. Distinguish an asset from money available to pay an invoice An estate can have valuable property while lacking cash for a bill due now. Access, sale timing, secured debt and administrative requirements affect when an amount becomes usable. British Columbia’s estate guide describes duties including listing assets and debts, paying valid obligations, filing returns and preparing accounts. Its guidance is specific to B.C.; other jurisdictions have their own requirements. This illustration tracks estate cash only. Starting cash is assumed accessible to the authorized representative, and a later asset sale supplies a separate receipt. No personal money from an executor or beneficiary is automatically included. The sale input means cash after selling costs and secured loans, before the separate tax and debt payment entered in the controls. It is not the gross property value. Entering a liability in both the net-sale figure and the separate payment would count the same obligation twice. Put immediate and recurring obligations on a calendar The example starts with CAD 25,000 of accessible cash and CAD 20,000 of immediate obligations, leaving CAD 5,000 at time zero. It then pays CAD 1,500 of carrying and administration costs each month for twenty-four months. A separate CAD 60,000 payment is scheduled at the end of month six. This input is a placeholder for a separately estimated tax or debt obligation. The model does not calculate an actual liability, determine claim priority or assign a statutory deadline. The later net sale receipt is CAD 250,000 in month nine. Under the model’s explicit convention, receipts arrive at the beginning of their selected month and bills settle at month-end. Actual settlement dates within a month can matter, so a monthly ledger should not replace a dated payment list when the margin is tight. Read the deepest shortage as well as the endpoint The selected cash path falls below zero before the sale. At the end of month six, after the separate payment, the position is negative CAD 64,000. Continuing carrying costs take it to negative CAD 67,000 after month eight, just before the modeled month-nine receipt. The maximum-additional-cash metric is therefore CAD 67,000. It is the amount which, if available at the start without interest or repayment, would keep this selected ledger from falling below zero. The tool does not establish that borrowing, an advance or any other funding source is available. The comparison curve moves the same receipt up to three months earlier while keeping every amount unchanged. A different receipt date can reduce the peak funding need even though the final balance remains identical. The curves connect month-end observations; they do not show every intra-month movement. Reconcile the totals without calling the remainder distributable The totals waterfall adds CAD 25,000 of starting cash and CAD 250,000 of later proceeds, then subtracts CAD 20,000 of immediate obligations, CAD 36,000 of recurring costs and the separate CAD 60,000 payment. It ends at CAD 159,000. That positive endpoint coexists with the earlier CAD 67,000 funding gap. Neither figure measures the full estate’s legal solvency or the amount beneficiaries may receive. Assets and obligations outside this ledger, later assessments, unresolved claims and professional costs could change the result. The CRA’s clearance-certificate guidance explains the representative’s tax exposure when assets are distributed without clearance and tax remains owing. A positive cash forecast does not replace clearance, legal advice or the other requirements applicable to a distribution. Stress the dates and document the assumptions The matrix changes the sale-receipt month and the separate payment month. Each cell finds the deepest cash shortage over the full twenty-four-month ledger after counting starting cash. Immediate obligations and monthly costs remain fixed. Same-month receipts precede bills by convention. Use the grid to identify a dependency that needs verification: a planned receipt may need confirmed authority, a completed sale and accessible settlement funds. The selected dates are neither predicted processing times nor permission to postpone an obligation. The ledger includes no interest on borrowing and no investment return on temporary cash. It assumes the monthly costs continue for the whole horizon and includes no beneficiary distribution. A practical review replaces placeholders with supported amounts and dates, records what remains uncertain, and checks who has authority to act before treating an apparent funding solution as available.

documents.title: Marginal versus average tax: see the income slices before applying a rate
documents.description: Use 2026 Canadian federal brackets in four graphics that explain income slices, the rate on the next dollar and the effect of an illustrative deduction.
documents.body: A bracket rate applies to an income slice. Compare the tax on an additional amount with the average across the full amount, and keep this limited calculation separate from total tax or take-home pay. Start with a clearly limited tax calculation The Canada Revenue Agency’s 2026 federal table applies 14% to the first CAD 58,523, then 20.5%, 26%, 29% and 33% to successive bands ending at CAD 117,045, CAD 181,440, CAD 258,482 and above. Each rate applies to its own portion of taxable income. This tool calculates that federal bracket arithmetic before credits. It does not apply the basic personal amount, other federal credits, provincial or territorial tax, Quebec abatement, CPP or EI, income-tested benefits or alternative minimum tax. Its result is not a tax-return estimate or take-home pay. The starting input is taxable income before the one illustrative deduction entered in the controls. It is not necessarily gross salary. The model does not decide how salary, dividends, capital gains or other receipts enter taxable income, nor whether a particular deduction is available to a person. Follow the amount charged within each band The first graphic calculates the income falling between each lower and upper threshold, multiplies that portion by its rate, and displays the resulting tax. Bands above the selected income have zero amounts. The total is the sum of the slice taxes. The default CAD 80,000 starting amount less an illustrative CAD 5,000 deduction leaves CAD 75,000 for the comparison. The first CAD 58,523 produces CAD 8,193.22 of bracket tax, and the remaining CAD 16,477 produces CAD 3,377.79 when rounded for display. The total is approximately CAD 11,571.01 before credits. Applying 20.5% to all CAD 75,000 would discard the lower rate on the first band. Moving into the second band changes the rate on that next portion; it does not replace the rate previously applied to every earlier dollar. Compare the next-dollar rate with the average The stepped curve shows the bracket rate applying to the next dollar of taxable income. The average curve divides the calculated bracket tax by taxable income. At the default CAD 75,000, those figures are 20.5% and about 15.43% respectively, before credits. At zero taxable income, the average ratio has a zero denominator and is not defined. The calculator reports that explicitly, and the average curve begins at CAD 1. Because credits are excluded, the curve below the first threshold is not a representation of the effective tax actually paid by a low-income household. The rates shown are also not a person’s combined effective marginal rate. Provincial taxes, credits and changes in benefits can alter the effect of additional income. Use these curves to understand the bracket mechanism, then use a complete, current calculation for the actual household question. Read what changes when income rises The stacked bars compare the selected amount with the amount after adding the extra taxable income. The same illustrative deduction applies in both cases. One component is bracket tax before credits; the other is taxable income less only that tax. In the default case, adding CAD 10,000 keeps that additional amount within the 20.5% band. It adds CAD 2,050 of federal bracket tax and CAD 7,950 to the arithmetic remainder. The remainder omits the other taxes, deductions and benefit effects listed above, so it should not be labelled a paycheque. The graph illustrates why a higher bracket rate does not automatically absorb all of a raise. It does not establish the after-tax value of a specific employment offer or the tax consequences of a transaction. A deduction may span several bands The matrix compares illustrative deductions at several taxable-income amounts. Each cell is the difference between bracket tax before and after the deduction. If the deduction crosses a threshold, its portions affect tax at different rates; multiplying the full deduction by one headline rate may then be inaccurate. The selected input deduction is applied once and taxable income is floored at zero. The fixed grid supplies its own alternative income and deduction amounts. It does not determine deductibility, carryforward treatment, refunds or the effect of credits. The rules in this article are fixed to 2026 and were reviewed on 25 October 2026. Recheck the applicable year and the full federal and provincial rules before using a tax assumption in a contribution, withdrawal or employment decision. A clear distinction between bracket arithmetic and a complete tax calculation keeps the planning comparison understandable.

documents.title: FHSA contribution timing: draw the room, the deposits and the balance
documents.description: Explore a simplified new-account calendar with four graphics that separate annual participation room, capped contributions and investment growth.
documents.body: Contribution room and account value measure different things. Track the opening year, usable room and actual deposits before projecting a home-saving balance. Know the case the calendar is modeling The CRA’s FHSA participation guidance gives CAD 8,000 of room in the year the first account opens. In the ordinary case illustrated here, subsequent room reflects the annual base, participation-room carryforward capped at CAD 8,000, and remaining ordinary lifetime capacity of CAD 40,000. The model assumes the first FHSA opens in year one and the person remains eligible throughout the selected horizon. There are no prior accounts, RRSP transfers, withdrawals, excess amounts, designated amounts or re-participation adjustments. Those omissions matter because the full CRA calculation covers more situations. The waiting input means an already open account receives no requested contributions for the initial years. It does not mean that the opening date is postponed. Room does not accumulate before the first account is opened, and opening also starts the maximum participation period , which this calculator does not determine. Follow annual room before each deposit The room chart compares available participation room with the contribution actually modeled each year. A requested deposit is limited to available room, and remaining ordinary lifetime capacity is checked separately. Requests that do not fit are recorded as unplaced cash rather than deposited as excess contributions. The default account waits two years before requesting CAD 10,000 annually. It has CAD 8,000 of room in year one and CAD 16,000 in year two. Another unused year does not make the ordinary carryforward unlimited. The modeled year-three room remains CAD 16,000. The first CAD 10,000 deposit leaves carryforward that supports room of CAD 14,000 in year four. The next selected deposits gradually use that carryforward. By the end of year six, cumulative deposits reach CAD 40,000, after which the ordinary lifetime constraint stops further modeled deposits. Keep unplaced cash distinct from the FHSA balance Across the default eight-year horizon, six annual requests of CAD 10,000 total CAD 60,000. The simplified calendar places CAD 40,000 in the account and records CAD 20,000 of requests that did not fit. The tool does not invest that unplaced amount elsewhere or include it in the account-value curve. This cap is a convention of the illustration. It does not check contributions or transfers made in actual accounts. Participation room applies across the holder’s FHSAs; opening another account does not supply a separate copy of the same room. Reconcile actual transactions and the applicable CRA calculations before depositing. The model also does not calculate a deduction or refund. The CRA’s FHSA overview distinguishes generally deductible contributions from RRSP-to-FHSA transfers, which are not deductible. Account room, deductible amounts and account value should not be treated as interchangeable figures. Separate contributions from investment growth Contributions arrive at year-end in this model. The existing balance first earns the selected annual return, then the allowed deposit is added. Under the default 4% assumption, the eight-year ending balance is CAD 45,929.75 from CAD 40,000 of contributions. The waterfall separates those contributions from modeled growth or loss. Investment income generally does not consume participation room, so an account value above CAD 40,000 does not by itself show excess contributions. Conversely, a lower balance after an investment loss does not reopen contribution capacity in this ordinary model. The comparison path removes the initial waiting period while keeping the same opening year, requested annual amount, return and finish date. Annual limits can change the actual deposit schedule, so this is a comparison of funding timing and constraints rather than investment performance. Use the calendar alongside the actual account rules The matrix varies the requested annual amount and the first contribution year, while retaining the selected finish date. Its cells show cumulative deposits that fit, not investment balances or tax deductions. They therefore remain unchanged when the investment-return input changes. The calendar freezes the reviewed rules for a hypothetical horizon. It does not determine eligibility to open, maximum participation deadlines, qualifying withdrawals, account closure, transfers out, tax on excesses or the treatment of any actual account history. Confirm those details in current CRA guidance and your records. A first-home plan also needs a purchase budget, closing costs, cash accessibility and an investment-risk review tied to the intended use date. Keep that wider funding need separate from the amount a registered account permits you to contribute. The four graphics explain the ordinary calendar without turning it into a personal room statement or a recommendation to open an account.

documents.title: How much cash does a move release? Reconcile both homes and both mortgages
documents.description: Use four graphics to separate a headline home-price difference from the cash remaining after loans, transaction costs and the replacement purchase.
documents.body: A cheaper replacement home does not automatically release the difference in prices. Mortgage balances, transaction costs and the funding of the replacement determine the cash result. Start with the proceeds available after selling The sale price is a gross amount. Before assigning it to another goal, account for the current mortgage repayment and the applicable selling costs. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s selling guide lists costs such as legal and discharge fees and possible commissions, moving expenses and mortgage prepayment charges. This model separates a percentage-based selling allowance from other sale-side costs and a tax provision. The percentages and fixed amounts are hypothetical inputs, not commission quotations, statutory tax rates or a calculation of a mortgage penalty. The default CAD 900,000 sale less CAD 36,000 of percentage-based costs, CAD 5,000 of other provisions and a CAD 250,000 mortgage repayment leaves CAD 609,000. The model does not determine whether a tax exemption applies or calculate tax due on the sale. Fund the replacement and the move The next step is the replacement purchase price, its purchase costs, and moving or setup costs, less the assumed new mortgage. The FCAC’s homebuying guide emphasizes upfront costs beyond the mortgage and lists examples of closing expenses. For a CAD 650,000 replacement, a 3% purchase-cost allowance adds CAD 19,500 and moving costs add CAD 5,000. The default 30% assumed mortgage finances CAD 195,000. The cash needed for those settlements is therefore CAD 479,500. The assumed mortgage percentage is a scenario input. It does not establish qualification, available proceeds, insurance treatment, interest rates or monthly affordability. A real plan needs confirmed financing and actual closing figures. The tool’s percentage-based cost allowances also cannot replace calculations of charges that follow different rules. Read the full reconciliation The waterfall adds sale proceeds, subtracts sale costs, repays the old loan, pays for the replacement and its costs, and adds the new financing. Its endpoint is cash released or additional cash needed under the selected assumptions. The default net cash release is CAD 129,500. The home-price difference alone is CAD 250,000, but mortgage debt falls by CAD 55,000 and entered transaction and moving costs total CAD 65,500. Those uses of funds explain why the price difference overstates the cash available for another goal. The step order is an accounting reconciliation, not a closing calendar. In particular, adding mortgage funding as a later step does not assert that the borrower must first pay the purchase price entirely in cash. The model assumes the settlements occur together; a different sequence requires a separate timing and bridging review. Separate liquidity from a change in wealth The home-value and mortgage bars show equity before costs for each property. More new borrowing can increase the cash released while leaving less equity in the replacement. That is a change in the financing mix, rather than a gain created by the move. The bookkeeping check is replacement home equity + signed cash released = current home equity − transaction and moving costs , within this simplified model. A negative cash-release figure means outside cash is needed, rather than negative money that can be assigned to a goal. For example, setting the default replacement mortgage to zero creates a CAD 65,500 additional cash requirement, even though the replacement price is lower. The mortgage-free purchase consumes the former equity, and the entered transaction costs still need funding. The debt choice therefore belongs alongside the desired use of the released cash. Test prices, costs and the post-move budget The cost bars make each allowance visible. The matrix then varies sale and replacement prices around the selected values. The current mortgage and fixed costs remain unchanged, while percentage-based costs and the assumed replacement mortgage scale with the relevant price. Each signed cell is a cash position, with no probability attached. A positive amount does not establish that the replacement is affordable over time, and a negative amount does not identify a source of additional funding. Consider actual sale conditions, deposit dates, lender funding and settlement costs separately. The ongoing budget may also change through mortgage payments, property costs, utilities, maintenance, transport or care needs. This tool computes the settlement ledger, not those future expenses or retirement-income adequacy. Review the cash release together with the new obligations before assigning the apparent surplus to spending, saving or another commitment.

documents.title: Understand an employer match: the contribution cap and the retirement balance
documents.description: Follow an illustrative matching formula through four graphics that separate personal saving, employer funding and investment growth.
documents.body: A matching percentage applies to a defined contribution base. Understand the eligible-pay cap and plan terms before translating the offer into a long-term savings projection. Identify what kind of workplace arrangement you have Workplace retirement arrangements can have different contribution, benefit and access rules. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s employer-plan overview distinguishes defined contribution and defined benefit pensions and describes group RRSPs. It notes that employer details vary and should be checked with the plan representative. This calculator illustrates a matching contribution formula. It assumes the employee and employer deposit money into an invested balance. It does not calculate a defined benefit pension promise, determine plan membership or reproduce the rules of a particular employer. Before entering real figures, identify eligible pay, the employee contribution required, the matching percentage, the cap and the timing of deposits. A phrase such as “50% match” is incomplete without the contribution base and limit. Other employer contributions may follow different formulas and are outside this example. Read where the match stops increasing The first chart shows first-year employer deposits as the employee contribution rate rises. The assumed formula is eligible annual pay × minimum of employee rate and eligible-pay cap × matching percentage . Rates are expressed as decimals in that calculation. With CAD 60,000 of eligible pay, a 6% employee rate and a 50% match on the first 6% of pay, the employee deposits CAD 3,600 and the employer deposits CAD 1,800 in year one. The employer amount is 3% of eligible pay, not 50% of salary. The curve flattens after the matching cap. Additional employee saving above that point still enters the modeled account but creates no extra matching deposit under this formula. A different actual employer formula could behave differently, so the plateau is a consequence of the entered assumptions rather than a general pension rule. Keep the personal contribution constant in the comparison The balance chart compares employee deposits alone with employee plus employer deposits. The employee contribution rate, eligible-pay growth, return and horizon are identical. That makes the effect of the employer-funded deposits visible without changing the employee’s gross saving effort between paths. Contributions arrive at month-end, and eligible pay increases once each year. The default 2% annual pay increase raises both employee deposits and the matching base. Both components earn the same assumed effective annual return, converted to an equivalent monthly rate. At a smooth 4% return over 20 years, the default total ending balance is CAD 193,863.35. This is a nominal amount before tax, fees and inflation. It does not show spendable retirement income or establish what could be withdrawn from the actual plan. Investment returns can differ materially from a constant rate. Separate employer funding from investment performance The waterfall adds total employee contributions, total employer contributions and modeled investment growth or loss. The first two amounts are deposits across different dates. The final step reconciles those deposits with the ending balance. A match is employer funding under the assumed arrangement. Expressing one matching deposit as a percentage of an employee deposit does not turn it into an annualized investment return. Later investment gains or losses on that money are a separate component, shown explicitly in the waterfall. The matrix compares first-year employer deposits across employee contribution rates and matching percentages. The selected eligible-pay cap remains fixed. Horizon, investment return and future pay growth do not affect those first-year cells; they matter to the long-term path. No cell represents an available job offer or plan entitlement. Connect payroll saving with the wider plan The employee contribution shown is a gross deposit, rather than an estimate of the change in take-home pay. Taxes, payroll treatment, registered-account room and other interactions need a separate review. The model assumes sufficient room and full entitlement to all employer deposits. Check eligibility dates, deposit timing, fees, available investments, vesting or ownership terms, transfer options and restrictions on access with the actual administrator. Also assess how the contribution fits current cash flow and other goals. A projected account balance does not replace a liquidity review. Revisit the assumptions after a pay change, plan amendment or job transition. Keep the written matching formula alongside the projection so changes can be traced to their source. The graphs explain the mechanics of a contribution-based arrangement while leaving plan-specific rights and retirement-income decisions for the relevant current documents and advice.

documents.title: Debt consolidation: compare the monthly relief with the full repayment cost
documents.description: Use four graphics to compare two existing repayment schedules with a proposed loan, including the effect of a financed setup fee and a longer term.
documents.body: A lower payment can come from a lower rate, a longer repayment period or both. Compare the debt-free date and total interest and fees before interpreting the relief. Start with a complete repayment comparison The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s consolidation guidance describes combining debts and explains that a lower-interest arrangement may still cost more if repayment is extended. It also emphasizes understanding the debts and the terms of a proposed product. This example begins with two balances and their nominal annual rates. Both current debts are assumed to amortize fully over the selected remaining years. The proposed loan refinances their combined principal and finances its setup fee. These are invented fixed-rate schedules, rather than the minimum-payment rules of actual credit cards or lines of credit. The default balances are CAD 12,000 at 18% and CAD 8,000 at 12%, each with two years remaining. The proposed alternative is 10% over five years with a CAD 300 financed fee. No rates shown here are offers or estimates of what a lender would approve. Read the payment reduction in its time context The monthly-payment bars compare the current combined payment with the proposed payment. In the default case, those amounts are CAD 975.68 and CAD 431.32. The difference provides recurring cash-flow relief while the schedules overlap. However, the current loans finish after 24 payments. The proposed arrangement continues for 60 payments. A comparison that stops at the first month misses those additional three years of obligations. The balance chart therefore keeps both paths visible through the longer horizon. After a current loan reaches zero, its plotted balance stays at zero. The calculator does not assume the released payment continues into another debt or an investment account. It compares scheduled loan cash flows; it is not a complete comparison of household wealth under different uses of the released money. Compare the cost of borrowing, with principal excluded Borrowing cost here means interest plus the setup fee, rather than the original principal. The original CAD 20,000 must be repaid in either arrangement, so separating it helps reveal the cost of obtaining and extending the credit. The default current schedules incur CAD 3,416.25 in interest. The proposed loan incurs CAD 5,878.90 in interest and the financed setup fee combined. Despite its lower rate and monthly payment, the proposed borrowing cost is CAD 2,462.65 higher under these assumptions. The stacked bars show interest and setup-fee principal separately. Interest charged on that financed fee is already included in the proposed interest amount. Adding the fee to the loan and then counting all loan repayments plus the fee again would count the fee principal twice. Use the matrix to separate the rate and term effects Each matrix cell recalculates the proposed arrangement at a displayed rate and term while retaining the selected original balances and setup fee. The amount is full-life borrowing cost. Read across a rate row to see the effect of duration, and down a term column to compare rates. The loan formula uses a monthly rate equal to the nominal annual rate divided by twelve, with payments at month-end. If B is the financed balance, r the monthly rate and n the payment count, the payment is Br ÷ [1 − (1 + r) −n ] . At zero interest, it is B ÷ n. A lender’s actual rate convention, fees, insurance, prepayment terms and variable-rate features can differ. The matrix does not include promotional-rate expiry, additional borrowing or future rate changes. Replacing an existing schedule with a new one requires the actual contractual figures for a meaningful comparison. Connect the proposed schedule with a sustainable budget A lower monthly obligation can matter when cash flow is tight, even when it increases total cost. Assess that trade-off explicitly: identify the amount of relief, the added repayment years and the change in borrowing cost, then compare them with the household’s available income and flexibility. The tool assumes no new spending on the cleared accounts. Reusing credit can create a different debt path from the one shown. It also does not assess collateral, credit history, eligibility or the consequences of converting unsecured obligations into secured borrowing. Review actual balances, payoff amounts, closure costs, proposed terms and an affordable payment schedule. The graphs organize those questions without selecting a provider or determining whether consolidation is appropriate. If the proposed payment still does not fit the budget, changing the loan label does not close that underlying cash-flow gap.

documents.title: Variable income in four charts: the annual total and the cash-flow buffer
documents.description: Compare three payment schedules with the same annual income, then see how the order and depth of low-income months change the cash needed at the start.
documents.body: An annual income figure cannot show whether each month’s payments are funded. Separate the annual budget from the cash needed to bridge the timing of receipts. Use income that is available for the household budget The Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy’s budgeting education discusses variable and irregular income, including commissions, contract work and seasonal earnings. It explains the role of saving in higher-income months and being careful about the receipts included in a budget. The annual income input here is net money available to the household. For a self-employed person, business receipts are not automatically the same amount: business costs and a provision for taxes or other obligations may need to be accounted for first. This calculator does not determine those deductions. All three illustrative schedules have the same annual total. The comparison therefore isolates timing, rather than assuming the seasonal household earns less. It does not estimate whether the entered annual income will actually arrive. Income uncertainty requires a separate downside test. Read how the same total is rearranged The even schedule divides annual income by twelve. In the low-first schedule, the selected number of low-income months arrives first. Each receives the chosen percentage reduction from the annual monthly average. The remaining months’ income is solved to preserve the full annual total. The high-first schedule reverses those same low and high amounts. With the default CAD 60,000 annual income and six months at 50% below average, the low months receive CAD 2,500 and the high months CAD 7,500. The even schedule receives CAD 5,000 every month. The income chart marks the payment levels as steps. A longer or deeper low period requires a larger amount in the remaining high months when the annual total is held fixed. That is an arithmetic constraint of this scenario, rather than evidence that the higher receipts are achievable or guaranteed. Follow the buffer after spending and goal transfers Each schedule pays the same CAD 4,000 of monthly household spending and transfers CAD 500 to other goals in the default example. That is CAD 4,500 leaving the modeled cash buffer each month. All receipts and outflows occur at month-end. With CAD 10,000 of starting cash, the low-first case reaches negative CAD 2,000 after month six, then recovers. All profiles end at CAD 16,000 because they share CAD 60,000 of receipts and CAD 54,000 of cash outflows. The matching endpoint does not eliminate the earlier shortage. A negative point is an unfunded cash-flow position, with no borrowing facility or interest cost assumed. The calculation does not establish that a bank will allow the payments. For a real schedule, also check bill dates and access to receipts within the month; month-end totals can hide an earlier gap. Separate a timing reserve from an emergency reserve The required starting buffer is the largest cumulative excess of planned cash outflows over income received so far, floored at zero. The bar chart compares that requirement across the three schedules before applying the entered existing cash. The default low-first schedule requires CAD 12,000 initially to avoid a negative month-end position. The selected CAD 10,000 leaves CAD 2,000 still to fund. This is a planned timing requirement. An additional shock, such as a missing payment or unexpected expense, creates a different need. Goal transfers leave this modeled buffer but remain household savings elsewhere. They are not consumption expenses or a second tax charge. If a goal transfer must be reduced or delayed to protect essential payments, test that change explicitly and record the effect on the other goal. Avoid treating one pool of money as fully available for several commitments at once. Stress the schedule without mistaking it for a forecast The matrix varies the number of low months and their reduction from average income. Each cell places the low period first, recalculates the high receipts needed to preserve annual income, and reports additional cash required after the selected starting buffer. These are deterministic alternatives, not probabilities or confidence intervals. A real downside may involve a lower annual total as well as later receipts. Test that by reducing annual net income and checking whether the plan has an ongoing annual deficit, a timing gap, or both. Review the buffer as invoices, payroll and recurring commitments become clearer. Track what was actually received, preserve money needed for taxes and business obligations outside this simplified household model, and update the next months’ calendar. An annual average helps describe the budget’s scale; the dated cash path shows whether the plan can meet its commitments on time.

documents.title: What does a car really cost? Map the loan, running costs and resale value
documents.description: Use four graphics to connect the monthly commitment with the full cost of ownership and the risk of owing more than the car is worth.
documents.body: The monthly loan payment is one cash-flow component. A full plan also includes acquisition costs, running costs, the ownership period and debt remaining when you sell. Separate the vehicle’s value from the amount financed The example starts with a vehicle purchase value and adds acquisition taxes and fees as a separate input. The down payment applies to that combined purchase cost. The loan finances the remainder, while the vehicle’s starting modeled resale value excludes those acquisition costs. In the default case, a CAD 35,000 vehicle plus CAD 4,000 of entered costs requires CAD 39,000. A 20% down payment is CAD 7,800, leaving CAD 31,200 financed. This distinction prevents a tax or fee payment from automatically appearing as additional vehicle value. All amounts are hypothetical, including the acquisition-cost allowance. They are not a dealer quote or a calculation of provincial taxes. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s financing overview describes different ways of financing a car; this tool models a fully amortizing purchase loan. Build the recurring cash requirement The default loan uses a 6% nominal annual rate divided by twelve, with equal month-end payments over five years. The scheduled monthly payment is CAD 603.18. Adding CAD 500 of initial running costs gives a first-month recurring requirement of CAD 1,103.18, before the separate down payment. Running costs can include insurance, fuel or charging, parking, maintenance and other regular vehicle expenses. Use a budget based on the vehicle and expected usage. A fixed monthly allowance simplifies the chart; actual repair bills can be uneven and may need their own periodic-bill reserve. The model increases running costs once per year at the selected rate. The loan payment remains fixed until the loan is repaid, then stops. A payment comparison that omits those timing changes can understate the ongoing commitment or assume loan payments continue after the debt has reached zero. Compare the asset path with the debt path The first chart follows vehicle value and remaining loan principal over the selected ownership period. Vehicle value declines at a constant assumed percentage each year. The debt follows the amortization schedule, which depends on the balance, rate and loan term. If debt exceeds modeled vehicle value, the household has negative equity at that date. Selling for that value would leave part of the loan to be funded from elsewhere. The FCAC’s discussion of car-financing risks explains negative equity and why long repayment terms deserve attention. Try a longer loan term and a faster value decline. A smaller monthly payment can coexist with more debt at the intended sale date. The depreciation assumption here is independently selected and smooth. It is not an appraisal, a source-reported depreciation schedule or a forecast of used-car prices. Reconcile what leaves the household over the whole period The waterfall adds the down payment, loan payments made during ownership and running costs. It then adds the loan balance that must be settled at sale and subtracts the vehicle’s modeled sale proceeds. The endpoint is the net cash cost of owning and exiting under these assumptions. For the default five-year case, the net cost is CAD 59,685.56. The same result can be checked as vehicle value lost, plus acquisition costs, plus loan interest, plus running costs. The remaining loan is zero at that endpoint because the ownership period matches the repayment term. These are two ways of describing the same cost. Adding depreciation again to the waterfall would count the loss of vehicle value twice. If the car is sold before the loan ends, include the remaining principal in the settlement; subtracting the full vehicle value while ignoring that debt would overstate the cash recovered. Review the exit date as well as the payment The matrix varies the loan rate and term while retaining the selected ownership horizon. Each cell settles any remaining debt at that date. The displayed amounts are total ownership costs, so they should not be read as monthly payments or as interest bills alone. At a positive rate, extending repayment can lower the scheduled payment while increasing the interest incurred before a given exit. At zero interest, different terms change the timing of principal payments, but settling the remaining balance at sale keeps the underlying principal cost consistent. The tool excludes investment opportunity cost, selling expenses, prepayment costs, balloon payments, insurance claims and differences between quoted and realized resale value. Review the actual financing contract, purchase costs and a realistic operating budget. Connect the commitment with the household’s other goals and its ability to handle an earlier-than-planned sale.

documents.title: Choosing an insurance deductible: compare the premium and the cash you retain
documents.description: Explore four graphics that separate recurring premiums, per-claim responsibility and the reserve needed for a covered loss.
documents.body: A premium reduction and a larger per-claim cash commitment belong in the same comparison. Check whether the household can fund the retained risk when a loss occurs. Identify the recurring price and the contingent amount A premium is paid to maintain the insurance arrangement. A deductible determines part of the loss the household retains when the relevant claim conditions apply. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s insurance overview explains these terms and notes that a higher deductible may be associated with a lower premium. The comparison uses two hypothetical policies with otherwise identical coverage for the eligible loss. Policy A defaults to a CAD 1,200 annual premium and CAD 500 per-claim deductible. Policy B defaults to CAD 900 and CAD 1,500 respectively. These inputs are not quotations or terms from an insurer. The annual premium saving in B is CAD 300. That recurring saving comes with an additional retained amount for some claims. The controls let either policy have the higher premium or deductible, so read the signs and the actual figures rather than assuming the labels A and B imply a ranking. Read how the deductible interacts with loss size The first chart shows household responsibility against the size of a fully eligible loss. In this simplified model, household share = minimum of covered loss and deductible . The assumed insurer share is the remaining eligible loss, with no limit or other cost sharing applied. If a covered loss is CAD 300 and the deductible is CAD 500, the household pays CAD 300, not CAD 500. Once the eligible loss exceeds the deductible, the retained amount stops increasing in this model. The curve therefore rises, then flattens at the selected deductible. This chart isolates deductible arithmetic. Real exclusions, sublimits, valuation methods, policy limits and settlement conditions can change the amount covered. Some policies also use other deductible structures. Verify those terms before treating two premium-and-deductible pairs as equivalent coverage. Compare several realized claim years The grouped bars add annual premiums to the retained amount for zero, one, two or three covered claims. Each claim has the loss amount entered in the controls, and a new deductible applies separately to each claim. The selected claim count is also a scenario input, without a probability attached. For the default CAD 5,000 eligible loss, one claim costs the household CAD 1,700 under A and CAD 2,400 under B, including the annual premium. With no claims, the comparison is simply CAD 1,200 versus CAD 900. The order can change because the recurring and contingent amounts respond differently. The model does not calculate an expected annual cost, predict claim frequency or apply a premium increase after a claim. A year with no claims does not show that coverage had no value, and a lower modeled cost in one scenario does not establish which policy is suitable. Check the retained amount against accessible cash The split bars show how the selected eligible loss is allocated between household and insurer under the assumptions. With a CAD 5,000 loss, B leaves CAD 1,500 with the household and CAD 3,500 with the insurer. Premiums are excluded from this per-claim split because they are already counted in the annual comparison. The default CAD 1,000 of cash allocated to a claim leaves a CAD 500 one-claim reserve gap under B. That gap is separate from the premium budget. If more than one claim occurs, or another emergency uses the reserve first, additional cash may be needed. Settlement timing can also matter. The retained share does not necessarily equal all the cash required before reimbursement arrives. The tool does not model repair deposits, temporary accommodation, claim delays or access restrictions on savings. Keep money already assigned to another goal out of the available-claim reserve unless replacement funding is planned. Read the matrix as a stress comparison The matrix varies claim size and count, showing B’s annual household cost minus A’s. A negative cell means B costs less within that scenario; a positive cell means B costs more. It uses the entered premiums and deductibles while replacing the selected claim size and count with the displayed alternatives. Use the matrix to locate the circumstances that change the result. Then consider whether the corresponding retained costs could be paid on time. Do not infer likelihood from the shading or select a policy solely because one cell is smaller. For a real review, compare coverage definitions and limits, the applicable deductible structure, accessible reserves, the premium schedule and the household’s tolerance for a large cash call. Obtain the actual policy terms and resolve coverage questions with the insurer or licensed representative. The graphs organize the funding trade-off while leaving underwriting and suitability outside the calculator.

documents.title: Plan a break from work: map the income drop and the reserve before you leave
documents.description: Follow temporary income, household spending and the cash reserve through a planned absence, then solve the additional saving required before it begins.
documents.body: A planned work break needs a dated income schedule. Fund the lowest cumulative cash position, including upfront costs and the months after temporary payments end. Start with the cash the household will actually receive A planned absence can involve parenting, study, caregiving or another life transition. Begin with the household’s continuing income, any temporary payments and the spending that remains due. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s budget guidance includes planning for life events and reviewing income, expenses and savings together. All income inputs here are net cash amounts, after any tax or payroll deductions you expect to apply. Continuing income remains throughout the break. Temporary income arrives for the selected number of months, then stops even if the absence continues. The model does not assume that taking time away creates eligibility for a benefit. For parental leave, the Government of Canada’s EI information explains that amounts and duration depend on the applicable program and circumstances, and that some employers provide top-ups. Confirm the actual arrangement before entering the cash-flow schedule. Put the end of temporary income on the chart The default household spends CAD 4,500 per month, receives CAD 2,500 of continuing monthly income and adds CAD 1,500 of temporary income for six months. Its first six monthly shortfalls are CAD 500 each. After the temporary payments end, the shortfall rises to CAD 2,000 a month. The income chart marks that change against the spending line. The two inputs have different roles: the length of the break controls how long expenses continue, while the temporary-income duration controls when that payment stops. Extending one does not automatically extend the other. Actual paydays, benefit processing, employer conditions and return-to-work timing can differ from a simple monthly schedule. A detailed plan should use confirmed payment dates and include any gap before the first receipt. The calculator assumes all monthly cash flows occur at month-end and does not estimate program eligibility, withholding or job-protected leave rights. Fund the worst cumulative position The reserve model begins by paying the entered upfront costs before month one. It then adds monthly income and subtracts spending. The required starting fund is the amount that keeps the lowest cumulative position at or above zero. For the default twelve-month break, CAD 3,000 of upfront costs plus six CAD 500 gaps and six CAD 2,000 gaps require CAD 18,000 at the start. With CAD 15,000 allocated, the additional saving requirement is CAD 3,000. Spreading that over twelve preparation months gives CAD 250 a month, with no interest assumed. Funding the lowest point matters even if the full period eventually produces a surplus. Upfront payments may need cash before later income arrives. Conversely, early monthly surpluses can help fund later shortfalls if that money remains available. The model retains both effects rather than simply adding every negative month while ignoring the positive ones. Compare the reserve path with the annual-style total The cash-balance chart shows the currently allocated savings and the fully funded starting reserve. A line below zero identifies spending that needs another funding source. It does not represent approved credit or include the cost of borrowing to fill the gap. The waterfall adds upfront and ongoing spending, then subtracts continuing income, temporary payments and allocated savings. A positive endpoint means a net shortfall by the final month; a negative endpoint means a surplus. Because it summarizes the full period, read it alongside the monthly path to catch any earlier shortage. The matrix changes the break’s duration and temporary monthly income while keeping the selected duration of those payments fixed. Each cell reruns the timing calculation and shows the additional fund required after allocated savings. Its income levels are hypothetical alternatives, not statutory benefit rates or employer offers. Include the transition back into the household plan The calculator leaves several items for a wider review: pension accrual, workplace insurance, employer top-up conditions, tuition, care costs, work-related savings, tax changes and costs on returning to work. Identify which are already included in spending and which need separate dated amounts. Check the consequence of a longer absence or a delayed restart of earnings. Also keep an emergency reserve distinct from the savings deliberately assigned to the break. A plan that uses every accessible dollar for known costs has less room for an unrelated shock. Before the break begins, reconcile the confirmed income schedule, planned expenses, available savings and preparation transfers. The calculated monthly saving amount must fit the current budget; it does not establish affordability by itself. Update the schedule as arrangements become definite, and review it again when the actual cash flows start.

documents.title: How long should retirement savings last? Read the survival curve
documents.description: Explore preliminary Canadian life-table statistics alongside separate funding scenarios that show the cost of planning for more years.
documents.body: An average remaining lifetime is a population summary. A retirement funding horizon must also consider the consequences of living longer than that average. Know what the statistical curve represents The first two graphics use Statistics Canada’s Canada-level 2022–2024 period life table, released on 13 January 2026. The source marks this period preliminary because late death registrations can lead to revisions. The chart preserves the publisher’s Males and Females categories. A period table summarizes a pattern of mortality for a reference period. It is not a forecast that follows today’s 65-year-olds through future changes in mortality. Its survivor counts describe a synthetic cohort, rather than a survey sample of the people now shown on the age axis. Each survival line starts at 100% at age 65. Later points divide the source’s survivor count at that age by its survivor count at 65, within the same sex category: conditional survival = l x ÷ l 65 . This conditioning matters because the comparison begins with people who have already reached 65. Read the birthdays beyond the average The published remaining life expectancy at 65 is 19.43 years for Males and 22.15 for Females in this preliminary table. Those are averages under the period’s mortality pattern. They do not mean that everyone dies at the average age or that half the group necessarily lives beyond it. The milestone bars show derived survival shares to 85, 90 and 95, conditional on reaching 65. For example, the age-90 shares are about 29.14% and 42.00% for the respective source categories. The data table retains the displayed percentages, and the source link identifies the original survivor counts and reference period. These population patterns provide context for a long funding horizon. They do not adjust for an individual’s health, family history or future circumstances. They also do not calculate the chance that at least one member of a couple survives. Household joint-survival analysis requires additional assumptions and should not be inferred by adding the two percentages. Keep the funding scenarios separate from the statistics The controls change the hypothetical funding illustrations only. They do not alter the official life-table observations. Enter the annual spending shortfall after other income, the years it needs to be funded, a real return assumption and the capital allocated to that need. The model funds a level shortfall in today’s purchasing-power dollars, paid at each year-end. For annual gap G, real return r and n years, the reserve is G[1 − (1 + r) −n ] ÷ r . At zero return, it is G × n. A negative real return increases the starting reserve required for the same future purchasing power. The default CAD 20,000 annual gap for 30 years at an assumed 2% real return requires CAD 447,929.11 today. After CAD 400,000 of allocated capital, the modeled gap is CAD 47,929.11. These are deterministic calculations, with constant returns and no market sequence, taxes or fees beyond what is already assumed in the real rate. Use longer horizons as a resilience test The grouped bars compare the funding requirement for 20, 25, 30 and 35 years with the same capital allocation. The matrix varies both the horizon and real return. Each cell reports additional capital needed, with zero as a floor when allocated capital already covers the modeled requirement. A zero cell is not a probability of success. The calculation assumes the selected return occurs smoothly and the shortfall remains constant in real terms. Different inflation exposure, investment losses, care needs or other spending could change the required payments. The model does not multiply each year’s essential spending by the chance of surviving to that year. Such weighting would describe a different expected-value question. It would not demonstrate that one household can fund every payment if it lives longer. Risk pooling, annuities and insurance require their own pricing, contract and suitability analysis. Connect longevity to an income plan List the spending that continues if retirement lasts longer, and the income sources that continue alongside it. Check their terms, inflation treatment and any changes after a spouse or partner dies. Keep dependable cash flows distinct from assets that may need to be sold. Test a longer funding period without simultaneously improving the return assumption. That exposes the cost of additional years. Then identify possible responses, such as different saving, spending, retirement timing or income arrangements, and assess their constraints in a fuller plan. Revisit the horizon as circumstances and source estimates change. These charts combine dated population context with transparent arithmetic; they do not select a personal lifespan, establish a safe withdrawal rate or guarantee that a particular reserve will be sufficient.

documents.title: The lifetime cost of recurring fees: follow the dollars and the growth
documents.description: Compare two fee assumptions with a common savings plan, then separate direct deductions from their effect on future investment growth.
documents.body: Recurring fees change both the money deducted and the balance left to compound. Compare costs, services and risk on a consistent basis when assessing a long-term plan. Compare costs against the same saving effort The charts hold the initial balance, monthly contributions, horizon and gross investment return constant. Only the recurring fee changes between the paths. This isolates the cost mechanism without claiming that two real investment arrangements provide identical investments, risks or services. The Canadian Securities Administrators’ fee overview identifies several types of charges associated with investment products, accounts, transactions and advice. Understanding the applicable charges helps clarify what the investor pays and what services are received. The no-fee line is a mathematical reference. It does not identify an available product or promise equivalent services at zero cost. Before comparing actual arrangements, check which costs are included, which are additional and whether the investment exposures and service scope are comparable. State how the percentage becomes a deduction This model treats the annual fee as an effective fraction of assets and converts it to an equivalent monthly fraction: monthly fee = 1 − (1 − annual fee) 1/12 . Each month the opening balance first earns the gross return, the fee is deducted from that grown balance, and the contribution then arrives at month-end. The resulting annual growth factor before contributions is (1 + gross return) × (1 − annual fee) . With 5% gross return and a 0.25% fee, the modeled net annual rate is 4.7375%. With a 1.75% fee, it is 3.1625%. Simply subtracting fee from gross return would use a different, approximate convention. Actual charges may accrue daily, apply to different valuation bases, include tax or use flat-dollar schedules. The tool’s convention is explicit so its results can be checked. If an entered return already includes a particular charge, deducting that same charge again would count it twice. Read the difference in ending wealth The default example begins with CAD 10,000 and adds CAD 500 each month for 30 years. At the selected 5% gross return, fee A of 0.25% leaves CAD 429,421.33. Fee B of 1.75% leaves CAD 322,759.38. The difference is CAD 106,661.95 under this smooth-return illustration. That difference is not a bill issued in the final year. It accumulates from deductions over time and the return those deducted amounts would otherwise have experienced. The common contributions remain the same, so the comparison does not disguise an additional saving effort in one case. Fee A and fee B are editable labels, not a fixed ranking. If B is set below A, the sign of the displayed A-minus-B difference changes. If both fees are equal, the paths and ending values coincide. Neither setting predicts how differently managed real portfolios will perform before costs. Separate direct fees from the return effect The fee bars total the monthly dollar deductions. They are nominal amounts paid at different dates, added without discounting or inflation adjustment. The waterfall starts with the no-fee reference, subtracts fee B’s direct deductions and reconciles the remaining return effect to fee B’s ending value. Under positive constant gross returns, money deducted earlier misses later positive growth. Under negative constant gross returns, the removed amounts would instead have experienced losses. The residual return effect can then reverse sign. This accounting effect is not a refund, another fee or evidence that charging a fee improves the investment. The matrix compares selected recurring fees over different horizons against the matching no-fee reference for each horizon. Darker cells show larger ending-wealth gaps. They are cumulative differences, with no probability attached, rather than annual fee rates expressed as dollars. Bring the cost assumption into the goal review Use a consistent after-cost return assumption when estimating whether a savings goal is funded. If a cost change reduces the modeled endpoint, quantify the resulting gap before choosing a response. Contributions, timing, spending goals and service arrangements are separate decisions. For an actual account, inventory recurring product charges, advisory costs, account fees and transaction costs, and identify any overlap. Compare that inventory with the investment and service terms. This calculator includes only the selected recurring percentage; it does not value advice, determine suitability or calculate a household’s tax treatment. Review fees when the account, product mix or service arrangement changes. A transparent cost assumption makes the long-term plan easier to assess, while leaving investment uncertainty and the value of the services as questions requiring their own evidence.

documents.title: Plan for annual bills: a sinking fund with a calendar
documents.description: Map four periodic expenses, follow the monthly reserve balance and see why a balanced annual budget can still run short before a bill arrives.
documents.body: The annual total tells you how much spending is planned. The calendar tells you when the cash must already be available. Give predictable bills their own place in the plan Some expenses arrive every month, while others arrive at particular points in the year. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s budgeting lesson includes irregular and periodic expenses in the budget and describes spreading a known expense over the months before it is due. A sinking fund is money earmarked over time for those planned payments. The label is less important than the amount, date and funding source. A future insurance renewal or booked trip can be planned separately from unexpected expenses whose timing and size are unknown. This example lists four hypothetical bills: insurance in month three, maintenance in month six, travel in month eight, and gifts or events in month twelve. The chart’s fixed dates make the timing visible. Actual maintenance and event costs can differ, so use your own records and payment notices when building a real calendar. An annual average can miss the first-year cash need The default bills total CAD 4,500, equivalent to CAD 375 a month over a full year. The example also starts with CAD 500 already reserved. At a CAD 375 monthly contribution, the year ends with CAD 500 still earmarked. However, after the month-eight travel bill, the projected balance is negative CAD 100. By that point, cumulative bills are CAD 3,600 while starting cash plus eight contributions totals CAD 3,500. A positive year-end amount does not pay a bill that falls before the later contributions arrive. The signed monthly line exposes that timing gap. A negative point means the scheduled spending lacks funding within this reserve. It is not an approved overdraft or a prediction that a bank will permit the payment. Identify another source or revise the plan before the due date. Solve for the contribution that covers each deadline For every month m, compare cumulative bills due by that month with the starting reserve R. A constant monthly contribution C must satisfy R + Cm ≥ cumulative bills through month m . The smallest non-negative C is the largest value of (cumulative bills − R) ÷ m across the twelve months, floored at zero. In the default calendar, month eight is the binding deadline. The required contribution is (CAD 3,600 − CAD 500) ÷ 8 = CAD 387.50. The comparison line uses that amount and avoids a negative month-end balance within the illustrated year. This is a timing calculation, not an affordability assessment. The solved amount must still fit the operating budget after other spending and saving. A larger initial reserve, a revised bill amount or a different payment schedule can change the requirement; any actual schedule change needs agreement with the relevant provider. Use all four graphics together The bill bars identify the amounts and deadlines. The line chart follows the signed reserve after each month’s contribution and payment. The waterfall reconciles starting cash plus twelve contributions less all listed bills to the year-end balance. The waterfall deliberately leaves the payment order out of its annual total. Use it to check arithmetic, then return to the monthly path to check availability. The matrix compares alternative starting reserves and monthly saving amounts, reporting the largest unfunded month-end balance in each case. The example assumes contributions arrive before bills at month-end. If a payment is due earlier than the transfer, an end-of-month model may hide an intra-month shortage. Add actual paydays, transfer settlement times and bill deadlines to the detailed plan. No interest is earned here, so the results depend on cash timing rather than an investment forecast. Keep the reserve and the budget consistent A transfer between your own accounts changes where cash is held and how it is earmarked; it does not itself consume household wealth. When reviewing a consolidated budget, avoid treating both the transfer and the later bill as two separate purchases. The bill is the spending; the transfer prepares the cash for it. Also avoid assigning the same opening reserve to several goals. If these dollars are committed to known annual bills, they are unavailable for another planned payment unless you replace the funding. Review the emergency reserve separately for genuinely unexpected costs. After each payment, update the actual amount, remaining balance and next deadline. This is a one-year illustration; it does not automatically assume the same opening balance in every future year. Recalculate as prices, plans and bill dates change, and connect the transfer schedule with the income that funds it.
