documents.title: RRSP versus TFSA in four charts: compare the same after-tax saving effort
documents.description: Follow the deduction, growth and withdrawal tax through a fair comparison. See why the tax-rate relationship matters when the saving budget is held constant.
documents.body: Compare the spendable outcome from the same net saving cost. A gross account balance alone does not show the money available after tax. Begin with the different tax timing The Canada Revenue Agency’s RRSP overview explains that deductible contributions can reduce tax, income inside the plan is usually sheltered while it remains there, and payments are generally taxable. The CRA’s TFSA overview explains that contributions are not deductible and qualifying account income and withdrawals are generally tax-free. The charts isolate those mechanics. They assume both accounts hold investments earning exactly the same return and both have enough available room for the modeled contribution. They do not select investments, calculate eligibility or estimate an individual’s actual tax bill. Tax relief and withdrawal tax are entered as constant percentages applying to the full relevant amount. Real deductions and withdrawals can span brackets and interact with other income, benefits and credits. The percentages here are hypothetical assumptions, not published federal or provincial tax rates. Hold the personal saving cost constant Suppose the available after-tax saving budget is B and the tax relief on a fully deductible RRSP contribution is t. The modeled gross RRSP contribution is B ÷ (1 − t) . Tax relief finances the difference between that contribution and B. The TFSA receives B directly. For a CAD 10,000 personal budget and 40% tax relief, the RRSP contribution is CAD 16,666.67. The assumed tax relief is CAD 6,666.67, leaving CAD 10,000 of net cost. The TFSA contribution is CAD 10,000. Comparing those gross deposits without their tax treatment would miss why they differ. This assumes the relief is usable immediately and funds the larger deposit, such as through a suitably arranged cash-flow process. A refund received later creates a timing or financing issue. If the refund is spent rather than included in saving, that is a different comparison with different consumption today. The tool does not model a refund delay or borrowing costs. Read the after-tax bars and the growth paths The ending-balance chart displays account value and modeled spendable value. For the RRSP, the second bar deducts the assumed withdrawal tax from the entire balance. For the TFSA, the two bars coincide under the qualifying tax-free treatment assumed here. With 20 years at 5%, the default TFSA reaches CAD 26,532.98. The grossed-up RRSP, after a hypothetical 30% tax on its full withdrawal, leaves CAD 30,955.14. The difference comes from the selected tax-rate relationship, with identical growth assumptions and net initial saving costs. The line chart shows the same comparison at earlier dates. Each RRSP point assumes a complete withdrawal at that date using the same selected tax rate. It is not a sequence of annual withdrawals, an income drawdown strategy or a calculation of mandatory registered-account payments. The selected return is smooth and uncertain in practice. Use the matrix to see the equal-rate result If the RRSP deduction relief and withdrawal rate are equal, the model produces the same spendable outcome as the TFSA. Algebraically, RRSP net ÷ TFSA = (1 − withdrawal rate) ÷ (1 − deduction-relief rate) . The common growth factor and starting budget cancel. The matrix displays that ratio minus one as a percentage difference. A positive cell means the modeled RRSP amount is larger; a negative cell means it is smaller. These are amounts relative to the TFSA outcome, not annualized investment returns. Changing the horizon or common investment return does not change this isolated ratio. The waterfall reconciles the gross RRSP balance, tax at withdrawal and TFSA comparison amount. Tax relief has already financed the gross contribution at the start. Adding the refund to the ending balance again would count the same resource twice. Add the rules and cash-flow constraints before deciding Actual account choice also depends on available contribution and deduction room, the use date, access needs, withdrawal rules, employer arrangements and the household’s wider tax situation. Check current CRA guidance for those questions rather than extending this simplified illustration beyond its assumptions. The tool assumes a single deposit and no additional tax drag inside either qualifying account. It omits fees, withholding mechanics, income-tested benefits, future account conversion rules, estate treatment and changes in tax law. A deduction that cannot be fully used now also breaks the immediate-relief assumption. Document the net saving cost, how the tax relief will be funded and used, and a plausible range for future withdrawal tax. Then compare the result with the goal’s timing and liquidity requirements. A transparent comparison helps identify the variables that need review; the largest gross balance alone does not settle the account decision.

documents.title: CPP at 60, 65 or 70: chart the timing trade-off and the income bridge
documents.description: Compare monthly CPP age adjustments, cumulative receipts and discounted payment timing with four graphics and a clearly stated common benefit assumption.
documents.body: A later start trades early cash flow for a larger payment later. Compare that trade-off with the cost of funding the waiting period and the household’s other needs. Separate the age adjustment from the entitlement estimate The Government of Canada’s CPP start-age guidance states that the standard start age is 65, with starts available from 60 to 70. Before 65, the monthly amount is reduced by 0.6% for each month early. After 65, it increases by 0.7% for each month delayed, through age 70. The first chart applies those factors to one common assumed age-65 entitlement. At the default CAD 1,000 per month, the illustrative payments are CAD 640 at 60, CAD 1,000 at 65 and CAD 1,420 at 70. The CAD 1,000 input is neither an official maximum nor an average payment. A personal CPP estimate also depends on the contribution record and applicable calculation rules. Working longer or changing future contributions can change that underlying entitlement. This tool freezes the entitlement to isolate the age adjustment. It does not retrieve a contribution history or calculate the pension that a particular person will receive. Read the cash-flow head start The cumulative chart counts the payments received by each birthday. At the chosen starting birthday, cumulative receipts are zero; the following birthday includes twelve month-end payments. The age axis begins at 60 so the years relevant to the comparison remain visible. Starting at 65 provides five years of payments before a start at 70 begins. Under the default assumption, that head start is CAD 60,000 in constant purchasing-power dollars. After 70, the later-start case receives CAD 420 more each month. It gradually makes up the difference if the person continues receiving payments. Ignoring discounting, tax and all other effects, the continuous arithmetic crossover is about age 81.9 for 65 versus 70. With month-end payments, the first crossover is at the 143rd payment after age 70. This is a conditional receipt calculation. It does not establish the age a person will live to or recommend waiting until 70. Account for when the money arrives A dollar available sooner and a dollar received decades later have different timing. The present-value bars discount each monthly payment back to age 60 using the selected real annual rate, converted to an equivalent monthly rate. All payments in the illustration are expressed in constant purchasing-power dollars. The discount rate must therefore also be real. Using a nominal investment return against these real cash flows would mix measurement bases. The tool does not separately forecast CPI or reproduce actual annual CPP indexation. A positive discount rate gives more weight to earlier payments. The matrix compares start-at-70 receipts with start-at-65 receipts over several final ages and discount rates. Each signed cell is a present-value difference at age 60. A negative cell favors the earlier receipts under that calculation; a positive cell favors the later receipts. There is no probability attached to a cell. Plan the years before the pension starts The charts count CPP receipts only. They do not deduct the resources needed to pay household expenses while waiting. If employment, other pensions or savings must cover that period, write down the annual shortfalls and identify their funding sources. A person who uses an investment portfolio for the bridge may make larger withdrawals before CPP starts. The portfolio’s return sequence, tax cost and remaining flexibility then matter. The sequence-risk guide explains why the same average investment return can produce different results when withdrawals occur. Conversely, a household with sufficient income from elsewhere may value the larger later monthly payment differently from one with immediate cash needs. A simple cumulative-payment crossover cannot represent all those circumstances. Compare a full household cash-flow plan alongside the receipt chart. Treat longevity and benefit interactions separately Every plotted receipt assumes the person is alive to receive it. The model applies no survival probabilities and computes no expected present value. A comparison through age 95 is an assumption about the payment horizon, rather than a prediction or a statement about population life expectancy. Taxes, income-tested benefits, survivor benefits, disability-related provisions, future contributions and QPP rules are outside the tool. These can affect an actual decision. A household review should also consider health, a spouse or partner’s cash flows, debt costs, flexibility and the consequence of living longer than initially planned. Use an up-to-date personal estimate and verify the applicable rules before implementing a start date. Keep the entitlement estimate, age adjustment, payment timing and bridge funding as distinct inputs. The four charts make one part of that decision visible while leaving room for the circumstances that a receipt-only model cannot resolve.

documents.title: Rent or buy? Compare the housing budget, invested savings and exit costs
documents.description: Explore four charts that give renting and buying the same starting capital and monthly budget, then track debt, carrying costs and invested differences.
documents.body: The comparison depends on the full cash flows and the holding period. Include the down payment’s alternative use, ownership costs and the costs of leaving. Give both households the same starting resources A useful comparison begins with homes that provide comparable housing services and households that start with the same money. A larger property with a different location or quality changes the living arrangement as well as the financing decision. The buyer uses starting capital for the down payment and purchase costs. The renter invests that same capital. In the default example, a CAD 600,000 home, 20% down payment and 2% purchase costs require CAD 132,000. The mortgage begins at CAD 480,000; the renter’s investment portfolio begins at CAD 132,000. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s homebuying guide emphasizes costs beyond the mortgage and lists examples of closing expenses. The percentages in these charts are hypothetical placeholders. They are not quotations for transfer tax, legal fees, commissions or a particular transaction. Invest the cost advantage in either direction Every month, the tool calculates each household’s housing cash outflow. It gives both households a common budget equal to the higher amount. Whichever option is cheaper invests the difference at month-end. This can be the renter or the owner, and the direction can change as rent and owner costs evolve. The owner pays mortgage principal and interest plus combined carrying costs. The carrying-cost assumption is a yearly percentage of the current modeled home value, allocated monthly. It can stand for a budget allowance for property tax, insurance, maintenance and similar expenses, but those actual bills need their own estimates. The renter pays the selected rent, increasing once a year at the assumed rate. The FCAC renting guide notes that additional rental expenses depend on the arrangement. Shared utilities and lifestyle costs are omitted here as equal in both cases. Add a difference to the budget before applying the comparison to unlike living arrangements. Distinguish the cash required from the cost consumed The first-year bars compare average monthly housing outflows before investing any cost difference. Mortgage principal is included because it must be paid, but it also reduces debt. Therefore, the outflow bars are not a pure economic-expense comparison between rent and interest. The mortgage uses a 25-year amortization and the same explicit semi-annual quoted-rate convention as the renewal guide. Its rate remains unchanged for the entire selected comparison. That simplifies the calculation but leaves renewal uncertainty out. Actual future payments may differ. Both portfolios earn the same effective annual investment return, converted to a monthly rate. Home value also changes smoothly each month at the selected annual assumption. Repairs can be uneven, investments fluctuate and neither growth rate is assured. A smooth path is a calculation convention, not a forecast of the experience of either household. Compare the resources available after an exit The owner’s line equals home value less assumed sale costs and outstanding mortgage debt, plus any investment portfolio accumulated from a monthly cost advantage. The renter’s line is the investment portfolio. Every point on the owner’s line assumes a sale at that date, including the starting point. That sale convention means the buyer starts below the renter after transaction costs. Purchase costs have been consumed, and the chart also allows for a hypothetical immediate sale cost. Longer holding periods give other cash flows and value changes more time to matter; they do not guarantee that either option wins. With the default assumptions, modeled year-ten resources are CAD 360,031.78 for the owner and CAD 287,564.12 for the renter. The waterfall reconciles the home value, sale costs, debt and both portfolios to show the difference. The endpoint measures relative modeled wealth, not the home’s investment profit or an annual return. Test assumptions that could reverse the comparison The matrix reruns the monthly comparison for different home-value changes and investment returns. Each signed cell is owner ending wealth minus renter ending wealth. It also recalculates the carrying costs tied to modeled home value. A positive result favors the owner within the model; a negative result favors the renter. Test a shorter stay, higher carrying costs, a weaker home-value path and different rent growth. Consider whether the assumed investments and regular saving would actually be maintained. A renter who spends the cost difference or an owner who faces an unbudgeted major repair follows a different path. The model excludes taxes and housing benefits, default insurance, moving expenses, detailed condominium assessments, rent-law constraints and the costs of mortgage changes. Its minimum down-payment input of 20% avoids modeling insured-mortgage premiums but does not establish eligibility or approval. Flexibility, location, stability and the household’s other goals also deserve weight. Use actual comparable-home costs and current contract terms before making the commitment.

documents.title: Mortgage renewal in four charts: the payment, the balance and the trade-off
documents.description: See how a future renewal rate changes monthly cash flow, principal repayment and the relationship between rate and amortization.
documents.body: A renewal changes the cost of financing the balance that remains. Test the payment against your budget while keeping the payoff date visible. Separate the next contract from the payoff horizon A mortgage term and its amortization answer different questions. The term describes the period covered by a particular contract. Amortization describes the repayment horizon used to calculate the scheduled payment. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s renewal guide explains these distinctions and the choices involved at renewal. This illustration starts with a balance today, a current quoted rate and a remaining amortization. The assumed first term lasts five years. After 60 month-end payments, the renewal scenario applies a new rate to the balance still owed and recalculates the payment for the remaining years. The comparison keeps the original payoff date. With the default CAD 400,000 balance, 20-year amortization and 4% quoted rate, the modeled monthly payment is CAD 2,416.99. A 6% renewal rate after five years changes it to CAD 2,750.51, an increase of CAD 333.53. These are original hypothetical calculations, not current lender offers or a forecast of rates. Why two balance paths can reach zero together The first chart compares continuing at the original rate with changing the rate after five years. Both balances reach the same scheduled end date because the renewal payment adjusts. A higher rate does not have to mean a longer loan when the payment increases enough to preserve amortization. Do not read the balance line as the amount paid. A payment contains both interest and principal. Interest is a financing cost; principal reduces the debt. The stacked chart separates those components for years one through five and years six through ten in the renewal scenario. Those two five-year periods start with different balances. Their interest amounts therefore reflect both the rate and the amount still owed. They are successive stages of one financing path, rather than two otherwise identical loans. For a rate-only comparison, use the matrix, which holds the initial balance constant across its cells. Turn the payment change into a cash-flow test The payment bars show the recurring budget effect more directly than the outstanding-balance lines. Compare the increase with the amount left after ordinary spending, other required debt payments and planned saving. A budget that balances only by suspending every other goal has little flexibility. Try a higher renewal rate and record the monthly difference. Multiply that difference by twelve to estimate the annual cash-flow adjustment, while keeping it separate from a change in total interest over the full loan. The annual budget effect and lifetime borrowing cost answer different questions. Property taxes, home insurance, condominium charges, repairs and utilities remain outside the payment calculation. A reserve for these costs can be necessary even when the mortgage payment itself fits. The emergency-fund guide provides a separate way to model an income interruption; mortgage affordability alone does not measure that resilience. Read across the amortization matrix Each cell shows the monthly payment for today’s selected starting balance, using the displayed rate and amortization. Reading across a row isolates the horizon change. Reading down a column isolates the rate change. The grid uses the starting balance, so its cells are not renewal quotes based on the smaller year-five balance. At a positive rate, a longer amortization lowers the scheduled payment but keeps money borrowed for longer. Under an unchanged rate and a fully repaid loan, total scheduled interest is payment × number of payments − original principal. A lower monthly payment can therefore accompany a larger cumulative interest bill. Actual renewal options may involve lender requirements, fees, insurance considerations, contractual restrictions or a reassessment of the application. The chart does not establish that a particular amortization is available. Obtain the actual terms before treating a modeled payment as an executable option. Keep the compounding convention explicit This example assumes a quoted nominal annual rate compounded semi-annually. If j is that annual rate as a decimal, the equivalent monthly rate is m = (1 + j ÷ 2) 1/6 − 1 . For balance B and N remaining monthly payments, the payment is Bm ÷ [1 − (1 + m) −N ] . At zero interest, it is B ÷ N. Each month’s interest is opening balance × m. The payment first covers that interest and the remainder reduces principal. At renewal, the formula uses the remaining balance and remaining number of payments. The selected renewal rate then stays constant until payoff in this model. The tool excludes fees, prepayments, default-insurance premiums and later rate changes. Contracts can use different conventions. Read the lender’s disclosed interest calculation and payment schedule, then compare the resulting cash flows with this illustration. A useful review records the actual renewal date, balance, payment options and planned source of any increase.

documents.title: How much family protection? Draw the funding gap before choosing coverage
documents.description: Map future household shortfalls, immediate costs and available resources with a present-value curve, a funding waterfall and sensitivity charts.
documents.body: Start with the household’s obligations and surviving resources. A salary multiple alone cannot explain the amount or duration of the funding need. Begin with the household shortfall A protection plan asks what the household would need to fund if an income earner died. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s life-insurance overview describes uses such as replacing income, supporting dependants and paying debts. It also distinguishes coverage types and emphasizes understanding the policy. The relevant income gap is the difference between future spending and the surviving household’s available income. It is not automatically the deceased person’s gross salary. Employment-related expenses might end, care costs might rise, and the surviving household may have its own earnings or benefits. Estimate those cash flows before entering a shortfall. The line chart starts with an annual after-tax gap and increases it each year at the selected escalation rate. The default CAD 40,000 first-year shortfall grows at 2% for 20 years. The first payment arrives at the end of year one. A need that begins immediately, varies by life stage or ends earlier requires a different cash-flow schedule. Translate future support into an amount today Adding future nominal shortfalls gives the total dollars expected to be paid across different dates. Present value asks what amount today could fund those payments if it earned the selected net return. This model discounts the cash flows at an assumed nominal rate after costs and tax. For first annual gap G, escalation g, discount rate d and n support years, the income amount today is Σ G(1 + g) t−1 ÷ (1 + d) t , summed from t = 1 to n. Immediate costs are then added without discounting. Escalation and discounting are different operations; using a real rate while also inflating the cash flows would mix conventions. The default 3% net discount rate produces a combined need of CAD 759,067.82, including CAD 50,000 of immediate costs. A discount rate is an assumption about funding the future payments. It is not a guaranteed return available from an investment or an insurance policy. A lower assumed rate increases the amount needed today for the same positive future shortfalls. Read the waterfall without counting resources twice The waterfall first adds immediate costs and the present value of income support. It then subtracts assets allocated to this need and existing death benefits. Teal steps add needs; gold steps subtract resources. The navy endpoint shows the modeled net gap or surplus. With CAD 100,000 of allocated assets and CAD 300,000 of existing benefits, the default additional funding gap is CAD 359,067.82. The figure is a planning estimate under the selected assumptions. It does not identify a suitable policy, establish insurability or determine a premium. Use a consistent treatment for debts. If immediate costs include paying off the mortgage, remove the corresponding mortgage payments from the future spending gap. If assets are assigned here, do not also promise the same dollars to education and retirement. A home or restricted account may not supply cash when the household needs it; this simplified model assumes the entered resources are fully available today. Test the support period and the discount rate together The grouped bars compare several support periods against the same available resources. A longer period includes more annual shortfalls. The matrix then varies both duration and discount rate, showing the additional gap after resources in each case. The shading represents amounts, not probabilities. A darker cell is not more likely. A zero cell means the specified resources cover the modeled need in that scenario; it does not establish that the existing coverage has suitable conditions, duration, ownership or beneficiaries. Different obligations can have different end dates. Childcare may end before education begins; a partner may retire later; an outstanding debt may be repaid along the way. A detailed plan can replace the single smooth income-gap curve with dated cash flows. Keeping those dates visible is more informative than hiding every obligation in one rounded salary multiple. Review the resources as carefully as the need Check whether employer coverage continues after a job change and whether the benefit amount, policy term and conditions match the period being modeled. Verify settlement timing, access to assets, beneficiary arrangements and tax treatment for the actual contract and household. These are separate from the present-value calculation. The charts assume a death occurs today and then fund the resulting household shortfalls. They do not apply mortality probabilities, compare expected insurance claims with premiums or value an insurance policy. They also omit underwriting, exclusions, premium affordability and changes in future coverage. Review the plan when dependants, debts, income, care needs or existing benefits change. Record which expenses are included, which resources are committed, and which assumptions would change the gap most. The result is a documented funding question to resolve with the relevant licensed professionals, rather than a coverage recommendation generated by a chart.

documents.title: Education funding in pictures: the cost calendar and the monthly savings gap
documents.description: Build an education reserve from annual costs, the start date, existing savings and monthly contributions. Explore four charts before choosing an account.
documents.body: An education goal has several payment dates. Estimate the whole cost calendar, then solve the saving requirement with explicit return and inflation assumptions. Define what one study year needs to cover Begin with an annual budget at today’s prices. Depending on the plan, that may include tuition, compulsory fees, books, supplies, housing, food, travel and equipment. A published tuition figure alone would not describe the entire cost of studying away from home. The default CAD 20,000 is a hypothetical all-in budget, not a Canadian tuition average or an institution’s quotation. Choose an amount for a specific study plan and document what it includes. Domestic or international status, program, location, living arrangements and the number of years can all change that starting budget. Every study year has its own price date. The cost bars inflate the starting annual budget separately to each study year. With study beginning in twelve years and 3% annual cost growth, year one costs more than today’s budget, while later study years are more expensive again. The 3% assumption is a sensitivity input, not an official education-price forecast. Know what the reserve target means This model reserves the full sum of the future nominal study costs when study begins. The reserve earns zero during study. That convention makes the cost calendar easy to inspect: each year’s nominal budget is funded at the start, without assuming investment earnings during the withdrawal period. For annual budget C today, cost-growth rate g, y years until study and s study years, the target is Σ C(1 + g) y+k , with k running from zero to s − 1. The default four-year reserve is CAD 119,297.03. This is the total modeled funding requirement before any scholarships, grants, work income or borrowing. A model that keeps unused funds invested during study could produce a different starting requirement and introduce additional investment risk. A monthly payment calendar could also differ from this annual illustration. Compare models only after aligning their cost dates, return assumptions and cash-flow timing. Compare the selected contribution with the solved contribution The savings chart shows two paths from the same starting balance. One uses the monthly amount selected in the controls. The other solves for the month-end contribution required to reach the reserve target by the study start date, using the same assumed effective annual return. The default CAD 10,000 already saved plus CAD 200 per month grows to CAD 52,728.71 after twelve years at an assumed 4% annual return. The solved monthly contribution is CAD 562.59. These paths use smooth returns; they do not describe the changing value of an actual investment portfolio. If existing savings alone already fund the target under the assumptions, the required new contribution is zero. The model does not invent a negative contribution or recommend withdrawing the excess. Future account rules, other education goals and uncertainty still need consideration. Use the waterfall and matrix to locate the pressure The waterfall adds each study year’s cost and subtracts the savings projected at the start. A positive endpoint is an unfunded reserve; a negative endpoint is a modeled surplus. Investment growth is already included in projected savings, so it must not be added again as a separate resource. The matrix changes the years until study and the return assumption. It recalculates the future cost target for every column. A longer waiting period provides more time to save and potentially compound, but it also allows more years of cost growth. The cells show the monthly saving required after both effects. Read several return rows rather than choosing the most convenient result. If a plan works only at a high assumed return, identify what else can change: contributions, the study budget, timing or outside funding. A higher target return brings uncertainty; it does not make the required outcome dependable. Add account benefits only after checking eligibility The Government of Canada’s education-savings overview explains RESPs and education-savings benefits. Eligibility and applicable rules require their own review. This calculator includes no grants, tax benefits, contribution limits or account withdrawal rules, and the solved contribution is not an RESP contribution recommendation. Keep a separate dated list of confirmed outside resources. Distinguish money already available from a possible scholarship, future student employment or a loan that must be repaid. Subtracting unconfirmed resources from the goal can make the displayed gap appear smaller without improving the underlying plan. Refresh the budget as a program and location become clearer. As the first payment approaches, review when cash must be available and how much value fluctuation the remaining horizon can tolerate. The plan should connect each cost date to an available source of money, then update as costs, family contributions and confirmed benefits change.

documents.title: Map your household net worth: assets, debts and financial resilience
documents.description: Use a waterfall, an asset-composition chart and stress comparisons to understand what net worth measures and how liquidity and debt change the picture.
documents.body: Net worth measures assets less liabilities on a date. Cash flow and accessible reserves answer different questions about the household’s ability to meet payments. Put every balance on the same date A household balance sheet records what you own and what you owe. Net worth is assets − liabilities . The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s financial-planning lesson explains this calculation using current values and distinguishes the balance sheet from the household budget. Use a common observation date. Mixing an old home estimate, today’s investment statement and a debt balance from last year can create a misleading total. Record valuation uncertainty alongside assets that have no readily observable market price. The default example lists a CAD 600,000 home, CAD 150,000 in market investments and CAD 30,000 in cash. Assets total CAD 780,000. Subtracting a CAD 350,000 mortgage and CAD 20,000 of other debts gives CAD 410,000 net worth. All figures are hypothetical and describe a simplified balance sheet. Follow the bridge from gross assets to net worth The waterfall adds each asset and subtracts each debt. The final navy bar is the net amount. Its endpoint can be negative: that means the listed liabilities exceed the listed asset values. A signed result is more informative than clipping the chart at zero. Keep the home and mortgage treatment consistent. This chart lists gross home value as an asset and the mortgage as a liability. Alternatively, a presentation could show home equity alone. Adding home equity and then subtracting the mortgage again would count the debt twice. Debt repayment and saving can affect the balance sheet in different ways. Paying principal with existing cash reduces cash and debt by the same amount, leaving net worth unchanged at that instant. Paying interest reduces cash without reducing principal. Future interest savings, fees, taxes and changes in asset values are separate effects rather than an immediate increase created by moving cash between rows. Read composition alongside accessibility The donut divides listed gross assets among the home, investments and cash. Its denominator is total listed assets before debt. It does not show an investment allocation, household spending shares or the fraction of net worth available to spend. A home can dominate gross assets while supplying little immediate liquidity. Accessing its value may require selling, borrowing, paying costs or changing living arrangements. An investment account may be easier to sell but exposed to price movements, settlement timing, account restrictions or tax consequences. Cash and deposits also need context: some may be committed to upcoming bills or a separate goal. Add a liquidity review alongside the net-worth total, listing which resources can meet which payments and when. The emergency-reserve tool starts from spending needs, rather than assuming that a positive balance sheet guarantees a sufficient cash buffer. Watch the equity cushion change under stress The grouped bars compare asset values with debts under separate home and investment declines, then both together. Cash and debt balances remain fixed in these instantaneous scenarios. A fall in a financed asset’s market value does not automatically reduce the amount owed. In the default combined stress, home value falls 20% and investments fall 25%. Assets become CAD 622,500 while debts remain CAD 370,000. Net worth becomes CAD 252,500, a CAD 157,500 reduction, or about 38.4% of starting net worth. The percentage change in net worth can exceed the percentage change in gross assets because the liabilities remain. The matrix expands this into combinations of home and market declines. Each signed cell reports resulting net worth in CAD. Gold negative cells mean debts exceed stressed assets. The selected stress percentages and matrix are alternative assumptions, with no probability attached and no forecast of property or investment prices. Connect the snapshot to the rest of the plan This simplified example omits pensions, businesses, other property, taxes triggered by sale, transaction costs and additional obligations. A more complete inventory can include those items with clear definitions. Be careful when combining amounts before and after tax or treating a future income entitlement as an immediately spendable lump sum. A rise in net worth can come from saving, debt reduction, asset-price changes or new information about values. Track those drivers separately when comparing dates. An increase caused by a property revaluation does not necessarily improve the monthly budget; a change in interest costs can tighten cash flow without immediately changing principal balances. Use the balance sheet with a cash-flow plan, emergency reserve and dated goals. Record the valuation date, sources and included obligations, then repeat on a consistent basis. The useful question is how the household’s resources support its commitments over time, rather than whether one headline number is above someone else’s.

documents.title: The savings plan you can see: time, contributions and compounding
documents.description: Use three charts and editable scenarios to see how regular saving, the starting date and return assumptions change a long-term goal.
documents.body: A savings plan has several adjustable parts. Begin with the contribution and time horizon you can sustain, then test a range of returns. Read the gap between saving and growth The first chart separates money contributed from the portfolio’s modeled value. The contribution line includes your initial savings and each monthly deposit. The difference between the lines is growth under the selected return assumption. With a negative return, that difference can be a loss. The curve is a mathematical illustration. It does not show the path of a real investment. Markets do not supply a smooth annual return, and an account can lose value even while you continue contributing. The Investor.gov compound-interest calculator also treats initial capital, contributions, time and the estimated rate as distinct inputs. Try setting the return to zero. The two lines should coincide. This is a useful baseline: the plan’s progress then comes entirely from your own deposits, making the required saving effort visible. Compare the same finish date The second chart compares starting monthly contributions now with delaying them by five or ten years. All cases share the selected finish date, contribution amount and return. Existing starting savings remain invested in every case. The delayed cases skip deposits rather than making larger catch-up payments later. This comparison changes both the amount contributed and the time each deposit has to grow. It should not be interpreted as a pure investment-performance comparison. Starting sooner can improve the modeled endpoint at a positive return, but it also requires setting money aside sooner. A practical follow-up is to ask what would make an earlier start feasible: a smaller initial transfer, redirecting an expense, or a gradual increase as income changes. A larger assumed return can make a spreadsheet balance without making the required outcome reliable. Use the matrix as a stress test The matrix varies the horizon and return while preserving your selected initial savings and monthly contribution. Each cell is an alternative scenario. Darker shading means a larger ending amount; it does not mean the outcome is more likely. For a goal with a firm deadline, read down one time column and compare several rates. For a flexible goal, compare what additional time might accomplish. Keep the return convention consistent: these are nominal returns before tax, fees and inflation. If only the most optimistic cell meets the goal, identify the funding gap. Possible changes include increasing contributions, changing the goal, delaying the deadline or finding other resources. Taking more risk creates a wider range of possible results; it does not guarantee the higher cell. Know exactly how the example compounds The annual return is an effective rate. The equivalent monthly rate is (1 + annual return) 1/12 − 1 . Each month, the existing balance grows by that rate and a deposit arrives at month-end. Using annual return divided by 12 would represent a different rate convention. For an initial amount B, monthly deposit C, monthly rate m and N months, the ending value is B(1 + m) N + C[(1 + m) N − 1] ÷ m . When m is zero, use B + CN. The tool uses a month-by-month recurrence, which also handles delayed deposits explicitly. Real account results depend on actual deposit dates, changing returns, costs and tax treatment. This calculator does not impose contribution limits or determine account eligibility. Use the relevant current account rules when turning an illustration into an implemented plan. Translate the chart into a monthly decision Describe the goal in today’s dollars and give it a date. Separate near-term cash needs from money that can remain invested. Choose a contribution that fits actual cash flow. Test a lower-return scenario and an interruption in deposits. Review progress as income, prices and the goal change. The ending balance is only one planning measure. Also record how much money you must contribute, whether the schedule leaves a cash reserve, and how flexible the goal is. Read the inflation guide next to translate a future balance into purchasing power.

documents.title: Inflation in pictures: what your future budget needs to buy
documents.description: Use charts and editable scenarios to explore future living costs, the purchasing power of unchanged cash and the difference between nominal and real returns.
documents.body: A future dollar amount needs a price-level assumption. Compare what the money can buy as well as the number printed on the account statement. Start with the cost of a familiar budget The first chart grows today’s monthly cost at the selected annual inflation rate. It holds the quantity and quality of the spending basket constant. If your family, housing or lifestyle changes, that is a separate planning adjustment rather than an inflation effect. A monthly budget of CAD 3,000 at a constant 3% inflation assumption becomes about CAD 6,281 after 25 years. This is an original calculation, not a forecast of Canadian prices. The increase compounds: applying 3% to the original budget every year without increasing the base would understate it. The Bank of Canada’s inflation overview describes CPI and its inflation-target framework. A policy target is not a promise that prices or your personal expenses will grow at that rate every year. Use more than one assumption for a long horizon. See the difference between stable dollars and stable purchasing power The second chart holds a cash amount at CAD 10,000 with no nominal interest. Its purchasing power is shown in today’s dollars after fixed comparison periods. The nominal balance remains unchanged, while positive inflation reduces the goods and services it can purchase. This is not an argument that every dollar should be invested in risky assets. Money needed for an imminent bill has a different role from long-term retirement capital. Liquidity and the ability to make a payment on time can justify holding cash even when its real return is low. Compare the emergency-fund guide for that distinction. An emergency reserve is designed to absorb a cash-flow shock. A growth portfolio is exposed to market risk and may be down precisely when the money is needed. Translate nominal return into a real return The matrix compares assumed nominal returns with inflation rates. A positive account return can still mean a loss of purchasing power. The exact relationship is real return = (1 + nominal return) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1 . For example, a 5% nominal return with 3% inflation gives a real return of about 1.94%, before tax and fees. Subtracting 3% from 5% is a useful approximation at modest rates, but it is not the exact compounding relationship. These cells are sensitivity calculations, not estimates of investment success. The matrix does not assign probabilities, and it does not allow you to choose a return simply because it is needed to meet a goal. Your spending basket can differ from the average A household that rents, a household with a fixed mortgage payment, and a household facing large care expenses may experience different pressures. An aggregate price index is useful context but cannot reconstruct every household’s cost changes. Build your own starting basket from actual recurring spending. Separate price changes from changes in quantity, such as moving to a larger home or adding a family member. For a detailed plan, examine major categories separately rather than hiding every uncertainty in one average rate. Do not combine a real return with a second inflation deduction. If both future cash flows and portfolio returns are expressed in today’s dollars, maintain that basis throughout the model. If the model is nominal, inflate the expenses and use nominal returns consistently. Put an inflation review into the plan Write the goal in today’s dollars and retain that baseline. Test at least a lower and higher inflation assumption. Identify expenses whose prices or quantities could change differently. Check whether income sources adjust with prices, and under what terms. Update the budget from observed spending rather than only changing the forecast rate. A spending plan becomes easier to review when nominal amounts, real amounts, dates and assumptions are clearly labelled. The charts are designed to make those relationships visible before a more detailed tax, benefit or investment model is added.

documents.title: Build a financial buffer: household spending and emergency reserves
documents.description: Compare official Canadian household-spending statistics, then build a reserve target from your own essential expenses and cash flow.
documents.body: Use household statistics for context. Build the emergency reserve from the expenses and risks your own household needs to cover. Read the official spending comparison carefully The first chart uses Statistics Canada’s Survey of Household Spending for 2021 and 2023, published on 21 May 2025. It shows average annual spending on goods and services among households in the provinces. It is a dated survey comparison, not a current monthly cost-of-living reading. The seven displayed categories sum to CAD 67,125 in 2021 and CAD 76,750 in 2023. Shelter is the largest displayed category. These are nominal dollar amounts. Changes can reflect prices, quantities, household circumstances and spending choices; they are not category inflation rates. The chart’s denominator is household consumption, not after-tax income. Savings, income taxes and other items outside this consumption definition are not an “unspent” residual. These averages are not a recommended allocation, a median budget, or an assessment of what a particular family should spend. Build your own essential-expense baseline List the spending you would need to maintain during an interruption in earnings: housing, basic food, utilities, transport, insurance and required payments. Identify which amounts could fall and which would remain due. Add a provision for predictable irregular costs in a separate budget. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada distinguishes unexpected expenses from occasional expenses that can be planned. Its emergency-fund guidance describes three to six months of regular expenses or income as possible starting points. The tool uses expenses rather than income so the coverage calculation stays explicit. Its six-month default is an example, not an assessment of your needs. Job stability, insurance, dependants, access to other resources and the ability to reduce spending can all affect an appropriate reserve. Read the reserve-building curve The second chart starts with your current cash reserve and adds the selected monthly saving. It stops new deposits once the target is reached. If the current reserve already exceeds the target, it retains the existing amount instead of pretending money has been withdrawn. At CAD 3,000 of monthly essential expenses and six months of coverage, the target is CAD 18,000. Starting with CAD 3,000 and adding CAD 500 per month takes 30 months to close the CAD 15,000 gap, assuming no interest, withdrawals or expense changes. Try a smaller first milestone if the full target feels distant. For example, the initial objective might be one month of essential expenses, followed by successive additions. The important point is to make the funding schedule fit the cash available after required bills. Test the cost of an expense shock The third chart raises essential expenses by 10% and 20% while keeping the selected number of coverage months fixed. This shows how a reserve can become inadequate even when its dollar balance does not fall. These increases are hypothetical stresses, not statistical confidence bounds. You could instead test a specific event such as a rent change, a car replacement or additional care needs. Keep the cost of a known upcoming purchase separate from the reserve for genuinely uncertain events. Also examine accessibility. A reserve intended for urgent payments needs to be available on the relevant timeline. Check withdrawal terms, settlement timing and possible penalties rather than treating every account balance as equally usable cash. Create a reserve routine Reconcile the essential-expense figure with recent bills. Choose an initial coverage target and a realistic monthly transfer. Keep predictable annual expenses in the regular budget. Review coverage after a housing, family or employment change. After using the reserve, write a replenishment schedule. The reserve is part of the overall plan. Balance its funding with required debt payments and other commitments. The debt guide shows the interest effect of repayment choices; it does not assume that eliminating every cash buffer is the right way to accelerate repayment.

documents.title: Debt repayment, visualized: the payment, the timeline and the interest
documents.description: Compare repayment paths, inspect principal and interest, and see how the rate and monthly payment change a debt-free date.
documents.body: A payment decision changes both the time in debt and the interest paid. Check that the payment reduces principal before relying on a payoff date. Follow the remaining balance The first chart compares your selected monthly payment with the same payment plus an extra amount. The interest rate and starting balance stay fixed. The final payment is reduced to the amount owed rather than collecting a full payment after the debt is cleared. At the start of the default example, CAD 10,000 at an assumed nominal annual rate of 18% incurs CAD 150 of interest over one simplified month. A CAD 300 payment therefore reduces principal by CAD 150 in that first month. Later interest falls as the balance declines. The chart is not a reconstruction of a credit-card statement. Actual products may use daily accrual, different transaction rates, grace periods, fees and changing minimum payments. Read the agreement and statement before treating any modeled date as a contractual payoff quote. Separate the amount borrowed from the financing cost The stacked bars divide a completed repayment schedule into original principal and cumulative interest. Both paths repay the same starting principal. Any reduction in total paid comes from a change in financing cost under the selected assumptions. Do not compare only the monthly payment. A lower payment can make the current budget easier while extending the repayment period and increasing interest. Conversely, a larger payment needs to be affordable; a plan that repeatedly forces new borrowing may fail to deliver the modeled saving. If the selected payment is no larger than the first month’s interest, it does not reduce principal in this simplified model. The tool reports “Not repaid” instead of inventing a payoff date. It also withholds a lifetime-interest total when the schedule is not completed within the model limit. Read the rate-and-payment matrix The matrix uses your starting balance with a fixed set of rates and payments. Each cell shows months to repay, including a partial final payment. NR means the debt is not repaid within the 600-month limit, including cases where the payment fails to reduce the balance. This is a sensitivity map. A lower rate is not assumed to be available, and a larger payment is not assumed to fit your budget. If a refinancing offer exists, compare fees, term, variable-rate risk and any collateral implications separately. A rate cut and an extra payment affect the model through different channels. The former reduces the charge on the outstanding balance; the latter reduces the balance more quickly. A genuine comparison needs both the repayment schedule and the total cost. Place the debt inside the whole budget Make a list of all obligations, interest rates, due dates and minimum payments. The Government of Canada’s Six Steps to Get Out of Debt discusses directing extra repayment toward high-rate debt and, alternatively, small balances for motivation, while maintaining required payments. The chart models one balance and cannot decide the entire order of repayment. Arrears, essential living costs, secured obligations, promotional terms and restrictions may change priorities. It also does not value employer matching contributions, tax effects or access to emergency cash. Keep the avoided borrowing cost distinct from a risky investment’s expected return. Repaying a fixed-rate balance changes an interest obligation under its terms; an investment forecast does not guarantee that it will outperform that cost. Check the recurrence and the implementation The monthly recurrence is new balance = old balance × (1 + annual nominal rate ÷ 12) − actual payment , with payment capped at the amount owed. No new purchases or fees are added. A completed schedule satisfies total payments approximately equal to principal plus modeled interest, subject to rounding. Use the statement’s actual rate and identify any separate balances. Keep required payments current. Choose an extra payment that leaves a workable cash-flow margin. Confirm any prepayment restrictions or charges. Reconcile the next statement with the planned progress. If the plan cannot cover essential costs and required payments, that is a cash-flow problem to address directly. A longer chart does not create the capacity to pay.

documents.title: Retirement withdrawals: why the order of returns changes the plan
documents.description: Compare two portfolios with the same ten returns in reverse order, then isolate what changes when retirement spending is withdrawn.
documents.body: Once a portfolio funds spending, the order of returns matters. A long-run average alone cannot describe the path of available retirement capital. Compare two paths with the same ingredients The first chart uses ten invented annual returns. One sequence begins with losses of 20% and 10%; the other reverses the entire sequence. Starting capital and the withdrawal rule are identical. Both sequences contain exactly the same returns. Withdrawals occur at the start of each year, before that year’s return applies. This convention is deliberately explicit because moving the payment date changes the result. The selected annual increase raises requested spending each year; it does not change the return series. Schwab’s sequence-risk explanation describes how early losses can be particularly damaging when a portfolio is funding withdrawals. Our chart uses its own invented return series and assumptions, rather than copying Schwab’s example or estimating a historical retirement outcome. Read the return bars before interpreting the balance The grouped bars show the annual return in each sequence. Negative values fall below zero. Their order differs, but their arithmetic average and no-withdrawal compounded return are the same. With no deposits or withdrawals, the ending balance is the starting amount multiplied by all ten return factors. Reordering multiplication does not change that product. Intermediate balances still differ, which can matter for liquidity and behaviour even in the no-withdrawal case. Set the withdrawal to zero and inspect the final balances. They should match up to rounding. That comparison acts as a control: it helps isolate the role of cash flows instead of attributing every difference to a change in average investment performance. Why the withdrawal changes the arithmetic When money is withdrawn, it no longer participates in subsequent gains or losses. A poor early return can leave a smaller balance supporting later withdrawals. The same dollar spending can then consume a greater fraction of the remaining portfolio. The recurrence used here is ending balance = (opening balance − funded withdrawal) × (1 + annual return) . Funded withdrawal cannot exceed available assets. If requested spending is larger, the remaining balance is zero and the unmet amount is recorded separately. The tool reports unfunded withdrawals because a zero balance must not look like a successfully financed spending plan. In a depleted path, actual funded spending can differ between the two sequences even though the requested rule is identical. Keep a teaching comparison separate from a retirement forecast Ten hand-picked returns cannot establish a sustainable withdrawal rate or a probability of success. There is no statistical confidence interval here, no simulation distribution and no claim that either sequence is likely to occur. A full plan also needs a longer horizon, longevity assumptions, pension and benefit cash flows, taxes, investment costs, asset allocation, inflation and spending flexibility. Currency and household obligations can add further constraints. Those items are outside this demonstration. Do not treat the first withdrawal as a recommended percentage of savings. It is an input that exposes the relationship. A plan that works under one invented sequence may fail under a different drawdown, a longer life or a larger spending need. Use the charts to ask better planning questions Which essential expenses are covered by reliable income outside the portfolio? How much spending could be delayed or reduced after a market decline? What liquid resources are available without selling volatile assets? How would a longer retirement or a higher cost level change the funding gap? When will the withdrawal plan be reviewed and adjusted? Flexibility can change the required cash flows, while asset allocation changes the range of investment paths. Neither can be assessed from a single average return. Use this visual explanation as a starting point for a plan with explicit obligations, documented assumptions and a review process.

documents.title: Canadian bank research & valuation
documents.description: In-depth Royal Bank, TD, BMO, Scotiabank and CIBC equity research with linked forecasts and interactive valuation models.
documents.body: Independent equity research / Canadian banks Five franchises. Five different valuation debates. Read the business, test the earnings, challenge the price. In-depth Canadian bank research with operating forecasts, credit and capital analysis, scenario valuation, and interactive return models. Four new analyses published 25 October 2026. Prices through 23 October; financials through 31 July. The existing RBC note keeps its separately dated snapshot. RY · Royal Bank Strong franchise, limited valuation cushion Read the original senior analysis, forecast model, credit and capital review, valuation scenarios and historical return research. Analysis 18 October · price 16 October 2026 Read RBC research ↗ BMO · BMO BMO: U.S. returns must earn the valuation premium Credit normalization and capital efficiency are rebuilding earnings. At more than twice July common book, the share price also requires lasting improvement in the return on capital committed to the U.S. franchise. Reference close C$236.87 Our FY2027 EPS C$17.15 Analysis 25 October · price 23 October 2026 Read BMO research ↗ BNS · Scotiabank Scotiabank: a better bank still needs a sensible entry price The turnaround is producing stronger earnings, but a price near twice July common book already anticipates more. Canadian funding, international credit and capital discipline determine whether the recovery can persist. Reference close C$130.00 Our FY2027 EPS C$9.56 Analysis 25 October · price 23 October 2026 Read Scotiabank research ↗ CM · CIBC CIBC: stronger returns, less room for an easy rerating Improved Canadian profitability and a steadier U.S. business strengthen the franchise. The valuation now requires those returns to persist after tax benefits, transaction charges and provision releases are normalized. Reference close C$159.59 Our FY2027 EPS C$11.56 Analysis 25 October · price 23 October 2026 Read CIBC research ↗ TD · TD TD: recovery has a price; controls still matter Capital return and a stronger earnings base support the franchise. A demanding starting valuation still requires durable U.S. execution, sound Canadian credit and lasting control improvements. These are research anchors, not a uniform return ranking. Each article explains its own earnings basis, forecast drivers, chosen multiples, risks and evidence gaps.
